They now approached the principality of Vladimir, and no army appeared to resist them on the frontiers. They advanced unimpeded to the capital, which, left to its fate by the grand prince, had nothing to expect, but the same cruel treatment which the neighbouring cities had received. Yury, with unpardonable negligence, was celebrating a marriage feast, when he ought to have been employed in collecting the means of defence against the enemy, of whose approach to his borders he had received timely intimation. The city of Vladimir, which contained the princess and two of her sons, was left to the protection of a chieftain, totally unqualified for its defence, and the inhabitants seemed to share the pusillanimity of their governor. Instead of annoying the enemy by occasional excursions, and preparing the means of defending the walls against a sudden attack, they gave themselves up to terror and despair; and as they conceived death to be inevitable, they prepared for it, by taking the habits of monks and nuns, in order to insure to themselves a blissful departure. A prey to fear and despondency, the city soon fell into the hands of the Tartars. They one morning scaled the walls, and meeting with little opposition, quickly made themselves masters of the place; when they cast aside every feeling of humanity, and like beasts of prey, glutted their appetite for blood among the wretched inhabitants. The grand princes, and other ladies of distinction, dreading the brutality of the relentless conquerors, had taken refuge in the choir of a church, an asylum which all the assurances of the Tartars that they should suffer no injury, could not prevail on them to abandon. It was therefore set on fire by the barbarians, who feasted their ears with the shrieks and groans of the women, as the flames surrounded them. Yury, incensed almost to desperation, at the fate of his capital, and the horrible death of his wife and children, was determined to take signal vengeance on the assailants. He assembled all the forces which he could draw together, and though his army was greatly inferior in numbers to the Tartars, he marched against the enemy, and attacked them with the most determined valour. The struggle was short, but bloody; the Tartars were victorious, and the body of Yury was found among the slain. This appears to have been the only vigorous stand made by the Russian princes. The Tartars pushed forward with rapidity, and successively overpowered the principalities of Novgorod and Kief. In the latter city they found immense booty; but this circumstance did not prevent them from repeating here the same bloody scenes which they had acted in the other capitals. The governor was preserved from the cruelties that had been inflicted on the inhabitants, by the courage he had displayed in defence of the city; and his noble demeanour, when he fell into the hands of the conqueror, acquired the esteem and affection of that chief, and enabled him to obtain a temporary repose to his country. The Tartars had now established themselves in the Russian territories, and their khan or chief, though he did not himself assume the nominal sovereignty, princes unregained as paramount lord, and placed on the throne any of the native princes whom he found most obsequious to his will, or who had ingratiated themselves by the magnificence of their presents. The throne was successively occupied by Yarolaf II. Alexander Yaroslavitch, Yarolaf Yaroslavitch, Vasilii Yaroslavitch, Dimitri Alexandrovitch, Andrei, Daniil, both brothers of Dimitri, Mikaila Yaroslavitch, Yury Danilovitch, Alexander Mikailovitch, Ivan Danilovitch, Simon Ivanovitch, and Ivan Ivanovitch. Among the princes whom we have enumerated, we must particularly notice Alexander the son of Yarolaf der Neffsky. II. This prince was installed grand prince of Russia by the Tartar khan in 1252, and continued to reign till 1264. He is remarkable chiefly for a decisive victory gained by him over the Danes on the banks of the Neva,—a victory which procured him the honourable surname of Neffsky (the conqueror). This victory is said to have taken place in 1239, while Alexander was governor of Novgorod, under his father Yarolaf, who then reigned at Vladimir. After his accession to the throne on the death of his father, he engaged in a successful war with Sweden. This prince is held in great veneration by the Russians, and several miracles are attributed to him. In particular it is said, that when the prayer of abolution was offered to his corpse previous to interment (a practice long customary in Russia), the hand hand of the dead body opened to receive it. His reputation for sanctity occasioned him to be ranked among the tutelary saints of the Greek church, where he still holds a distinguished place, by the title of St Alexander Nevsky. During these several reigns, which all historians have passed over for want of records concerning them, the miseries of a foreign yoke were aggravated by all the calamities of intestine discord and war; whilst the knights of Livonia, or brothers of the short sword, as they are sometimes called, a kind of military order of religious, on one side, and the Poles on the other, catching at the opportunity, attacked Russia, and took several of its towns, and even some considerable countries. The Tartars and Ruthians, whose interests were in this case the same, often united to oppose their common enemy; but were generally worsted. The Livonians took Pleikow, and the Poles made themselves masters of Black Russia, the Ukraine, Podolia, and the city of Kief. Casimir the Great, one of their kings, carried his conquests still farther. He asserted his pretensions to a part of Russia, in right of his relation to Boleslaus duke of Kalitz, who died without issue, and forcibly possessed himself of the duchies of Perzemylia, Kalitz, and Luckow, and of the districts of Sanock, Lubatczow, and Terebowla; all which countries he made a province of Poland. The newly-conquered Ruthians were ill disposed to endure the government of the Poles, whose laws and customs were more contrary to their own than those of the Tartars had been. They joined the latter to rid themselves of the yoke, and assembled an army numerous enough to overwhelm all Poland, but destitute of valour and discipline. Casimir, undaunted by this deluge of barbarians, presented himself at the head of a few troops on the borders of the Vistula, and obliged his enemies to retire. About the year 1362 Dimitri Ivanovitch received the sovereignty from the Tartar chief, and established the seat of his government at Mosco. This prince possessed considerable ambition, and contrived to inspire the other Ruthian princes with so much respect for his person and government, that they consented to hold their principalities as fiefs under Dimitri. This increased the consequence of the Ruthian prince, excited the jealousy of Mamai the Tartar khan, who determined to take measures for maintaining his superiority. He began by demanding an increase of tribute, but when Dimitri seemed to demur at consenting to this new encroachment, the khan not only inflicted on his demand, but required the grand prince to appear before him in person. This requisition Dimitri thought proper to refuse, and prepared to support his refusal by force of arms. The terror with which the Tartars had inspired the inhabitants of Russia had now considerably subsided, while the hatred which the Ruthians bore these haughty masters, was kept alive by the barbarity of their manners, and the difference of their religion. The Christian ministers, justly dreading that the Tartars, in their furious progress, might extirpate Christianity, contributed all in their power to confirm the spirit of revolt among the people; and they promised the crown of martyrdom to such as should fall in battle against the infidels. Thus, the contest into which the grand prince determined to enter in support of his authority, became in some measure a holy war, undertaken in defence of the national religion. This combination of favourable circumstances operated so strongly in favour of Dimitri, and the princes that had confederated with him, that they soon collected an army of 200,000 men. With this force the grand prince left Mosco, and marched towards the Don, on the southern bank of which the Tartars were encamped. Arrived at this river, he left it to the choice of his troops, either to cross the river, and encounter the enemy on the other side, or to await the attack where they were. The general voice declared for passing over to the assault. The grand prince accordingly transported his battalions across the river, that he might cut off all hope of escaping by retreat. The fight now commenced, and though the numbers of the foe far exceeded their own, the Ruthians defended themselves valiantly against the furious onset of the Tartars; but as these barbarians were continually relieved by fresh reinforcements, they appeared to be gaining ground. Indeed, nothing but the impossibility of retreating across the river, and the firm persuasion that death would immediately transport them to the mansions of eternal bliss, restrained the Ruthians from a general flight. At the moment when the day seemed entirely lost, a detachment of the grand prince's army which he had stationed in reserve, and had remained out of the view of the enemy, came up with unabated force, fell on the rear of the Tartars, threw them into such terror and confusion, that they fled with Mamai at their head, and left the Ruthians masters of the field. This contest must have been extremely bloody, as we are told that eight days were employed by the remains of the Ruthian army, in burying the bodies of their slaughtered companions, while those of the Tartars were left uninterred upon the ground. This glorious victory, which took place in 1380, was attended with numerous advantages to the Ruthian cause. In particular, it taught the native princes that the Tartars were not unconquerable; that nothing was wanting to relieve them from the galling yoke under which they had long groaned, but mutual union, courage, and prudence. The Tartars appear to have been so much humbled by this defeat, that for a time they left the Ruthians to enjoy peace in their recovered liberty. This forbearance, however, was not of long duration. Before the death of Dimitri they returned with increased numbers, laid siege to Mosco, which, after an obstinate defence, was at length induced to surrender, and Russia once more submitted to her old masters. Dimitri died in 1389, and was succeeded by his son Vasilii Dimitrievitch. In the reign of this prince a new incursion of the Tartars took place, under the great Timur or Tamerlane, who after having subdued all the neighbouring Tartar hordes, extended his conquests to the Ruthian territories, carried Mosco by assault, and carried off immense plunder. The grand principality of Vladimir, or as it may now comparatively be called, of Mosco, had, at the end of the 14th century, attained its greatest height, while that of Kief had proportionally declined. This latter principality was, at the time of which we are now writing, under the dominion of the Poles, having been seized on in 1320 by Gedemin, duke of Lithuania. The latter end of the 14th century forms a splendid epoch in the Ruthian history. At this time, viz., from

RUST

Pages 28-28

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> oxide of a metal, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, for instance, formed by exposure to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or by corroding and dissolving its superficial parts by some menstruum. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in producing rust; and hence oils, and other fatty bodies, secure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> from rust; water being no menstruum for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and therefore not able to make its way through it. Almost all metals are liable to rust. The rust of iron is not merely an oxide of that metal; it contains besides a portion of carbonate.

RUSTIC

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, implies a manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, rather than according to the rules of art. See Architecture. RUSTIC Gods, dii ruficii, in antiquity, were the gods of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those who presided over <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, &c. Varro invokes the 12 dii confentes, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> among the rustic gods; viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, Tellus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, Rubigus, Flora, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, Venus, Lympha, and Good Luck. Besides these 12 <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-rustic gods, there were an infinity of lesser ones; as Pales, Vertumnus, Tutelina, Fulgor, Sterculius, Mellona, Jugatimus, Collinus, Vallonia, Terminus, Sylvanus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIAPUS">Priapus</a>. Struvius adds the Satyrs, Fauns, Sileni, Nymphs, and even Tritons; and gives the empire over all the rustic gods to the god <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. RUSTIC Order, that decorated with rustic quoins, rustic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, &c. RUSTIC Work, is where the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, &c. of a building, instead of being smooth, are hatched, or picked with the point of a hammer.

RUSTRE

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> shape, pierced through in the middle with a round hole. See HERALDRY.

RUTA

Pages 28-28

RUE; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decidua clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 26th order, Multiflorae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Rue has a strong ungrateful smell, and a bitter penetrating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>: the leaves, when full of vigour, are extremely acid, infomuch as to inflame and blister the skin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> much handled. With regard to their medicinal virtues, they are powerfully stimulating, attenuating, and detergent; and hence, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> phlegmatic habits, they quicken the circulation, dissolve tenacious juices, open obstructions of the excretory glands, and promote the fluid secretions. The writers on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a> in general have entertained a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the virtues of this plant. Boerhaave is full of its praises; particularly of the essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and the distilled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> co-habated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> re-distilled several times from fresh parcels of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. After extravagantly commending other waters prepared in this manner, he adds, with regard to that of rue, that the greatest commendations he can bestow upon it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of its merit: "What medicine (says he) can be more efficacious for promoting sweat and perspiration, for the cure of the hydric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> and of epilepsies, and for expelling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>?" Whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> rue may be of in the two last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it undoubtedly has its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the others: the cohabited water, however, is not the most efficacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of it. An extract made by rectified spirit contains in a small compass the whole virtues of the rue; this menstruum taking up by infusion all the pungency and flavour of the plant, and elevating nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. With water, its peculiar flavour and warmth arise; the bitterness, and a considerable share of the pungency, remaining behind. Ruta Baga, or Swedish turnip. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of cultivation, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> Index. Book of RUTH, a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; being a kind of appendix to the book of Judges, and an introduction to those of Samuel; and having its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from the person whose story is here principally related. In this story are observable the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of kindred and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>; and the manner of buying the inheritance of the deceased, with other particulars of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> and antiquity. The canonicals of this book was never disputed; but the learned are not agreed about the epocha of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> it relates. Ruth the Moabitels is found in the genealogy of our Saviour. Matth. i. 5. RUTILUS. See CYPRINUS, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index.

RUTHERGLEN

Pages 28-29
or by contraction Ruglen, the head borough of the nether ward of Lanarkshire in Scotland, is situated in N. Lat. 55° 51', and W. Long. 4° 13'; about two miles south-east of Glasgow, and nine west of Hamilton. Few towns in Scotland can lay greater claim to antiquity than Rutherglen. Maitland, in his History of the Antiquities of Scotland, vol. i. p. 92, tells us, that it was founded by a King Reuther, from whom it derived its name; and a tradition of the same import prevails among the inhabitants. But without laying any stress on the authority of tradition, which is often false and always doubtful, we find, from several original charters still preserved, that it was erected into RUT a royal borough by King David I. about the year 1126. The territory under the jurisdiction of the borough was extensive, and the inhabitants enjoyed many distinguished privileges, which were however gradually wrested from them, by political influence, in favour of Glasgow, which in latter times rose into consequence by trade and manufactures. The ancient dimensions of the place are now unknown; but in the fields and gardens towards the east the foundations of houses are occasionally discovered. It is now of a very reduced size, consisting but of one principal street and a few lanes, and containing about 1631 inhabitants. About 150 yards to the south of the main street is a kind of lane, known by the name of Dins-dykes. A circumstance which befell the unfortunate Queen Mary, immediately after her forces were routed at the battle of Langside, has ever since continued to characterize this place with an indelible mark of opprobrium. Her majesty, during the battle, stood on a rising ground about a mile from Rutherglen. She no sooner saw her army defeated than she took her precipitate flight to the south. Dins-dykes unfortunately lay in her way. Two ruffians, who were at that instant cutting grass hard by, seeing her majesty fleeing in haste, rudely attempted to intercept her, and threatened to cut her in pieces with their scythes if she presumed to proceed a step further. Neither beauty, nor even royalty itself, can at all times secure the unfortunate when they have to do with the unfailing or the revengeful. Relief, however, was at hand; and her majesty proceeded in her flight. Adjoining to a lane called the Back-row stood the castle of Rutherglen, originally built at a period coeval, it is reported, with the foundation of the town. This ancient fortress underwent several sieges during the unhappy wars in the days of King Robert Bruce, and it remained a place of strength until the battle of Langside; soon after which it was destroyed by order of the regent, to revenge himself on the Hamilton family, in whose custody it then was. The foundations of the buildings are now erased, and the site converted into dwelling-houses and gardens. The church of Rutherglen, an ancient building of the Saxon-Gothic style, was rendered famous by two transactions, in which the fate of Sir William Wallace and his country was deeply concerned. In it a truce was concluded between Scotland and England in the year 1297 (Henry's Life of Wallace, book vi. verse 862.), and in it Sir John Monteath bargained with the English to betray Wallace his friend and companion (Life of Wallace, book xi. verse 796.). This ancient building, having become incommodes, was, in 1794, pulled down, and one of a modern style was erected in its place. Buried in the area were found vast quantities of human bones, and some relics of antiquity. No borough probably in Britain possesses a political constitution or felt more free and unembarrassed than Rutherglen. It was anciently under the influence of a self-elected magistracy, many of whom lived at a distance from the borough, and who continued long in office without interruption. Negligence on the one hand, and undue exertion of power on the other, at length excited the burgesses, about the middle of the last century, to apply an effectual remedy to this evil. The community who, at that period, possessed the power of reforming the abuses that had long prevailed in the management of the borough, were much assisted in their exertions by a Mr David Spens, town-clerk, a gentleman unbaffled by false politics, and who was animated with a high degree of true patriotism. Great opposition was at first made to the reform; but the plan adopted by the burgesses was wisely laid, and was prosecuted with unremitting fidelity. They were proof against the influence and bribery of a party that struggled to continue the old practice; and having at length surmounted every difficulty, they formed a new constitution and set for the borough, which, in 1671, was approved of by all the inhabitants of the town, and afterwards inserted in the records of the general convention of the royal boroughs of Scotland. Rutherglen, in conjunction with Glasgow, Renfrew, and Dumbarton, sends a member to the British parliament. The fairs of this town are generally well attended, and have long been famous for a great flow of horses, of the Lanarkshire breed, which are esteemed the best draught-horses in Britain. The inhabitants of this borough still retain some customs of a very remote antiquity. One of these is the making of Rutherglen four cakes. The operation is attended with some peculiar rites, which lead us to conclude that the practice is of Pagan origin. An account of these rites is given in Ure's History of Rutherglen and Kilbride, p. 94; from whence we have taken the above account of this place, and which we do not hesitate to recommend to the attention of such of our readers as are fond of natural and local history, being persuaded that they will find it to be both an useful and entertaining performance.

RUTLANDSHIRE

Pages 29-29

is the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in England, being but 40 miles in circumference; in which are two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 48 parishes, 3263 houses, and 16,336 inhabitants. However, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> it may be compared with any other county; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> being good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fertile both for tillage and pastures; and it not only affords plenty of corn, but feeds a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of horned cattle and sheep. It is well watered with brooks and rivulets; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Weland and the Wath. It is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>; on the south by the river Weland, which parts it from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>; and on the west and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>. It has only two market-towns; namely, Okeham, where the assizes and sessions are held, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UPPINGHAM">Uppingham</a>.

RUYSCH

Pages 29-30

FREDERIC, one of the most eminent anatomists of which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> can boast, was born at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1638. After making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress at home, he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and there prosecuted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of anatomy and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. He studied next at Franeker, where he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic. He then returned to the Hague; and marrying in 1661, dedicated his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the study of his profession. In 1665 he published a treatise, entitled Dilucidatio vascularum de varia lymphaticis et lacteis; which raised his reputation so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that he was chosen professor of anatomy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> he accepted with the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, because his situation at Amsterdam would give him easy access to every requisite help for cultivating anatomy and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. After he settled in Amsterdam, he was perpetually engaged in dissecting and in examining with the most inquisitive eye the various parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. He improved the RUYSCH Ruytch science of anatomy by new discoveries; in particular, he found out a way to preserve dead bodies many years from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. His anatomical collection was curious and valuable. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of fetishes of all sizes, from the length of the little finger to that of a new-born infant. He had also bodies of full grown persons of all ages, and a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of animals almost of every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> on the globe, besides a great many other natural curiosities. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great of Russia, in his tour through Holland in the year 1698, visited Ruytch, and was so charmed with his conversation, that he passed whole days with him; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of departure came, he left him with regret. He set so high a value on Ruytch's cabinet of curiosities, that when he returned to Holland in 1717, he purchased it for 30,000 florins, and sent it to Pittsburgh. In 1685 he was made professor of medicine, an office which he discharged with great ability. In 1728 he got his thigh-bone broken by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in his chamber. The year before this misfortune happened he had been deprived of his son Henry, a youth of talents, and well skilled in anatomy and botany. He had been created a doctor of physic, and was supposed to have afflicted his father in his discoveries and publications. Ruytch's family now consisted only of his youngest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. This lady had been early inspired with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for anatomy, the favourite science of her father and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and had studied it with success. She was therefore well qualified to assist her father in forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> collection of curiosities in natural history and anatomy, which he began to make after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Russia had purchased the first. Ruytch is said to have been of a healthy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, that though he lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 93, yet during that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he did not labour under the infirmities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. From the time he broke his thigh he was indeed disabled from walking without a support; yet he retained his vigour both of mind and body without any sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, till in 1731 his strength at once deserted him. He died on the 22d of February the same year. His anatomical works are printed in 4 vols 4to. The style of his writings is simple and concise, but sometimes inaccurate. Instruction, and not ostentation, seems to be his only aim. In anatomy he undoubtedly made many discoveries; but from not being sufficiently conversant in the writings of other anatomists, he published as discoveries what had been known before. The Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1727 elected him a member in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, who was lately deceased. He was also a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.

RUYSCHIA

Pages 30-30

a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those that are doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

RUYTER

Pages 30-30

MICHAEL ADRIAN, a distinguished naval officer, was born at Fleeslingue, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, in 1607. He entered on a seafaring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> when he was only 11 years old, and was first a cabin-boy. While he advanced successively to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of mate, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, he acquired himself with ability and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> in all these employments. He repulsed the Irish, who attempted to take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English. He made eight voyages to the West Indies and ten to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>. He was then promoted to the rank of rear-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, and sent to assist the Portuguese against the Spaniards. When the enemy came in sight, he advanced boldly to meet them, and gave such unquestionable proofs of valour as drew from the Portuguese monarch the warmest applause. His gallantry was still more conspicuous before Salée, a town of Barbary. With one single vessel he sailed through the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in defiance of five Algerine corsairs who came to attack him. In 1653 a squadron of 70 vessels was dispatched against the English under the command of Van Tromp. Ruyter, who accompanied the admiral in this expedition, seconded him with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill and bravery in the three battles which the English so gloriously won. He was afterwards stationed in the Mediterranean, where he captured several Turkish vessels. In 1659 he received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to join the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Swedes; and he not only maintained his former reputation, but even raised it higher. As the reward of his services, the king of Denmark ennobled him and gave him a pension. In 1661 he ran ashore a vessel belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, released 40 Christian slaves, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the Tunisians, and reduced the Algerine corsairs to submission. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as a testimony of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for such illustrious services, raised him to the rank of vice-admiral and commander-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. To the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, the highest that could be conferred upon him, he was well intitled by the signal victory which he obtained over the combined fleets of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought in 1672 about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The battle was maintained between the English and Dutch with the obstinate bravery of nations which were accustomed to dispute the empire of the main. Ruyter having thus made himself master of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, conducted a fleet of Indians safely into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEXEL">Texel</a>; thus defending and enriching his country, while it had become the prey of hostile invaders. The next year he had three engagements with the fleets of France and England, in which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, his bravery was still more distinguished than ever. De Frettes the French vice-admiral wrote to Colbert in these words: "I would purchase with my life the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of De Ruyter." But he did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy the triumphs which he had so honourably won. In an engagement with the French fleet off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, he lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and received a mortal wound, which put an end to his life in a few days. His corpse was carried to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, and a magnificent monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was there erected by the command of the states-general. The Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> bestowed on him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, and transmitted a patent investing him with that dignity; but he died before it arrived. When some person was congratulating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. upon De Ruyter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, telling him he had now got rid of one dangerous enemy; he replied, "Every one must be sorry at the death of so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>." RYE. See SECALE, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and also <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> Index. RYE-GRAFS. See AGRICULTURE Index.

RYCHOPS

Pages 31-31

a genus of birds belonging to the order of anseres. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

RYE

Pages 30-31

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> on Wednesdays and Saturdays, but no fair. It is one of the cinque-ports; is a handsome well-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, governed by a mayor and jurats, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> built with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and a town <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and consists of three streets, paved with stone. One One side of the town has been walled in, and the other is guarded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It has two gates, and is a place of considerable trade in the shipping way. From thence <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of corn are exported, and many of the inhabitants are fishermen. It is 34 miles south-east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, and 64 on the same point from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The mouth of the harbour is of late choked up with sand; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well opened, it would be a good station for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> that cruise against the French. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 50. N. Lat. 51. o.

RYMER

Pages 31-31

THOMAS, Esq. the author of the Feadera, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, and educated at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school of Northallerton. He was admitted a scholar at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, then became a member of Gray's Inn, and at length was appointed historiographer to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Mr Shadwell. He wrote A View of the Tragedies of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">Age</a>, and afterwards published a tragedy named Edgar. For a critic he was certainly not well qualified, for he wanted candour; nor is his judgement much to be relied on, who could condemn Shakespeare with such rigid severity. His tragedy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> show, that his talents for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> were by no means equal to those whole poems he has publicly censured. But though he has no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the appellation of poet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> critic, as an antiquarian and historian his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> be preserved. His Feadera, which is a collection of all the public transactions, treaties, &c. of the kings of England with foreign princes, is esteemed one of our most authentic and valuable records, and is often referred to by the best English historians than perhaps any other book in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It was published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the beginning of the present century in 17 volumes folio. Three volumes more were added by Sanderson after Rymer's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The whole were reprinted at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 10 vols in 1730. They were abridged by Rapin in French, and inserted in Le Clerc's Bibliothèque, a translation of which was made by Stephen Whatley, and printed in 4 vols 8vo, 1731. Rym died 14th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1731, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Clement's Danes. Some specimens of his poetry are preserved in the first volume of Mr Nichol's Select Collection of Miscellaneous Poems, 1780.

RYOTS

Pages 31-31

in the policy of Hindoostan, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name by which the renters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> are distinguished. They hold their possessions by a lease, which may be considered as perpetual, and at a rate fixed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> surveys and valuations. This arrangement has been fo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> established, and accords so well with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the natives, concerning the distinction of casts, and the functions allotted to each, that it has been invariably maintained in all the provinces subject either to Mahometans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Europeans; and to both it serves as the basis on which their whole system of finance is founded. Reflecting the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, however, in which the ryots of Hindoostan held their possessions, there is much diversity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are very impartially delineated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> iv. to the Appendix of Robertson's Historical Disquisition, &c. concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, p. 345, to which we refer such of our readers as are interested in this subject of finance.

RYSWICK

Pages 31-31

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> village in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> and Delft, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which stands about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> farther. It is a very noble structure, all of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, but perhaps not proportionally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. It is adorned with a marble staircase, marble floors, and a magnificent terrace. There is a good prospect of it from the canal between Delft and the Hague. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded here in 1697 between England, Germany, Holland, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 20. N. Lat. 52. 8. S. S, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> s, the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> and 14th consonant of our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of which is formed by driving the breath through a narrow passage between the palate and the tongue elevated near it, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the lower jaw and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> towards the upper, the lips being a little way open; with such a configuration of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mouth and larynx, as renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> somewhat sibilous and hissing. Its sound, however, varies; being strong in some words, as this, thus, &c. and soft in words which have a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> e, as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, wife, &c. It is generally doubled at the end of words, whereby they become hard and harsh, as in kifs, lofs, &c. In some words it is silent, as fife, yland, wif, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a>, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, the long character s is generally used at the beginning and middle of words, but the short s at the end. In abbreviation, S stands for socieas or socius; as, R. S. S. for regiae societatis socius, i.e. fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. In medicinal prescriptions, S. A. signifies secundum artem, i.e. according to the rules of art: And in the notes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, S stands for Sextus; S. P. for Spurius; S. C. for senatus consultum; S. P. Q. R. for senatus populiisque Romanus; S. S. S. for stratum super stratum, i.e. one layer above another alternately; S. V. B. E. E. Q. V. for si valeas bene ef, ego quoque valeo, a form used in Cicero's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in the beginning of letters. Used as a numeral, S anciently denoted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>; in the Italian music, S signifies solo: And in books of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, S stands for south; S. E. for south-east; S. W. for south-west; S. S. E. for south-south-east; S. S. W. for south-south-west, &c.

SAAVEDRA

Pages 31-32

MICHAEL DE CERVANTES, a celebrated Spanish writer, and the inimitable author of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in the year 1541. From his infancy he was fond of books; but he applied himself wholly to books of entertainment, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> of all kinds, especially Spanish and Italian authors. From <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, either to serve <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Aquaviva, to whom he was chamberlain at Rome; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> else to follow the profession of a soldier, as he did some years under the victorious banners of Marco Antonio Colonna. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>, fought in the year 1571; in which he either lost his left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of an harquebus, or had it so maimed that he lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. After this he was taken by the Moors, and carried to Algiers, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a captive five years and a half. Then he returned to Spain, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of comedies and tragedies; and he composed several, all of which were well received by the public, and acted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. In the year 1584 he published his Galatea, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> in six books; which he presented to Alcanio Colonna, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, as the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which has done him the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immortalize his name, is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Don Quixote; the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was printed at Madrid in the year 1605. This is a satire upon books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-errantry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the sole, end of it was to destroy the reputation of those books, which had so infatuated the greater part of mankind, and especially those of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. This work was universally read; and the most eminent painters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>-workers, engravers, and sculptors, have been employed in representing the history of Don Quixote. Cervantes, even in his lifetime, obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of having his work receive a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> approbation. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> III. was standing in a balcony of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Madrid, and viewing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he observed a student on the banks of the river Manzanares <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> in a book, and from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time breaking off and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> his forehead with extraordinary tokens of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and delight: upon which the king said to those about him, "That scholar is either mad, or reading Don Quixote:" the latter of which proved to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. But virtus laudatur et alget: notwithstanding the vast applause his book everywhere met with he had not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> enough to procure a small pension, for he could scarcely keep himself from starving. In the year 1615, he published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part; to which he was partly moved by the presumption of some scribbler, who had published a continuation of this work the year before. He wrote also several novels; and among the rest, "The Troubles of Perifles and Sigismunda." He had employed many years in writing this novel, and finished it but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; for he did not live to see it published. His sickness was of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that he himself was able to be, and actually was, his own historian. At the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the Troubles of Perifles and Sigismunda, he represents himself on horseback upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and a student, who had overtaken him, engaged in conversation with him: "And happening to talk of my illness (says he), the student soon let me know my doom, by saying it was a drop of I had got; the thirst attending which all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the ocean, though it were not <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, would not suffice to quench. Therefore Senior Cervantes, says he, you must drink nothing at all, but do not forget to eat; for this alone will recover you without any other physic. I have been told the same by others, answered I; but I can no more forbear tippling, than if I were born to do nothing else. My <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> to an end; and from the daily journal of my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, I shall have finished my course by next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> at the farthest.—But adieu, my merry friends all, for I am going to die; and I hope to see you ere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the other world, as happy as heart can wish." His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> increased, and at last proved fatal to him; yet he continued to say and to write bon mots. He received the last sacrament on the 18th of April 1616; yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after wrote a dedication of the Troubles of Perifles and Sigismunda to the conde de Lemos. The particular day of his death is not known.

SABA

Pages 32-32

a Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near St Eustatia in the West Indies. It is a steep rock, on the summit of which is a little ground, very proper for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>. Frequent rains, which do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, give growth to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of an exquisite flavour, and cabbages of an extraordinary size. Fifty European families, with about one hundred and fifty slaves, here raise cotton, spin it, make stockings of it, and sell them to other colonies for as much as ten crowns a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>. Throughout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> there is no blood so pure as that of Saba; the women there preserve a freshness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, which is not to be found in any other of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Happy colony! elevated on the top of a rock between the sky and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it enjoys the benefit of both elements without dreading their storms; it breathes a pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, lives upon vegetables, cultivates a simple commodity, from which it derives ease without the temptation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; is employed in labours less troublesome than useful, and possesses in peace all the blessings of moderation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. This is the temple of peace, from whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> may contemplate at leisure the errors and passions of men, who come like the waves of the sea, to strike and dash themselves on the rich coasts of America, the spoils and possession of which they are perpetually contending for, and wresting from each other: hence may he view at a distance the nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> in the midst of the ocean, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> with the flames of ambition and avarice under the heats of the tropics; devouring <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> without ever being satisfied; wading through seas of blood to amass those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, those pearls, those diamonds, which are used to adorn the oppressors of mankind; loading innumerable ships with those precious casks, which furnish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> with purple, and from which flow pleasures, effeminacy, cruelty, and debauchery. The tranquil inhabitant of Saba views this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of follies, and spins his cotton in peace. SABÆANS. See Sabians.

SABAZIA

Pages 32-32

in Greek antiquity, were nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Sabazius. All the initiated had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> put in at their breasts, and taken out at the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their garments, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Jupiter's ravishing Proserpina in the form of a serpent. There were also other feasts and sacrifices distinguished by this appellation, in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRAS">Mithras</a>, the deity of the Persians, and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, who was thus denominated by the Sabians, a people of Thrace.

SABBATARIANS

Pages 32-32
or Seventh Day Baptists, a sect of anabaptists; thus called, because they observed the Jewish or Saturday-Sabbath, from a persuasion that it was never abrogated in the New Testament by the institution of any other.

SABBATH

Pages 32-38

SABBATH, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies rest. The seventh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was denominated the Sabbath, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> day of rest, because that in it God had rested from all his works which he created and made. From that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the seventh day seems to have been set apart for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> services; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, was afterwards observed by the Hebrews as a holyday. They were commanded to let it apart for sacred purposes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and likewise in memorial of their own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> from Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. The importance of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> may be gathered from the different laws respecting it. When the ten commandments were published from Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a> in tremendous pomp, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the Sabbath held a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in what is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and by subsequent statutes the violation of it was to be punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Six days were allowed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; but the seventh day God referred to himself, and appointed it to be observed as a stated time for holy offices, and to be spent in the duties of piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. On this day the ministers of the temple entered upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; and those who had attended on the temple service the preceding week went out at the same time. New loaves of shew-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> were placed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> table, and the old ones taken away. Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> for a burnt-offering, with a certain proportion of fine flour, mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, for a bread-offering, and wine for a libation, were offered. The Sabbath, as all other festivals, was celebrated from evening to evening. It began at six in the evening on Friday, and ended at the same time the next day. Concerning the time at which the Sabbath was first instituted, different opinions have been held. Some have maintained, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANCTIFICATION">sanctification</a> of the seventh day, mentioned in Gen. ii., is only there spoken of in anticipation; and is to be understood of the Sabbath afterwards enjoined the children of Israel at the commencement of the Mosaic dispensation. But without entering into a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of all the arguments adduced to support this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, a few observations, it is presumed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to show that it rests on no <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation. It cannot easily be supposed that the inspired penman would have mentioned the sanctification of the seventh day amongst the primeval transactions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such sanctification had not taken place until 2500 years afterwards. Writers, ambitious of that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> elegance which the rules of criticism have established, often bring together in their narratives events which were themselves far distant, for the sake of giving form to their discourse; but Moses appears to have despised all such flimsy refinements, and to have constructed his narrative in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> conformity to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of events. From the accounts we have of the religious service practised in the patriarchal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, it appears that, immediately after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> was restored to favour through a Mediator, a stated form of public worship was instituted, which man was required to observe, in testimony, not only of his dependence on the Creator, but also of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and hope in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> made to our first parents, and seen afar off. Of an institution, then, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and important, no circumstance would be omitted that is necessary to preserve it, or that contributes to render the observance of it regular and solemn. That determined times are necessary for the due celebration of divine service, cannot be denied. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of man, that he must have particular times set apart for particular services. He is doomed to toil and labour; to earn his bread in the sweat of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; and is capable of performing religious duties only in such a manner as is consistent with his situation in the world. If stated times for religious solemnities had not been enjoined, the consequence would have been, that such solemnities would have been altogether neglected; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> shows, that if mankind were left at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> when and how often they should perform religious offices, these offices would not be performed at all. It is the observation of holy times that preserves the practice of holy services; and without the frequent and regular returns of hallowed days, man would quickly forget the duty which he owes to God, and in a short time no vestige of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> would be found in the world. Among the ordinances which God vouchsafed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people, we find that the pious observation of the holydays was particularly insisted upon; and the Sabbath was enjoined to be kept holy, in the most solemn manner, and under the severest penalties. Can it then be supposed that He would suffer mankind, from the creation of the world to the Mosaic era, to remain without an institution so expedient in itself, and as well fitted to answer the end proposed by it, under the one dispensation, as ever it could be under the other? No; we have every imaginable reason to conclude, that when religious services were enjoined, religious times were appointed also; for the one necessarily implies the other. It is no objection to the early institution of the Sabbath, that there is no mention of it in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the patriarchal age. It would have swelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> to a most enormous size, had the sacred historian given a particular account of all the transactions of those times; besides, it would have answered no end. When Moses wrote the book of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, it was unnecessary to relate minutely transactions and institutions already well known by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>: accordingly we see, that his narrative is everywhere very concise, and calculated only to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the most important facts. However, if we take a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-service of the patriarchal age, we shall find that what is called the legal dispensation, at least the liturgic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, was no new system, but a collection of institutions observed from the beginning, and republished in form by Moses. The Scriptures inform us that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> offered sacrifices; and the account which is given of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of the one, and the rejection of the other, evidently shows that stated laws respecting the service had then taken place. "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time," at the end of the days, "Abel brought an offering." Here was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, altar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of sacrifice, appointed time, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to sacrifice, atonement made, and accepted. The distinction of animals into clean and unclean before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s sacrifice immediately after his deliverance, without any new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, is an unanswerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. It is testified of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, by God himself, that he kept his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, his commandments, his statutes, and his laws. These expressions comprehend the various branches, into which the law given at Sinai was divided. They contain the moral precepts, affirmative and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, the matter of religious service, a body of laws. laws to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> obedience, and to which man was to conform his conduct in every part of duty. Agreeably to this, we find that sacrifices were offered, altars and places of worship consecrated, and the Sabbath also mentioned as a well-known solemnity, before the promulgation of the law. It is expressly taken notice of at the fall of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a>; and the incidental manner in which it is then mentioned, is a convincing proof that the Israelites were no strangers to the institution: for had it been a new one, it must have been enjoined in a positive and particular manner, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of it must have been laid open and explained, otherwise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> would have conveyed no meaning. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of time into weeks, or periods of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days, which obtained so early and almost universally, is a strong indication that one day in seven was always distinguished in a particular manner. Weeks, and seven days, are in scripture language <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms. God commanded Noah, seven days before he entered the ark, to introduce into it all sorts of living creatures. When the waters of the flood began to abate, Noah sent forth a dove, which, finding no rest for the sole of her foot, returned to him. After seven days he sent forth the dove a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, and again she returned to the ark. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of other seven days he let go the dove a third time: and a week is spoken of (Gen. xxix.) as a well-known space of time. This septenary division of time has been, from the earliest ages, uniformly observed over all the eastern world. The Israelites, Assyrians, Egyptians, Indians, Arabians, and Persians, have always made use of a week, consisting of seven days. Many vain attempts have been made to account for this uniformity; but a practice so general and prevalent could never have taken place, had not the septenary distribution of time been instituted from the beginning, and handed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by tradition. From the same source also must the ancient heathens have derived their notions of the sacredness of the seventh day. That they had such notions of it is evident from several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the Greek poets quoted by Aristobulus, a learned Jew, by Clement of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and Eusebius. That they likewise held the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> seven in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation has been thrown by a learned, though sometimes fanciful, author*, with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> as to enforce conviction. The Pythagoreans call it the venerable number, εὐσεβεῖς ἀριθμός, worthy of veneration, and held it to be perfect and most proper to religion. They denominated it fortune, and also styled it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, music, because no doubt, seven distinct notes comprehend the whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of music, beyond which neither voice nor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> can go, but must return from the seventh, and begin again anew. They likewise designed it ἐπίσημον, leading to the end. Sabbath. Seven, in the Hebrew language, is expressed by a word that primarily signifies fulness, completion, sufficiency, and is applied to a week, or seven days, because that was the full time employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of creation; to the Sabbath, because on it all things were completed; and to an oath, because it is sufficient to put an end to all strife. This opening of the Hebrew root will enable us to come at the meaning of those expressions of the heathens, and also let us see whence they derived their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and modes of speaking, and that the knowledge of the transactions at the creation, though much perverted, was never entirely lost by them. It has been supposed by some, that the heathens borrowed the notion of the sacredness of the seventh day from the Jews. But this opinion will not readily be admitted, when it is considered that the Jews were held in the greatest contempt by the surrounding nations, who derided them no less for their sabbaths than for their circumcision. All sorts of writers ridiculed them on this account. Seneca <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> them with spending the seventh part of their time in sloth. Tacitus said, that not only the seventh day, but also the seventh year, was unprofitably wasted. Juvenal brings forward the same charge; and Perius upbraided them with their recutia Sabbati. Plutarch said that they kept it in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. Tacitus affirmed, that it was in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>; but the most abominable affront of all is that of Apion, who said that they observed the Sabbath in memory of their being cured on that day of a shameful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, called by the Egyptians <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. Some perceiving the force of this objection have contended, that time was divided into weeks of seven days, that each of the planetary gods, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and Saturn, who were the Dii majorum gentium, might have a day appropriated to his service. But if such was the origin of weeks, how came the great and ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Tellus to be omitted? She was worshipped by the early idolaters as well as the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, and must surely have been deemed by them as worthy of a particular day set apart to her honour as the planet Saturn, who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> undiscovered, afterwards seen but occasionally, and at all times considered as of malign aspect. (See Remphan.) Others have supposed, that as the year was divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months of something more than 28 days, it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to divide the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> from the different phases of the moon, which would produce as many weeks of seven days. But this supposition is less tenable than the former. The phases of the moon are not so precisely marked at the quarters as to attract to them any particular notice, nor are the quarterly appearances of one month commonly like those of another. We cannot, therefore, conceive what should have induced the earliest observers of the phases of the moon to divide the month into four parts rather than into three, or five, or seven. Had the ancient week consisted of 14 days, it might have been inferred, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of plausibility, that its length was regulated by the phases of the moon, because the shape of that luminary, at the end of the second <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, is very precisely marked; but there is nothing which, in the present <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, could have everywhere led mankind to make their weeks consist of seven days. This division of time, therefore, can can be accounted for only by admitting the primeval institution of the Sabbath, as related by Moses in the book of Genesis.
