That institution was absolutely necessary to preserve among men a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of religion; and it was renewed to the Jews at the giving of the law, and its observance enforced by the severest penalties. It was accordingly observed by them with more or less strictness in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of their commonwealth, and there is none of the institutions of their divine lawgiver which, in their present state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>, they more highly honour. They regard it, indeed, with a superstitious reverence, call it their "joy," their delight, and speak of it in the most magnificent terms. They have often varied in their opinions of the manner in which it ought to be kept. In the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>, they carried their respect for the Sabbath so very high, that they would not on that day defend themselves from the attacks of their enemies. But afterwards they did not scruple to stand upon their necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, although they would do nothing to prevent the enemy from carrying on their operations. When our Saviour was on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, it was no sin to loose a beast from the stall, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and if he had chanced to fall into a ditch, they pulled him out: but now it is absolutely unlawful to give a creature in that situation any other assistance than that of food; and if they lead an animal to water, they must take care not to let the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> or halter hang loose, otherwise they are transgressors. As the law enjoins rest on that day from all servile employments, in order to comply with the injunction, they undertake no kind of work on Friday but such as can easily be accomplished before evening. In the afternoon they put into proper places the meat that they have prepared to eat the day following. They afterwards set out a table covered with a clean cloth, and place bread upon it, which they also cover with another cloth; and during the Sabbath the table is never moved out of its place. About an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> before sunset, the women <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> the Sabbath lamps, which hang in the places where they eat. They then stretch forth their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to the light, and pronounce the following benediction. "Blessed be thou, O God, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the world, who hast enjoined us, that are sanctified by thy commandments, to light the Sabbath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>." These lamps are two or more in number, according to the size of the chamber in which they are suspended, and continue to burn during the greatest part of the night. In order to begin the Sabbath well, they wash their hands and faces, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and pare their nails, beginning at the fourth finger, then going to the second, then the fifth, then the third, and ending with the thumb. If a Jew calls the parings of his nails to the ground, he is rafcah, that is, a wicked man; for Satan has great power over those parings of nails; and it seems they are of great use to the wizards, who know how to employ them in their enchantments. If he buries them in the earth, he is rafedie, that is, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> man; if he burns them in the fire, he is cheful, that is, worthy of honour, an holy man. When they have performed these preparatory ceremonies, they repair to the synagogue, and enter upon their devotions. As soon as prayers begin, the departed souls <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> out of the purgatorial flames, and have liberty to cool themselves in water while the Sabbath lasts; for which reason the Jews prolong the continuance of it as much as they can; and the Rabbins have strictly commanded them not to exhaust all the water on the Sabbath day, lest those miserable souls should by that means be deprived of the refreshing element. When they have ended their prayers, they return home, and salute one another, by wishing a good Sabbath. They then sit down to table. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the family takes a cup full of wine, and lifting up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, says, "Blessed be thou, O God our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, king of the world, who hast created the fruit of the vine.—Blessed be thou, O God our Lord, king of the world, who hast sanctified us by thy commandments, and given us thy holy Sabbath; and of thy good will and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> hast left it to us an inheritance, the memorial of thy works of creation. For it is the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of saints, and the memorial of the coming out of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. And thou hast also chosen us from all other people, and sanctified us, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and pleasure hast left thy holy Sabbath an inheritance. Blessed be thou, O God, who sanctifiest the Sabbath." After this benediction is ended, he drinks, and gives the cup to all that are present. He then removes the cloth, and taking bread, says, "Blessed be thou, O God our Lord, king of the world, who bringest bread out of the earth." Then he breaks off a bit, and eats, and also gives a piece of it to every one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. On the morning of the Sabbath, the Jews do not rise so early as they do at other times. Thinking, the greater pleasure they take on that day, the more devoutly they keep it. When they come into the synagogue, they pray as usual, only the devotions are somewhat longer, being intermingled with psalmody, in honour of the Sabbath. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a> is then produced, and seven sections of it are read in order by seven persons chosen for the purpose. Several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> are likewise read out of the prophets, which have some relation to what was read out of the law. After morning prayers they return to their houses, and eat the second Sabbath-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, shewing every token of joy, in honour of the festival. But if one has seen anything ominous in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>; if he has dreamed that he burnt the book of the law; that a beam has come out of the walls of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> have fallen out;—then he fails until very late at night, for all such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> are bad ones. In the afternoon they go again to the synagogue, and perform the evening service, adding to the ordinary prayers some lessons that respect the Sabbath. When the devotional duties are ended, they return home, and light a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> resembling a torch, and again sit down to eat. They remain eating until near six, and then the master of the family takes a cup, and pouring wine into it rehearses some benedictions; after which he pours a little of the wine upon the ground, and says, "Blessed be thou, O Lord, King of the world, who hast created the fruit of the vine." Then holding the cup in his left hand, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> he takes a box of sweet spices, and says, "Blessed be thou, O Lord God, who hast created various kinds of sweet spices." He smells the spices, and holds them out to the rest, that they may do the same. He then takes the cup in his right hand, and going to the candle views the left very narrowly, and pronounces a blessing. With the cup in the left hand, he examines the right in the same manner. Again, holding the cup in his right hand, he rehearses another benediction, and at the same time pours some of the wine. on the ground. After this he drinks a little of it, and then hands it about to the rest of the family, who finish what remains. In this manner the Sabbath is ended by the Jews, and they may return to their ordinary employments. Those who meet pay their compliments, by wishing one another a happy week. The Rabbins have reckoned up <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> and thirty primary prohibitions, which ought to be observed on the Sabbath festival; but their circumstances and dependents, which are also obligatory, are almost innumerable. The 39 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> are, Not to till the ground; to sow; to reap; to make hay; to bind up sheaves of corn; to thresh; to winnow; to grind; to sift meal; to knead the dough; to bake; to shear; to whiten; to comb or card <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; to spin; to twine or twist; to warp; to dye; to tie; to untie; to sew; to tear or pull in pieces; to build; to pull down; to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> with a hammer; to hunt or fish; to kill a beast; to flay it; to dress it; to scrape the skin; to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> it; to cut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; to write; to scratch out; to rule <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; to kindle a fire; to extinguish it; to carry a thing from place to place; to expose any thing to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. These are the primary prohibitions, and each of these has its proper consequences, which amount to an incredible number; and the Jews themselves say, that if they could keep but two Sabbaths as they ought, they would soon be delivered out of all their troubles. If a Jew on a journey is overtaken by the Sabbath in a wood, or on the highway, no matter where, nor under what circumstances, he sits down; he will not stir out of the spot. If he falls down in the dirt, he lies there; he will not rise up. If he should tumble into a privy, he would rest there; he would not be taken out (A). If he sees a flea skipping upon his clothes, he must not catch it. If it bites him he may only remove it with his hand; he must not kill it; but a louse meets with no such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, for it may be destroyed. He must not wipe his hands with a towel or cloth, but he may do it very lawfully with a cow's tail. A fresh wound must not be bound up on the Sabbath day; a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> that had been formerly applied to a sore may remain on it; but if it falls off, it must not be put on anew. The same may use a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> must not. These particulars, and a great many more of the same nature, are observed by the Jews in the strictest manner. But if any one wishes to know more of the practice of that devoted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, he may consult Buxtorf's "Judaica Synagogae," chap. x. xi., where he will find a complete detail of their customs and ceremonies on the Sabbath; and likewise see the primary prohibitions branched out into their respective circumstances. As the seventh day was observed by the Jewish church, in memory of the rest of God after the works of creation, and their own deliverance from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>'s tyranny; so the first day of the week has always been observed by the Christian church, in memory of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, by which he completed the work of man's redemption on earth, and rescued him from the dominion of him who has the power of death. This day was denominated by the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> the Lord's day. It was also sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>; which was the name given to it by the heathens, who dedicated it to the sun. And indeed, although it was originally called Sunday by the heathens, yet it may very properly retain that name among Christians, because it is dedicated to the honour of "The true light," which lighteth every man that cometh into the world, of Him who is styled by the prophet "The Sun of righteousness," and who on this day arose from the dead. But although it was, in the primitive times, indifferently called the Lord's day or Sunday, yet it was never denominated the Sabbath; a name confidently appropriated to Saturday, or the seventh day, both by sacred and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers. Of the change from the seventh to the first day of the week, or even of the institution of the Lord's day of its festival, there is no account in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. However, it may be fairly inferred from it, that the first day of the week was, in the apostolic age, a stated time for public worship. On this day the apostles were assembled, when the Holy Ghost came down visibly upon them to qualify them for the conversion of the world. On this day we find St Paul preaching at Troas, when the disciples came to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> bread: and the directions which the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> gives to the Corinthians concerning their contributions for the relief of their suffering brethren, plainly allude to their religious assemblies on the first day of the week. Thus it would appear from several passages in the New Testament, that the religious observation of the first day of the week is of apostolical appointment; and may indeed be very reasonably supposed to be among those directions and instructions which our blessed Lord himself gave to his disciples, during the 40 days between his resurrection and ascension, wherein he conversed with them, and spoke of the things pertaining to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of God. Still, however, it must be owned that those passages, although the plainest that occur, are not sufficient to prove the apostolical institution of the Lord's day, or even the actual observation of it. In order, therefore, to place the matter beyond all controversy, recourse must be had to ecclesiastical testimony. From the consistent evidence and uniform practice of the primitive church, and also from the attestation of Pliny, an heathen of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> both in learning and power, we find that the first day of the week was observed in the earliest ages as a holyday or festival, in honour of the resurrection of Christ. Now there are but two sources whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> could possibly have arisen. It must have been instituted either by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> or divine authority: by human authority it was not instituted; for there was no general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in those early times, and without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of a general council it was impossible that any ecclesiastical institution could (A) This, it seems, was once really the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. A Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> fell into a privy on a Saturday. He might have been taken out; but he told those who offered him their assistance to give themselves no trouble, for there he was determined to keep holy the Sabbath day. The bishop, when he heard of it, resolved that he should sanctify the next day also in the same place; and so, betwixt them, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> Jew lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. could have been universally established at once. It remains, therefore, that it must have been instituted by divine authority; and that it really was so, will further appear from the following considerations. It is certain that the apostles travelled over the greatest part of the world, and planted churches in the remotest parts of it. It is certain also that they were all led by the same spirit; and their desire was, that unity and uniformity should be observed in all the churches which they had founded. It is not therefore surprising that, in the primitive times, the same doctrine, the same worship, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and customs, should prevail all over the Christian world; nay, it would have been unaccountable had the case been otherwise. For this reason we may conclude that every custom, universally observed in the early ages of the Christian church, and not instituted by a general council, was of original appointment. As the Lord's day is sanctified, that is, set apart to Christians for the worship and service of God, their Creator, Redeemer, and Sanctifier, a little consideration will easily discover how it ought to be observed. Although a day separated from worldly business, yet it is in no sense a day of idleness, but a season appropriated to the works of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> and labours of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. In the primitive times this holy day was observed in the most solemn manner. From the monuments of those early ages we learn, that it was spent in a due and constant attendance on all the offices of divine worship. On it they held their religious assemblies, in which the writings of the apostles and prophets were read to the people; and the doctrines of Christianity further pressed upon them by the exhortations of the clergy. Solemn prayers and praises were offered up to God, and hymns sung in honour of Christ; the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> was constantly celebrated; and collections were made for the maintenance of the clergy and the relief of the poor. On this day they abstained, as much as they could, from bodily labour. They looked upon it as a day of joy and gladness; and therefore all fasting on it was prohibited, even during the season of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, their great annual fast.—Such was the zeal of those times, that nothing, nor the severest persecutions, hindered them from celebrating holy offices on this day. They were often betrayed, and as often slaughtered in consequence of cruel edicts from emperors, those very emperors for whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and prosperity they always offered up their fervent prayers. For this cause, when they could not meet in the daytime, they assembled in the morning before it was light; and when sick, in exile, or in prison, nothing troubled them more than that they could not attend the service of the church. No trivial pretences were then admitted for any one's absence from public worship; for severe censures were passed upon all who were absent without some urgent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. When the empire became Christian, Constantine and his successors made laws for the more solemn observation of the Lord's day. They prohibited all prosecutions and pleadings and other juridical matters to be transacted on it, and also all unnecessary labour; not that it was looked upon as a Jewish Sabbath, but because these things were considered as inconsistent with the duties of the festival. But although the primitive Christians did not indulge themselves in the practice of unnecessary labour or trifling amusements, yet they did not wholly abstain from working, if great necessity required it. The council of Laodicea enjoined that men should abstain from work on the Lord's day if possible; but if any were found to Judaize, they were to be censured as great transgressors. So circumspect were the primitive Christians about their conduct on this festival, that on the one hand they avoided all things which tended to profane it, whilst on the other they censured all those who insisted it should be observed with Pharisaical rigour. The primary duty of the Lord's day is public worship. The nature and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Christian religion sufficiently shows the necessity and importance of assembling for the duties of devotion. The whole operation of Christianity is to bring us to an union with God, which cannot be obtained or preserved without frequent communications with him; and the reasons which show religious intercourse to be the indispensable duty of Christians in a private capacity, will bind it with equal or more force on them considered as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. The advantages of public worship, when duly performed, are many and great. There are two, however, which deserve to be considered in a particular manner. It gives Christians an opportunity of openly professing their faith, and testifying their obedience to their Redeemer in the wisest and best manner; and in an age when atheism has arisen to an alarming height, when the Son of God is crucified afresh, and put to open shame, every man, who has any regard for religion, will cheerfully embrace all opportunities of declaring his abhorrence of the vicious courses pursued by those degenerate apostates. He will with pleasure lay hold on every occasion to testify that he is neither afraid nor ashamed to confess the truth; and will think it his indispensible duty openly to disavow the sins of others, that he may not incur the guilt of partaking of them. Public worship preserves in the minds of men a sense of religion, without which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> could not exist. Nothing can keep a body of men together and unite them in promoting the public good, but such principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> as may reach and govern the heart. But these can be derived only from a sense of religious duties, which can never be so strongly impressed upon the mind as by a constant attendance upon public worship. Nothing can be more weak than to neglect the public worship of God, under the pretence that we can employ ourselves as acceptably to our Maker at home in our closets. Both kinds of worship are indeed necessary; but one debt cannot be paid by the discharge of another. By public worship every man professes his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in that God whom he adores, and appeals to Him for his sincerity, of which his neighbour cannot judge. By this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> he endears himself more or less to others. It creates confidence; it roots in the heart benevolence, and all other Christian virtues, which produce, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> life, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of mutual love and general peace. People in general are of opinion that the duties of the Lord's day are over when public worship is ended. But they seem to forget for what purposes the day was set apart. It is not only appropriated to the duties of public worship, but also sanctified to our improvement in the knowledge of the doctrines of Christianity. SABBATH is an institution calculated to alleviate the condition of the laborious classes of mankind, and, in consequence of that, to afford rest to beggars also. It is proper, it is necessary, that man should reflect on his condition in the world, that he should examine the state of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and inquire what progress he has made in that work which was given him to do. Those that have children or servants are obliged to look after their instruction as well as their own. These are the ends which the institution of Sunday was designed to answer. Every man must allow that these things must be done at some time or other; but unless there be set times for doing them, the generality of mankind would wholly neglect them. Visiting and travelling (though very common) are enormous profanations of this holy day. Families are thereby robbed of their time; a loss for which no amends can ever be made them; Servants, instead of having leisure to improve themselves in spiritual knowledge, are burdened with additional labour: And in a man of any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, it must excite many painful sensations, when he reflects how often the useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> on that day experiences all the anguish of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, torn sides, and battered <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. Every kind of amusement, every kind of common labour, is an encroachment on the particular duties of the Lord's day; and consequently men profane the day by spending it in any amusements, or undertaking upon it any ordinary employment unless it be a work of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> necessity. SABBATH-Breaking, or profanation of the Lord's day, is punished by the municipal laws of England. For, besides the notorious indecency and scandal of permitting any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> business to be publicly transacted on that day in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> professing Christianity, and the corruption of morals which usually follows its profanation, the keeping one day in seven holy, as a time of relaxation and refreshment, as well as for public worship, is of admirable service to a state, considered merely as a civil institution. It humanizes, by the help of conversation and society, the manners of the lower classes; which would otherwise degenerate into a ferocious and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> selfishness of spirit: it enables the industrious workman to pursue his occupation in the ensuing week with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and cheerfulness: it imprints on the minds of the people that sense of their duty to God so necessary to make them good citizens; but which yet would be worn out and defaced by an unremitting continuance of labour, without any stated times of recalling them to the worship of their Maker. And therefore the laws of King Athelstan forbade all merchandising on the Lord's day, under very severe penalties. And by the statute 27 Hen. VI. c. 5, no fair or market shall be held on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> festivals, Good Friday, or any Sunday (except the four Sundays in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>), on pain of forfeiting the goods exposed to sale. And, since, by the statute 1 Car. I. c. 1, no persons shall assemble, out of their own parishes, for any sport whatsoever, upon this day; nor, in their parishes, shall use any bull or bear-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a>, interludes, plays, or other unlawful exercises or pastimes; on pain that every offender shall pay 3s. 4d. to the poor. This statute does not prohibit, but rather implicitly allows, any innocent recreation or amusement, within their respective parishes, even on the Lord's day, after divine service is over. But by statute 29 Car. II. c. 7, no person is allowed to work on the Lord's day, or use any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or barge, or expose any goods to sale, except meat in Sabelians' public houses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> at certain hours, and works of necessity or charity, on forfeiture of 5s. Nor shall any drover, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>, or the like, travel upon that day, under pain of 20s.

SABELLIANS

Pages 38-38

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the 3rd century, that embraced the opinions of Sabellius, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, who openly taught that there is but one person in the Godhead. The Sabellians maintained, that the Word and the Holy Spirit are only virtues, emanations, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> functions of the Deity; and held, that he who is in heaven is the Father of all things, that he descended into the virgin, became a child, and was born of her as a son; and that having accomplished the mystery of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, he diffused himself on the apostles in tongues of fire, and was then denominated the Holy Ghost. They explained by resembling God to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the illuminative virtue or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of which was the Word, and its warming virtue the Holy Spirit. The Word, they taught, was darted, like a divine ray, to accomplish the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>; and that being re-ascended to heaven, the influences of the Father were communicated after a like manner to the apostles.

SABINA

Pages 38-38

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territories of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Umbria, on the east by Farther Abruzzo, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of Rome, and on the west by the patrimony of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. It is 22 miles in length, and almost as much in breadth; watered by several small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and wine. There is no walled town in it; and Magliano is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

SABINIANS

Pages 38-38

an early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of idolaters, which continues to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and worships the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and stars. See POLYTHEISM, No. 10, 11, 12.

SABINUS

Pages 38-38

GEORGE, a celebrated Latin poet, born in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> in 1568. His poem Res gestae Caesarum Germanorum, spread his reputation all over Germany, and procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of all the princes who had any regard for polite literature: he was made professor of the belles lettres at Frankfort on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, rector of the new academy of Konigslburg, and councillor to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Brandenburg. He married two wives, the first of whom was the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the famous reformer Melanchthon; and died in 1560. His poems are well known, and have been often printed.

SABLE

Pages 39-40

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, signifies "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>;" and is borrowed from the French, as are most terms in this science: in engraving it is expressed by both <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> and perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> crossing each other. Sable of itself signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, learning, and grief; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heralds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that when it is compounded with The occasion that introduced this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> into heraldry is thus related by Alexander Nifbet, p. 8. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Anjou, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, after the loss of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, appeared at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a> in Germany all in black, with his shield of that tincture, *semé de larmes*, i.e. belprinkled with drops of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to represent tears, indicating by that both his grief and loss.

SABLESTAN

Pages 40-40
or **SABLUSTAN**, a province of Asia, in Persia, on the frontiers of India; bounded on the north by Khorasan; on the east, by the mountains of Balk and Candahar; on the south, by Sagistan or Segestan; and on the west, by Heri. It is a mountainous country, very little known to Europeans; nor is it certain which is the capital town.

SABRE

Pages 40-40

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scimitar, with a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and heavy blade, thick at the back, and a little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCATED">falcated</a> or crooked towards the point. It is the ordinary weapon worn by the Turks, who are said to be very expert in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it.

SABURRA

Pages 40-40

in Medicine, usually denotes any collection of half putrid indigested <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in the stomach and intestines, by which the operation of digestion is impeded. **SABURÆ**, gritts, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>; a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, found in minute masses. They are of various colours, as flaky and sparry grits, of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> greyish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> flaky grits; green flaky grits; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> grits; blackish grits. **SACÆA**, a feast which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Babylonians and other orientals held annually in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the deity Anaitis. The Sacæa were in the East what the Saturnalia were at Rome, viz. a feast for the slaves. One of the ceremonies was to choose a prisoner condemned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and allow him all the pleasures and gratifications he would wish, before he were carried to execution.

SACCADE

Pages 40-40

in the manege, is a jerk more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less violent, given by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in pulling or twitching the reins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> all on a sudden and with one pull, and that when a horse lies heavy upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or obstinately arms himself. This is a correction used to make a horse carry well; but it ought to be used discreetly, and not seldom.

SACCHAROMETER

Pages 40-40

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the value of worts, and the strength of different kinds of malt liquor. The name signifies a measurer of sweetness. An instrument of this kind has been invented by a Mr Richardson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>, on the following principle. The menstruum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, employed by the brewer, becomes more dense by the addition of such parts of the materials as have been dissolved or extracted by, and thence incorporated with it: the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, and its subsequent cooling, still adds to the density of it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>; so that when it is submitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, it is denser than at any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In passing through this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> operation, a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The fluid no sooner begins to ferment than its density begins to diminish; and as the fermentation is more or less perfect, the fermentable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, whose accretion has been traced by the increase of density, becomes more or less attenuated; and in place of every particle thus attenuated, a spirituous particle, of less density than water, is produced; so that when the liquor is again in a state of rest, it is so much specifically <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than it was before, as the action of fermentation has been capable of attenuating the component parts of its acquired density; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the whole were attenuated in this manner, the liquor would become lighter, or less dense than water, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of spirit produced from the fermentable matter, and occupying its place, would diminish the density of the water in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of proportion to that in which the latter has increased it.

SACCHARUM

Pages 40-40
Sugar, or the Sugar-Cane, a genus of plants belonging to the triandria clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 4th order, Graminae. See Botany Index. This plant is a native of Africa, the East Indies, and of Brazil; from whence it was introduced into our West India islands soon after they were settled. The sugar-cane is the glory and the pride of those islands. It amply rewards the industrious planter, enriches the British merchant, gives bread to thousands of manufacturers and seamen, and brings an immense revenue to Saccharum the crown. For the process of making sugar, see Sugar. Sugar, formerly a luxury, is now become one of the necessaries of life. In crop-time every negro on the plantations, and every animal, even the dogs, grow fat. This sufficiently points out the nourishing and healthy qualities of sugar. It has been alleged, that the eating of sugar spoils the colour of, and corrupts, the teeth; this, however, proves to be a mistake, for no people on the earth have finer teeth than the negroes in Jamaica. Dr Allion, formerly professor of botany and materia medica at Edinburgh, endeavoured to obviate this vulgar opinion: he had a fine set of teeth, which he ascribed solely to his eating great quantities of sugar. Externally too it is often useful: mixed with the pulp of roasted oranges, and applied to putrid or ill-diposed ulcers, it proves a powerful corrector.

SACCULUS

Pages 40-40

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of saccus, signifies a little bag, and is applied to many parts of the body.

SACHEVEREL

Pages 40-41

Dr Henry, a famous clergyman of the Tory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; who distinguished himself by indecent and furious sermons and writings against the dissenters and revolution principles. He owed his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, however, to being indirectly prosecuted by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords for his affizsermon at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and his 5th of November sermon at St Paul's in 1729; in which he asserted the doctrine of non-resistance to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and reflected severely on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of toleration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> parties were very violent at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of Sacheverel inflamed the high-church party to dangerous riots and excesses: he was, however, suspended for three years, and his sermons burned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hangman. The Tories being in administration when Sacheverel's suspension expired, he was freed with every circumstance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and public rejoicing; was ordered to preach before the commons on the 29th of May, had the thanks of the house for his discourse, and obtained the valuable rectory of St Andrew's, Holborn.

SACK

Pages 41-41

a wine used by our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, which some have taken to be Rhineilh and some Canary wine.—Venner, in his Via Recta <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> Vitam Longam, printed in 1628, says that sack is "completely not in the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and that some affect to drink sack with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and some without; and upon no other ground, as I think, but as it is best pleasing to their palate." He goes on to say, "that sack, taken by itself, is very hot and very penetrative; being taken with sugar, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is both somewhat allayed, and the penetrative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> thereof retarded." He adds farther, that Rhineilh, &c., decline after a twelvemonth, but sack and the other stronger wines are best when they are two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three years old. It appears to be highly probable that sack was not a sweet wine, from its being taken with sugar, and that it did not receive its name from having a saccharine flavour, but from its being originally stored in sacks or borachios. It does not appear to have been a French wine, but a strong wine the production of a hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. Probably it was what is called dry mountain, or some Spanish wine of that kind. This conjecture is the more plausible, as Howell, in his French and English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, printed in the year 1650, translates sack by the words vin d'Espagne, vin fée. SACK of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">Wool</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wool containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> 22 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> 14 pounds. In Scotland, a sack is 24 stones, each stone containing 16 pounds. SACK of Cotton Wool, a quantity from one hundred and a half to four hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. SACKS of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, in Fortification, are canvas bags filled with earth. They are used in making retrenchments in haste, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on parapets, or the head of the breaches, &c., to repair them, when beaten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>.

SACKBUT

Pages 41-41

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind, being a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, though different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> trumpet both in form and size; it is fit to play a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, and is contrived to be drawn out <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shortened, according to the tone required, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> or acute. The Italians call it trombone, and the Latins tuba ductilis.

SACKVILLE

Pages 41-42
Charles, earl of Dorset, a celebrated wit and poet, descended from the foregoing, was born in 1637. He was, like Villiers, Rochester, Sedley, &c., one of the libertines of King Charles's court, and sometimes indulged himself in inexcusable excesses. He openly disdained the violent measures of James II, and engaged early for the prince of Orange, by whom he was made lord chamberlain of the household, and taken Sacrament taken into the privy-council. He died in 1706, and left several poetical pieces, which, though not considerable enough to make a volume by themselves, may be found among the works of the minor poets, published in 1749. SACRAMENT is derived from the Latin word sacramentum, which signifies an oath, particularly the oath taken by soldiers to be true to their country and general. The words of this oath, according to Polybius, were, obtemperatus sum et facturus quicquid mandabitur ab imperatoribus justa vires. The word was adopted by the writers of the Latin church, and employed, perhaps with no great propriety, to denote those ordinances of religion by which Christians came under an obligation, equally sacred with that of an oath, to observe their part of the covenant of grace, and in which they have the assurance of Christ that he will fulfil his part of the same covenant. Of sacraments, in this sense of the word, Protestant churches admit of but two; and it is not easy to conceive how a greater number can be made out from Scripture, if the definition of a sacrament be just which is given by the church of England. By that church, the meaning of the word sacrament is declared to be "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace given unto us, ordained by Christ himself as a means whereby we receive the same, and a pledge to assure us thereof." According to this definition, baptism and the Lord's Supper are certainly sacraments; for each consists of an outward and visible sign of what is believed to be an inward and spiritual grace; both were ordained by Christ himself, and by the reception of each does the Christian come under a solemn obligation to be true to his divine master, according to the terms of the covenant of grace. (See Baptism and Supper of the Lord.) The Romanists, however, add to this number confirmation, penance, extreme unction, ordination, and marriage, holding in all seven sacraments; but two of those rites not being peculiar to the Christian church cannot possibly be Christian sacraments, in contradiction to the sacraments or obligations into which men of all religions enter. Marriage was instituted from the beginning, when God made man male and female, and commanded them to be fruitful, and multiply and replenish the earth; and penance, as far as it is of the same import with repentance, has a place in all religions which teach that God is merciful, and men fallible.—The external severities imposed upon penitents by the church of Rome (see Penance) may indeed be in some respects peculiar to the discipline of that church, though the penances of the Hindoos are certainly as rigid; but none of these severities were ordained by Christ himself as the pledge of an inward and spiritual grace; nor do they, like baptism and the Lord's Supper, bring men under obligations which are supposed to be analogous to the meaning of the word sacramentum. Confirmation has a better title to the appellation of a sacrament than any of the other five popish rites of that name, though it certainly was not considered as such by the earliest writers of the Christian church, nor does it appear to have been ordained by Christ himself, (see Confirmation). Ordination is by many churches considered as a very important rite; but as it is not administered to all men, nor has any particular form appropriated to it in the New Testament, it cannot be considered as a Christian sacrament conferring grace generally necessary to salvation. It is rather a form of authorizing certain persons to perform certain offices, which respect not themselves but the whole church; and extreme unction is a rite which took its rise from the miraculous powers of the primitive church vainly claimed by the succeeding clergy. (See Ordination and Extreme Unction). These considerations seem to have some weight with the Romish clergy themselves; for they call the eucharist, by way of eminence, the holy sacrament. Thus to expose the holy sacrament, is to lay the consecrated host on the altar to be adored.—The procession of the holy sacrament is that in which this host is carried about the church, or about a town. Numerous as we think the sacraments of the Romish church, a sect of Christians sprung up in England early in the current century who increased their number.—The founder of this sect was a Dr Deacon, we think, of Manchester, where the remains of it subsisted very lately, and probably do so at present. According to these men, every rite and every phrase in the book called the Apolitical Constitutions were certainly in use among the apostles themselves. Still, however, they make a distinction between the greater and the lesser sacraments. The greater sacraments are only two, baptism and the Lord's supper. The lesser are no fewer than ten, viz. five belonging to baptism, exorcism, anointing with oil, the white garment, a taste of milk and honey, and anointing with chrism or ointment. The other five are, the sign of the cross, imposition of hands, unction of the sick, holy orders, and matrimony. Of the nature of these lesser sacraments, or the grace which they are supposed to confer, our limits will permit us to give no account.—Nor is it necessary that we should. The sect which taught them, if not extinguished, is certainly in its last wane. It has produced, however, one or two learned men; and its founder's Full, True, and Comprehensive View of Christianity, in two Catechisms, is a work which the Christian antiquary will read with pleasure for information, and the philosopher for the materials which it contains for meditation on the workings of the human mind. It was published in 8vo, in the year 1748. Congregation of the Holy SACRAMENT, a religious establishment formed in France, whose founder was Autherius, bishop of Bethlehem, and which, in 1644, received an order from Urban VIII. to have always a number of ecclesiastics ready to exercise their ministry among pagan nations, wherever the pope, or congregation de propaganda, should appoint.

SACRAMENTARIANS

Pages 42-42

a general name given to all such as have published <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> held erroneous doctrines of the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly applied among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, by way of reproach, to the Lutherans, Calvinists, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>.

SACRAMENTARY

Pages 42-42

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-book, which contains all the prayers and ceremonies practised at the celebration of the sacraments. It was wrote by Pope Gelasius, and afterwards revised, corrected, and abridged, by St Gregory.

SACRE

Pages 42-43
or SAKER, in Ornithology, the name of a species of falcon, called by authors Falco sacer, and differently described by different authors, but by all agreed to be an extremely bold and active bird. It is a native of of the northern regions of Europe; and a variety called by some writers the speckled partridge hawk is found at Hudson's class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay, North America.

SACRED

Pages 43-43

something holy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is solemnly offered and consecrated to God, with benedictions, uncions, &c. Kings, prelates, and priests, are reckoned sacred persons; abbots are only blest.—The deaconhood, sub-deaconhood, and priesthood, are all sacred orders, and are said to impress a sacred indelible character. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of consecrating kings with holy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is derived (says Gurlingius) from the Hebrews; among whom, he agrees with Grotius, it was never used but to kings who had not an evident <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by succession. He adds, that the Christian emperors never used it before Justin the younger; from whom he takes it to have passed to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, &c. Sacred is also applied to things belonging to God and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Church-lands, ornaments, &c. are held sacred.—The sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> is that of the cardinals.

SACRED MAJESTY

Pages 43-43

is applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England; yet Lovelace says it is blasphemy. See MAJESTY. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> held a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> struck with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> as sacred. In the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, sacred place chiefly denotes that where a person deceased has been interred. SACRED Elixir. See ELIXIR.

SAILING ALSO

Pages 60-62

g also implies a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, formed on the principles, and regulated by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. Hence we say, Plain Sailing, Mercator's, Middle-latitude, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>-circle Sailing. See the article Navigation. Sail-Making, the art of making sails. See Sail and Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Sailor, the same with Mariner and Seaman. Saint, means a person eminent for piety and virtue, and is generally applied by us to the apostles and other holy persons mentioned in Scripture. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> make its application much more extensive. Under the word Canonization we have already said something on their practice of creating saints. Our readers, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not, we trust, be displeased with the following more enlarged account, which they themselves give of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The canonization of saints, then, they tell us, is the enrolment of any person in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> catalogue of those who are called saints; or, it is a judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, by which it is declared, that a deceased person was eminent for sanctity during his lifetime, and especially towards the end of it; and that consequently he must now be in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with God, and deserves to be honoured by the church on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with that veneration which she is wont to pay to the blest in heaven. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> with regard to this matter has varied. It would seem that in the first ages every bishop in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> was wont to declare what persons were to be honoured as saints by his people. Hence St Cyprian, about the middle of the third century, B. 3. ep. 6, requires that he be informed of those who should die in prison for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, that so he might make mention of them in the holy sacrifice with the martyrs, and might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> them afterwards on the anniversary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of their happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This veneration <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> sometimes to be confined to one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but sometimes it extended to distant provinces, and even became universal all over the church. It was thus that St Laurence, St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, St Augustine, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, and many others, appear to have been canonized by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and universal persuasion. In those ages none were reckoned saints but the apostles, the martyrs, and very eminent confessors, whose sanctity was notorious everywhere. Afterwards it appears that canonizations were wont to be performed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> synods under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the metropolitan. It was thus that St Isidore of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> was canonized in the 7th century, by the 8th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, 14 years after his death. This manner of canonization continued occasionally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the 12th century. The last instance of a saint canonized in that way, is that of St Walter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Pontaise, who was declared a saint by the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in the year 1153. In the 12th century, in order to prevent mistakes in so delicate a matter, Pope Alexander III. judged it proper to reserve this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> to the holy see of Rome exclusively; and decreed that no one should for the future be honoured by the church as a saint without the express approbation of the pope. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the canonization of saints has been carried on in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>; and there is at Rome a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of cardinals, called the congregation of holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, who are assisted by several divines under the name of confessors, who examine such matters, and prepare them for the decision of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>. When therefore any pontificate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> body, think fit, they apply to the pope for the canonization of any person. The first juridical step in this business must be taken by the bishop in whose diocese the person for whom the application is made had lived and died, who by his own authority calls witnesses to attest the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the holiness, the virtues, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, of the person in question. When the deceased has resided in different dioceses, it may be necessary that different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> take such depositions; the originals of which are preserved in the archives of their respective churches, and authentic copies sealed up are sent to Rome by a special messenger, where they are deposited with the congregation of rites, and where they must remain for the space of ten years without being opened. They are then opened, and maturely examined by the congregation, and with their advice the pope allows the cause to go on or not as he thinks proper. The solicitors for the canonization are then referred by his holiness to the said congregation, which, with his authority, gives a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to one or more bishops, or other respectable persons, to examine, on the spot and in the places where the person in question has lived and died, into his character and whole behaviour. These commissioners summon witnesses, take depositions, and collect letters and other writings of the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and get all the intelligence they can concerning him, and the opinion generally entertained of him. The report of these commissioners is considered attentively and at length by the congregation, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it discussed by the confessors, when the congregation determines whether or not they can permit the process to go on. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it be allowed to proceed, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, who is called pontiff, undertakes to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in that affair. The first question then that comes to be examined is, whether or not the person proposed for canonization can be proved to have been in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> endued with the moral virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, fortitude, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>; and with the theological virtues of faith, hope, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>? All this is canvassed with great deliberation; and there is a distinguished ecclesiastic called the promoter of the holy faith, who is sworn to make all reasonable objections to the proofs that are adduced in favour of the canonization. If the decision be favourable, then the proofs of miracles done to show the sanctity of the person in question are permitted to be brought forward; when two miracles must be verified to the satisfaction of the congregation, both as to the reality of the facts, and as to their having been truly above the power of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. If the decision on this comes out likewise favourable, then the whole is laid before the pope and what divines he chooses (a). Public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and fasting are likewise prescribed, in order to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and direction from heaven. After all this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> procedure, when the pope is resolved to give his approbation, he issues a bull, first of beatification, by which the person is declared blessed, and afterwards another of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANCTIFICATION">sanctification</a>, by which the name of saint is given him. These bulls are published in St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s church with very great solemnity. A person remarkable for holiness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, even before he is canonized, may be venerated as such by those who are persuaded of his eminent virtue, and his prayers may be implored; but all this must rest on private opinion. After his canonization, his name is inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">Martyrology</a>, or catalogue of saints, of which the respective portion is read every day in the choir at the divine office. A day is also appointed for a yearly commemoration of him. His name may be mentioned in the public church <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and his intercession with God besought. His relics may be enshrined; he may be painted with rays of glory, and altars and churches may be dedicated to God in honour of him, and in thanksgiving to the divine goodness for the blessings bestowed on him in life, and for the glory to which he is raised in heaven. The affair of a canonization is necessarily very expensive, because so many persons must be employed about it; so many journeys must be made; so many writings for and against it must be drawn out. The expense altogether amounts to about 25,000 Roman crowns, or 600l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. But it is generally con- --- (a) His holiness generally appoints three consistories; in the first of which the cardinals only assist, and give their opinion; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, a preacher pronounces a speech in praise of the candidate before a numerous audience; to the third, not only the cardinals, but all the bishops who are at Rome, are invited, and all of them give their vote by word of mouth. trived to canonize two or three at a time, by which means the particular expense of each is very much lessened, the solemnity being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. It often happens that the solicitors for a canonization are unsuccessful. Thus the Jesuits, even when their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at Rome was greatest, could not obtain the canonization of Bellarmine; and it is remarkable, that the objection is said to have been, his having defended the indirect power of the pope over Christian princes even in temporals. Several authors have written on canonization, and particularly Prosper Lambertini, afterwards pope under the name of Benedict XIV. who had held the office of promoter of the faith for many years. He published on it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in several volumes, in folio, of which there is an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> in French. In this learned performance there is a full <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the canonization of saints in general, and of all the particular processes of that kind that are on record: an account is given of the manner of proceeding in these extraordinary trials; and it is shown, that, besides the affluence of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, which is implored and expected in what is so much connected with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, all prudent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> means are made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, in order to avoid mistakes, and to obtain all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of which the matter is susceptible, and which must appear more than sufficient to every impartial judge. See POPE, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">POPERY</a>, &c. SAINT Catherine, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, not far distant from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>. It was visited by La Perouse, who ascertained it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between 27° 19' 10" and 27° 49' N. Lat. and its most northerly point to lie in 49° 49' W. Long. from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Its breadth from east to west is only six miles, and it is separated from the main <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> by a channel only about 200 fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. On the point stretching farthest into this channel is situated the city of Nostra Senora del Defter, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the governor's residence. It contains about 400 houses, and 3000 inhabitants, and has an exceedingly pleasant appearance. In the year 1712, this island served as a retreat to vagabonds, who effected their escape from different parts of the Brazils, being only nominal subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. Its whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> has been estimated at 20,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is extremely fertile, producing all sorts of fruit, vegetables, and corn, almost spontaneously. The whale fishery is very successful; but it is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and is farmed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, which has three considerable establishments upon the coast. Every year they kill about 400 whales, the produce of which, both <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and spermaceti, is sent to Lisbon by the way of Rio Janeiro. The inhabitants are idle spectators of this fishery, from which they derive not the smallest advantage. A very amiable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, however, is given of their hospitality to strangers, by M. La Perouse. SAINT Foin, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hedyarum. See HEDYARUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> Index.

SAINTES

Pages 62-62

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of France, in the department of Lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Saintonge, and before the revolution was a bishop's see. It contained likewise several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, a Jesuit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> remarkable for its steeple, which is said to be one of the loftiest in France. It is seated on an eminence, 37 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, and 262 south-south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., 8° 38' N. Lat. 45° 54'. The castle is seated on a rock, and is reckoned impregnable. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was a Roman colony; and those conquerors of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, who polished the nations they subdued, have left behind them the traces of their magnificence. In a hollow valley between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and almost adjoining to one of the suburbs, are the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. Though now in the last stage of decay, its appearance is august and venerable. In some parts, scarcely any of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> are to be seen; but the east end is still in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of preservation. From its situation in a valley, and from the ruins of an aqueduct which conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the town from near three leagues distance, it has been supposed that Naumachiae were represented in it; but this amounts only to conjecture. A triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, on which is an inscription in Roman letters, merits likewise <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It was erected to Germanicus, on the news of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, so universally lamented throughout the empire. The river Charente surrounds this city, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> does that of Shrewsbury, describing the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>. Except the remains of Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> yet visible at Saintes, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> contains very little to detain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> amuse a traveller. It is built with great irregularity; the streets are narrow and winding, the houses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, and almost all of them are some centuries old. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> has been repeatedly defaced and destroyed by Normans and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>, who made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> alike on every monument of art or piety. One tower only escaped their rage, which is said to have been built as early as the year 800 by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. It is of an enormous magnitude, both as to height and circumference. These circumstances have probably conduced more to its preservation during the fury of war, than any veneration for the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of its founder, or for the sanctity of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>.

SAINTOGNE

Pages 62-62

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, now forming with the province of Aunis the department of Lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a> and Perigord, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Poitou and the territory of Aunis, on the west by the ocean, and on the south by Bourdelois and Giron, about 62 miles in length and 30 in breadth. The river Charente runs through the middle of it, and renders it one of the finest and most fertile provinces in France, abounding in all sorts of corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; and it is said the best <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is made here.

SAJENE

Pages 62-63

a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length, equal to about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> English feet. SAKRADAWENDRA is the name of one of the Ceylonese deities, who commands and governs all the rest, and formerly answered the prayers of his worshippers; but according to the fabulous account which is given of him, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, on which he sat, and the foot of which was made of wax, that was softened by their prayers and tears, and sunk downward, so that he could take notice of their requests and relieve them, being disposed of among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, they no longer derive any benefit from him, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pay him any reverence. See Budun. SAL. See <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">SALT</a>.

SALACIA

Pages 64-64

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandria clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SALADIN

Pages 63-63

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, equally renowned as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. He supported himself by his valour, and the influence of his amiable character, against the united efforts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Christian potentates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who carried on the most unjust wars against him, under the false appellation of Holy Wars. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Egypt and Croisades.

SALAMANCA

Pages 63-63
