an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon, situated on the river Tormes, about 75 miles west from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. It is said to have been founded by Teucer the son of Telamon, who called it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Salamanica, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the ancient Salamis. Here is an university, the greatest in Spain, consisting of 24 colleges, and perhaps inferior to none in the whole world, in respect at least to its revenues, buildings, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scholars, and masters. Here are also many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and magnificent palaces, squares, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, churches, colleges, chapels, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. The bishop of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is suffragan to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>, and has a yearly revenue of 1000 ducats. A Roman way leads from hence to Merida and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, and there is an old Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river. Of the colleges in the university, four are appropriated to young men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and near it is an infirmary for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> sick scholars. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6.10. N. Lat. 41.0. SALAMANDER. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>, Erpetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SALAMIS

Pages 63-64

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34.0. N. Lat. 37.32.—It was famous in antiquity for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between the Greek and Persian fleets. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> held among the Persians on this occasion, all the commanders were for engaging, because they knew this advice to be most agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s inclinations. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> was the only person who opposed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. She was queen of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>; and followed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> in this war with five ships, the best equipped of any in the fleet, except those of the Sidonians. This princess distinguished herself on all occasions by her singular courage, and still more by her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and conduct. She represented, in the council of war we are speaking of, the dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of engaging a people that were far more expert in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs than the Persians; alleging, that the loss of a battle at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> would be attended with the ruin of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; whereas, by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> out the war, and advancing into the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, they would create jealousies and divisions among their enemies, who would separate from one another, in order to defend each of them their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and that the king might, almost without striking a blow, make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Greece. This advice, though very prudent, was not followed, but an engagement unanimously resolved upon. Xerxes, in order to encourage his men by his presence, caused a throne to be erected on the top of an eminence, whence he might safely behold whatever happened; having several scribes about him, to write <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the names of such as should signalize themselves against the enemy. The approach of the Persian fleet, with the news that a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> from the army was marching against Cleombrotus, who defended the isthmus, struck such a terror into the Peloponnesians, that they could not by any intrigues be prevailed upon to stay any longer at Salamis. Being therefore determined to put to sea, and sail to the isthmus, Themistocles privately dispatched a trusty friend to the Persian commanders, informing them of the intended flight; and exhorting them to lend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their fleet round the island, in order to prevent their escape. The same messenger assured Xerxes, that Themistocles, who had sent him that advice, designed to join the Persians, as soon as the battle began, with all the Athenian ships. The king giving <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to all he said, immediately caused a strong squadron to sail round the island in the night in order to cut off the enemy's flight. Early next morning, as the Peloponnesians were preparing to set sail, they found themselves encompassed on all sides by the Persian fleet; and were against their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> obliged to remain in the straits of Salamis and expose themselves to the same dangers with their allies. The Grecian fleet consisted of 380 sail, that of the Persians of 2000 and upwards. Themistocles avoided the engagement till a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which rose regularly every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and which was entirely contrary to the enemy, began to blow. As soon as he found himself favoured by this wind, he gave the signal for battle. The Persians, knowing that they fought under their king's eye, advanced with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resolution; but the wind blowing directly in their faces, and the largeness and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their ships embarrassing them in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> so strait and narrow, their courage soon abated; which the Greeks observing, used such efforts, that in a short time breaking into the Persian fleet, they entirely disordered them; some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> towards Phalarus, where their army lay encamped; others laying themselves in the harbours of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The Ionians were the first that betook themselves to flight. But Queen Artemisia distinguishing herself above all the rest, her ships being the last that fled: which Xerxes observing, cried out that the men behaved like women, and the women with the courage and intrepidity of men. The Athenians were incensed against her, that they offered a reward of 10,000 drachmas to any one that should take her alive; but she, in spite of all their efforts, got clear of the ships that pursued her, and arrived safe on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. In this engagement, which was one of the most memorable actions we find recorded in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the Grecians lost 40 ships; and the Persians 200, besides a great many more that were taken, with all the men and ammunition they carried. The island of Salamis is of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> shape; it was reckoned 70 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 80 stadia, i.e. 8 or 10 miles long, reaching westward as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called Kerata or The Horns. Paullanias informs us, that on one side of this island stood in his time a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, and on the other a trophy for a victory obtained by Themistocles, together with the temple of Cycnreus, the site of which is now thought to be occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Nicholas. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Salamis was demolished by the Athenians, because in the war with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSANDER">Cassander</a> it surrendered to the Macedonians, from disaffection. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, when it was visited by Paulanias, some ruins of the Agora or market-place remained, with a temple and image of Ajax; and not far from the port was shown a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, SALAMIS on which, they related, Telamon sat to view the Salaminian ships on their departure to join the Grecian fleet at Aulis. The walls may still be traced, and it has been conjectured were about four miles in circumference. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> space within them was now covered with green corn. The port is choked with mud, and was partly dry. Among the scattered marbles are some with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>. One is of great antiquity, before the introduction of the Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. On another, near the port, the name of Solon occurs. This renowned lawgiver was a native of Salamis, and a statue of him was erected in the market-place, with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> covered by his veil, the modest attitude in which he was accustomed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> the people of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. An inscription on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble was also copied in 1676 near the ruin of a temple, probably that of Ajax. The island of Salamis is now inhabited by a few Albanians, who till the ground. Their village is called Ampelaki, "the Vineyard," and is at a distance from the port, standing more inland. In the church are marble fragments and some inscriptions.

SALARY

Pages 64-64

a recompense <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> consideration made to a person for his pains and industry in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s business. The word is used in the statute 23 Edw. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 1. Salarium at first signified the rents or profits of a falle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> (and in Gascoigne they now call the seats of the gentry salars, as we do halls); but afterwards it was taken for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, stipend, or annual allowance.

SALE

Pages 64-64

is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of a commodity for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> permutation, is the exchange of one commodity for another. When the bargain is concluded, an obligation is contracted by the buyer to pay the value, and by the seller to deliver the commodity, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> agreed on, or immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> no time be specified. In this, as well as other mercantile contracts, the safety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> requires the utmost good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and veracity. Therefore, although by the laws of England, a sale above the value of £10 be not binding, unless <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> be paid, or the bargain confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, a merchant would lose all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> who refused to perform his agreement, although these legal requisites were omitted. When a specific thing is sold, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, even before delivery, is in some respect vested in the buyer; and if the thing perishes, the buyer must bear the loss. For example, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> dies before delivery, he must pay the value: but if the bargain only determines the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the goods, without specifying the identical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, and the seller's warehouse, with all his goods, be burned, he is entitled to no payment. He must also bear the loss if the thing perish through his fault; or when a particular time and place of delivery is agreed on, if it perish before it be tendered, in terms of the bargain. If a person purchase goods at a shop without agreeing for the price, he is liable for the ordinary market-price at the time of purchase. If the buyer proves insolvent before delivery, the seller is not bound to deliver the goods without payment or security. If the importation, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the commodities sold, be prohibited by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or if the buyer knows that they were smuggled, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies for delivery. The property of goods is generally presumed, in favour of commerce, to belong to the possessor, and cannot be challenged in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an onerous purchaser. But to this there are some exceptions. By the Scots law, stolen goods may in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> be reclaimed by the proprietor, and also by the English law, unless they were bought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide in open market; that is, in the accustomed public places, on stated days, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or in a shop in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and horses may be reclaimed, unless the sale be regularly entered by the book-keeper of the market. In all cases, if the goods be evicted by the lawful proprietor, the seller is liable to the purchaser for the value. Actions for payment of shop accounts, as well as other debts not constituted by writing, are limited in England to five years. The testimony of one witness is admitted; and the seller's books, although the person that kept them be dead, are good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for one year. In Scotland, merchant's books may be proved within three years of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the last article, by one witness, and the creditor's books and oath in supplement. After three years, they can only be proved by the oath or writ of the debtor. A merchant's books are in all cases good evidence against him.

SALEP

Pages 64-65

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, the dried root of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of orchis. See ORCHIS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Several methods of preparing salep have been proposed and practised. Geoffroy has delivered a very judicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for this purpose in the Histoire de l'Academie Royale des Sciences, 1740; and Retmus, in the Swedish Translations, 1764, has improved Geoffroy's method. But Mr Moult of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCHDALE">Rochdale</a> has lately favoured the public with a new manner of curing the orchis root; by which salep is prepared, at least equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, to any brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The new root is to be washed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> skin which covers it is to be separated by means of a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the root in hot water, and rubbing it with a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth. When a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of roots have been thus cleaned, they are to be spread on a tin-plate, and placed in an oven heated to the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, where they are to remain fix or ten minutes, in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have lost their milky whiteness, and acquired a transparency like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, without any diminution of bulk. Being arrived at this state, they are to be removed, in order to dry and harden in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which will require several days to effect; or by using a very gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, they may be finished in a few hours. Salep thus prepared, may be afforded in those parts of England where labour bears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> value, at about eightpence or tenpence per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>: And it might be sold still cheaper, if the orchis were to be cured, without separating from it the brown skin which covers it; a troublesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the process, and which does not contribute to render the root either more palatable or salutary. Whereas the foreign salep is now sold at five or six shillings per pound. Salep is said to contain the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vegetable nourishment in the smallest bulk. Hence a very judicious writer, to prevent the dreadful calamity of famine at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, has lately proposed that the powder of it should constitute part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of every ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. company. This powder and portable soup, dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, form a rich thick jelly, capable of supporting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for a considerable length of time. An ounce of each of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, with two quarts of boiling water, will be sufficient subsistence for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and as being a mixture of animal and vegetable food, must prove more nourishing than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>-cake, made by boiling rice in water; which last, however, sailors are often obliged solely to subsist upon for several months; especially in voyages to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, when the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and flour are exhausted, and the beef and pork, having been falted in hot countries, are become unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. "But as a wholesome nourishment (says Dr Percival*), rice is much inferior to salep. I digested several alimentary mixtures prepared of mutton and water, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up with bread, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>-biscuit, salep, rice-flower, sagopowder, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>, old cheese, &c. in a heat equal to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. In 48 hours they had all acquired a vinous smell, and were in brick <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, except the mixture with rice, which did not emit many air-bubbles, and was but little changed. The third day several of the mixtures were sweet, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to ferment; others had lost their intestine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and were sour; but the one which contained the rice was become putrid. From this experiment it appears, that rice as an aliment is slow of fermentation, and a very weak corrector of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. It is therefore an improper diet for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>-patients; but more particularly for sailors in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages; because it is incapable of preventing, and will not contribute much to check, the progress of that fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, the sea fever. Under certain circumstances, rice seems disposed of itself, without mixture, to become putrid; for by long keeping it sometimes acquires an offensive flavor. Nor can it be considered as a very nutritive kind of food, on account of its difficult solubility in the stomach. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> confirms the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this conclusion; for it is observed by the planters in the West Indies, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> grow thin, and are less able to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, whilst they subsist upon rice. "Salep has the singular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of concealing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> water; a circumstance of the highest importance at sea, when there is a scarcity of fresh water. I dissolved a dram and a half of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt in a pint of the mucilage of salep, so liquid as to be potable, and the same quantity in a pint of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water. The salep was by no means disagreeable to the taste, but the water was rendered extremely unpalatable. This experiment suggested to me the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the orchis root as a corrector of acidity, a property which would render it a very useful diet for children. But the solution of it, when mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, seemed only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> like an equal proportion of water, and not to cover its sharpness. Salep, however, appears by my experiments to retard the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a> fermentation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and consequently would be a good thing for milk-pottage, especially in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the cattle being fed upon sour dairies must yield acidulent milk. "Salep in a certain proportion, which I have not yet been able to ascertain, would be a very useful and profitable addition to bread. I directed one ounce of the powder to be dissolved in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of water, and the mucilage to be mixed with a sufficient quantity of flour, salt, and yeast. The flour amounted to two pounds, the yeast to two ounces, and the salt to 80 grains. The loaf when baked was remarkably well fermented, and weighed three pounds two ounces. Another loaf, made with the same quantity of flour, &c. weighed two pounds and 12 ounces; from which it appears that the salep, though used in so small a proportion, increased the gravity of the loaf six ounces, by absorbing and retaining more water than the flour alone was capable of. Half a pound of flour and an ounce of salep were mixed together, and the water added according to the usual method of preparing bread. The loaf when baked weighed 13 ounces and a half; and would probably have been heavier if the salep had been previously dissolved in about a pint of water. But it should be remarked, that the quantity of flour used in this trial was not sufficient to conceal the peculiar taste of the salep. "The restorative, mucilaginous, and demulcent qualities of the orchis root, render it of considerable use in various diseases. In the sea fever it powerfully obtunds the acrimony of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and at the same time is easily assimilated into a mild and nutritious chyle. In diarrhoeas and the dysentery it is highly serviceable, by strengthening the internal coat of the intestines, by abating irritation, and gently correcting putrefaction. In the symptomatic fever, which arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of pus from ulcers in the lungs, from wounds, or from amputation, salep used plentifully is an admirable demulcent, and well adapted to resist the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the crusts of the blood, which is so evident in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. And by the same mucilaginous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, it is equally efficacious in the strangury and dysuria; especially in the latter, when arising from a venereal cause, because the discharge of urine is then attended with the most exquisite pain, from the ulceration about the neck of the bladder and through the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>. I have found it also an useful aliment for patients who labour under the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or gravel." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> chemists appear to have entertained a very high <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the orchis root, as appears from the secretia secretorum of Raymund Lully, a work dated 1565.

SALERNO

Pages 65-65

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Hither Principato, with an archbishop's see, a castle, harbour, and an university chiefly for medicine. It is situated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 53'. N. Lat. 40° 35'.

SALET

Pages 65-65

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> covering <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> armour for the head, anciently worn by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LIGHT_HORSE">light-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, only different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a> in that it had no crest and was little more than a bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>.

SALIANT

Pages 65-65

SAILIANT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> SAILLANT, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is applied to a lion, or other beast, when its fore-legs are raised in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> posture.

SALIC

Pages 65-66
or SALIQUE, LAW, (Lex Salica), an ancient and fundamental law of the kingdom of France, usually supposed to have been made by Pharamond, or at least by Clovis; in virtue of which males only are to inherit. Some, as Poffellus, would have it to have been called Salie, q. d. Gallie, because peculiar to the Gauls. Fer. Montanus infits, it was because Pharamond was at first called Salicus. Others will have it to be so named, as having been made for the falc lands. These were noble fiefs which their first kings used to bestow on the falians, that is, the great lords of their falle or court, without any other tenure than military service; and for this reason, such fiefs were not to descend to women, as being by nature unfit for such a tenure. Some, again, derive the origin of this word from the Sallians, a tribe of Franks that settled in Gaul in the reign of Julian, who is said to have given them lands on condition of their personal service in war. He even passed the conditions into a law, which the new conquerors acquiesced in, and called it salic, from the name of their former countrymen.

SALICORNIA

Pages 66-66

jointed glass-wort, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Saltwort: a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, Holoraceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The inhabitants near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts where these plants grow, cut them up toward the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when they are fully grown; and, after having dried them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, they burn them for their ashes, which are used in making glaas and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. These herbs are by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people called kelp, and promiscuously gathered for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>.

SALII

Pages 66-66

in Roman antiquity, priests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, whereof there were 12, instituted by Numa, wearing painted, multicoloured garments, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> bonnets; with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> cuirass on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. They were called salii, from saltare "to dance"; because, after afflicting at sacrifices, they went <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> about the streets, with bucklers in their left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a rod in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, striking musically with their rods on one another's bucklers, and singing hymns in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods.

SALINO

Pages 66-66

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIPARI_ISLANDS">Lipari <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, consists of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, both in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> state of cultivation. The one lying more towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> than the other is rather the highest of the two, and is called del Capo, "the head." The other is called della Foja felice, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the "happy valley." One third of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of these hills from the bottom to the summit is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> orchard, consisting of vines, olive, fig, plum, apricot, and a vast diversity of other trees. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> roofs of the houses, which are everywhere interspersed amid this diversity of verdure and foliage, contribute to variegate the prospect in a very agreeable manner. The back <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of almost all the houses is shaded by an arbour of vines, supported by pillars of brick, with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> to sustain the branches and foliage of the vines. These arbours shelter the houses from the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of which is quite scorching in these southern regions. The vines are extremely fruitful; the poles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. The scenes in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> are more interesting to the lover of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> than to the antiquarian. See Reticulum. On the south side of the island, however, there are still to be seen some fine ruins of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bath, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. They consist of a wall 10 or 11 fathoms in extent, and terminating in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, of which only a small part now remains. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> seems to have been reduced to its present state rather by the ravages of men than the injuries of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Almost all the houses in the island are built of materials which have belonged to ancient monuments. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of fresh as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in this island; for whenever the present habitations have occasion for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of fresh water, they have only to dig a pit on the shore, and pure sweet water flows in great abundance. There were formerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> here, from which the inhabitants drew a very considerable yearly revenue. But whether they are exhausted, or whatever circumstance may have caused them to be given up, they are now no longer known. The island abounds in a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. On the east side it is very populous. There are two places which are both called Lingua, "the tongue," and which contain a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants; the one is near Salino, the other is distinguished by the name of St Marina: there are besides these two other villages. All these places together may contain about 4000 inhabitants: the circumference of the island may be about 14 miles.

SALISBURY

Pages 66-67

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Wiltshire in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 55'. N. Lat. 51° 3'. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> owed its first rise to its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which was begun in 1219, and finished in 1288. According to an estimate delivered in to Henry III, it cost forty thousand marks. It is a Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and is certainly the most elegant and regular in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The doors and chapels are equal in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to the months, the windows to the days, and the pillars and pilasters to the hours in a year. It is built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>, with a spire in the middle, and nothing but buttresses and glaas windows on the outside. The spire is the highest in the kingdom, being 410 feet, which is twice the height of the Monument in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The pillars and pilasters in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> are of suffe marble; the art of making which is now either entirely lost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> little known. This magnificent church has lately undergone most beautiful alterations; with an addition of two fine windows, and an organ presented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which is 50 feet in diameter and 150 in circumference, bears entirely upon one slender pillar, which is such a curiosity as can hardly be matched in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> of the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> through the city in the reign of Edward III, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage to it. The chancellorship of the most noble order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, which is annexed to this see, was first conferred on Bishop Richard Beauchamp. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of St Michael's, near this city, was founded by one of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. Dr Seth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, bishop of this see in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, contributed greatly to the making the river Avon navigable to Christchurch in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. The same prelate, in 1683, built an hospital for the entertainment of the widows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> clergymen. There are three other churches besides the cathedral, which is without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the city, and a greater number of boarding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, especially for young ladies, than in any other town in England. Here is a manufacture of druggets, flannels, bonelace, and those cloths called Salisbury whites; in consideration of which, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, affizes, Salisbury boarding-schools, and clergy; the city may be justly said to be in a flourishing condition. It was incorporated by Henry III.; and is governed by a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, recorder, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-recorder, 24 aldermen, and 30 assistants or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men. The number of souls is about 7668. A new council chamber, with proper courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, was built here in the year 1794, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Radnor; to which Mr Hulley was also a great benefactor. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> called the Clove, where the canons and prebendaries live, is like a fine city of itself. In this town are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-schools; the expense of one of them is entirely defrayed by the bishop. The city gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the noble family of Cecil. SALISBURY Plain. The extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> in Wiltshire, which are thus denominated, form in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> one of the most delightful parts of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. It extends 28 miles west of Weymouth, and 25 east to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>; and in some places is near 40 miles in breadth. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> about Salisbury is a chalky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and is famous for feeding numerous flocks of sheep. Considerable portions of this tract are now enclosed, the advantages of which are so great, that it is hoped the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> undergo so beneficial a change. This plain contains, beside the famous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a>, numerous other remains of antiquity.

SALIVA

Pages 67-67

is that fluid by which the mouth and tongue are continually moistened in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state; and is supplied by glands which form it, that are called salivary glands. This humour is thin and pellucid, incapable of being concreted by the fire, almost without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell. By chewing, it is expressed from the glands which separate it from the blood, and is intimately mixed with our food, the digestion of which it greatly promotes. In hungry persons it is acid, and copiously discharged; and in those who have failed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> it is highly acid, penetrating, and revolting. A too copious evacuation of it produces thirst, loss of appetite, bad digestion, and an atrophy.

SALIVATION

Pages 67-67

in Medicine, a promoting of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of saliva, by means of medicines, mostly by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of salivation is in diseases belonging to the glands and membranes adipose, and principally in the cure of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; though it is sometimes also used in epidemic diseases, cutaneous diseases, &c., whose crises tend that way.

SALIX

Pages 67-67

the WILLOW, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 5th order, Amentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Willow trees have been frequently the theme of poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Horace, and in Ovid, we have many exquisite allusions to them and their several properties; and for a melancholy lover <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a contemplative poet, imagination cannot paint a fitter retreat than the banks of a beautiful river, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a drooping willow. The Babylonian, Babylonian pendulous salix, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called weeping willow, grows to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size, having numerous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, slender, pendulous branches, hanging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> lovelily all around in a curious manner, and long, narrow, spear-shaped, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, smooth leaves. This curious willow is a native of the east, and is retained in our hardy plantations for ornament; and exhibits a most agreeable variety, particularly when disposed singly by the verges of any piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or in spacious openings of grassy ground. All the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of salix are of the tree kind, very hardy, remarkably fast growers, and several of them attaining a considerable stature when permitted to run up to standards. They are mostly of the aquatic tribe, being generally the most abundant and of most profuse growth in watery situations: they however <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow freely almost anywhere, in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and exposure; but grow considerably the fattest and strongest in low moist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, particularly in marshy situations, by the verges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, brooks, and other waters; likewise along the sides of watery ditches, &c., which places often lying waste, may be employed to good advantage, in plantations of willows, for different purposes.

SALLEE

Pages 67-67

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, with a harbour and several ports. The harbour of Sallee is one of the best in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and yet, on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> that lies across it, ships of the smallest draught are forced to unload and take out their guns before they can get into it. There are docks to build ships; but they are hardly ever used, for want of skill and materials. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, divided by the river Guero into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been famous for its rovers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pirates, which make prizes of all Christian ships that come in their way, except there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> to the contrary. The town of Sallee in its present state, though large, presents nothing worthy the observation of the traveller, except a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of 24 pieces of cannon fronting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and a redoubt at the entrance of the river, which is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and penetrates several miles into the interior country. W. Loug. 6. 30. N. Lat. 34°.

SALLET

Pages 67-67
or SALAD, a dish of eatable herbs, ordinarily accompanying roast meat; composed chiefly of crude fresh herbage, seasoned with salt, oil, and vinegar. Menage derives the word from the Latin salata; of sal, "salt;" others from salcedo; Du Cange from salgamma, which is used in Antonius and Columella in the same sense. Some add mustard, hard eggs, and sugar; others, pepper, and other spices, with orange-peel, saffron, &c. The principal salad-herbs, and those which ordinarily make the basis of our English salads, are lettuce, celery, endive, cresses, radish, and rape; along with which, by way of additional, are used purslane, spinach, sorrel, tarragon, burnet, corn-fallet, and chervil. The gardeners call some plants small herbs in salads; these should always be cut while in the seed-leaf: as cresses, mustard, radish, turnip, spinach, and lettuce; all which are raised from seeds sown in drills, or lines, from the middle of February to the end of March, under glass or frames; and thence to the middle of May, upon natural beds, warmly exposed; and during the summer heats in more shady places; and afterwards in September, as in March, &c.; and lastly, in the rigour of the winter, in hot-beds. If they chance to be frozen in very frosty weather, putting them in spring-water two hours before they are used recovers them.

SALLO

Pages 67-68

DENIS DE, a French writer, famous for being being the projector of literary journals, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1626. He studied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was admitted a counsellor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris in 1652. It was in 1664 he schemed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the Journal des Scavans; and the year following began to publish it under the name of Sieur de Heronville, which was that of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre. But he played the critic so feverishly, that authors, surprised at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of such attacks, retorted so powerfully, that M. de Sallo, unable to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> the storm, after he had published his third Journal, declined the undertaking, and turned it over to the abbe Gallois; who, without presuming to criticize, contented himself merely with giving titles, and making extracts. Such was the origin of literary journals, which afterwards sprang up in other countries under different titles; and the success of them, under judicious management, is a clear <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their utility. M. de Sallo died in 1669.

SALLUSTIUS

Pages 68-68
CAIUS CRISPUS, celebrated Roman historian, was born at Amiternum, a city of Italy, in the year of Rome 669, and before Christ 85. His education was liberal, and he made the best use of it. His Roman s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history in five books, from the death of Sylla to the conspiracy of Catiline, the great work from which he chiefly derived his glory among the ancients, is unfortunately lost excepting a few fragments; but his two detached pieces of history which happily remain entire, are sufficient to justify the great encomiums he has received as a writer. He has had the singular honour to be twice translated by a royal hand: first by our Elizabeth, according to Camden; and secondly, by the present Infant of Spain, whose version of this elegant historian, lately printed in folio, is one of the most beautiful books that any country has produced since the invention of printing. No man has inveighed more sharply against the vices of his age than this historian; yet no man had fewer pretensions to virtue. His youth was spent in a most lewd and profligate manner; and his patrimony almost squandered away when he had scarcely taken possession of it. Marcus Varro, a writer of undoubted credit, relates, in a fragment preserved by Aulus Gellius, that Sallust was actually caught in bed with Fausta the daughter of Sylla, by Milo her husband; who scourged him very severely, and did not suffer him to depart till he had redeemed his liberty with a considerable sum. A. U. C. 694, he was made quæstor, and in 702 tribune of the people; in neither of which places is he allowed to have acquitted himself at all to his honour. By virtue of his quæstorship, he obtained an admission into the senate; but was expelled thence by the censors in 704, on account of his immoral and debauched way of life. In the year 705 Caesar restored him to the dignity of a senator; and to introduce him into the house with a better grace, made him quæstor a second time. In the administration of this office he behaved himself very scandalously: exposed every thing to sale for which he could find a purchaser; and if we may believe the author of the invective, thought nothing wrong which he had a mind to do: *Nihil non venale habuerit, cujus aliquis emptor fuit, nihil non sequam et verum duxit, quod ipsi facere colibuisse.* In the year 707, when the African war was at an end, he was made praetor for his services to Cæsar, and sent to Numidia. Here he acted the same part as Verres had done in Sicily; outrageously plundered the province; and returned with Sallustian such immense riches to Rome, that he purchased a most magnificent building upon Mount Quirinal, with those gardens which to this day retain the name of Sallustian gardens, besides his country house at Tivoli. How he spent the remaining part of his life, we have no account from ancient writers. Eusebius tells us that he married Terentia, the divorced wife of Cicero; and that he died at the age of 52, in the year 710, which was about four years before the battle of Actium. Of the many things which he wrote, beside his Histories of the Catilinarian and Jugurthine wars, we have some orations or speeches, printed with his fragments.

SALLY-PORTS

Pages 68-68

in fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pofern-Gates, as they are sometimes called, are those under-ground passageways which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> from the inner works to the outward ones; such as from the higher flank to the lower, or to the tenailles, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> from the middle of the curtain to the ravelin. When they are made for men to go through only, they are made with steps at the entrance and going out. They are about 6 feet wide and 8½ feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. There is also a gutter or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> made under the sally-ports, which are in the middle of the curtains, for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which runs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the streets to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the ditch; but this can only be done when they are wet ditches. When sally-ports serve to carry guns through them for the out-works, instead of making them with steps, they must have a gradual slope, and be 8 feet wide.

SALMASIUS

Pages 68-68

CLAUDIUS, a French writer of uncommon abilities and immense erudition, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near Semur in 1596. His mother, who was a Protestant, infused her notions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> into him, and he at length converted his father: he settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; and in 1650 paid a visit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who is reported to have shown him extraordinary marks of regard. Upon the violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. of England, he was prevailed on by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, then in exile, to write a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; which was answered by our famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in 1651, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> intitled Defensio pro Populo Anglicano contra Claudii Salmasii Defensionem Regiam. This book was read over all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and conveyed such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the writer's abilities, that he was respected even by those who hated his principles. Salmasius died in 1653; and some did not scruple to say, that Milton killed him by the acuteness of his reply. His works are numerous, and of various kinds; but the greatest monuments of his learning are, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a> in Historiae Auguifae Scriptores, and his Exercitationes Pliniiane in Solinum.

SALMO

Pages 68-68

the SALMON; a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SALMON. See Salmo, Ichthyology Index. Salmon-Fishery. See Salmon-Fishery.

SALON

Pages 68-69
or SALOON, in architecture, a lofty, spacious sort of hall, vaulted at top, and usually comprehending two stories, with two ranges of windows. The falcon is a grand room in the middle of a building, or at the head of a gallery, &c. Its faces, or sides, are all to have a symmetry with each other; and as it usually takes up the height of two stories, its ceiling, Daviler observes, should be with a moderate sweep. The faloon is a state-room much used in the palaces in Italy; and from thence the mode came to us. Ambassadors, and other great visitors, are usually received in the faloon. It is sometimes built square, sometimes round or oval, sometimes octagonal, as at Marly, and sometimes in other forms.

SALONA

Pages 69-69

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, fended on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. It was formerly a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and its ruins show that it was 10 miles in circumference. It is 18 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Spalato, and subject to Venice. It is now a wretched village, preserving few distinguishable remains of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendor. Doubtless the two last ages have destroyed all that had escaped the barbarity of the northern nations that demolished it. In a valuable MS. relation of Dalmatia, written by the senator Giambattista Guiflaminian, about the middle of the 16th century, there is a hint of what existed at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, and magnificence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Salona, may be imagined from the vaults and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which are seen at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; from the vast <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the finest marble, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> scattered on, and buried in the fields; from the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of three pieces of marble, which is still standing in the place where they say the arsenal was, towards the seashore; and from the many arches of surprising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, supported by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> marble columns; the height of the arches is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-throw, and above them there was an aqueduct, which reached from Salona to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>. There are to be seen many ruins and vestiges of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> palaces, and many ancient epitaphs may be read on fine marble stones; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is increased, has buried the most ancient stones, and the most valuable things." E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 29. N. Lat. 24. 15.

SALONICHI

Pages 69-69

formerly called Thessalonica, a seaport town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, with an archbishop's see. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and rich, being about 10 miles in circumference. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, carried on principally by the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> and Jews, the former of which have 30 churches, and the latter as many synagogues; the Turks also have a few mosques. It is surrounded with walls flanked with towers, and defended on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-side by a citadel, and near the harbour with three forts. It was taken from the Venetians by the Turks in 1431. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merchandise is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. It is seated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of the same name, partly on the top, and partly on the side of a hill, near the river Vardar. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 13. N. Lat. 40. 41.

SALSES

Pages 69-69

a very strong castle of France, in Roussillon, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. It was taken from the Spaniards by the French in 1642; and is seated on a lake of the same name, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERPIGNAN">Perpignan</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. o. N. Lat. 43. 35.

SALSETTE

Pages 69-69

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the East Indies, adjacent to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, from which it is in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> divided only by a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> fordable at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is about 26 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is rich, and by a proper cultivation capable of producing any thing that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow in tropical climates. It is everywhere well watered, and when in the possession of the Portuguese furnished such quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, that it was called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">Granary</a> of Goa. It abounds also in all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, both of the four-footed and feathered kind. It has pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and there is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> that the whole was thrown up from the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of which it is said, that on the top of the highest hill there was found, some years ago, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, such as was anciently used by the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here we meet with the ruins of a place called Canara, where there are excavations of rocks, supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with those of Elephanta. They are much more numerous, but not comparable to the former either in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> or workmanship. The island of Salsette lately formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Portuguese dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. It ought to have been ceded to the English along with Bombay, as part of the dower of Catherine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, espoused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. The fulfilment of this article, however, being evaded, the island remained in possession of the Portuguese; and notwithstanding the little care they took of it, the revenue of it was valued at 60,000l. Such was the negligence of the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, that they took no care to fortify it against the attacks of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>, from whose dominions Salsette was only separated by a very narrow pass fordable at low water. Here they had only a miserable redoubt of no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, till, on the appearance of an approaching <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Mahrattas, they began to build another, which indeed would have answered the purpose of protecting the island, provided the Mahrattas had allowed them to finish it. This, however, was not their intention. They allowed them indeed to go on quietly with their works till they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them almost completed, when they came and took possession of them. The Mahrattas thus became dangerous neighbours to the English at Bombay, until it was ceded to the latter by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded with these people in 1780. E. Long. 72. 15. N. Lat. 19. 0.

SALSOLO

Pages 69-69

Glass-wort, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, Holaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. All the sorts of glasswort are sometimes promiscuously used for making the sal kali, but it is the third sort which is deemed best for this purpose. The manner of making it is as follows: Having dug a trench near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> laths across it, on which they lay the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in heaps, and, having made a fire below, the liquor, which runs out of the herbs, drops to the bottom, which at length thickening, becomes sal kali, which is partly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and partly of an ash-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, very sharp and corrosive, and of a saltish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. This, when thoroughly hardened, becomes like a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and in that state is transported to different countries for making of glass.

SALT

Pages 69-74

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bodies. The characteristic marks of salt have usually been reckoned its power of affecting the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and of being soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. But this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not distinguish salt from quicklime, which also affects the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of taste, and dissolves in water; yet quicklime has been universally reckoned an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and not a salt. The only distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of salts, therefore, is their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> in water: but this does not belong to all salts; for the nitrous and marine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, though allowed on all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to be salts, are yet incapable of crystallization, at least. least by any method hitherto known. Several of the imperfect neutral salts also, such as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of the nitrous, muriatic, and vegetable acids, with some kinds of earths, crystallize with very great difficulty. However, by the addition of spirit of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other substances which absorb <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the water, keeping the liquor in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, &c., all of them may be reduced to crystals of one kind or other. Salt, therefore, may be defined a substance affecting the organs of taste, soluble in water, and capable of crystallization, either by itself or in conjunction with some other body; and, universally, every salt capable of being reduced into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form, is also capable of crystallization per se. Thus the class of saline bodies will be sufficiently distinguished from all others; for quicklime, though soluble in water, cannot be crystallized without addition either of fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> or some other acid; yet it is most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in a solid state. The precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, bafaltes, &c., though supposed to be formed by crystallization, are nevertheless distinguished from salts by their infusibility and insolubility in water. But acids and alkalis, and combinations of both, when in a concrete form, are salts, and of the purest form. Hence we conclude, that the bodies, to which the name of salts more properly belongs, are the concretions of those substances; which are accordingly called acid salts, alkaline salts, and neutral salts. These last are combinations of acid and alkaline salts, in such proportion as to render the compounds neither four nor alkaline to the taste. This proportionate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> is called saturation: thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> salt is a neutral salt, composed of muriatic acid and soda combined together to the point of saturation. The appellation of neutral salts is also extended to denote all those combinations of acids, and any other substance with which they can unite, so as to lose, wholly or in great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, their acid properties. But although this general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of salts is commonly received, yet there are many writers, especially mineralogists, who confine the denomination of salts in the manner we first mentioned, viz., to those substances only which, besides the general properties of salts, have the power of crystallizing, that is, of arranging their particles so as to form regular shaped bodies, called crystals, when the water superfluous to their concrete existence has been evaporated. Common SALT, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Salt, the name of that salt extracted from the waters of the ocean, which is used in greater quantities for preserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, &c. It is a perfect neutral salt, composed of marine or muriatic acid, saturated with mineral alkali. It has a saline but agreeable flavour. It requires about four times its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water to be dissolved, and nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, according to Macquer. But according to Kirwan, it only requires 2.5 its weight of water to be dissolved in the temperature of sixty degrees of Fahrenheit. This salt always contains some part formed with a calcareous base; and, in order to have it pure, it must be dissolved in distilled water; then a solution of mineral alkali is to be poured in it until no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> precipitation appears; then by filtrating and evaporating the solution, a pure common salt is produced. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is perfectly cubic, and those hollow pyramids, or tremies as the French call them, as well as the parallelopipeds formed sometimes in its crystallization, consist all of a quantity of small cubes disposed in those forms. Its decrepitation on the fire, which has been reckoned by some as a characteristic of this salt, although the vitriolated tartar, nitrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and other salts, have the same property, is owing chiefly to the water, and perhaps also to the air of its crystallization. Its specific gravity is 2.120 according to Kirwan. The acid of tartar precipitates nothing from it. One hundred parts of common salt contain thirty-three of real acid, fifty of mineral alkali, and seventeen of water. It is commonly found in salt water and salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, in the proportion of even thirty-five per cent. It is found also in coals, and in beds of gypsum. This salt is unalterable by fire, though it fuses, and becomes more opake: nevertheless a violent fire, with the free access of air, causes it to evaporate in white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which adhere to the neighbouring bodies. It is only decomposed, as Macquer affirms, by the sulphuric and nitric acids; and also by the boracic or sodaive salt. But although nitre is decomposed very easily by arsenic, this neutral marine salt is nowise decomposed by the same. According to Monge, the fixed vegetable alkali, when caustic, decomposes all this marine salt. It preserves from corruption almost all sorts of animal food much better for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> than any other salt, as it preserves them without destroying their taste and qualities; but when applied in too small a quantity, it then promotes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. Of this most useful commodity there are ample stores on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> as well as in the ocean. There are few countries which do not afford vast quantities of rock or fossil salt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">Mines</a> (a) of it have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been discovered and wrought in England, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and other countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In several parts of the world, there are huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which wholly consist of fossil salt. Of this kind are two mountains in Russia, near Astrakhan; several in the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> and Algiers, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; and several also in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> almost entirely consists of fossil salt. The new world is likewise stored with treasuries of this useful mineral, as well as with all other kinds of subterranean productions.
