Moreover, the sea affords such vast plenty of common salt, that all mankind might thence be supplied with quantities sufficient for their occasions. There are also innumerable springs, ponds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, impregnated with common salt, from which the inhabitants of many countries are plentifully supplied therewith. In some countries which are remote from the sea, and have little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and which are not blessed with mines of salt or salt-waters, the necessities of the inhabitants have forced them to invent a method of extracting --- (a) Amongst the salt mines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> are those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTHWICH">Northwich</a> in Cheshire, Altemonte in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a> in Tyrol, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDONA">Cardona</a> in Catalonia; also those stupendous mines at Wilczek in Poland, to be noticed in the sequel of this article, and Soowar in Upper Hungary; of which see accounts in Phil. Trans. No. 61. and 413. ting their common salt from the ashes of vegetables. The muriatic salt of vegetables was described by Dr Grew under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *liviviated marine salt*. Leeuwenhoek obtained cubic crystals of this salt from a livivium of soda or kelp, and also from a solution of the livivial salt of carduns benedictus; of which he hath given figures in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, published in No. 175. of their Transactions. Dr Dagner, in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a>. Acad. N. C.* vol. v. obl. 150., takes notice of great quantities of it which he found mixed in potatoes. And the ingenious Dr Fothergill extracted plenty of it from the ashes of fern: See *Medical Essays*, vol. v. article 13. The muriatic salt which the excellent Mr Boyle extracted from silex, and supposed to be produced from the materials used in making glass, was doubtless separated from the kelp made use of in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. Kunckel also informs us, that he took an alkaline salt; and after calcining it with a moderate fire, dissolved it in pure water, and placing the solution in a cool cellar, obtained from it many crystals of a neutral salt. He supposes, that the alkaline salt was by the process converted into this neutral salt. But it is more reasonable to believe, that the alkaline salt which he applied was not pure, but mixed with the muriatic salt of vegetables, which by this process was only separated from it. It is doubtless chiefly this muriatic salt which, in some of the inland parts of Asia, they extract from the ashes of duck-weed and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>'s fig-tree, and use for their common salt. That they are able in those countries to make common salt to profit from vegetables, ought not to be wondered at, since in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, capitals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, salt is so scarce as usually to be sold for half-a-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. We may therefore give some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to Marco <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLO">Polo</a>, when he informs us, that in the inner parts of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the world, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASHMERE">Cashmere</a>, lying west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>, the natives used salt instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, it being first made up in cakes, and sealed with the stamp of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and that they made great profit of this money by exchanging it with the neighbouring nations for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>. We are also told by Ludolfus, in his *Hyphoria Ethiopica*, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Abyssines there are mountains of salt, the which when dug out is soft, but soon grows hard; and that this salt serves them instead of money to buy all things. The same is confirmed by Ramulio. Mr Boyle discovered common salt in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood and urine. "I have observed it (says Mr Brownrigg), not only in human urine, but also in that of dogs, horses, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. It may easily be discovered in these, and many other liquids impregnated with it, by certain very regular and beautiful starry figures which appear in their surfaces after congelation. These figures I first observed in the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> in the year 1739. The dung of such animals as feed upon grass or grain, doth also contain plenty of common salt." Naturalists, observing the great variety of forms under which this salt appears, have thought fit to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the several kinds of it under certain general classes; distinguishing it, most usually, into rock or fossil salt, sea-salt, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> or fountain salt. To which classes, others might be added, of those muriatic salts which are found in vegetable and animal substances. These several kinds of common salt often differ from each other in their outward form and appearance, or in such accidental properties as they derive from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> substances with which they are mixed. But when perfectly pure, they have all the same qualities; so that chemists, by the exactest inquiries, have not been able to discover any essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them; for which reason we shall distinguish common salt after a different manner, into the three following kinds, viz. into rock or native salt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> salt, and white salt. By rock salt, or native salt, is understood all salt dug out of the earth, which hath not undergone any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. Under the title of bay salt may be ranked all kinds of common salt extracted from the water wherein it is dissolved, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and the operation of the air; whether the water from which it is extracted be sea-water, or natural brine drawn from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and springs, or salt water stagnating in ponds and lakes. Under the title of white salt, or boiled salt, may be included all kinds of common salt extracted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> from the water wherein it is dissolved; whether this water be sea water, or the salt water of wells, fountains, lakes or rivers; or water of any sort impregnated with rock-salt, or other kinds of common salt. The first of these kinds of salt is in several countries found so pure, that it serves for most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> uses, without any previous preparation (triturate excepted); for all natural salts rock-salt is the most abundantly furnished by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in various parts of the world, being found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, occupying great tracts of land. It is generally found in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> under the surface of the earth, as in Hungary, Muscovy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, Poland, Calabria, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, Ethiopia, and the East Indies. "In England (says Magellan), the salt mines at Northwich are in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ground, and contain it in layers or strata of various colours, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> are the most plentiful, as I have observed on the spot, which I visited in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1782, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with my worthy and learned friend Mr Volta, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and well known by his great abilities, and many discoveries in that branch of knowledge. The mine into which we descended was excavated in the form of a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> or vault under ground, supported by various columns of the salt, that were purposely left to support the incumbent weight. And the workmen having lighted a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of candles all round its circumference, it furnished us with the most agreeable and surprising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, whilst we were descending in the large tub, which serves to bring up the lumps that are broken from the mine," &c. Wraxall gives the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the famous salt mines near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> in Poland. "After being let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> (says he) by a rope to the depth of 230 feet, our conductors led us through galleries of the mines, which, for loftiness and breadth, seemed rather to resemble the avenues of some subterraneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, than palaces cut in a mine. They were perfectly dry in every part, and terminated in two chapels composed entirely of salt, hewn out of the solid walls. The images which adorn the altars, as well as the pillars and ornaments, were all of the same transparent materials; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and spars of which, reflecting the rays of light from the lamps which the guides held in their hands, produced an effect equally <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> and beautiful. Descending lower..." er into the earth by means of ladders, I found myself in an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> or cavern of salt, many hundred feet in height, length, and dimensions, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> and sides of which were cut with exact regularity. A thousand persons might dine in it without inconvenience, and the eye in vain attempted to trace or define its limits. Nothing could be more sublime than this vast subterranean apartment, illuminated by flambeaux, which faintly discover its prodigious magnitude, and leave the imagination at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to enlarge it indefinitely. After remaining about two hours and a half under ground, I was drawn up again in three minutes with the greatest facility." See also an account of the same mines by Mr Bernard, Journal de Physique, vol. xvi. for 1780, in which the miraculous tales concerning those subterraneous habitations, villages, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, are reduced to their proper magnitude and estimate. The English fossil salt is unfit for the uses of the kitchen, until by solution and coction it is freed from several impurities, and reduced into white salt. The British white salt also is not so proper as several kinds of bay salt for curing fish and such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-meats as are intended for sea provisions, or for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> into hot countries. So that for these purposes we are obliged, either wholly or in part, to use bay salt, which we purchase in France, Spain, and other foreign countries. However, it does not appear that there is any other thing requisite in the formation of bay salt than to evaporate the sea-water with an exceedingly gentle heat; and it is even very probable, that our common sea-salt by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> solution and crystallization might attain the requisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity. Without entering into any particular detail of the processes used for the preparation of bay-salt in different parts of the world, we shall content ourselves with giving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of the best methods of preparing common salt. At some convenient place near the sea-shore is erected the faltern. This is a long, low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, consisting of two parts; one of which is called the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>-house, or boiling-house. The fore-house serves to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and cover the workmen; and in the boiling-house are placed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and pan in which the salt is made. Sometimes they have two pans, one at each end of the faltern; and the part appropriated for the fuel and workmen is in the middle. The furnace opens into the fore-house by two mouths, beneath each of which is a mouth to the ash-pits. To the mouths of the furnace doors are fitted; and over them a wall is carried up to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, which divides the fore-house from the boiling-house, and prevents the dust of the coal and the ashes and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the furnace from falling into the salt pan. The fore-house communicates with the boiling-house by a door, placed in the wall which divides them. The body of the furnace consists of two chambers, divided from each other by a brick partition called the mid-feather; which from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> base terminates in a narrow edge nigh the top of the furnace; and by means of short pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> erected upon it, supports the bottom of the salt pan; it also fills up a considerable part of the furnace, which otherwise would be too large, and would consume more coals than, by the help of this contrivance, are required. To each chamber of the furnace is fitted a grate, through which the ashes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the ash-pits. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> are made of long bars of iron, supported underneath by strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bars of the same metal. They are not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the farthest part of the furnace, it being unnecessary to throw in the fuel so far; for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> is driven from the fire on the grate to the farthest part of the furnace; and from thence passes together with the smoke, through two flues into the chimney; and thus the bottom of the salt pan is everywhere equally heated. The salt pans are made of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, flat at the bottom, with the sides erected at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; the length of some of these pans is 15 feet, in breadth 12 feet, and the depth 16 inches; but at different works they are of different dimensions. They are commonly made of plates of iron, joined together with nails, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> are filled with a strong cement. Within the pan five or six strong beams of iron are fixed to its opposite sides, at equal distances, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other and to the bottom of the pan, from which they are distant about eight inches. From these beams hang down strong iron hooks, which are linked to other hooks or clamps of iron firmly nailed to the bottom of the pan; and thus the bottom of the pan is supported, and prevented from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> down or changing its figure. The plates most commonly used are of malleable iron, about four feet and a half long, a foot broad, and the third of an inch in thickness. The Scots prefer smaller plates, 14 or 15 inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Several make the sides of the pan, where they are not exposed to the fire, of lead; those parts, when made of iron, being found to consume salt in rust from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of the pan. Some have used plates of cast iron, five or six feet square, and an inch in thickness; but they are very subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> when unequally heated, and shaken (as they frequently are) by the violent boiling of the liquor. The cement most commonly used to fill the joints is <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> made of lime. The pan, thus formed, is placed over the furnace, being supported at the four corners by brick <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but along the middle, and at the sides and ends, by round pillars of cast iron called tripods, which are placed at three feet distance from each other, being about eight inches high, and at the top, where smallest, four inches in diameter. By means of these pillars the heat of the fire penetrates equally to all parts of the bottom of the pan, its four corners only excepted. Care is also taken to prevent the smoke of the furnace from passing into the boiling-house, by bricks and strong cement, which are closely applied to every part of the salt pan. In some places, as at Blyth in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, besides the common salt pans here described, they have a preparing pan placed between two salt pans, in the middle part of the building, which in other works is the fore house. The sea-water being received into this preparing pan, is there heated and in part evaporated by the flame and heat conveyed under it through flues from the two furnaces of the salt pans. And the hot water, as occasion requires, is conveyed through troughs from the preparing pan into the salt pans. Various other contrivances have been invented to lessen the expense of fuel, and several patents have been obtained for that purpose; but the salt-boilers have found their old methods the most convenient. Between the sides of the pan and walls of the boil- ing-house, there runs a walk five or six feet broad, where the workmen stand when they draw the salt, or have any other bunsels in the boiling-house. The same walk is continued at the end of the pan, next to the chimney; but the pan is placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the wall at the end adjoining to the fore-house. The roof of the boiling-house is covered with boards fastened on with nails of wood, iron nails quickly mouldering into rust. In the roof are several openings, to convey off the watery vapours; and on each side of it a window or two, which the workmen open when they look into the pan whilst it is boiling. Not far distant from the saltern, on the sea-shore, between full sea and low-water marks, they also make a little pond in the rocks, or with stones on the land, which they call their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. From this pond they lay a pipe, through which, when the tide is in, the sea-water runs into a well adjoining to the saltern; and from this well they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> it into troughs, by which it is conveyed into their ship or cistern, where it is stored up until they have occasion to use it. The cistern is built close to the saltern, and may be placed most conveniently between the two boiling-houses, on the back side of the fore-house; it is made either of wood, or brick and clay; it sometimes wants a cover, but ought to be covered with a shed, that the salt water contained therein may not be weakened by rains, nor mixed with foot and other impurities. It should be placed so high, that the water may conveniently run out of it, through a trough, into the salt pans. Besides the buildings already mentioned, several others are required; as store houses for the salt, cisterns for the bittern, an office for his majesty's salt-officers, and a dwelling-house for the salt-boilers. All things being thus prepared, and the sea-water having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> in the cistern till the mud and sand are settled to the bottom, it is drawn off into the salt pan. And at the four corners of the salt pan, where the flame does not touch its bottom, are placed four small lead pans, called scratch pans, which, for a salt pan of the size above-mentioned, are usually about a foot and a half long, a foot broad, and three inches deep; and have a bow or circular handle of iron, by which they may be drawn out with a hook, when the liquor in the pan is boiling. The salt pan being filled with sea-water, a strong fire of pit-coal is lighted in the furnace; and then, for a pan which contains about 400 gallons, the salt-boiler takes the whites of three eggs, and incorporates them well with two or three gallons of sea-water, which he pours into the salt pan while the water contained therein is only lukewarm; and immediately stirs it about with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>, that the whites of eggs may everywhere be equally mixed with the salt water. Instead of whites of eggs, at many salterns, as at most of those nigh <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, they use blood from the butchers, either of sheep or black cattle, to clarify the sea-water: And at many of the Scots salterns they do not give themselves the trouble of clarifying it. As the water grows hot, the whites of eggs separate from it a black frothy scum, which arises to the surface of the water, and covers it all over. As soon as the pan begins to boil, this scum is all risen, and it is then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to skim it off. The most convenient instruments for this purpose are skimmers of thin ash boards, six or eight inches broad, and so long that they may reach above half way over the salt pan. These skimmers have handles fitted to them; and the salt-boiler and his assistant, each holding one of them on the opposite sides of the pan, apply them so to each other that they overlap in the middle, and beginning at one end of the pan, carry them gently forward together, along the surface of the boiling liquor, to the other end; and thus, without breaking the scum, collect it all to one end of the pan, from whence they easily take it out. After the water is skimmed, it appears perfectly clear and transparent; and they continue boiling it briskly, till so much of the fresh or aqueous part is evaporated, that what remains in the pan is a strong brine almost fully saturated with salt, so that small saline crystals begin to form on its surface; which operation, in a pan filled 15 inches deep with water, is usually performed in five hours. The pan is then filled up a second time with clear sea-water drawn from the cistern; and about the time when it is half filled, the scratch-pans are taken out, and being emptied of the scum found in them, are again placed in the corners of the salt pan. The scum taken out of these pans is a fine white calcareous earth found in the form of powder, which separates from the sea-water during its coction, before the salt begins to form into grains. This subtile powder is violently agitated by the boiling liquor, until it is driven to the corners of the pan, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the liquor being more gentle, it subsides into the scratch pans placed there to receive it, and in them it remains undisturbed, and thus the greatest part of it is separated from the brine. After the pan hath again been filled up with sea-water, three whites of eggs are mixed with the liquor, by which it is clarified a second time, in the manner before described; and it is afterwards boiled down to a strong brine as at first; which second boiling may take up about four hours. The pan is then filled up a third time with clear sea-water; and after that, a fourth time; the liquor being each time clarified and boiled down to a strong brine, as before related; and the scratch-pans being taken out and emptied every time that the pan is filled up. Then, at the fourth boiling, as soon as the crystals begin to form on the surface of the brine, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a> the fire, and only suffer the brine to simmer, or boil very gently. In this heat they constantly endeavour to keep it all the time that the salt corns or granulates, which may be <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten hours. The salt is said to granulate, when its minute crystals cohere together into little masses or grains, which sink down in the brine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at the bottom of the salt pan. When most of the liquor is evaporated, and the salt thus lies in the pan almost dry on its surface, it is then time to draw it out. This part of the process is performed by raking the salt to one side of the pan into a long heap, where it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> a while from the brine, and is then filled out into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> or other proper vessels, and carried into the store-house, and delivered into the custody of his majesty's officers. And in this manner the whole process is performed in 24 hours; the salt being usually drawn every morning. In the store-house the salt is put hot into drabs, which are partitions like stalls for horses, lined on three sides and at the bottom with boards, and having a sliding-board on the fore-side to put in or draw out as occasion requires. The bottoms are made shelving, being highest at the back-side, and gradually inclining forwards; by which means the saline liquor, which remains mixed with the salt, easily drains from it; and the salt, in three or four days, becomes sufficiently dry; and is then taken out of the drabs, and laid up in large heaps, where it is ready for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The saline liquor which drains from the salt is not a pure brine of common salt, but hath a sharp and bitter taste, and is therefore called bittern; this liquor, at some works, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> for particular uses, at others throw away. A considerable quantity of this bittern is left at the bottom of the pan after the process is finished; which, as it contains much salt, they suffer to remain in the pan, when it is filled up with sea-water. But at each process this liquor becomes more sharp and bitter, and also increases in quantity: so that, after the third or fourth process is finished, they are obliged to take it out of the pan; otherwise it mixes in such quantities with the salt, as to give it a bitter taste, and disposes it to grow soft and run in the open air, and renders it unfit for domestic uses. After each process there also adheres to the bottom and sides of the pan, a white stony crust, of the same calcareous substance with that before collected from the boiling liquor. This the operators call <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-scratch, distinguishing the other found in the lead-pans by the name of powder-scratch. Once in eight or ten days they separate the stone-scratch from their pans with iron picks, and in several places find it a quarter of an inch in thickness. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this stony crust is suffered to adhere to the pan much longer, it grows so thick that the pan is burnt by the fire, and quickly wears away. In M. de Pagés's Travels round the World, we find the following important fact. "I had been anxious (says that author) to ascertain by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, whether sea-water contains salt in greater quantity under the torrid than under the other zones; and my experiments on this subject served to show, contrary to what I expected, that sea-water is impregnated with salt in less quantity within than without the tropics." These experiments were made on a hundred pounds of sea-water, taken at the depth of ten fathoms, and weighed in water-cales. M. de Pagés has given a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of these experiments, from which it appears that 100 lb. of sea-water in 46° 12' S. lat. gave 4½ lb. of salt, and in 1° 16' only 3½ lb.; and that in 74° N. lat. it gave 4½ lb. and in 4° 22' only 3½ lb., these being the highest and lowest latitudes in which the experiments were made, and also the greatest and least quantities of salt. Duty on Salt, is a distinct branch of his majesty's extraordinary revenue, and consists in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> of 3s. 4d. per bushel imposed upon all salt, by several statutes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William and other subsequent reigns. This is not generally called an excise, because under the management of different commissioners: but the commissioners of the salt-duties have, by statute 1 Ann. c. 21. the same powers, and must observe the same regulations, as those of other excises. This tax had usually been only temporary: but by statute 26 Geo. II. c. 3. was made perpetual. Salts, effects of in producing great degrees of cold. In the account of the remarkable effects of frigorific mixtures, in which saline bodies act so important a part, given in our article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, some errors had crept in. These errors through the liberal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of Mr. Walker of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, whose researches on this subject have been carried farther than any other chemist, we are enabled to correct by laying before our readers the following tables, most obligingly communicated to us by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>.

SALTPETRE

Pages 78-79
or NITRE, (nitrate of potash), a compound of nitric acid and potash. See POTASH, Chemistry Index. The importance of this fact in various manufactures renders every information relative to its production valuable. The following method has been long practised by the farmers of Appenzell in Switzerland. In so hilly a country, most houses and stables are built on slopes, one side of the edifice resting on the hill, and the other being supported by two strong poles, elevated two or three feet above the ground; so that the air has a free current under the saltpetre building. Immediately under the stable a pit is dug, usually occupying both in breadth and length the whole space of ground covered by the building; and instead of the clayey earth which is dug out, the pit is filled up with sandy soil. This is the whole process, and all the rest is done by nature. The animal water, which is continually oozing through the planks of the floor, having drenched the earth contained in the pit for the space of two or three years, the latter is emptied, and the saltpetre is refined and prepared in the usual manner. That manner, however, is not the best; and the French chemists, during the incessant wars occasioned by the revolution, have, for the sake of supplying their armies with gunpowder, turned their attention to the best method of refining saltpetre. The following are directions given for this purpose by Chaptal, Champy, and Bonjour. The crude saltpetre is to be beaten small with mallets, in order that the water may more easily attack every part of the mats. The saltpetre is then to be put into tubs, five or six hundred pounds in each tub. Twenty per cent. of water is to be poured into each tub, and the mixture well stirred. It must be left to macerate or digest until the specific gravity of the fluid ceases to augment. Six or seven hours are sufficient for this first operation, and the water acquires the density of between 25 and 35 degrees. (Sp. gr. 1.21, and 1.306, ascertained by Baumé's hydrometer.) The first water must then be poured off, and a second portion of water must be poured on the same saltpetre amounting to 10 per cent.; after which the mixture must be stirred up, suffered to macerate for one hour, and the fluid drawn or poured off. Five per cent. of water must then be poured on the saltpetre; and after stirring the whole, the fluid must be immediately drawn off. When the water is drained from the saltpetre, the salt must be thrown into a boiler containing 50 per cent. of boiling water. When the solution is made, it will mark between 66 and 68 degrees of the hydrometer. (Sp. gr. 1.848, and 1.898.) The solution is to be poured into a proper vessel, where it deposits by cooling about two-thirds of the saltpetre originally taken. The precipitation begins in about half an hour, and terminates in between four and six hours. But as it is of importance to obtain the saltpetre in small needles, because in this form it is more easily dried, it is necessary to agitate the fluid during the whole time of the crystallization. A slight motion is communicated to this liquid mass by a kind of rake; in consequence of which the crystals are deposited in very slender needles. In proportion as the crystals fall down, they are scraped to the borders of the vessel, whence they are taken with a skimmer, and thrown to drain in baskets placed on trellises, in such a manner that the water which passes through may either fall into the crystallizing vessel, or be received in basins underneath. The saltpetre is afterwards put into wooden vessels in the form of a mill-hopper or inverted pyramid with a double bottom. The upper bottom is placed two inches above the lower on wooden ledges, and has many small perforations through which water may pass to the lower bottom, which likewise affords a passage by one single aperture. A reservoir is placed beneath. The crystallized saltpetre is washed in these vessels with 5 per cent. of water; which water is afterwards employed in the solution of saltpetre in subsequent operations. The saltpetre, after sufficient draining, and being dried by exposure to the air upon tables for several hours, may then be employed in the manufacture of gunpowder. But when it is required to use the saltpetre in the speedy and immediate manufacture of gunpowder, it must be dried much more strongly. This may be effected in a stove, or more simply by heating it in a flat metallic vessel. For this purpose the saltpetre is to be put into the vessel to the depth of five or six inches, and heated to 40 or 50 degrees of the thermometer (or about 135° of Fahrenheit). The saltpetre is to be stirred for two or three hours, and dried to such a degree that, when strongly pressed in the hand, it shall acquire no consistence, nor adhere together, but resemble a very fine dry sand. This degree of dryness is not required when the powder is made by pounding. From these circumstances, we find that two saline liquids remain after the operation; (1) the water from the washing; and (2) that from the crystallizing vessels. We have already remarked, that the washing of the saltpetre is performed in three successive operations, in which, upon the whole, the quantity of fluid made use of amounts to 35 per cent. of the weight of the crude saltpetre. These washings are established on the principle, that cold water dissolves the muriates of soda, and the earthy nitrates and muriates, together with the colouring principle, but scarcely attacks the nitrate of potash. The water of these three washings therefore contains the muriate of soda, the earthy salts, the colouring principle, and a small quantity of nitrate of potash; the amount of which is in proportion to that of the muriate of soda, which determines its solution. The water of the crystallizing vessels contains a portion of the muriates of soda, and of the earthy salts which escaped the operation of washing, and a quantity of nitrate of potash, which is more considerable than that of the former solution. The waters made use of at the end of the operation, to whiten and wash the crystals deposited in the pyramidal vessel, contain nothing but a small quantity of nitrate of potash. These waters are therefore very different in their nature. The water of the washings is really a mother water. It must be collected in vessels, and treated with potash by the known processes. It must be evaporated to 66 degrees (or 18.48 lbs. gr.), taking out the muriate of soda as it falls. This solution is to be saturated with 2 or 3 per cent. of potash, then suffered to settle, decanted, and poured into crystallizing vessels, where 20 per cent. of water is to be added to keep the whole of the muriate of soda suspended. The waters which are thus obtained by treatment of the mother water may be mixed with the water of the first crystallization. From these the marine salt may be separated by simple evaporation; and the nitrate of potash, which they hold in solution, may be afterwards obtained by cooling. The small quantity of water made use of to wash and whiten the refined saltpetre, contains nothing but the nitrate of potash: it may therefore be used in the solution of the saltpetre when taken from the tubs. From this description it follows, that a manufactory for the speedy refining of saltpetre ought to be provided with mallets or rammers for pounding the saltpetre; tubs for washing; a boiler for solution; a crystallizing vessel of copper or lead, in which the saltpetre is to be obtained by cooling; baskets for draining the saltpetre; scales and weights for weighing; hydrometers and thermometers, to ascertain densities and temperatures; rakes to agitate the liquor in the crystallizing vessel; skimmers to take out the crystals, and convey them to the baskets; syphons or hand-pumps to empty the boilers. The number and dimensions of these several articles must vary according to the quantity of saltpetre intended to be refined.

SALUTE

Pages 82-83

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, a testimony of deference <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> homage rendered by the ships of one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to another, or by ships of the same nation to a superior or equal. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is variously performed, according to the circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, or situation, of the parties. It consists in firing a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cannon, or volleys of small arms; in striking the colours or top-gallants; or in one or more general shouts of the whole ship's crew, mounted on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> or rigging for that purpose. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> regulations with regard to salutes in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> navy are as follow: "When a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> officer salutes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> and commander-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the fleet, he is to give him fifteen guns; but when captains salute him, they are to give him seventeen guns. The admiral and commander-in-chief of the fleet is to return two guns less to flag-officers, and four less to captains. Flag-officers saluting their superior or senior officer, are to give him thirteen guns. Flag-officers are to return an equal number of guns to flag-officers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> their flags on the same mast, and two guns less to the rest, as also to captains. "When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> salutes an admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or blue, he is to give him fifteen guns; but to vice and rear admirals, thirteen guns. When a flag officer is saluted by two or more of his majesty's ships, he is not to return the salute till all have finished, and then to do it with such a reasonable number of guns as he shall judge proper. "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the meeting of two squadrons, the two chiefs only are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> salutes. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> single ships meet a squadron consisting of more than one flag, the principal flag only is to be saluted. No salutes shall be repeated by the same ships, unless there has been a separation of six months at least. "None of his majesty's ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, commanded only by captains, shall give or receive salutes from one another, in whatsoever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world they meet. "A flag officer commanding in chief shall be saluted, upon his first hoisting his flag, by all the ships present, with such a number of guns as is allowed by the first, third, or fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. "When any of his majesty's ships shall meet with any ship or ships belonging to any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state, within his majesty's seas (which extend to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>), it is expected, that the said foreign ships do strike their top-gallant, and take in their flag, in acknowledgment of his majesty's sovereignty in those seas; and if any shall refuse or offer to resist, it is enjoined to all flag officers and commanders to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their utmost endeavours to compel them thereto, and not suffer any dishonour to be done to his majesty. And if any of his majesty's subjects shall so much forget their duty, as to omit striking their top-gallant in passing by his majesty's ships, the name of the ship and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and from whence, and whither bound, together with affidavits of the fact, are to be sent up to the secretary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, in order to their being proceeded against in the admiralty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. And it is to be observed, that in his majesty's seas, his majesty's ships are in nowise to strike to any; and that in other parts, no ship of his majesty's is to strike her flag or top-gallant to any foreigner, unless such foreign ship shall have first struck, or at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> strike, her flag or top-gallant to his majesty's ship. "The flag-officers and commanders of his majesty's ships are to be careful to maintain his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon all occasions, giving protection to his subjects, and endeavouring, what in them lies, to secure and encourage them in their lawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and they are not to injure, in any manner, the subjects of his majesty's friends and allies. "If a foreign admiral meet with any of his majesty's ships, and salutes them, he shall receive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> for gun. If he be a vice-admiral, the admiral shall answer with two guns less. If a rear-admiral, the admiral and vice-admiral shall return two less. But if the ship be commanded by a captain only, the flag-officer shall give two guns less, and captains an equal number. "When any of his majesty's ships come to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in a foreign port or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, within cannon-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of its forts, the captain may salute the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with such a number of guns as have been customary, upon good assurance of having the like number returned, but not otherwise. But if the ship bears a flag, the flag-officer shall first carefully inform himself how flags of like rank, belonging to other crowned heads, have given or returned salutes, and to insist upon the same terms of respect. "It is allowed to the commanders of his majesty's ships in foreign parts, to salute the persons of any admirals, commanders in chief, or captains of ships of war of foreign nations, and foreign noblemen, or strangers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as also the factories of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects, coming on board to visit the ship; and the number of guns is left to the commander, as shall be suitable to the occasion and the quality of the persons visiting; but he is nevertheless to remain accountable for any excesses in the abuse of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. If the ship visited be in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>... pany with other ships of war, the captain is not to make use of the civilities allowed in the preceding articles but with leave and consent of the commander in chief or the senior captain. "Merchant-ships, whether foreigners or belonging to his majesty's subjects, saluting the admiral of the fleet, shall be answered by five guns less; when they salute any other flag-ships, they shall be answered by four guns less; and if they salute men of war commanded by captains, they shall be answered by two guns less. If several merchant-ships salute in company, no return is to be made till all have finished, and then by such a number of guns as shall be thought proper; but though the merchant-ships should answer, there shall be no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> return. "None of his majesty's ships of war shall salute any of his majesty's forts or castles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, on any pretence whatsoever."

SALUZZO

Pages 83-83

the marquisate of, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Dauphiny and the province of the Four Valleys, on the east by those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAVIGNANO">Savignano</a> and Fossano, on the south by that of Cona and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, and on the west by Barcelonetta. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy in 1601.

SALZBURG

Pages 79-82

an archbishopric of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, bounded on the east by Styria and the Upper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Tyrol, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Bavaria, and on the south by the duchy of Carinthia and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIXEN">Brixen</a>. It is said to be about 100 miles from east to west, and upwards of 60 from north to south. With respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it is very mountainous, yielding, however, excellent pasturage, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that, abounding in cattle, and horses remarkable for their mettle and hardiness. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is particularly noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> it produces, and its strong palaces and castles. Here are also considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> calcinatus, with quarries of marble, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> hot-bath. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Salza, the Inn, the Enz, and Muerz; which, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and other streams, are well-stored with fish. The peasants here are all allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of arms, and trained to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> duty. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> in the country, and most of the lands belong to the clergy. The estates consist of the prelates, the cities, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Notwithstanding this country is under the power of a Popish ecclesiastic, and the violent, arbitrary, and oppreotive manner in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have always been treated, great numbers of them still remained in it till the year 1732, when no less than 30,000 of them withdrew from it, dispersing themselves in the several Protestant states of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and some of them were even sent from Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to the American colonies. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares, and all sorts of arms and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of coarse cloth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> here. The archbishop has many and great prerogatives: he is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire, and perpetual legate of the holy see in Germany, of which he is also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>. He has the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the diet of this circle, and next to the electors in that of the empire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes, in which he and the archduke of Austria preside by turns. No <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lies from him either in civil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes, but to the pope alone: and he is entitled to wear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. He has also the nomination to several bishoprics; and the canonicates that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> vacant in the months in which the popes, by virtue of the concordat, are allowed to nominate, are all in his gift. His suffragans are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Freisingen, Ratibon, Brixen, Gurk, Chiemsee, Seckan, and Lavant; and of these, the four last are nominated, and even confirmed by him and not by the pope. At the diet of the empire, Salzburg, his envoy takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of all the princes that are present, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>. His revenue is said to amount to near 200,000l. a-year, a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it arising from the salt-works. He is able to raise 25,000 men; but keeps in constant pay, besides his guards, only one regiment, consisting of 1000 men. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> is very magnificent; and he has his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> great officers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> colleges. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> consists of 24 canons, who must be all noble, but are obliged only to four months residence. At his accession to the see, the archbishop must pay 100,000 crowns to Rome for the pall. There is an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> here, instituted in 1711, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St Rupert, who was the first bishop of Salzburg, about the beginning of the 8th century. Salzburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a German archbishopric of the same name, and which takes its own from the river Salza, on which it stands, and over which it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is a very handsome place, well fortified, and the residence of the archbishop. The houses are high, and all built of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; the roofs are in the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and you may walk upon them. The castle here is very strong, and as strongly garrisoned, and well provided with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and warlike stores. The archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is magnificent; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> before it is a fountain, esteemed the largest and grandest in Germany. The stables are very lofty; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the horses usually kept by the archbishop is said to be upwards of 200. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, of which one part stands on a steep rock, is well built, but the streets are narrow and badly paved. Besides the above mentioned, there are two other flatly palaces belonging to the archbishop, one of which is called the Nuebau, and the other Mirabella. The latter of these has a very beautiful garden; and the number of trees in the orangery is so great, that Mr Keyfeler tells us, 20,000 oranges have been gathered from them in one year. The river Salza runs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the walls of this garden. There are a great many other fine structures in the city, public and private, such as palaces, monasteries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and churches. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dedicated to St Rupert (the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of Bavaria, and a Scotchman by birth), all the altars are of marble of different kinds, and one of the organs has above 3200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. The whole structure is extremely handsome. It is built of freestone in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s at Rome. The portico is of marble, and the whole is covered with copper. Before the portico there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quadrangular place, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> and galleries, in which is the prince's residence; and in the middle of this place there is a statue of the Virgin in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>; it is a fine piece of art, but of an unnatural size. There are large areas encompassed with handsome buildings on both sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the middle of that which is to the left, there is a most magnificent fountain of marble, and some valuable figures of gigantic size. There is likewise a fountain in that to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, but it is not to be compared with the former one, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> of it makes but a very pitiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. This town contains many more excellent buildings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, which remind one that the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> are not far distant. The winter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> riding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> here are noble structures. The university was founded in 1629, and committed to the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>. Besides it, there are two colleges, in which the young noblemen are educated. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 33. Salvadora o. N. Lat. 47. 45. Salvadora, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clas; and in the natural method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Salvage-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, a reward allowed by the civil and statute <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> for the saving of ships or goods from the danger of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, pirates, or enemies.—Where any ship is in danger of being stranded, or driven on shore, justices of the peace are to command the constables to assemble as many persons as are necessary to preserve it; and, on its being preserved by their means, the persons afflicting therein shall, in 30 days after, be paid a reasonable reward for their salvage; otherwise the ship or goods shall remain in the custody of the officers of the customs as a security for the same. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">Salvation</a>, means the safety or preservation of any thing which is or has been in danger, and is generally used in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, when it means preservation from eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, or reception to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of heaven, which is now offered to all men by the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> upon certain conditions. The Hebrews but rarely make use of concrete terms as they are called, but often of abstracted. Thus, instead of saying that God saves them and protects them, they say that God is their salvation. Thus the word of salvation, the joy of salvation, the rock of salvation, the shield of salvation, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> of salvation, &c. is as much as to say, The word that declares deliverance; the joy that attends the escaping a great danger, a rock where any one takes refuge, and where he may be in safety from his enemy; a buckler, that secures him from the arm of the enemy; a horn or ray of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, of happiness and salvation, &c. See <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, &c. Salvator Rosa. See Rosa. Salve <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">Regina</a>, among the Romanists, the name of a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, addressed to the Virgin, and sung after complines, as also upon the point of executing a criminal. Durandus says, it was composed by Peter bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of ringing the salve regina at the close of the office was begun by order of St Dominic, and first in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, about 1237. Gregory IX. first appointed it to be general. St Bernard added the conclusion, O dulcis! O pia, &c. Salvia, sage, a genus of plants belonging to the dignia clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillate. See Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVIANUS">Salvianus</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> father of the Christian church, who flourished in the 5th century, and was well skilled in the sciences. It is said he lived in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> with his wife Palladia, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been his sister; and that he was so afflicted at the wickedness of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that he was called the Jeremiah of the fifth century. He acquired such reputation for his piety and learning, that he was named the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the bishops. He wrote a Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; another on Avarice; and some epistles, of which Baluze has given an excellent edition; that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Ritterhusius, in 2 vols octavo, is also esteemed. Salutation, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of saluting, greeting, or paying respect and reverence to any one. When men (writes the compiler of L'Esprit des Usages Salutation. Usages et des Coutumes) salute each other in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> manner; it signifies little whether they move a particular part of the body, or practise a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. In these actions there must exist different customs. Every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> imagines it employs the most reasonable ones; but all are equally simple, and none are to be treated as ridiculous. This infinite number of ceremonies may be reduced to two kinds; to reverences or salutations; and to the touch of some part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> and prostrate oneself to express sentiments of respect, appears to be a natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; for terrified persons throw themselves on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> when they adore invisible beings. The affectionate touch of the person they salute, is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of tenderness. As nations decline from their ancient simplicity, much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> and grimace are introduced. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a>, the manners of a people, and their situation, influence the modes of salutation; as may be observed from the instances we collect. Modes of salutation have sometimes very different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and it is no uninteresting speculation to examine their shades. Many display a refinement of delicacy, while others are remarkable for their simplicity, or for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. In general, however, they are frequently the same in the infancy of nations, and in more polished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. Respect, humility, fear, and esteem, are expressed much in a similar manner; for these are the natural consequences of the organization of the body. These demonstrations become, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, only empty civilities, which signify nothing; we shall notice what they were originally, without reflecting on what they are. The first nations have no peculiar modes of salutation; they know no reverences, or other compliments, or they despise and disdain them. The Greenlanders laugh when they see an European uncover his head and bend his body before him whom he calls his superior. The islanders, near the Philippines, take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or foot of him they salute, and with it they gently rub their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. The Laplanders apply their nose strongly against that of the person they salute. Dampier says, that at New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> they are satisfied in placing on their heads the leaves of trees, which have ever passed for symbols of friendship and peace. This is at least a picturesque salute. Other salutations are very inconvenient and painful; it requires great practice to enable a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be polite in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated in the straits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a>. Houtman tells us, they saluted him in this odd way: "They raised his left foot, which they passed gently over the right leg, and from thence over his face." The inhabitants of the Philippines bend their body very low, in placing their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, and raising at the same time one foot in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, with their knee bent. An Ethiopian takes the robe of another, and ties it about his own waist, so that he leaves his friend half naked. This custom of undressing on these occasions takes other forms; sometimes men place themselves naked before the person whom they salute; it is to show their humility, and that they are unworthy of appearing in his presence. This was practised before Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, when he received the visit of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> Otaheitans. Their innocent simplicity, no doubt, did not appear immodest in the eyes of the virtuous. Sometimes they only undress partially. The Japanese only take off a slipper; the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRACAN">Arracan</a>, their sandals in the Salutation street, and their stockings in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the progress of time, it appears feasible to uncover one's self. The grandees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> claim the right of appearing covered before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, to show that they are not so much subjected to him as the rest of the nation; and (this writer observes) we may remark, that the English do not uncover their heads so much as the other nations of Europe. In a word, there is not a nation (observes the humorous Montaigne), even to the people who, when they salute, turn their backs on their friends, but that can be justified in their customs. It must be observed of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, that they are lovers of ludicrous actions, and thus make all their ceremonies farcical. The greater part pull the fingers till they crack. Snellgrave gives an odd representation of the embassy which the king of Dahomy sent to him. The ceremonies of salutation consisted in the most ridiculous contortions. When two negro monarchs visit, they embrace in snapping three times the middle finger. Barbarous nations frequently imprint on their salutations the dispositions of their character. When the inhabitants of Carneia (says Athenaeus) would show a peculiar mark of esteem, they breathed a vein, and presented for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a> of their friend the blood as it issued. The Franks tore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> from their head, and presented it to the person they saluted. The slave cut off his hair, and offered it to his master. The Chinese are singularly affected in their personal civilities; they even calculate the number of their reverences. These are their most remarkable postures. The men move their hands in an affectionate manner, while they are joined together on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and bow their head a little. If they respect a person, they raise their hands joined, and then lower them to the earth in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> the body. If two persons meet after a long separation, they both fall on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and bend the face to the earth, and this ceremony they repeat two or three times. Surely we may differ here with the sentiment of Montaigne, and confess this ceremony to be ridiculous. It arises from their national affection. They substitute <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> ceremonies for natural actions. Their expressions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> as little as their ceremonies. If a Chinese is asked how he finds himself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>? he answers, Very well; thanks to your abundant felicity. If they would tell a man that he looks well, they say, Prosperity is painted on your face; or, Your air announces your happiness. If you render them any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, they say, My thanks should be immortal. If you praise them, they answer, How shall I dare to persuade myself of what you say of me? If you dine with them, they tell you at parting, We have not treated you with sufficient distinction. The various titles they invent for each other it would be impossible to translate. It is to be observed, that all these answers are prescribed by the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, or academy of compliments. There are determined the number of bows; the expressions to be employed; the genuflexions, and the inclinations which are to be made to the right or left hand; the salutations of the master before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> where the stranger is to be seated, for he salutes it most profoundly, and wipes the dust away with the skirts of his robe; all these and other things are noticed, even to the silent gestures, by which you are entreated to enter the house. The lower class of people are equally nice Salutation, nice in these punctilios; and ambassadors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> 40 days in practising them before they are enabled to appear at court. A tribunal of ceremonies has been erected, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> very odd decrees are issued, to which the Chinese most religiously submit. The marks of honour are frequently arbitrary; to be seated, with us, is a mark of repose and familiarity; to stand up, that of respect. There are countries, however, in which princes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> only be addressed by persons who are seated, and it is considered as a favour to be permitted to stand in their presence. This custom prevails in despotic countries: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> cannot suffer without disgust the elevated figure of his subjects; he is pleased to bend their bodies with their genius: his presence must lay those who behold him prostrate on the earth: he defies no eagerness, no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; he would only inspire terror. The pope makes no reverence to any mortal except the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, to whom he stoops a very little when he permits him to kiss his lips.

SAMA

Pages 83-83

a town and fort in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Dutch on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, stands on an eminence, the fort being watered by the pleasant river of St George, that discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The town contains above 200 houses, which seem to form three distinct villages, one of which is immediately under the cannon of the Dutch fort St Sebastian. Des Marchais deems this town to be one of the largest on the whole coast, Barbot likewise agreeing with him in its situation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants. The sole employment of the natives is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; a circumstance which easily accounts for their poverty. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is republican, the magistrates having the supreme power, being subject to periodical changes, and under the authority of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Gavi, who seldom however interferes in the affairs of the state. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> resides some leagues distant from the sea, is rich, and much respected by his neighbours.

SAMANEANS

Pages 83-83

in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> philosophers, have been confounded by some with the Bramins. They proceeded from Ariana, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and the neighbouring countries, spread themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and taught new doctrines. The Bramins, before their arrival, it is said, were in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, were the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> of India, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence was on the banks of the Ganges, and in the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; while the Samaneans were settled towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. Others say, that the Bramins acquired all their knowledge from the Samaneans, before whose arrival it would be difficult to prove that the Bramins were the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> teachers of the Indians. The most celebrated and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of the Samanean doctors was Bouddha, or Buddha, who was born 683 years before Christ. His scholars paid him divine honours; and his doctrine, which consisted chiefly in the transmigration of souls, and in the worship of cows, was adopted not only in India, but also in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. It was propagated according to M. de Sainte Croix, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>, in the 8th century, and succeeded there the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Zamolxis. The Samaneans, or Buddhas, were entirely destroyed in India by the jealous rage of the Bramins, whose absurd practices and fables they affected to treat with contempt; but several of their books are still preserved and respected on the coasts of Malabar. We are told, too, that several of the Brahmin orders have adopted their manner of living, and openly profess the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their doctrines. L'Excurion d'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, ou Ancien Comment du Vedam, published by M. de S. Croix, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1779. See BRAHMIN.

SAMAR

Pages 83-83

a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> not far from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a> in the East Indies, is called Samar on the side which looks towards the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and Iloabao on that next the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> ocean. Its greatest length, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Baliquaton, which, with the point of Manilla, makes the strait of St Bernardino, in 13 deg. 30 min. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, extends to that of Guiguan in 11 deg. towards the south.
