The other two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, making the greatest breadth of the island, are Cabo de Espiritu Santo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cape of the Holy Ghost, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of which are the first discovered by ships from New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and that which lying opposite to Leyte westward, makes another strait, scarce a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>'s throw over. The whole compass of the island is about 130 leagues. Between Guiguan and Cape Espiritu Santo is the port of Borognon, and not far from thence those of Palapa and Catubig, and the little island of Bin, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Catarman. Vessels from countries not yet discovered are very frequently <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away on the before-mentioned coast of Palapa. Within the straits of St Bernardino, and beyond Baliquaton, is the coast of Samar, on which are the villages of Ibatan, Bangahon, Cathalogan, Paramos, and Calviga. Then follows the strait of St Juanillo, without which, standing eastward, appears the point and little island of Guiguan, where the compass of the island ends. It is mountainous and craggy, but the few plains which it contains are very fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are much the same as those of Leyte; but there is one particular sort, called by the Spaniards chico, and by the Chinese, who put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value on it, jeyza, without kernels.

SAMARA

Pages 83-83

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the te-trandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAMARCAND

Pages 83-84
or SARMACAND, an ancient and famous town of Asia, capital of the kingdom of the same name in the country of the Ubeck Tartars, with a castle and a famous university. The houses are built with stones, and it carries on a trade in excellent fruits. It is pleasantly seated near the river Sogde, a branch of the Amu. E. Long. 69° 0', N. Lat. 39° 50'. This town was the capital of the kingdom of Sogdia in the time of Alexander the Great, when it was called Maracanda. It was afterwards the capital of the empire of Tamerlane the Great. In the time of Jenghiz Khan, it was forced to yield to the arms of that cruel conqueror; by whom the garrison, amounting to 30,000 men, were butchered; 30,000 of the inhabitants, with their wives and Samaria and children, were presented to his generals; the rest were permitted to live in the city, on paying a tribute of 300,000 dinars or crowns of gold.

SAMARIA

Pages 84-87

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Samaria, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the ten tribes. It was built by Omri <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, who began to reign in the year of the world 3079, and died 3086 (1 Kings xvi. 24.). He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, or for the sum of 684l. 7s. 6d. It took the name of Samaria from Shemer the owner of the hill; though some think there were already some beginnings of a city, because, before the reign of Omri there is mention made of Samaria (1 Kings xiii. 32.) in the year of the world 3030. But others take this for a prolepsis, or an anticipation, in the discourse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of God, who speaks of Samaria under the reign of Jeroboam. However this be, it is certain that Samaria was no considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and did not become the capital city of the kingdom of Israel till after the reign of Omri. Before him, the kings of Israel dwelt at Shechem, or Tirzah. Samaria was situated upon an agreeable and fruitful hill, in an advantageous situation, and was 12 miles from Dothaim, 12 from Merom, and four from Atharoth. Josephus says, it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Besides, though it was built upon an eminence, yet it must have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in abundance; since we find medals struck in this city, whereon is represented the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Astarte treading a river under foot; which proves it to have been well watered. And Josephus observes, that when it was taken by John Hircanus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Jews, he entirely demolished it, and caused even the brook to flow over its ruins, to obliterate all the footsteps of it. The kings of Samaria omitted nothing to make this city the strongest, the finest, and the richest, that was possible. Ahab built there a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> (1 Kings xxii. 39.), that is, in which there were many ornaments of ivory. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a> describes Samaria under Jeroboam II. as a city sunk into all excesses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and effeminacy (Amos iii. 15. and iv. 1, 2.). Ben-hadad king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> built public places or streets in Samaria (1 Kings xx. 34.) probably for traffic, where his people dwelt to promote trade. His son Ben-hadad besieged this place under the reign of Ahab (1 Kings xx. 1, 2, 3., &c.) in the year of the world 3103. The following year, Ben-hadad brought an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> into the field, probably with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against Samaria; but his army was again cut in pieces. Some years after this, Ben-hadad came a third <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before Samaria, and reduced it to such necessities by famine, that a mother was there forced to eat her own child; but the city was relieved by a sensible effect of the protection of God. Lastly, it was besieged by Shalmaneser king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, in the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel (2 Kings xvii. 6, 7, &c.), which was the fourth of Hezekiah king of Judah. It was taken three years after, in the year of the world 3283. The prophet Hosea speaks of the cruelties exercised by Shalmaneser against the besieged (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOF">Hof</a>. x. 4, 8, 9. xiv. 1.) and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MICAH">Micah</a> says, that this city was reduced to a heap of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> (Mic. i. 6.). The Cuthites that were sent by Esarhaddon to inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Samaria, did not think it worth their while to repair the ruins of this city; they dwelt at Shechem, which they made the capital city of their state. They were still upon this footing when Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> came into Phoenicia and Judea. However, the Cuthites had rebuilt some of the houses of Samaria, even from the time of the return from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, since <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> then speaks of the inhabitants of Samaria (Ezra iv. 17. Nehem. iv. 2.) and that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, being jealous of the favours that Alexander the Great had conferred on the Jews, revolted from him while this prince was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and burnt Andromachus alive, whom Alexander had left governor of Syria. Alexander marched against them, took Samaria, and put in Macedonians to inhabit it; giving the country round it to the Jews; and to encourage them to cultivate it, he granted them an exemption from tribute. The king of Egypt and Syria, who succeeded Alexander, deprived them of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this country. But Alexander Balas king of Syria restored to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> Maccabeus the cities of Lydda, Ephrem, and Ramatha, which he cut off from the country of Samaria (1 Mac. x. 32, 33, and xi. 28, 34.). Lastly, the Jews re-entered into the full possession of this whole country under John Hircanus the Asmonæan, who took Samaria, and ruined it in such a manner, according to Josephus, that he made the river run through its ruins. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this condition to the year of the world 3947, when Aulus Gabinius, the proconsul of Syria, rebuilt it, and gave it the name of Gabiniiana. But it was yet but very inconsiderable, till Herod the Great restored it to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> lustre, and gave it the Greek name of Sebaste, which in Latin is Augusta, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus, who had given him the property of this place. The sacred authors of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> speak but little of Samaria; and when they do mention it, it is rather in respect of the country about it, than of the city itself. (See Luke xvii. 11. John iv. 4, 5.).—It was there our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> had the conversation with the woman of Samaria, that is, with a Samaritan woman of the city of Sychar. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of St Stephen, (Acts viii. 1, 2, 3.), when the disciples were dispersed through the cities of Judea and Samaria, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the deacon withdrew into the city of Samaria, where he made several converts. When the apostles heard that this city had received the word of God, they sent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and John thither, to communicate the Holy Ghost to such as had been baptized. It was there they found Simon Magus, who offered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the apostles, being in hopes to buy this power of communicating the Holy Ghost. Samaria is never called Sebaste in the books of the New Testament, though strangers hardly knew it by this name. St Jerome says, that it was thought Obadiah was buried at Samaria. They also showed there the tombs of Elitha and of St John the Baptist. There are found Samaritans found many ancient medals that were struck at Sebastae, or Samaria, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of this city have subscribed to the ancient councils. SAMARITANS. We have already spoken of the Samaritans under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTH">CUTH</a>. The Samaritans are the people of the city of Samaria, and the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of which Samaria was the capital city. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it should seem that we might give the name of Samaritans to the Israelites of the ten tribes, who lived in the city and territory of Samaria. However, the sacred authors <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> give the name of Samaritans only to those strange people whom the kings of Assyria sent from beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> to inhabit the kingdom of Samaria, when they took away captive the Israelites that were there before. Thus we may fix the epoch of the Samaritans at the taking of Samaria by Salmanezer, in the year of the world 3283. This prince carried away captive the Israelites that he found in the country, and assigned them dwellings beyond the Euphrates, and in Assyria, (2 Kings xvii. 24.) He sent other inhabitants in their stead, of which the most considerable were the Cutheites, a people descended from Cuth, and who are probably of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> knew by the name of Scythians. After Salmanezer, his successor Esar-haddon was informed, that the people which had been sent to Samaria were infected by lions that devoured them, (2 Kings xvii. 25.) this he imputed to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the people in the manner of worshipping the god of the country. Wherefore Esar-haddon sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the God of Israel that he might teach them the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Hebrews. But they thought they might blend this religion with that which they professed before; so they continued to worship their idols as before, in conjunction with the God of Israel, not perceiving how absurd and incompatible these two religions were. It is not known how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> they continued in this state; but at the return from the captivity of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, it appears they had entirely quitted the worship of their idols; and when they asked permission of the Israelites that they might labour with them at the rebuilding of the temple of Jerusalem, they affirmed, that from the time that Esar-haddon had brought them into this country they had always worshipped the Lord, (Ezra iv. 1, 2, 3.) And indeed, after the return from the captivity, the Scripture does not anywhere reproach them with idolatrous worship, though it does not dissemble either their jealousy against the Jews, nor the ill offices they had done them at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">flanders</a> and calumnies, or the stratagems they contrived to hinder the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem.—(Nehem. ii. 10, iv. 2, &c. vi. 1, 2, &c.) It does not appear that there was any temple in Samaria, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all these people who came thither from beyond the Euphrates, before the coming of Alexander the Great into Judea. Before that time, everyone was left to his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, and worshipped the Lord where he thought fit. But they presently comprehended, from the books of Moses which they had in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and from the example of the Jews their neighbours, that God was to be worshipped in that place only which he had chosen. So that since they could not go to the temple of Jerusalem, which the Jews would not allow of, they betook themselves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a temple of their own upon Mount Gerizim, near the city Samaritans, of Shechem, which was then their capital. Therefore <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANBALLAT">Sanballat</a>, the governor of the Samaritans, applied himself to Alexander, and told him he had a son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, son to Jaddus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priest of the Jews, who had retired to Samaria with a great number of other persons of his own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; that he desired to build a temple in this province, where he might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the high-priesthood; that this undertaking would be to the advantage of the king's affairs, because in building a temple in the province of Samaria, the nation of the Jews would be divided, who are a turbulent and factious people, and by such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> would be made weaker, and less in a condition to undertake new enterprises. Alexander readily consented to what Sanballat desired, and the Samaritans presently began their building of the temple of Gerizim, which from that time they have always frequented, and still frequent to this day, as the place where the Lord intended to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of his people. It is of this mountain, and of this temple, that the Samaritan woman of Sychar spoke to our Saviour, (John iv. 20.) See GARIZIM. The Samaritans did not long continue under the obedience of Alexander. They revolted from him the very next year, and Alexander drove them out of Samaria, put Macedonians in their room, and gave the province of Samaria to the Jews. This preference that Alexander gave to the Israelites contributed not a little to increase that hatred and animosity that had already obtained between these two people. When any Israelite had deserved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for the violation of some important point of the law, he presently took refuge in Samaria or Shechem, and embraced the way of worship according to the temple of Garizim. When the Jews were in a prosperous condition, and affairs were favourable to them, the Samaritans did not fail to call themselves Hebrews, and pretended to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>. But no sooner were the Jews fallen into discredit or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, but the Samaritans immediately disowned them, would have nothing in common with them, acknowledged themselves to be Phoenicians originally, or that they were descended from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> and Manasseh his son. This used to be their practice in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes. The Samaritans, having received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, or the five books of Moses, from the priest that was sent by Esar-haddon, have preserved it to this day, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and character it was then, that is, in the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> or Phoenician character, which we now call the Samaritan, to distinguish it from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Hebrew character, which at present we find in the books of the Jews. These last, after their captivity, changed their old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and took up those of the Chaldean, which they had been used to at Babylon, and which they continue still to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It is wrong, says F. Calmet, to give this the name of the Hebrew character, for that can be said properly only of the Samaritan text. The critics have taken notice of some variations between the Pentateuch of the Jews and that of the Samaritans; but these varieties of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> chiefly regard the word Gerizim, which the Samaritans seem to have purposely introduced to favour their pretensions, that Mount Gerizim was the place in which the Lord was to be adored. Samaritans adored. The other various readings are of small importance. The religion of this people was at first the Pagan. Every one worshipped the deity they had been used to in their own country (2 Kings xvii. 25, 30, 31.). The Babylonians worshipped Succoth-benoth; the Cuthites, Nergal; the Hamathites, Ashima; the Avites, Nibhaz and Tartak; the Sepharvites, Adrammelech and Ananmelech. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we would enumerate all the names of false gods to whom the Samaritans have paid a sacrilegious worship, we should have enough to do. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is sufficiently perplexed, by reason of the different names by which they were adored by different nations, inasmuch that it would be almost impossible to clear up this affair. See Succoth-benoth, &c. Afterwards, to this profane worship the Samaritans added that of the Lord, the God of Israel, (2 Kings xvii. 29, 30, 31, 32.). They gave a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their little regard to this worship of the true God, when under Antiochus Epiphanes they consecrated their temple at Gerizim to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Argivus. In the time of Alexander the Great, they celebrated the sabbatical year, and consequently the year of jubilee also. We do not know whether they did it exactly at the same time with the Jews, or whether they observed any other epoch; and it is to little purpose that some critics have attempted to ascertain the first beginning of it. Under the kings of Syria they followed the epoch of the Greeks, or that of the Seleucidae, as other people did that were under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Seleucidae. After that Herod had re-established Samaria, and had given it the name of Sebastae, the inhabitants of this city, in their medals, and all public acts, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of this new establishment. But the inhabitants of Samaria, of which the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> were Pagans or Jews, were no rule to the other Samaritans, who probably reckoned their years according to the reigns of the emperors they were subject to, till the time they fell under the jurisdiction of the Mahometans, under which they live at this day; and they reckon their year by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, or, as they speak, according to the reign of Ishmael, or the Ishmaelites. Such of our readers as desire to be further acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the ancient Samaritans, we refer to the works of Josephus, where they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find that subject largely treated of. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, it is objected to them, that they receive only the Pentateuch, and reject all the other books of Scripture, chiefly the prophets, who have more expressly declared the coming of the Messiah.—They have also been accused of believing God to be corporeal, of denying the Holy Ghost, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ reproaches them (John iv. 22.) with worshipping they know not what; and in the place already referred to he seems to exclude them from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, when he says, that "Salvation is of the Jews." True it is, that these words might only signify, that the Messiah was to proceed from the Jews; but the crime of schism alone, and a separation from the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was sufficient to exclude them from salvation. The Samaritan woman is a sufficient testimony that the Samaritans expected a Messiah, who they hoped would clear up all their doubts (John iv. 25.). Several of the inhabitants of Shechem believed at the preaching of Jesus Christ, and several of Samaritans believed at that of St Philip; but it is said, they soon fell back to their former errors, being perverted by Simon Magus. The Samaritans at present are very few in number. Joseph Scaliger, being curious to know their usages, wrote to the Samaritans of Egypt, and to the high priest of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who resided at Neapolis in Syria. They returned two answers to Scaliger, dated in the year of the Hegira 968. These were preserved in the French king's library, and were translated into Latin by Father Morin, and printed in England in the collection of that father's letters, in 1682, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Antiquitates Ecclesiae Orientalis. By these letters it appears, that they believe in God, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Moses, the holy law, the mountain Gerizim, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God, the day of vengeance and of peace; that they value themselves upon observing the law of Moses in many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> more rigidly than the Jews themselves.—They keep the Sabbath with the utmost strictness required by the law, without flinching from the place they are in, but only to the synagogue. They go not out of the city, and abstain from their wives on that day. They never delay circumcision beyond the eighth day. They still sacrifice to this day in the temple on Mount Gerizim, and give to the priest what is enjoined by the law. They do not marry their own nieces, as the Jews do, nor do they allow themselves a plurality of wives. Their hatred for the Jews may be seen through all the history of Josephus, and in several places of the New Testament. The Jewish historian informs us, that under the government of Coponius, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a> night, when they opened the gates of the temple, some Samaritans had scattered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of dead men there, to insult the Jews, and to interrupt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of the festival. The evangelists shew us, that the Jews and Samaritans held no correspondence together (John iv. 9.) "The Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." And the Samaritan woman of Sychar was much surprized that Jesus talked with her, and asked drink of her, being a Samaritan. When our Saviour sent his apostles to preach in Judea, he forbade them to enter into the Samaritan cities, (Mat. x. 5.) because he looked upon them as schismatics, and as strangers to the covenant of Israel. One day when he sent his disciples to provide him a lodging in one of the cities of the Samaritans, they would not entertain him, because they perceived he was going to Jerusalem, (Luke ix. 53.) "Because his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> was as though he would go to Jerusalem." And when the Jews were provoked at the reproaches of Jesus Christ, they told him he was a Samaritan (John viii. 48.), thinking they could say nothing more severe against him. Josephus relates, that some Samaritans having killed several Jews as they were going to the feast at Jerusalem, this occasioned a kind of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between them. The Samaritans continued their fealty to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, when the Jews revolted from them; yet they did not escape from being involved in some of the calamities of their neighbours. There are still at this day some Samaritans at Shechem, otherwise called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAPLOUS">Naplous</a>. They have priests there, who say they are of the family of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>. They have a high-priest, who resides at Shechem, or at Gerizim, who offers sacrifices there, and who declares the feast of the passover, Sambucus, palfower, and all the other feats, to all the dispersed Samaritans. Some of them are to be found at Gaza, some at Damascus, and some at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>.

SAMBUCUS

Pages 87-87

elder, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 43d order, Dumo/se. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. All the sorts of elder are of the deciduous tribe, very hardy, and grow freely anywhere; are generally free shooters, but particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> elder and varieties, which make remarkably strong, jointed hoots, of several feet in length, in one season; and they flower mostly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, except the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>-mote elder, which generally begins flowering in April; and the branches being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, spreading, and very abundant, are exceedingly conspicuous; but they emit a disagreeable odour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are succeeded in most of the sorts by large bunches of ripe berries in autumn, which, although very unpalatable to eat, are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation for making that well known cordial liquor called elder wine, particularly the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-berried elder. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, the elder is both useful and ornamental, especially in extensive grounds.

SAMIAN EARTH

Pages 87-87

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, the name of two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> used in medicine, viz. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> kind, called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> collyrium saminum, being astringent, and therefore good in diarrhoeas, dyteries, and haemorrhages; they also used it externally in inflammations of all kinds. 2. The brownish white kind, called oster famius by Dioscorides; this also stands recommended as an astringent.

SAMIELS

Pages 87-87

the Arabian name of a hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. It blows over the desert in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, and sometimes it continues with all its violence to the very gates of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, but never affects any body within the walls. Some years it does not blow at all, and in others it appears six, eight, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ten times, but seldom continues more than a few minutes at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It often passes with the apparent quickness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. The Arabians and Persians, who are acquainted with the appearance of the sky at or near the time this wind arises, have warning of its approach by a thick haze, which appears like a cloud of dust arising out of the horizon; and they immediately upon this appearance throw themselves with their faces to the ground, and continue in that position till the wind is passed, which frequently happens almost instantaneously; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, on the contrary, they are not careful or brisk enough to take this precaution, which is sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and they get the full force of the wind, it is instant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The above method is the only one which they take to avoid the effects of this fatal blast; and when it is over, they get up and look round them for their companions; and if they see any one lying motionless, they take hold of an arm or leg, and pull and jerk it with some force; and if the limb thus agitated separates from the body, it is a certain sign that the wind has had its full effect; but if, on the contrary, the arm or leg does not come away, it is a sure sign there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> remaining, although to every outward appearance the person is dead; and in that case they immediately cover him or them with clothes, and administer some warm diluting liquor to cause a perspiration, which is certainly but slowly brought about.

SAMOJEDA

Pages 87-87

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Russian empire, between Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> and Archangel, lying along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The inhabitants are extremely rude and barbarous. They travel on the snow on sledges, drawn by an animal like a rein-deer, but with the horns of a stag. Their stature is short; their shoulders and faces are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with flat broad noses, hanging lips, and staring eyes; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> is dark, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; and they have very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they have any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at all, it is idolatry, though there has been some attempt of late to convert them. Their huts are made of birch bark sewed together, and laid upon stakes set in the ground; at the top is a hole to let out the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; the fire is made in the middle, round which they repose in the night.—Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment is hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>.

SAMOLUS

Pages 87-87
water pimpernel; a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria clas, and in the natural method ranking under the 21st order, Precia. See Botany Index.

SAMOS

Pages 87-88

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the promontory Mycale, on the continent of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and opposite to Ephesus; the distance only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stadia (Strabo); a free island, in compass 87 miles (Pliny); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 100 (Isidorus); with a cognominal town (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Horace); famous for the worship and temple of Juno, with a noted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Strabo, Tacitus); and hence their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> exhibited a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a> (Atheneus): The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who, to avoid the opprobrium of tyrants, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of freedom. Samos, though not so happy in producing wine, which Strabo wonders at, all the adjoining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> yielding a generous sort, yet abounds in all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Vasa Samia, among earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, were held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> repute. Samii, the people. Samos (Ovid).—The island is now in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. It is about 32 miles in length, and 22 in breadth, and extremely fertile. The inhabitants live at their ease, their <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> by the Turks being moderate. The women are very nasty and ugly, and they never shift above once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. They are clothed in the Turkish manner, except a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> coif; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hanging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their backs, with plates of silver or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>-tin fastened to the ends.—They have abundance of melons, lentils, kidney-beans, and excellent muscadine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. They have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> figs four times as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort, but not so well salted. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> is very fine, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax admirable; besides which, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> are excellent: they have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and most of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of a ruddy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: they have also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are of white marble. The inhabitants are about 12,000, who are almost all Greeks; and the monks and priests occupy most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island. They have a bishop who resides at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORA">Cora</a>. See Poly-

SAMPAN

Pages 88-88

is a Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, looking almost like a trough; they are made of different dimensions, but are mostly covered. These boats are as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as sloops, but broader, almost like a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> trough; and have at the end one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more decks of bamboo sticks: the cover or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is made of bamboo sticks, arched over in the shape of a grater; and may be raised or lowered at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: the sides are made of boards, with little holes, with shutters instead of windows: the boards are fastened on both sides to posts, which have notches like steps on the inside, that the roof may be let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and rest on them: on both ends of the deck are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> two little doors, at least there is one at the hindmost end. A fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> smooth carpet spread up as far as the boards makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which in the middle consists of loose boards; but this carpet is only made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on. As these boats greatly differ from ours in shape, they are likewise rowed in a different manner; for two rowers, poising themselves at the back end of the sampan, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it forwards very readily by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of two oars; and can almost turn the vessel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they please: the oars, which are covered with a little hollow quadrangular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, are laid on iron swivels, which are fastened in the sides of the sampan: at the iron the oars are pierced, which makes them look a little bent: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, a rower sits before with a short oar; but this he is forced to lay aside when he comes near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> throng of sampans; and this inconvenience has confirmed the Chinese in their old way of rowing. Instead of pitch, they make use of a cement like our putty, which we call chinam, but the Chinese call it kiang. Some authors say that this cement is made of lime and a resin exuding from the tree tong yea, and bamboo ockam. Besides a couple of chairs, they have the following furniture: two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> tables or boards on which some Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are drawn; a lanthorn for the night-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and a pot to boil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> in. They have also a little cover for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> god, decorated with gilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and other ornaments: before him stands a pot filled with ashes, into which the tapers are put before the idol. The candles are nothing else than bamboo chips, to the upper end of which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a>-wood is stuck on with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>. These tapers are everywhere lighted before the idols in the pagodas, and before the doors in the streets; and, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cities, occasion a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> very pernicious to the eyes. Before this idol stands some jinjo, or Chinese brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c. We ought to try whether the Chinese would not like to use juniper-wood instead of sandal-wood; which latter comes from Suratte, and has almost the same smell with juniper.

SAMSON

Pages 88-88

one of the judges of Israel, memorable for his supernatural strength, his victories over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, and his tragic end, as related in the book of Judges. SAMSON's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">Post</a>, a sort of pillar erected in a ship's hold, between the lower deck and the kelson, under the edge of a hatchway, and furnished with several notches that serve as steps to mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> descend, as occasion requires. This post being firmly driven into its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, not only serves to support the beam and fortify the vessel in that place, but also to prevent the cargo or materials contained in the hold, from shifting to the opposite side, by the rolling of the ship in a turbulent and heavy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Books of SAMUEL, two canonical books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, as being usually ascribed to the prophet Samuel. The books of Samuel and the books of Kings are a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reigns of the kings of Israel and Judah; for which reason the books of Samuel are likewise styled the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> books of Kings. Since the first 24 chapters contain all that relates to the History of Samuel, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the first book and all the second include the relation of events that happened after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that prophet, it has been supposed that Samuel was author only of the first 24 chapters, and that the prophets Gad and Nathan finished the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The first book of Samuel comprehends the transactions under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELI">Eli</a> and Samuel, and under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; and also the acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> while he lived under Saul; and is supposed to contain the space of 101 years. The second book contains the history of about 40 years, and is wholly spent in relating the transactions of David's reign.

SAN FERNANDO

Pages 98-98

near the entrance of the Golfo Dolce, in 15 degrees 18 minutes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, has lately been fortified by the Spaniards, for the purpose of checking the Mosquito-men, logwood-cutters, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>-men. It is a very good harbour, with safe anchorage from the north and east winds, in eight fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

SAN JUAN DE PUERTO RICO

Pages 100-100

usually called *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>*, one of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, is situated in about 18° N. Lat. and between 65° 36' and 67° 45' W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, and is about 40 leagues long and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is beautifully diversified with woods, valleys, and plains, and is extremely fertile. It is well watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, abounds with meadows, is divided by a ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> running from east to west, and has a harbour so spacious that the largest ships may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in it with safety. Before the arrival of the Spaniards it was inhabited by 400,000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 500,000 people, who, in a few years, were extirpated by its merciless conquerors. Raynal says, that its whole inhabitants amount at present only to 1,500 Spaniards, Metisses, and Mulattoes, and about 3,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. Thus one of the finest islands in the West Indies has been depopulated by the cruelty, and left uncultivated by the indolence, of its possessors. But it is the appointment of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, who seldom permits flagrant crimes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unpunished, that poverty and wretchedness should be uniform consequences of oppression.

SANA

Pages 88-89
or SANAA, a large, populous, and handsome town of Asia, capital of Arabia Felix, is situated in Proper Yemen, at the foot of Mount Nikkum, on which are still to be seen the ruins of a castle, which the Arabs suppose to have been built by Shem. Near this mountain stands the castle; a rivulet runs upon the other side; and near it is the Buffan el Metwokkel, a spacious garden, which was laid out by Imam Metwokkel, and has been embellished with a fine garden by the reigning imam. The walls of the city, which are built of bricks, exclude this garden, which is inclosed within a wall of its own. The city, properly so called, is not very extensive: one may walk round it all in an hour. The city-gates are seven. Here are a number of mosques, some of which have been built by Turkish pachas. Sana has the appearance of being more populous than it actually is; for the gardens occupy a part of of the space within the walls. In Sana are only 12 public baths; but many noble palaces, three of the most splendid of which have been built by the reigning imam. The palace of the late imam El Manzor, with some others, belong to the royal family, who are very numerous. The Arabian palaces are built in a style of architecture different from ours. The materials are, however, burnt bricks, and sometimes even hewn stones; but the houses of the common people are of bricks which have been dried in the sun. There are no glass windows, except in one palace, near the citadel. The rest of the houses have, instead of windows, merely shutters, which are opened in fair weather, and shut when it is foul. In the last case, the house is lighted by a round wicket, fitted with a piece of Mulcove glass; some of the Arabians use small panes of stained glass from Venice. At Sana, and in the other cities of the East, are great simferas or caravanserais for merchants and travelers. Each different commodity is sold in a separate market. In the market for bread, none but women are to be seen; and their little shops are portable. The several classes of mechanics work, in the same manner, in particular quarters in the open street. Writers go about with their desks, and make out briefs, copybooks, and instruct scholars in the art of writing, all at the same time. There is one market where old clothes are taken in exchange for new. Wood for the carpenter's purpose is extremely dear through Yemen; and wood for the fire at Sana is no less so. All the hills near the city are bleak and bare, and wood is therefore to be brought hither from the distance of three days' journey; and a camel's burden commonly costs two crowns. This scarcity of wood is particularly supplied by the use of a little pit-coal. Peats are burnt here; but they are so bad, that straw must be intermixed to make them burn. Fruits are, however, very plentiful at Sana. Here are more than 20 different species of grapes, which, as they do not all ripen at the same time, continue to afford a delicious refreshment for several months. The Arabs likewise preserve grapes, by hanging them up in their cellars, and eat them almost through the whole year. The Jews make a little wine, and might make more if the Arabs were not such enemies to strong liquors. A Jew convicted of conveying wine into an Arab's house is severely punished; nay, the Jews must even use great caution in buying and selling it among themselves. Great quantities of grapes are dried here; and the exportation of raisins from Sana is considerable. One sort of these grapes is without stones, and contains only a soft grain, the presence of which is not perceptible in eating the raisin. In the castle, which stands on a hill, are two palaces. "I saw (says Niebuhr) about it some ruins of old buildings, but, notwithstanding the antiquity of the place, no remarkable inscriptions. There is the mint, and a range of prisons for persons of different ranks. The reigning imam resides in the city; but several princes of the blood-royal live in the castle. The battery is the most elevated place above these buildings; and there I met with what I had no expectation of, a German mortar, with this inscription, Jorg Selos Gofnick, 1513. I saw also upon the same battery seven iron cannons, partly buried in the sand, and partly set upon broken carriages. These seven small cannons, with six others near the gates, which are fired to announce the return of the different festivals, are all the artillery of the capital of Yemen."

SANADON

Pages 89-89

Noël Étienne, a Jesuit, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1676, and was a distinguished professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a>. He there became acquainted with Huet bishop of Arranches, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was similar to his own. Sanadon afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and was entrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Conti, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Du Morceau. In 1728 he was made librarian to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV., an office which he retained to his death. He died on the 21st September 1733, in the 58th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His works are, 1. Latin Poems, in 12mo, 1715, and reprinted by Barbou, in 8vo, 1754. His style possesses the graces of the Augustan age. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is pure and nervous; his verses are harmonious, and his thoughts are delicate and well chosen; but sometimes his imagination flags. His Latin poems consist of Odes, Elegies, Epigrams, and others, on various subjects. 2. A translation of Horace, with Remarks, in 2 vols. 4to, printed at Paris in 1727; but the best edition of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1735, in 8 vols. 12mo, in which are also inserted the versions and notes of M. Dacier. Sanadon translated with elegance and taste; but he has not preserved the sublimity of the original in the odes, nor the energy and precision in the epistles and satires. In general, his version is rather a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> than a faithful translation. Learned men have justly censured him for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> which he has taken in making considerable changes in the order and structure of the odes. He has also given offence by his uncouth orthography. 3. A Collection of Discourses delivered at different times, which afford strong proofs of his knowledge of oratory and poetry. 4. A book entitled Prières et Instructions Chrétiennes.

SANBALLAT

Pages 89-90

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor of the Cutites or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, was always a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy to the Jews. He was a native of Horon, or Horonaim, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> beyond Jordan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Moabites. He lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Nehemiah, who was his great opponent, and from whose book we learn his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. There is one circumstance related of him which has occasioned some dispute among the learned; and the state of the question is as follows: When Alexander the Great came into Phoenicia, and sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before the city of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, Sanballat quitted the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and went at the head of 8000 men to offer his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to Alexander. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> readily entertained him, and being much solicited by him, gave him leave to erect a temple upon Mount Gerizim, where he constituted his son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. But this story carries a flagrant anachronism: for 120 years before this, that is, in the year of the world 3550, Sanballat was governor of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>; wherefore the learned Dr Prideaux (in his Connection of the Histories of the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>) supposes two Sanballats, and endeavours to reconcile it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, by showing it to be a mistake of Josephus. This author makes Sanballat to flourish in the time of Darius Codomannus, and to build his temple upon Mount Sanballat, Mount Gerizim by licence from Alexander the Great; whereas it was performed by leave from Darius Nothus, in the 15th year of his reign. This takes away the difficulty arising from the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Sanballat, and brings him to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Nehemiah, as the Scripture history requires.

SANCHEZ

Pages 90-90

FRANCOIS, called in Latin Sanctius, was of Las Brocas in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and has been dignified by his own countrymen with the pompous titles of le Pere de la Langue Laine, et le Docteur de tous les Gens de lettres. He wrote, 1. An excellent treatise intitled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> de Caufis Linguae Latinae, which was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1714, in 8vo. The authors of the Port-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Methode de la Langue Latine have been much indebted to this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. 2. The Art of Speaking, and the Method of translating Authors. 3. Several other learned pieces on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>. He died in the year 1600, in his 77th year. We must be careful to distinguish him from another Francois Sanchez, who died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> in 1632. This last was a Portuguese physician who settled at Toulouse, and, though a Christian, was born of Jewish parents. He is said to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. His works have been collected under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> Medica. His juncti sunt tractatus quidam philosophici non infutilis. They were printed at Toulouse in 1636.

SANCHONIATHO

Pages 90-94

a Phenician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and historian, who is said to have flourished before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Semiramis. Of this most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writer, the only remains extant are sundry fragments of cosmogony, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the gods and first mortals, preserved by Eusebius and Theodoret; both of whom speak of Sanchoniatho as an accurate and faithful historian; and the former adds, that his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which was translated by Philo-Byblius from the Phenician into the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, contains many things relating to the history of the Jews which deserve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, both because they agree with the Jewish writers, and because the author received these particulars from the annals of Hierombalus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the god Jao. Several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, however, of great learning, have called in question the very existence of Sanchoniatho, and have contended with much plausibility, that the fragments which Eusebius adopted as genuine upon the authority of Porphyry, were forged by that author, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the pretended translator Philo, from enmity to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and that the Pagans might have something to show of equal antiquity with the books of Moses. These opposite opinions have produced a controversy that has filled volumes, and of which our limits would hardly admit of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>. We shall therefore in few words state what to us appears to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and refer such of our readers as are desirous of fuller information to the works of the authors (A) mentioned at the bottom of the page. The controversy respecting Sanchoniatho resolves itself into two questions: 1. Was there in reality such a writer? 2. Was he of the very remote antiquity which his translator claims for him? That there was really such a writer, and that the fragments preserved by Eusebius are indeed parts of his history, interpolated perhaps by the translator (B), we are compelled to believe by the following reasons. Eusebius, who admitted them into his work as authentic, was one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and a diligent searcher into antiquity. His conduct at the Niceene <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> shows, that on every subject he thought for himself, neither biased by authority to the one side, nor carried over by the rage of innovation to the other. He had better means than any modern writer can have of satisfying himself with respect to the authenticity of a very extraordinary work, which had then but lately been translated into the Greek language, and made generally known; and there is nothing in the work itself, or at least in those parts of it which he has preserved, that could induce a wise and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to obtrude it upon the public as genuine, had he himself suspected it to be spurious. Too many of the Christian fathers were indeed very credulous, and ready to admit the authenticity of writings without duly weighing the merits of their claim; but then such writings were always believed to be favourable to the Christian cause, and inimical to the cause of Paganism. That no man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> could suppose the cosmogony of Sanchoniatho favourable to the cause of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, a farther <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> cannot be requisite than what is furnished by the following extract. "He supposeth, or affirms, that the principles of the universe were a dark and windy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> made of dark air, and a turbulent evening <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>; and that these things were boundless, and for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time had no bound or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. But when this wind fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with his own principles, and a mixture was made, that mixture was called desire or cupid (πάθος). "This mixture completed, was the beginning of the (κτίσις) making of all things. But that wind did not know its own production; and of this, with that wind was begotten Mot, which some call Mud, others the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> of a watery mixture. And of this came all the seed of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of the universe. "But there were certain animals, which had no sense, out of which were begotten intelligent animals, and were called Zophhefemin, that is, the furies or overseers of Heaven; and were formed alike in the shape of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. Thus shone out Mot, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, the lefs and the greater stars. "And the air shining thoroughly with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, by its fiery (A) Bochart, Scaliger, Vossius, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, Dodwell, Stillingfleet, Mosheim's Cudworth, and Warburton. (B) Of these there are indeed several proofs. Philo makes Sanchoniatho speak of Byblus as the most ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Phenicia, which, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, it was not. We read in the book of Judges of Berith or Berytus, the city where Sanchoniatho himself lived; but not of Byblus, which was the native city of Philo, and to which he is therefore partial. He makes him likewise talk of the Greeks at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> long before any of the Grecian states were known or probably peopled. Sanchoniatho's fiery influence on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, winds were begotten, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> and great defluxions of the heavenly waters. And when all these things first were parted, and were separated from their proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the sun, and then all met again in the air, and dalled against one another, and were so broken to pieces; whence thunders and lightnings were made: and at the stroke of their thunders the fore-mentioned intelligent animals were awakened, and frighted with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> stirred in the earth and in the sea: This is their generation of animals. "After these things our author (Sanchoniatho) goes on saying: These things are written in the Cosmogony of Taautus, and in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>; and out of the conjectures, and surer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> signs which his mind <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and found out, and wherewith he hath enlightened us. "Afterwards declaring the names of the winds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south and the rest, he makes this epilogue. But these first men consecrated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out of the earth, and judged them gods, and worshipped them; upon whom they themselves lived, and all their posterity and all before them: to these they made their meat and drink offerings." Then he concludes: "these were the devices of worship agreeing with the weakness and want of boldness in their minds." Let us suppose Eusebius to have been as weak and credulous as the darkest monk in the darkest age of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, a supposition which no man <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make who knows anything of the writings of that eminent historian; what could he see in this senseless jargon, which even a dreaming monk would think of employing in support of Christianity? Eusebius calls it, and calls it truly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> atheism; but could he imagine that an ancient system of atheism would contribute so much to make the Pagans of his age admit as divine revelations the books of the Old and New Testaments, that he should be induced to adopt, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, an impudent forgery not 200 years old as genuine remains of the most remote antiquity? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this Phenician cosmogony be a fabrication of Porphyry, or of the pretended translator, it must surely have been fabricated for some purpose; but it is impossible for us to conceive what purpose either of these writers could have intended to serve by forging a system so extravagantly absurd. Porphyry, though an enemy to the Christians, was not an atheist, and would never have thought of making an atheist of him whom he meant to obtrude upon the world as the rival of Moses. His own principles were those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> Platonists; and had he been the forger of the works which bear the name of Sanchoniatho, instead of the incomprehensible jargon about dark wind, evening chaos, Mot, the overseers of heaven in the shape of an egg, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a> proceeding from the sound of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, we should doubtless have been amused with refined speculations concerning the operations of the Demiurge and the other persons in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> Triad. See Platonism and Porphyry. Father Simon of the oratory imagines * that the purpose for which the history of Sanchoniatho was forged, was to support Paganism, by taking from it its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> and allegories, which were perpetually objected to it by the Christian writers; but this learned man totally mistakes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The primitive Christians were too much attached to allegories themselves to reflect their objections to Paganism on such a foundation: what they objected to that system was the immoral stories told of the priests. To this the pagan priests and philosophers replied, that these stories were only mythologic allegories, which veiled all the great truths of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, Ethics, and Physics. The Christians said, this could not be; for that the stories of the gods had a substantial foundation in fact, these gods being only dead men deified, who, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, had like passions and infirmities with other mortals. This then was the objection which the forger of the works of Sanchoniatho had to remove, if he really forged them in support of Paganism; but, instead of doing so, he gives the genealogy and history of all the greater gods, and shows, that they were men deified after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for the exploits, some of them grossly immoral, which they had performed in this world. We have elsewhere (Polytheism, No. 17.) given his account of the deification of Chrylo, and Ouranos, and Ge, and Hylas, and Mithra; but our readers may not perhaps be ill pleased to accompany him through the history of Ouranos and Cronus, two of his greatest gods; whence it will appear how little his writings are calculated to support the tottering cause of Paganism against the objections which were then urged to it by the Christian apologists. "Ouranos (says he), taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of his father, married Ge his sister, and by her had four sons; Iapetos, who is called Cronus; Betylos; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a>, who is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, or the god of corn; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. But by other wives Ouranos had much issue, wherefore Ge being grieved at it and jealous, reproached Ouranos, so as they parted from each other. But Ouranos, though he parted from her, yet by force invading her, and lying with her when she lifted, went away again; and he also attempted to kill the children he had by her. Ge also often defended or avenged herself, gathering auxiliary powers unto her. But when Cronus came to man's age, using Hermes Trismegistus as his counsellor and attendant (for he was his secretary), he opposed his father Ouranos, avenging his mother. But Cronus had children, Persephone and Athena; the former died a virgin, but by the counsel of the latter Athena, and of Hermes, Cronus made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> a scimitar and a spear. Then Hermes, speaking to the attendants of Cronus with enchanting words, wrought in them a keen desire to fight against Ouranos in behalf of Ge; and thus Cronus warring against Ouranos, drove him out of his kingdom, and succeeded in the imperial power or office. In the fight was taken a well-beloved concubine of Ouranos big with child. Cronus gave her in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to Dagon, and she brought forth at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> what she had in her womb by Ouranos, and called him Demaroon. After these things Cronus builds a wall round about his house, and founds Byblus the first city in Phoenicia. Afterwards Cronus, suspecting his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Atlas, with the advice of Hermes, throwing him into a deep hole of the earth, there buried him, and having a son called Sadid, he dispatched him with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, having a suspicion of him, and deprived his own son of life with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He also cut off the head of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, so that all the gods were amazed at the mind of Cronus. But in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, Ouranos being in flight, or banishment, sends his daughter Astarte, with two other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> Rhea and Dione, to cut off... Sanchotho off Cronus by deceit, whom Cronus taking, made wives of these filters. Ouranos, understanding this, sent Eimarmene and Hore, Fate and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a>, with other auxiliaries, to war against him; but Cronus, having gained the affections of these also, kept them with himself. Moreover, the god Ouranos devised Bactulia, contriving <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> that moved as having life. But Cronus begat on Aftarte <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> daughters called Titanides or Artemides; and he begat on Rhea seven sons, the youngest of whom, as soon as he was born, was consecrated a god. Also by Dionos he had daughters, and by Aftarte moreover two sons, Pothos and Eros, i.e., Cupid and Love. But Dagon, after he had found out <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, corn, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, was called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZEUS">Zeus</a> Aratrius. To Sydye, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, one of the Titanides bare Asklepios. Cronus had also in Persea three sons, 1. Cronus his father's namesake. 2. Zeus Belus. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. Is it conceivable, that a writer so acute as Porphyry, or indeed that any man of common sense, either in his age or in that of Philo, would forge a book filled with such stories as these, in order to remove the Christian objections to the immoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the Pagan divinities? The very supposition is impossible to be made. Nor let any one imagine that Sanchoniatho is here <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> allegorically, and by his tales of Ouranos, and Ge and Cronus, is only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSONIFYING">personifying</a> the heaven, the earth, and time. On the contrary, he affirms us, that Ouranos, or Epigeus, or Autochton (for he gives him all these names) was the son of one Elianus or Hippolitus, who dwelt about Byblus, and that from him the element which is over us was called heaven, on account of its excellent beauty, as the earth was named Ge after his sister and wife. And his translator is very angry * with the Neoteric Greeks, as he calls them, because that, "by a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of force and straining, they laboured to turn all the stories of the gods into allegories and physical discourses." This proves unanswerably, that the author of this book, whoever he was, did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to veil the great truths of religion under the cloak of mythologic allegories; and therefore, if it was forged by Porphyry in support of Paganism, the forger so far mistook the state of the question between him and his adversaries, that he contrived a book, which, if admitted to be ancient, totally overthrew his own cause. The next thing to be inquired into with respect to Sanchoniatho is his antiquity. Did he really live and write at so early a period as Porphyry and Philo pretend?
