We think he did not; and what contributes not a little to confirm us in our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is that mark of national vanity and partiality, common to after-times, in making the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> original, and conveyed from Phoenicia into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. This, however, furnishes an additional proof that Porphyry was not the forger of the work; for he well knew that the mysteries had their origin in Egypt (see Mysteries), and would not have fallen into such a blunder. He is guilty, indeed, of a very great anachronism, when he ranks Sanchoniatho <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Semiramis, and yet pretends that what he writes of the Jews is compiled from the records of Hierombalus the priest of the god Jao; for Bochart has made it appear in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> probable †, that Hierombalus or Jeromb <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">baal</a> is the Jerub-baal or Gideon of Scripture. Between the reign of Semiramis and the Trojan war a period elapsed of near 800 years, whereas Gideon flourished not above seventy years before the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. But supposing Sanchoniatho to have really consulted the records of Gideon, it by no means follows that he flourished at the same period with that judge of Israel. He speaks of the building of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> as an ancient thing, while our best chronologers ‡ place it in the time of Gideon. Indeed, were we certain that any writings had been left by that holy man, we should be obliged to conclude, that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract of time had intervened between the death of their author and their falling into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Sanchoniatho; for, surely, they could not, in a short period, have been so completely corrupted as to give any countenance to his impious absurdities. His atheistic cosmogony he does not indeed pretend to have got from the annals of the priest of Jao, but from records which were deposited in his own town of Berytus by Thoth a Phoenician philosopher, who was afterwards made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Egypt. But surely the annals of Gideon, if written by himself, and preserved pure to the days of Sanchoniatho, must have contained so many truths of the Mosaic religion, as must have prevented any man of sense from adopting so impossible a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> as Thoth's, though sanctioned by the greatest name of profane antiquity. Stillingsfeet indeed thinks it most probable that Sanchoniatho became acquainted with the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the life of Jerub-baal from annals written by a Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. He observes, that immediately after the death of Gideon, the Israelites, with their usual propensity to idolatry, worshipped Baal-berith, or the idol of Berytus, the town in which Sanchoniatho lived; and from this circumstance he concludes that there must have been such an intercourse between the Hebrews and Berytians, that in process of time the latter people might assume to themselves the Jerub-baal of the former, and hand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his actions to posterity as those of a priest instead of a great commander. All this may be true; but if so, it amounts to a demonstration that the antiquity of Sanchoniatho is not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> by many ages as that which is claimed for him by Philo and Porphyry, though he may still be more ancient, as we think Volfius has proved him to be *, than any other profane historian whose writings have come down to us either entire or in fragments. But granting the authenticity of Sanchoniatho's history, what, it may be asked, is the value of his fragments, that we should be at any trouble to ascertain whether they be genuine remains of high antiquity, or the forgeries of a modern impostor? We answer, with the illustrious Stillingsfeet, that though these fragments contain such absurdities as it would be a disgrace to reason to suppose credible; though the whole cosmogony is the grossest fling of atheism; and though many persons make a figure in the history, whose very existence may well be doubted; yet we, who have in our hands the light of divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, may in this dungeon discover many excellent relics of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, which throw no feeble light upon many passages of holy scripture, as they give us the origin and progress of that idolatry which was so long the opprobrium of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They furnish too a complete refutation of the extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, and show, if they be genuine, that the world is indeed not older than it is said to be by Moses. We shall conclude the article by earnestly recommending to our readers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANCTIFICATION">Sanctification</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of sanctifying, or rendering a thing holy. The reformed divines define sanctification to be an act of God's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, by which a person's desires and affections are alienated from the world; and by which he is made to die to sin, and to live to righteousness; or, in other words, to feel an abhorrence of all vice, and a love of religion and virtue. Sanction, the authority given to a judicial act, by which it becomes legal and authentic. Sanctorius, or Sanctorio, a most ingenious and learned physician, was professor in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, in the beginning of the 17th century. He contrived a kind of statical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, by means of which, after estimating the aliments received, and the sensible discharges, he was enabled to determine with great exactness the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of insensible perspiration, as well as what kind of victuals and drink increased or diminished it. On these experiments he erected a curious system, which he published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of De Medicina Statica; which is translated into English by Dr Quincy. Sanctorius published several other treatises, which showed great abilities and learning. Sanctuary, among the Jews, also called Sanctum sanctorum, or Holy of holies, was the holiest and most retired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, in which the ark of the covenant was preserved, and into which none but the high-priest was allowed to enter, and that only once a year, to intercede for the people. Some distinguish the sanctuary from the sanctum sanctorum, and maintain that the whole temple was called the sanctuary. To try and examine anything by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the sanctuary, is to examine it by a just and equal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>; because, among the Jews, it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the priests to keep <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> weights, to serve as standards for regulating all weights by, though these were not at all different from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> or profane weights. Sanctuary, in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, is also used for that part of the church in which the altar is placed, encompassed with a rail or balustrade. Sanctuary, in our ancient customs, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">Asylum</a>. Sand, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural History</a>, properly denotes small particles of siliceous stones. Sands are subject to be variously blended, both with different substances, as that of tacks, &c.; and hence, as well as from their various colours, are subdivided into, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> sands, whether pure or mixed with other arenaceous or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> particles; of all which there are several kinds, differing no less in the fineness of their particles than in the different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, from a bright and shining white, to a brownish, yellowish, greenish, &c., white. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and reddish sands, both pure and impure. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> sands, whether pure or mixed, are also very numerous. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> sands, distinguished in the same manner. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sands, of which there are only two varieties, viz. a fine shining greyish-black sand, and another of a fine shining reddish-black colour. 6. The green kind; of which there is only one known <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. a coarse variegated dulky green sand, common in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>. Sand is of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the glass manufacture; a white kind of sand being employed for making of the white glass, and a coarse greenish-looking sand for the green glass. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> it seems to be the office of sand to render uncultivated or clayey earths fertile, and fit to support vegetables, by making them more open and loose. Sand-bags, in the art of war. See Sacks of Earth. Sand-eel. See Ammodytes, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Sand-floods, a name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of sand so common in the deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. Mr Bruce gives the following accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of some that he saw in travelling through that long and dreary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. "At one o'clock (says he) we alighted among some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a> trees at Waad el Haliboub, having gone twenty-one miles. We were here at once surprised and terrified by a sight surely one of the most magnificent in the world. In that vast expanse of desert from west and to north-west of us, we saw a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prodigious pillars of sand at different distances, at times moving with great celerity, at others flanking on with a majestic flowness; at intervals we thought they were coming in a few minutes to overwhelm us; and small quantities of sand did actually more than once reach us. Again they would retreat so as to be almost out of sight, their tops reaching to the very clouds. There the tops often separated from the bodies; and these, once disjointed, dispersed in the air, and did not appear more. Sometimes they were broken near the middle, as if struck with a large cannon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. About noon they began to advance with considerable swiftness upon us, the wind being very strong." strong at north. Eleven of them ranged alongside of us about the distance of three miles. The greatest diameter of the largest appeared to me at that distance as if it would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> ten feet. They retired from us with a wind at south-east, leaving an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon my mind to which I can give no name, though surely one ingredient in it was fear, with a considerable deal of wonder and astonishment. It was in vain to think of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, the swiftest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or fastest failing ship could be of no use to carry us out of this danger; and the full persuasion of this riveted me as if to the spot where I stood, and let the camels <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> on me so much in my state of lameness, that it was with some difficulty I could overtake them. "The same appearance of moving pillars of sand presented themselves to us this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in form and disposition like those we had seen at Waadi Halboub, only they seemed to be more in number and less in size. They came several times in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> upon us, that is, I believe, within less than two miles. They began immediately after sunrise, like a thick wood, and almost darkened the sun; his rays shining through them for near an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, gave them an appearance of pillars of fire. Our people now became desperate: the Greek shrieked out, and said it was the day of judgement. Ifmael pronounced it to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, and the Tocorories, that the world was on fire. I asked Idris if ever he had before seen such a sight? He said he had often seen them as terrible, though never worse; but what he feared most was that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> redness in the air, which was a sure prelude of the coming of the simoom." See SIMOON. The flowing of sand, though far from being so tremendous and hurtful as in Arabia, is of very bad consequences in this country, as many valuable pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> have thus been entirely lost; of which we give the following instances from Mr Pennant, together with a probable means of preventing them in future. "I have more than once (says he), on the eastern coasts of Scotland, observed the calamitous state of several extensive tracts, formerly in a most flourishing condition, at present covered with sands, unstable as those of the deserts of Arabia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Furlie, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Aberdeen, is now reduced to two farms, and above £500. a year lost to the Errol family, as appears by the oath of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> in 1600, made before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of session, to ascertain the minister's salary. Not a vestige is to be seen of any buildings, unless a fragment of the church. "The estate of Coubin, near Forres, is another melancholy instance. This tract was once worth £2000. a-year, at this time overwhelmed with sand. This strange inundation was still in motion in 1769, chiefly when a strong wind prevailed. Its motion is so rapid, that I have been assured, that an apple-tree has been covered with it in one season, that only the very summit appeared. This distress was brought on about ninety years ago, and was occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down some trees, and pulling up the bent or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> which grew on the sand hills; which at last gave rise to the act of 15 George III. c. 33, to prohibit the destruction of this useful plant. "I beg leave to suggest to the public a possible means of putting a stop to these destructive ravages. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> hath kindly formed this plant to grow only in pure sand. Mankind was left to make, in after-times, an application of it suitable to their wants. The sand-hills, on a portion of the Flinthire shores, in the parish of Llanasa, are covered with it naturally, and kept firm in their place. The Dutch perhaps owe the existence of part at least of their country to the sowing of it on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOBILE">mobile</a> forum, their sand-banks. "My humane and amiable friend, the late Benjamin Stillingtonfleet, Esq. recommended the sowing of this plant on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> wilds of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, that its matted roots might prevent the deluges of sand which that country experiences. It has been already remarked, that wherefoever this plant grows the salutary effects are soon observed to follow. A single plant will fix the sand, and gather it into a hillock; these hillocks, by the increase of vegetation, are formed into larger, till by degrees a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> is made often against the encroachments of the sea; and might as often prove preventative of the calamity in question. I cannot, therefore, but recommend the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> to the inhabitants of many parts of North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The plant grows in most places near the sea, and is known to the Highlanders by the name of murah; to the English by that of bent-flar, mat-graft, or marram. Linnaeus calls it arundo arenaria. The Dutch call it helm. This plant hath stiff and sharp-pointed leaves, growing like a rush, a foot and a half long: the roots both creep and penetrate deeply into their sandy beds: the stalk bears an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> five or six inches long, not unlike rye; the seeds are small, brown, and roundish. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, as old Gerard observes, no cattle will eat or touch this vegetable, allotted for other purposes, subservient to the use of mankind." SAND-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIPER">Piper</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRINGA">TRINGA</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">SAND-Stone</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> stone of which there are numerous varieties, arising not only from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, but also in the nature and proportions of the constituent parts. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a> Index. There is a singular variety of sand-stone, which consists of small grains of hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a> which strike fire with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> united with some micaceous particles. This variety is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, the flexibility depending on the micaceous part and softness of the gluten with which the particles are cemented. This elastic stone is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>. There are also two tables of white marble, kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Borghese at Rome, which have the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. But the sparry particles of their substance, though transparent, are rather soft, and may be easily separated by the nail. They effervescence with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and there is a small mixture of minute particles of talk or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICA">mica</a>. Sand-stones are of great use in buildings which are required to resist air, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and fire. Some of them are soft in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, but become hard when exposed to the air. The loose ones are most useful, but the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and hard ones crack in the fire, and take a polish when used as grindstones. Stones of this kind ought therefore to be nicely examined before they are employed for valuable purposes.

SANDAL

Pages 94-96

in antiquity, a rich kind of slipper worn on the feet by the Greek and Roman ladies, made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other precious stuff; consisting of a sole, with an hollow at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to embrace the ankle, but leaving the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foot bare. Sandal, is also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> or slipper worn by the pope and other Romish prelates when they officiate. SANDARACH. It is also the name of a sort of slipper worn by several congregations of reformed monks. This last consists of no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> sole, fastened with latches or buckles, all the rest of the foot being left bare. The Capuchins wear sandals; the Recollets, clogs; the former are of leather, and the latter of wood. **SANDAL-WOOD.** See SAUNDERS. **SANDARACH,** in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>,* a very beautiful native fossil, though too often confounded with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fictitious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> arsenic, and with the red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> formed by melting the common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>. It is a pure substance, of a very even and regular structure, is throughout of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> which our dyers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> fusculet, and is considerably transparent even in the thickest pieces. But though, with respect to colour, it has the advantage of cinnabar while in the mats, it is vastly inferior to it when both are reduced to powder. It is moderately hard, and remarkably heavy; and, when exposed to a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, melts and flows like <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> set on fire, it burns very briskly. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and is sold to the painters, who find it a very fine and valuable red: but its virtues or qualities in medicine are no more ascertained at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than those of the yellow orpiment. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">Gum</a> SANDARACH,** is a dry hard resin, usually in the form of loose granules, of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-bean, or larger; of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> whitish yellow colour, transparent, and of a resinous smell, brittle, very inflammable, of an acid and aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and diffusing a very pleasant smell when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> the prevailing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this gum was obtained from the *juniperus communis*; but this plant does not grow in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> only sandarach is produced; for the gum sandarach of the shops is brought from the southern provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>. About five or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred quintals of it are exported every year from Santa Cruz, Mogador, and Safi. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the country it is called el graffa. The tree which produces it is a *Thuja,* found also by M. Vahl in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. It was made known several years ago by Dr Shaw, who named it *Cupressus frutica quadivalvis, Equifeti inflar articulatis*; but neither of these learned men was acquainted with the economical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this tree; probably because, being not common in the northern part of Barbary, the inhabitants find little advantage in collecting the resin which exudes from it. M. Schoutboe (a), who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of *Thuja* in question, says that it does not rise to more than the height of 20 or 30 feet at most, and that the diameter of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> does not exceed ten or twelve inches. It distinguishes itself, on first view, from the two other species of the same genus, cultivated in gardens, by having a very distinct trunk, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a real tree; whereas in the latter the branches rise from the root, which gives them the appearance rather of bushes. Its branches also are more articulated and brittle. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are not very apparent, shew themselves in April; and the fruit, which are of a spherical form, Sandarach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in September. When a branch of this tree is held to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it appears to be interpered with a multitude of transparent vesicles which contain the resin. When these vesicles burst in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, a resinous juice exudes from the trunk and branches, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in other coniferous trees. This resin is the sandarach, which is collected by the inhabitants of the country, and carried to the ports, from which it is transported to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is employed in making some kinds of sealing-wax, and in different sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. In 1793 a hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of it cost in Morocco from 13 to 13½ piastres, which make from about £1. 5s. to £1. 7s. 6d. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The duty on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> was about 7s. 6d. sterling per quintal. Sandarach, to be good, must be of a bright-yellow colour, pure and transparent. It is an article very difficult to be adulterated. Care, however, must be taken, that the Moors do not mix with it too much sand. It is probable that a tree of the same kind produces the gum sandarach of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, which is exported in pretty considerable quantities. **Pounded SANDARACH.** See POUNCE. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDEMANIANS">SANDEMANIANS</a>,** in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> that originated in Scotland about the year 1728; where it is at this time distinguished by the name of Glaister, after its founder Mr John Glaist, who was a minister of the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in that kingdom; but being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of subverting the national covenant, and tapping the foundation of all national establishments by the kirk judiciary, was expelled by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> from the church of Scotland. His sentiments are fully explained in a tract published at that time, intitled, "The Testimony of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> of Martyrs," and preserved in the first volume of his works. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of Mr Glaist's expulsion, his adherents formed themselves into churches, conformable in their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> to what they apprehended to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the first churches recorded in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Soon after the year 1755, Mr Robert Sandeman, an elder in one of these churches in Scotland, published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters addressed to Mr Hervey, occasioned by his Theron and Aspasio; in which he endeavours to show, that his notion of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> is contradictory to the scripture account of it, and could only serve to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> men, professedly holding the doctrines <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Calvinistic, to establish their own righteousness upon their frames, inward feelings, and various acts of faith. In these letters Mr Sandeman attempts to prove, that faith is neither more nor less than a simple assent to the divine testimony concerning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, recorded in the New Testament; and he maintains, that the word faith, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, is constantly used by the apostles to signify what is denoted by it in common discourse, viz. a persuasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of any proposition, and that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between believing any common testimony, and believing the apostolic testimony, except that which results from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the testimony itself. This led the way to a controversy, among those who were called Calvinists, concerning the nature of justifying faith; and those who adopted Mr Sandeman's notion... Sandemanians, formed themselves into church order, in strict fellowship with the churches in Scotland, but holding no kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with other churches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> opinions and practices in which this sect differs from other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, are, their weekly administration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-feasts, of which every member is not only allowed but required to partake, and which consist of their dining together at each other's houses in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the morning and afternoon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; their kifs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> used on this occasion, at the admission of a new member, and at other times, when they deem it to be necessary or proper; their weekly collection before the Lord's Supper, for the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and defraying other expenses; mutual exhortation; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from blood and things strangled; washing each other's feet, the precept concerning which, as well as other precepts, they understand literally; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of goods, so far as that every one is obliged to give all that he has in his possession and power as liable to the calls of the poor and church; and the unlawfulness of laying up treasures on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, by setting them apart for any distant, future, and uncertain use. They allow of public and private diversions, so far as they are not connected with circumstances really sinful; but apprehending a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to be sacred, disapprove of playing at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, dice, &c. They maintain a plurality of elders, pastors, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, in each church; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the presence of two elders in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of discipline, and at the administration of the Lord's Supper. In the choice of these elders, want of learning, and engagements in trade, &c. are no sufficient objection; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriages disqualify for the office; and they are ordained by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and fasting, imposition of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and giving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of fellowship. In their discipline they are strict and severe; and think themselves obliged to separate from the communion and worship of all such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> as appear to them not to profess the simple truth for their only ground of hope, and who do not walk in obedience to it. We shall only add, that in every church transaction, they esteem unanimity to be absolutely necessary. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the account which they have published of their tenets and practices, it does not seem to be probable that their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> should be very considerable.

SANDIVER

Pages 96-96

an old name for a whitish substance which is thrown up from the metal, as it is called, of which glass is made; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on its surface, is skimmed off. Sandiver is also plentifully ejected from volcanoes; some is of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and others tinged bluish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> yellowish. Sandiver is said to be detergent, and good for foulnesses of the skin. It is also used by gilders of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>.

SANDIX

Pages 96-96

a kind of minium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, made of ceruse, but much inferior to the true minium.

SANDOMIR

Pages 96-96

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the same name, in Little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>. The Swedes blew up the castle in 1656; and here, in 1659, was a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between the Tartars and Russians. It is 84 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>. Lat. 49. 26. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20. 10.

SANDORICUM

Pages 96-96

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23d order, Trilliatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SANDPU

Pages 96-96
or SANPOO, the vulgar name of a river in the East Indies, which is one of the largest in the world; but it is better known by that of Burrampooter. Of this most majestic body of waters we have the following very animated account in Maurice's Indian Antiquities. "An object equally novel and grand now claims our attention; so novel, as not to have been known to Europeans in the real extent of its magnificence before year 1765, and so awfully grand, that the astonished geographer, thinking the language of prose inadequate to convey his conception, has had recourse to the more expressive and energetic language of poetry: Scarce the Muse herself Dares stretch her wing o'er this enormous mass Of rushing waters; to whose dread expanse, Continuous depth, and wondrous length of course, Our floods are rills. This stupendous object is the Burrampooter, a word which in Sanscrit signifies the son of Brahma; for no meaner origin could be assigned to so wonderful a progeny. This supreme monarch of Indian rivers derives its source from the opposite side of the same mountain from which the Ganges springs, and taking a bold sweep towards the east, in a line directly opposite to the course of that river, washes the vast country of Tibet, where, by way of distinction, it is denominated Sanpoor, or the river. Winding with a rapid current through Tibet, and, for many a league, amidst dreary deserts and regions remote from the habitations of men, it waters the borders of the territory of Lalla, the residence of the grand Lama; and then deviating with a cometary irregularity, from an east to a south-east course, the mighty wanderer approaches within 200 miles of the western frontiers of the vast empire of China. From this point its more direct path to the ocean lay through the gulf of Siam; but with a deftly course peculiar to itself, it suddenly turns to the west through Assam, and enters Bengal on the north-east quarter. Circling round the western point of the Garow mountains, the Burrampooter now takes a southern direction; and for 60 miles before it meets the Ganges, its sister in point of origin, but not its rival in point of magnitude, glides majestically along in a stream which is regularly from four to five miles wide, and but for its freshness, Mr Rennell says, might pass for an arm of the sea. About 40 miles from the ocean these mighty rivers unite their streams; but that gentleman is of opinion that their junction was formerly higher up, and that the accumulation of two such vast bodies of water, scooped out the amazing bed of the Megna lake. Their present confluence is below Luckipoor; and by that confluence a body of fresh running water is produced, hardly equalled, and not exceeded, either in the old or the new hemisphere. So stupendous is that body of water, that it has formed a gulf of such extent as to contain islands that rival our Isle of Wight in size and fertility; and with such restless violence does it rush into the ocean, that in the rainy season the sea itself, or at least its surface, is perfectly fresh for many leagues out."

SANDS

Pages 96-98

GOODWIN, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Godwin, are dangerous sand banks. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, a town of Kent, and one of the cinque ports, having the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an earldom. It consists of about 1500 houses, most of them old, and built with wood, though there are a few new ones built with brick and flints. It has three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow streets paved, and thirty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-streets or alleys, with about 6000 inhabitants, but no particular manufacture. The town is walled round, and also fortified with ditches and ramparts; but the walls are much decayed, on account of the harbour being so choked up with sand that a ship of 100 tons burthen cannot get in. E. Long. 1° 20'. N. Lat. 51° 20'. Sandwich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of islands in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lying near <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NEW_IRELAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, were among the last discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, who so named them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sandwich, under whose administration these discoveries were made. They consist of 11 islands, extending in latitude from 18° 34' to 22° 15' N. and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from 150° 54' to 160° 24' W. They are called by the natives, Owhyhee, Mowee, Ranai, Motrotot, Tahoorowa, Woahoo, Attoo, Nechecheewu, Oreehoua, Morotinne, and Tahoraa, all inhabited except the two last. An account of the most remarkable of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in their alphabetical order, in their proper places in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of these islands differs very little from that of the West Indies in the same latitude, though perhaps more temperate; and there are no traces of those violent winds and hurricanes, which render the stormy months in the West Indies so dreadful. There is also more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> at the Sandwich isles, where the mountainous parts being generally enveloped in a cloud, successive showers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the inland parts, with fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and a clear sky, on the sea shore. Hence it is, that few of those inconveniences, to which many tropical countries are subject, either from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or moisture, are experienced here. The winds, in the winter months, are generally from east-south-east to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east. The vegetable productions are nearly the same as those of the other islands in this ocean; but the taro root is here of a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit trees thrive not in such abundance as in the rich plains of Otaheite, but produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fruit. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes are of a very unusual size, some of them measuring 11 inches and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> in circumference, and having 14 feet eatable. There is also a root of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, shaped like a yam, and from six to ten pounds in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, the juice of which is very sweet, of a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and is an excellent substitute for sugar. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> are confined to the three usual sorts, hogs, dogs, and rats. The fowls are also of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort; and the birds are beautiful and numerous, though not various. Goats, pigs, and European seeds, were left by Captain Cook; but the possession of the goats soon gave rise to a contest between two districts, in which the breed was entirely destroyed. The inhabitants are undoubtedly of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> that possesses the islands south of the equator; and in their persons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, customs, and manners, approach nearer to the New Zealanders than to their less distant neighbours, either of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> or Friendly Islands. They are in general about the middle size, and well made; they walk very gracefully, run nimbly, and are capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fatigue. Many of both sexes have fine open countenances; and the women in particular Sandwich have good eyes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, with a sweetness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of look, that render them very engaging. There is one peculiarity, characteristic of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of these islands, that even in the handsomest faces there is a fulness of the nostril, without any flatness or spreading of the nose. They suffer their beards to grow, and wear their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> after various fashions. The dress of both men and women nearly resemble those of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and both sexes wear necklaces of small variegated shells. Tattowing the body is practised by every colony of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and arms of the women are also very neatly marked, and they have the singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of tattowing the tip of the tongue. Like the New Zealanders, they have adopted the method of living together in villages, containing from 100 to 200 houses, built pretty closely together, without any order, and having a winding path between them. They are generally flanked, towards the sea, with detached walls, which are meant both for shelter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. These walls consist of loose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the inhabitants are very dexterous in shifting them suddenly to such places as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the attack may require. In the sides of the hills, or surrounding eminences, they have also little holes, or caves, the entrance to which is also secured by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of the same kind. They serve for places of retreat in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of extremity, and may be defended by a single person against several assailants. Their houses are of different sizes, some of them being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and commodious, from 40 to 50 feet long, and from 20 to 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; while others are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> hovels. The food of the lower class consists principally of fish and vegetables, to which the people of higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> add the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of dogs and hogs. The manner of spending their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> admits of little variety. They rise with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and, after enjoying the cool of the evening, retire to rest a few hours after luncheon. The making of canoes, mats, &c., forms the occupations of the men; the women are employed in manufacturing cloth, and the servants are principally engaged in the plantations and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. Their idle hours are filled up with various amusements, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOXING">boxing</a>, wrestling, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> bear a great resemblance to those of the Southsea islands. Their plantations, which are spread over the whole sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, consist of the taro, or eddy-root, and sweet potatoes, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the clove-trees set in rows. The bottoms of their canoes are of a single piece of wood, hollowed out to the thickness of an inch, and brought to a point at each end. The sides consist of three boards, each about an inch thick, neatly fitted and lashed to the bottom part. Some of their double canoes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> 70 feet in length, three and a half in depth, and twelve in breadth. Their cordage, fish-hooks, and fishing-tackle, differ but little from those of the other islands. Among their arts must not be forgotten that of making <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which they have in great abundance, and of a good quality. Their instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> are spears, daggers, clubs, and slings; and for defensive armour they wear strong mats, which are not easily penetrated by such weapons as theirs. As the islands are not united under one sovereign, wars are frequent among them, which, no doubt, contribute greatly to reduce the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants, which, according to the proportion assigned to each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, does not exceed 400,000. The same system of subordination prevails here here as at the other illands, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority on the part of the chiefs, and the same unresisting submission on the part of the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is likewise monarchical and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. At Owhyhee there is a regular society of priests living by themselves, and distinct in all respects from the rest of the people. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> sacrifices are here frequent; not only at the commencement of a war, or any signal enterprise, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of every considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> calls for a repetition of these horrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>. Notwithstanding the irreparable loss in the death of Captain Cook, who was here murdered through sudden resentment and violence, they are acknowledged to be of the most mild and affectionate disposition. They live in the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and friendship with each other; and in hospitality to strangers they are not exceeded even by the inhabitants of the Friendly Islands. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> capacity seems, in no respect, below the common standard of mankind; and their improvements in agriculture, and the perfection of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, are certainly adequate to the circumstances of their situation, and the natural advantages which they enjoy.

SANDYS

Pages 98-98

GEORGE, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the foregoing Sir Edwin, and youngest son of Archbishop Sandys, was born in 1577. He was a very accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; travelled over several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and the East; and published a relation of his journey in folio, in 1615. He made an elegant translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses; and composed some poetical pieces of his own, that were greatly admired in the times of their being written. He also paraphrased the Psalms; and has left behind him a Translation, with Notes, of one Sacred Drama written originally by Grotius, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Christus Patiens; on which, and Adamus Exul, and Mænianus, is founded Lauder's impudent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of plagiarism against our immortal Mitton. Our author became one of the privy chamber to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and died in 1643.

SANHEDRIM

Pages 98-99
or SANHEDRIN, from the Greek word Συνέδριον, which signifies a council or assembly of persons sitting together, was the name whereby the Jews called the great council of the nation, assembled in an apartment of the temple of Jerusalem to determine the most important affairs both of their church and state. This council consisted of seventy senators. The room they met in was a rotunda, half of which was built without the temple, and half within; that is, one semicircle was within the compass of the temple; the other semicircle, they tell us, was built without, for the senators to sit in; it being unlawful for any one to sit down in the temple. The Nasi, or prince of the sanhedrin, sat upon a throne at the end of the hall, having his deputy at his right hand, and his sub-deputy on his left. The other senators were ranged in order on each side. The rabbins pretend, that the sanhedrin has always subsisted in their nation from the time of Moses down to the destruction of the temple by the Romans. They date the establishment of it from what happened in the wilderness, some time after the people departed from Sinai (Num. xi. 16), in the year of the world 2514. Moses, being discouraged by the continual murmurings of the Israelites, addressed himself to God, and desired to be relieved, at least, from some part of the burden of the government. Then the Lord said to him, "Gather unto me 70 men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them unto the tabernacle of the congregation, that they may stand there with thee: And I will come down and talk with thee there; and I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone." The Lord, therefore, poured out his spirit upon these men, who began at that time to prophesy, and have not ceased from that time. The sanhedrin was composed of 70 counsellors, or rather 72, six out of each tribe; and Moses, as president, made up the number 73. To prove the uninterrupted succession of the judges of the sanhedrin, there is nothing unattempted by the partisans of this opinion. They find a proof where others cannot so much as perceive any appearance or shadow of it. Grotius may be consulted in many places of his commentaries, and in his first book De jure belli et pacis, c. 3. art. 20. and Selden de Synedriis veterum Hebræorum. Also, Calmet's Dissertation concerning the polity of the ancient Hebrews, printed before his Comment upon the Book of Numbers. As to the personal qualifications of the judges of this bench, their birth was to be untainted. They were often taken from the race of the priests or Levites, or out of the number of the inferior judges, or from the lesser Sanhedrim, lesser sanhedrim, which consisted only of 23 judges. They were to be skilful in the law, as well traditional as written. They were obliged to study magic, divination, fortune-telling, physic, astrology, arithmetic, and languages. The Jews say, they were to know to the number of 70 tongues; that is, they were to know all the tongues, for the Hebrews acknowledged but 70 in all, and perhaps this is too great a number. Eunuchs were excluded from the sanhedrim, because of their cruelty, infamers, decrepid persons, players at games of chance, such as had any bodily deformities, those that had brought up pigeons to decoy others to their pigeon-houses, and those that made a gain of their fruits in the sabbatical year. Some also exclude the high-priest and the king, because of their too great power; but others will have it, that the kings always presided in the sanhedrim, while there were any kings in Israel. Lastly, it was required, that the members of the sanhedrim should be of a mature age, a handsome person, and of considerable fortune. We speak now according to the notions of the rabbins, without pretending to warrant their opinions. The authority of the great sanhedrim was vastly extensive. This council decided such causes as were brought before it by way of appeal from the inferior courts. The king, the high-priest, the prophets, were under its jurisdiction. If the king offended against the law, for example, if he married above 18 wives, if he kept too many horses, if he hoarded up too much gold and silver, the sanhedrim had him stripped and whipped in their presence. But whipping, they say, among the Hebrews was not at all ignominious; and the king bore this correction by way of penance, and himself made choice of the person that was to exercise this discipline over him. Also the general affairs of the nation were brought before the sanhedrim. The right of judging in capital cases belonged to this court, and this sentence could not be pronounced in any other place, but in the hall called Laachar-haggazith, or the hall paved with stones, supposed by some to be the Astheggeos, or pavement, mentioned in John xix. 13. From whence it came to pass, that the Jews were forced to quit this hall when the power of life and death was taken out of their hands, 40 years before the destruction of their temple, and three years before the death of Jesus Christ. In the time of Moses this council was held at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony. As soon as the people were in possession of the land of promise, the sanhedrim followed the tabernacle. It was kept successively at Gilgal, at Shiloh, at Kirjath-jearim, at Nob, at Gibeon in the house of Obed-edom; and lastly, it was settled at Jerusalem, till the Babylonish captivity. During the captivity it was kept up at Babylon. After the return from Babylon, it continued at Jerusalem to the time of the Sicarii, or Assassins. Then finding that these profligate wretches, whose number increased every day, sometimes escaped punishment by the favour of the president or judges, it was removed to Hanoth, which were certain abodes situated, as the rabbins tell us, upon the mountain of the temple. From thence they came down into the city of Jerusalem, withdrawing themselves by degrees from the temple. Afterwards they removed to Jamia, thence to Jericho, to Uzzah, to Sepharvaim, to Bethanaim, to Sephoris, last of all to Tiberias, where they continued to the time of their utter extinction. And this is the account the Jews themselves give us of Sanhedrim, the sanhedrim. But the learned do not agree with them in all this. Father Petavius fixes the beginning of the sanhedrim not till Gabinius was governor of Judea, who, according to Josephus, erected tribunals in the five principal cities of Judea; at Jerusalem, at Gadara, at Amathus, at Jericho, and at Sephora or Sephoris, a city of Galilee. Grotius places the origin of the sanhedrim under Mozes, as the rabbins do; but he makes it determine at the beginning of Herod's reign. Mr Balfour at first thought that the sanhedrim began under Gabinius; but afterwards he places it under Judas Maccabeus, or under his brother Jonathan. We see indeed, under Jonathan Maccabeus, (1 Macc. xii. 6.), in the year 3860, that the senate with the high-priest sent an embassy to the Romans. The rabbins say, that Alexander Janneus, king of the Jews, of the race of the Asmoneans, appeared before the sanhedrim, and claimed a right of sitting there, whether the senators would or not. Josephus informs us, that when Herod was but yet governor of Galilee, he was summoned before the senate, where he appeared. It must be therefore acknowledged, that the sanhedrim was in being before the reign of Herod. It was in being afterwards, as we find from the Gospel and from the Acts. Jesus Christ in St Matthew (v. 22.) distinguishes two tribunals—“Whoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgement.” This, they say, is the tribunal of the 23 judges. “And whosoever shall fall to his brother Raca, shall be in danger of the council;” that is, of the great sanhedrim, which had the right of life and death, at least generally, and before this right was taken away by the Romans. Some think that the jurisdiction of the council of 23 extended to life and death also; but it is certain that the sanhedrim was superior to this council. See also Mark xiii. 9. xiv. 55. xv. 1.; Luke xxii. 52, 66.; John xi. 47.; Acts iv. 15. v. 21. where mention is made of the synedrion or sanhedrim. From all this it may be concluded, that the origin of the sanhedrim is involved in uncertainty; for the council of the 70 elders established by Mozes was not what the Hebrews understand by the name of sanhedrim. Besides, we cannot perceive that this establishment subsisted either under Joshua, the judges, or the kings. We find nothing of it after the captivity, till the time of Jonathan Maccabeus. The tribunals erected by Gabinius were very different from the sanhedrim, which was the supreme court of judicature, and fixed at Jerusalem; whereas Gabinius established five at five different cities. Lastly, it is certain that this senate was in being in the time of Jesus Christ; but the Jews themselves inform us that they had no longer then the power of life and death (John xviii. 31.).

a people inhabiting the Curdiistan, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, subsisting chiefly by plunder, and the scanty pittance afforded by their own mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. “They were much reduced (says Mr Ives) by the late bailaw Achmet of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, who pursued them in person to their subterranean retreats, and destroyed many by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and carried off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of prisoners, who were sold for slaves.” Notwithstanding this check, in the year 178, they again became so daring that they would attack <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> of 700 men, men, and sometimes carry all off. They are said to be worshippers of the evil principle.

SANNAZARIUS

Pages 100-100

JAMES**, in Latin *Aelius Cinnensis Sannazarius*, a celebrated Latin and Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1458. He by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> ingratiated himself into the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Frederic; and, when that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was dethroned, attended him into France, where he stood with him till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1524. Sannazarius then returned into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he applied himself to polite literature, and particularly to Latin and Italian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. His gay and facetious humour made him sought for by all companies; but he was so afflicted at the news that Philibert prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, general of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, had demolished his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, that it threw him into an illness, of which he died in 1535. It is said, that being informed a few days before his death, that the prince of Orange was killed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, he called out, "I shall die contented, since <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> has punished this barbarous enemy of the Mules." He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Italian and Latin poems: among those in Latin, his *De Partu Virginis* and *Eclogues* are chiefly esteemed; and the most celebrated of his Italian pieces is his *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>*.

SANSANDING

Pages 100-100

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated near the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, in N. Lat. 14° 24' and 2° 23' W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. It is inhabited by Moors and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of from eight to ten thousand. The Negroes are kind, hospitable, and credulous; the Moors are at Sansanding, as everywhere else in the interior parts of Africa, fanatical, bigotted, and cruel.

SANTA CRUZ

Pages 100-102
or St Croix, a small and unhealthy island, situated in about 64 degrees west longitude and 18 north latitude. It is about eighteen leagues in length, and from three to four in breadth. In 1643 Raynal says it was inhabited by Dutch and English, who soon became enemies to each other; and in 1650 were both the East driven out by 1,200 Spaniards, who arrived there in five and seven ships. The triumph of these lasted but a few months, Indians. The remains of that numerous body, which were left p. 293, for the defence of the island, surrendered without resistance to 160 French, who had embarked in 1651, from St Christopher's, to make themselves masters of the island. These new inhabitants lost no time in making themselves acquainted with a country so much disputed. On a foil, in other respects excellent, they found only one river of a moderate size, which, gliding gently almost on a level with the sea through a flat country, furnished only a brackish water. Two or three springs, which they found in the innermost parts of the island, made but feeble amends for this defect. The wells were for the most part dry. The construction of reservoirs required time. Nor was the climate more inviting to the new inhabitants. The island being flat, and covered with old trees, scarcely afforded an opportunity for the winds to carry off the poisonous vapours with which its marshes clogged the atmosphere. There was but one remedy for this inconvenience: which was to burn the woods. The French set fire to them without delay; and, getting on board their ships, became spectators from the sea, for several months, of the conflagration they had raised in the island. As soon as the flames were extinguished, they went on shore again. They found the soil fertile beyond belief. Tobacco, cotton, arnotto, indigo, and sugar, flourished equally in it. So rapid was the progress of this colony, that in 11 years from its commencement there were upon it 822 white persons, with a proportional number of slaves. It was rapidly advancing to prosperity, when such obstructions were thrown in the way of its activity as made it decline again. This decay was as sudden as its rise. In 1696 there were no more than 147 men, with their wives and children, and 623 blacks remaining; and these were transported to St Domingo. Some obscure individuals, some writers unacquainted with the views of government, with their secret negotiations, with the character of their ministers, with the interests of the protectors and the protected; who flatter themselves that they can discern the reason of events amongst a multitude of important or frivolous causes, which may have equally occasioned them; who do not conceive, that among all these causes the most natural may possibly be the farthest from the truth; who after having read the news, or journal of the day, with profound attention, decide as peremptorily as if they had been placed all their lifetime at the helm of the state, and had assisted at the council of kings; who are never more deceived than in those circumstances in which they display some share of penetration; writers as absurd in the praises as in the blame which they bestow upon nations, in the favourable or unfavourable opinion they form of ministerial operations: these idle dreamers, in a word, who think they are persons of importance, because their attention is always engaged on matters of consequence, being convinced that courts are always governed in their decisions by the most comprehensive views of profound policy, have supposed that the court Santa of Verfailles had neglected Santa Cruz, merely because they wished to abandon the small islands in order to unite all their strength, industry, and population, in the large ones; but this is a mistaken notion: This determination arose from the farmers of the revenue, who found that the contraband trade of Santa Cruz with St Thomas was detrimental to their interests. The spirit of finance hath in all times been injurious to commerce; it hath destroyed the source from whence it sprung. Santa Cruz continued without inhabitants, and without cultivation, till 1733, when it was sold by France to Denmark for 397,500l. Soon after the Danes built there the fortres of Christianshadt. Then it was that this northern power seemed likely to take deep root in America. Unfortunately, she laid her plantations under the yoke of exclusive privileges. Industrious people of all sorts, particularly Moravians, strove in vain to overcome this great difficulty. Many attempts were made to reconcile the interests of the colonists and their oppressors, but without success. The two parties kept up a continual struggle of animosity, not of industry. At length the government, with a moderation not to be expected from its constitution, purchased, in 1754, the privileges and effects of the company. The price was fixed at 412,500l., part of which was paid in ready money, and the remainder in bills upon the treasury, bearing interest. From this time the navigation to the islands was opened to all the subjects of the Danish dominions. Of 345 plantations, which were seen at Santa Cruz, 150 were covered with sugar canes, and every habitation is limited to 3000 Danish feet in length, and 2000 in breadth. It is inhabited by 2136 white men, by 22,244 slaves, and by 155 freedmen. **Santa Cruz**, in Teneriffe. See **Teneriffe**. **Santa Cruz**, a town of Africa, on the coast of Barbary, and in the province of Suez and kingdom of Morocco, with a harbour and a fort. The Moors took it from the Portuguese in 1536. It is seated at the extremity of Mount Atlas, on the Cape Aguier. W. Long. 10° 7'. N. Lat. 30° 38'. **Santa Cruz de la Sierra**, a town of South America, and capital of a province of that name in Peru, and in the audience of Los Charcas, with a bishop's see. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, in a country abounding in good fruits, on the river Guaypi. W. Long. 59° 35'. S. Lat. 20° 40'. **Santa Fe de Bogota**, a town of South America, and capital of New Granada, with an archbishop's see, a supreme court of justice, and a university. The city is situated at the foot of a steep and cold mountain, at the entrance of a vast and superb plain. In 1774 it contained 1770 houses, 3246 families, and 16,233 inhabitants. Population must necessarily increase there, since it is the seat of government, the place where the coin is struck, the staple of trade; and lastly, since it is the residence of an archbishop, whose immediate jurisdiction extends over 31 Spanish villages, which are called towns; over 193 Indian colonies, anciently subdued; and over 28 missions, established in modern times. This archbishop hath likewise, as metropolitan, a seat of inspection over the diocese of Quito, of Panama, of Caracas, of St Martha, and of Cartagena. It is by this last place, though at the distance 100 leagues, and by the river Magdalena, that Santa Fe keeps up its communication with Europe. There Santalum are silver mines in the mountains about the city. W. Long. 60° 5'. N. Lat. 3° 58'. **Santalum**, a genus of plants belonging to the octandra class; and in the natural method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See **Botany Index**. **Santaren**, a handsome town of Portugal in Estremadura, seated on a mountain near the river Tajo, 55 miles N. E. from Lisbon, in a country very fertile in wheat, wine, and oil. They get in their harvest here two months after they have sown their corn. It was taken from the Moors in 1447. W. Long. 8° 25'. N. Lat. 39° 2'. **Santagustine**. See **Augustine**. **Santen**, a town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and in the duchy of Cleves. It is seated on the Rhine, 15 miles S. E. from Cleves. It has a handsome church belonging to the Roman Catholics, wherein is an image of the Virgin Mary, which it is pretended performs a great many miracles. Here the fine walks begin that run as far as Weel, from which it is five miles distant to the north-west. E. Long. 6° 33'. N. Lat. 51° 38'. **Santerre**, the former name of a small territory of France, in Picardy; bounded on the north by Cambresis, on the east by Vermandois, on the west by Amiens, and on the south by the river Somme. It is very fertile, and the capital town is Peronne. **Santeuil**, or rather **Santeul**, John Baptist de, in Latin *Santolius Victorinus*, an excellent Latin poet, was born at Paris in 1620. Having finished his studies in Louis the Great's college, he applied himself entirely to poetry, and celebrated in his verse the praises of several great men; by which he acquired universal applause. He enriched Paris with a great number of inscriptions, which are to be seen on the public fountains, and the monuments consecrated to posterity. At length, some new hymns being to be composed for the Breviary of Paris, Claude Santeuil his brother, and M. Botueil, persuaded him to undertake that work; and he succeeded in it with the greatest applause. On which the order of Clugny desiring him to compose some for their Breviary, he complied with their request; and that order, out of gratitude, granted him letters of filiation, with an annual pension. Santeuil was cared for by all the learned men of his time; and had for his admirers the two princes of Condé, the father and son, from whom he frequently received favours. Louis XIV. also gave him a proof of his esteem, by bestowing a pension upon him. He attended the duke of Bourbon to Dijon, when that prince went thither in order to hold the states of Burgundy; and died there in 1697, as he was preparing to return to Paris. Besides his Latin hymns, he wrote a great number of Latin poems, which have all the fire and marks of genius discoverable in the works of great poets. To Santeuil we are indebted for many fine church-hymns, as above-mentioned. Santeuil read the verses he made for the inhabitants of heaven with all the agonies of a demoniac. Defreux said he was the devil whom God compelled to praise saints. He was among the number of poets whose genius was as impecunious as his muse was decent. La Bruyere has painted the character of this singular and truly original poet in the most lively colours. "Image a man of great felicity of temper, complaisant and docile; in an instant violent, choleric, passionate, and capricious. A man simple, credulous, playful, volatile, puerile; in a word, a child in gray hairs: but let him collect himself, or rather call forth his interior genius, I venture to say, without his knowledge or privacy, what follies! what elevation! what images! what latinity! Do you speak of one and the same person, you will ask? Yes, of the same; of Theodas, and of him alone. He shrieks, he jumps, he rolls upon the ground, he roars, he storms; and in the midst of this tempest, a flame influes that thines, that rejoices. Without a figure, he rattles like a fool, and thinks like a wise man. He utters truths in a ridiculous way; and, in an idiotic manner, rational and sensible things. It is nothing to find good sense discolored itself from the bosom of buffoonery, accompanied with grimaces and contortions. What shall I say more? He does and he says better than he knows. These are like two souls that are unacquainted with each other, which have each their turn and separate functions. A feature would be wanting in this extraordinary portrait, if I omitted saying, that he has at once an infatuated thirst for praise, ready to throw himself at the mercy of the critics, and at the bottom so docile as to profit by their censure. I begin to persuade myself that I have been drawing the portraits of two different persons: it would be impossible to find a third in Theodas; for he is a good man, a pleasant man, an excellent man." This poet ought not to be confounded with Claude de Santeuil, his brother, a learned ecclesiastic, who also wrote several hymns in the Paris Breviary, under the name of Santolius Magiorcanus, a name given him from his having lived a long time in the seminary of St Maggiore at Paris, in quality of secular ecclesiastic. He was esteemed not only for his poetical abilities, but also for his profound erudition and his exemplary piety. He wrote several other pieces of poetry, besides his hymns, which are printed with his brother's works.

SANTORINI

Pages 102-102
