or Santorin, an island of the Archipelago, to the north of Candia, and distant from it about 90 leagues, and to the south-west of Naphlio. It is eight miles in length, and nearly as much in breadth, and almost covered with pumice-stone, whence the soil in general must be dry and barren; it is, however, greatly improved by the labour and industry of the inhabitants, who have turned it into a garden. It affords a great deal of barley, plenty of cotton, and large quantities of wine. Fruit is scarce, except almonds and figs; and there is neither oil nor wood. The partridge and the hare, so common in the other islands of the Archipelago, are scarce at Santorin; but quails are met with in abundance. The inhabitants are all Greeks, and are about 10,000 in number. Pyrgos is the capital town, beside which, there are several little towns and villages. There is but one spring of water in the island, for which reason the rain-water is preserved in cisterns. Though subject to the Turks, they choose their own magistrates. E. Long. 25. 5. N. Lat. 39. 10.

SAONE

Pages 102-102

a considerable river of France, which has its source in Mount Vosgue, near Darney; runs through the Franche Comte, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, Beaujolais; and falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> at Lyons. It passes by Gray, Chalons, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACON">Macon</a>.

SAP

Pages 102-103

the juice found in vegetables. We observed, when treating of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>, that it has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> disputed whether the sap of plants be analogous to the blood of animals, and circulates in the same manner. We also mentioned the conclusions that Dr Hales drew from his numerous experiments, which were all in opposition to the doctrine that the sap circulates. Dr Walker, late professor of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, has published, in the 1st volume of the Philosophical Transactions of Edinburgh, an account of a course of experiments on this subject, accompanied with some observations and conclusions. It is well known that in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> vegetables contain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sap; and there are some trees, as the birch and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> wounded, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> discharge a great portion of it. Whence is this moisture derived? Whether is it imbibed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> does it flow from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> through the roots? These are the questions which require first to be answered; and Dr Walker's experiments enable us to answer them with confidence. He selected a vigorous young birch, 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 26 inches in circumference at the ground. He bored a hole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the ground on the 1st of February, and cut one of its branches at the extremity. He repeated this every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but no moisture appeared at either of the places till the 5th of May, when a small quantity flowed on making an incision near the ground. He then cut 21 incisions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the tree, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, at the distance of a foot from one another, and reaching from the ground to the height of 20 feet. The incisions were <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> triangles, each side being an inch long and an inch deep, and penetrating through the bark and wood. Dr Walker visited the tree almost every day for two months, and marked exactly from which of the incisions the sap flowed. He observed that it flowed from the lowest incision first, and gradually ascended to the highest. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> will show the progress of the sap upwards, and its correspondence with the thermometer. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> is the day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> on which the observation was made; the second expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of incisions from which the sap flowed on the day of the month opposite; and the third column the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the thermometer at noon. Some days are omitted in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, as the incisions, though made on the 5th, did not bleed till the 11th. Some days are also passed palled over in April, because no observation was made on account of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. | March | N. of In. Ther. Noon. | March | N. of In. Ther. Noon. | |-------|----------------------|-------|----------------------| | 5 | 46 | 30 | 8 | | 11 | 2 | 49 | 31 | | 12 | 2 | 49 | 7 | | 13 | 1 | April | 2 | | 14 | 4 | 48 | 4 | | 15 | 5 | 52 | 7 | | 16 | 5 | 47 | 8 | | 17 | 4 | 44 | 9 | | 18 | 5 | 47 | 10 | | 19 | 6 | 48 | 11 | | 20 | 5 | 44 | 12 | | 21 | 7 | 48 | 13 | | 22 | 7 | 45 | 14 | | 23 | 8 | 46 | 15 | | 24 | 9 | 47 | 16 | | 25 | 9 | 42 | 18 | | 26 | 7 | 39 | 19 | | 27 | 8 | 45 | 20 | | 28 | 8 | 49 | 21 | | 29 | 8 | 46 | 22 | Dr Walker found that the sap ascends through the wood, and still more copiously between the wood and the bark; but none could be perceived ascending through the pith or the bark. He found also, that when the thermometer at noon is about 49°, or between 46° and 50°, the sap rises about one foot in 24 hours; that when the thermometer is about 45° at noon, it ascends about one foot in two days; and that it does not ascend at all unless the mid-day <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> be above 40°. He observed that it moves with more velocity through young than through old branches. In one young branch it moved through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in one day, the thermometer being at 49°, while it moved in the trunk of the tree only seven feet in seven days. Dr Walker has thus explained the reason why the buds on the extremities of branches unfold first; because they are placed on the youngest wood, to which the sap flows most abundantly. The effects produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the sap deserve to be attended to. In those parts to which it has mounted, the bark easily separates from the wood, and the ligneous circles may, without difficulty, be detached from one another. The buds begin to swell and their scales to separate, while those branches to which the sap has not ascended remain closely folded. When the sap has reached the extremities of the branches, and has thus pervaded the whole plant, it is soon covered with opening buds and scales to bleed. The bleeding ceases first in the upper parts of the tree, and in the lower parts successively downwards, and the wood becomes dry. An <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> branch flows more copiously when cut than those which are erect. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the ascent of the sap is not occasioned by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which has risen in a small glass tube by this attraction will not descend when the tube is inverted. It is evident that there is an intimate connection between heat and the ascent of the sap. It did not begin to flow till the thermometer stood at a certain point: when it fell below 49°, it was arrested in its progress. The fourth side of the tree, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was bright, bled more profusely than the north side; and at sunset the incisions at the top ceased to bleed, where it was exposed most to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, while it still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to flow from the incisions next to the ground; the ground retaining its heat longer than the air. Sap, in sieges, is a trench, or an approach made under cover, of 10 or 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, when the besiegers come near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the fire from the garrison grows so dangerous that they are not able to approach uncovered.—There are several sorts of saps; the single, which has only a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, having one on each side; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, made with gabions, &c. In all saps traverses are left to cover the men. Sap, or Sopp, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, as to sap a wall, &c. is to dig out the ground from beneath it, so as to bring it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> all at once for want of support.

SAPHIES

Pages 103-103

a kind of charms, consisting of some scrap of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a> believe capable of protecting them from all evil. The Moors sell scraps of the Koran for this purpose; and indeed any piece of writing may be sold as a saphie; but it would appear that the Negroes are disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> greater confidence in the saphies of a Christian than in those of a Moor. When Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a> was at Koolikorro, a considerable town near the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> market for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, his landlord, hearing that he was a Christian, immediately thought of procuring a saphie. For this purpose he brought out his wadla, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> writing board, assuring me (says our author) that he would dress me a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I would write him a saphie to protect him from wicked men. The proposal was of too great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to me to be refused; I therefore wrote the board full, from top to bottom, on both sides; and my landlord, to be certain of having the whole force of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, washed the writing from the board into a calabash with a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and having said a few prayers over it, drank this powerful draught; after which, lest a single word should escape, he licked the board until it was quite dry. A saphie writer was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of too great consequence to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> concealed: the important information was carried to the Dooty, who sent his son with half a sheet of writing-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, desiring me to write him a napulha saphie (a charm to procure wealth). He brought me, as a present, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and when I had finished the saphie, and read it to him with an audible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, he seemed highly satisfied with his bargain, and promised to bring me in the morning some milk for my breakfast.

SAPINDUS

Pages 103-103

the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">SOAP</a>-BERRY TREE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the oecandria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23d order, Trichilace. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAPONARIA

Pages 103-103

Soapwort; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 22d order, Caryophyllace. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAPOR

Pages 103-103
Taste. See Taste, and Anatomy, No. 139. SAPOTA PLUM. See ACHRAS, Botany Index.

SAPPERS

Pages 103-104

are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, whose business it is to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at the saps, for which they have an extraordinary pay. A brigade of sappers generally consists of eight men, divided equally into two parties; SAP parties; and whilst one of these parties is advancing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a>, the other is furnishing the gabions, fascines, and other necessary implements. They relieve each other alternately.

SAPPHIRA

Pages 104-104

was the wife of a rich merchant in Gueldres, and equally distinguished for her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and her virtue. Rhinfauld, a German officer, and governor of the town of Gueldres, fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with her; and not being able to seduce her either by promises <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> presents, he imprisoned her husband, pretending that he kept up a traitorous correspondence with the enemies of the state. Sapphira yielded to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of the governor in order to relieve her husband from chains; but private orders had already been given to put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His unhappy widow, overwhelmed with grief, complained to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. He ordered Rhinfauld to marry her, after having made over to her all his possessions. As soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> was signed, and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> over, Charles commanded him to be put to death. Thus the children of a wife whom he had seduced, and of a husband whom he had murdered, became lawful heirs to all his wealth.

SAPPHIRE

Pages 104-104

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of a blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAPPHO

Pages 104-104

a famous poetess of antiquity, who for her excellence in her art has been called the Tenth Muse, was born at Mitylene, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, about 610 years before Christ. She was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Stesichorus and Alceus; which last was her countryman, and some think her suitor. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of this poet, in which he intimates to her his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, is preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, Rhet. lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 9. together with the fair damsel's answer. ALC. I fain to Sappho would a wish impart, But fear locks up the secret in my heart. SAP. Thy downcast looks, respect, and timid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, Too plain the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of thy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> declare. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> lawless, wild, inordinate desire, Did not with thoughts impure thy bosom fire, Thy tongue and eyes, by innocence made bold, Ere now the secret of thy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> had told. M. la Fevre observes, that Sappho was not in her usual good humour when she gave so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> an answer to a request, for which, at another <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, perhaps she would not have waited.—It has been thought, too, that Anacreon was one of her lovers, and his editor Barnes has taken some pains to prove it; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> will not admit this; since, upon inquiry, it will be found that Sappho was probably dead before Anacreon was born. Of the numerous poems this lady wrote, there is nothing remaining but some small fragments, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> scholiasts have cited; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Venus, preserved by Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>; and an ode to one of her mistresses*: which last piece confirms a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> delivered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from antiquity, that her amorous passion extended even to persons of her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and that she was willing to have her mistresses as well as her gallants. Ovid introduces her making a sacrifice to Phaon, one of her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> paramours; from which we learn, that Sappho's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for her own sex did not keep her from loving ours. She fell desperately in love with Phaon, and did all she could to win him; but in vain: upon which she threw herself headlong from a rock, and died. It is said that Sappho could not forbear following Phaon into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, whither he retired that he might not see her; and that during her stay in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> she probably composed the hymn to Venus, still extant, in which she begs so ardently the affluence of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. Her prayers, however, proved ineffectual: Phaon was cruel to the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The unfortunate Sappho was forced to take the dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>; she went to the promontory Leucas, and threw herself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The cruelty of Phaon will not surprise us so much, if we reflect, that she was a widow (for she had been married to a rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the isle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROS">Andros</a>, by whom she had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, named Cleis); that she had never been handsome; that she had observed no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in her passion to both sexes; and that Phaon had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> known all her charms. She was, however, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and for that alone deserves to be remembered. The Mitylenians held her merit in such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, that they paid her foreign honours after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and stamped their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> with her image. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> afterwards erected a noble statue of porphyry to her; and in short, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> as well as moderns have done <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Wolfius says, that none of the Greek poets excelled Sappho for sweetness of verse; and that he made Archilochus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of her style, but at the same time took care to soften the severity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. It must be granted, says Rapin, from what is left us of Sappho, that Longinus had great reason to extol the admirable genius of this woman; for there is in what remains of her something delicate, harmonious, and impassioned to the last degree.

SARABAND

Pages 104-104

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in triple <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the motions of which are slow and serious. Saraband is also a dance to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, which usually terminates when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> that beats the time falls; and is otherwise much the same as the minuet. The saraband is said to be originally derived from the Saracens, and is usually danced to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the guitar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> citternettes.

SARACA

Pages 104-104

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the delphinae clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SARACENS

Pages 104-104

the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; so called from the word saru, which signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, as the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Arabia is; and this being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Mahomet, his disciples were called Saracens.

SARACOLETS

Pages 104-105

a Negro <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> occupying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>. They are a laborious people, cultivate their lands with care, are plentifully supplied with all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and inhabit handsome and well built villages; their houses, of a circular form, are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> terraced; the others are covered with reeds as at Senegal: they are inclosed with a mud wall a foot thick, and the villages are surrounded with one of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that solidity. There are several gates, which are guarded at night for fear of a surprize. This nation is remarkably brave, so that it is very uncommon to find a Saracolet slave. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> principles of this people are nearly allied to Mahometanism, and still more to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. They acknowledge one God; and believe that those who steal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> are guilty of any crime, are eternally punished. They admit a plurality of wives, and believe their souls to be immortal like their own. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this country is unknown. It is governed by four powerful princes, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the name. SARACOLETS name of Fouquet. The least considerable, according to the testimony of the Saracolets, is that of Tuago, who can assemble 30,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and whose subjects occupy a territory two hundred leagues in extent, as well on the Senegal as on the tract that reaches beyond the Felou; a rock which, according to the same report, forms cataracts, from whence proceed the Senegal and the river Gambia, equally considerable.

SARAGOSA

Pages 105-105

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon, with an archbishop's see, an university, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>. It is said to have been built by the Phoenicians; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sent a colony here in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus, whence it had the name of Caesar Augustus, which by corruption has been changed into Saragossa. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and well-built town. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, well paved, and very clean, and the houses from three to six stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. It is adorned with many magnificent buildings; and they reckon 17 large churches, and 14 handsome monasteries, not to mention others less considerable. The river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EBRO">Ebro</a> runs across the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, dividing it into two; and on its banks is a handsome quay, which serves for a public walk. The Holy-street is the largest, and so broad that it may be taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and here they have their bull-fights: in this street there are several noblemen's families, particularly that of the viceroy. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> are handsome and richly adorned, as well as the churches. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, after the Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but the finest church is that of Nuestra Signora del Pilar, seated on the side of the Ebro, and is a place of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> in Spain. They tell us the Virgin appeared to St James, who was preaching the gospel, and left him her image, with a handsome pillar of jasper: it is still in this church, which they pretend is the first in the world built to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. This image stands on a marble pillar, with a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> in her arms; but the place is so dark, that it cannot be seen without the assistance of lamps, which are 50 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and all of silver. These are also chandeliers and balustrades of massy silver. The ornaments of this image are the richest that can be imagined, her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> being full of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of an inestimable price; in short, there is scarce anything to be seen but <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and jewels, and a vast number of people come in pilgrimage hither. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a sumptuous structure, adorned with fine columns: in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> are the pictures of all the kings of Arragon; and in a corner of it St George on horseback, with a dragon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble under him. It is seated in a very large plain, where the Ebro receives two other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; and over it are two bridges, one of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and the other of wood, which last has been thought the most beautiful in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. A victory was obtained here over the French and Spaniards in 1719, but it was abandoned by the allies soon after. It is 97 miles west by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARRAGONA">Tarragona</a>, 137 west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, and 150 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. W. Long. 0° 48'. N. Lat. 41° 47'. SARANNE. See Lilium.

SARCASM

Pages 105-105

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a keen bitter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which has the true point of satire, by which the orator scoffs and insults his enemy: such as that of the Jews to our Saviour; "He saved others, himself he cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a>."

SARCOCELE

Pages 105-105

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a spurious rupture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a>, wherein the testicle is considerably tumefied or indurated, like a scirrhus, or much enlarged by a fleshy excrescence, which is frequently attended with acute pains, so as to degenerate at last into a cancerous disposition. See Surgery.

SARCOLOGY

Pages 105-105

is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of anatomy which treats of the soft parts, viz. the muscles, intestines, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, veins, nerves, and fat.

SARCOPHAGUS

Pages 106-106
or Lapis Albus, in the href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history of the ancients, a stone much used among the Greeks in their sepultures, is recorded to have always perfectly consumed the flesh of human bodies buried in it in forty days. This property it was much famed for, and all the ancient naturalists mention it. There was another very singular quality also in it, but whether in all, or only in some peculiar pieces of it, is not known: that is, its turning into stone any thing that was put into vessels made of it. This is recorded only by Mutianus and Theophratus, except that Pliny had copied it from these authors, and some of the later writers on these subjects from him. The account Mutianus gives of it is, that it converted into stone the shoes of persons buried in it, as also the utensils which it was in some places customary to bury with the dead, particularly those which the person while living most delighted in. The utensils this author mentions, are such as must have been made of very different materials; and hence it appears that this stone had a power of consuming not only flesh, but that its petrifying quality extended to substances of very different kinds. Whether ever it really possessed this last quality has been much doubted; and many, from the seeming improbability of it, have been afraid to record it. What has much encouraged the general disbelief of it is, Mutianus's account of its taking place on substances of very different kinds and textures; but this is no real objection, and the whole account has probably truth in it. Petrifications in those early days might not be distinguished from incrustations of sparry and stony matter on the surfaces of bodies only, as we find they are not with the generality of the world even to this day; so the incrustations of spar on moles and other substances in some of our forings, being at this time called by many petrified moles, &c., and incrustations like these might easily be formed on substances enclosed in vessels made of this stone, by water passing through its pores, dislodging from the common mass of the stone, and carrying with it particles of such spar as it contained; and afterwards falling in repeated drops on whatever lay in its way, it might again deposit them on such substances in form of incrustations. By this means, things made of very different matter, which happened to be inclosed, and in the way of the passage of the water, would be equally incrusted with and in appearance turned into stone, without regard to the different configuration of their pores and parts. The place from whence the ancients tell us they had this stone was Assos, a city of Lycia, in the neighbourhood of which it was dug; and De Boot informs us, that in that country, and in some parts of the East, there are also stones of this kind, which, if tied to the bodies of living persons, would in the same manner consume their flesh. Hill's Notes on Theophratus, p. 14.

SARCOTICS

Pages 106-106

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, medicines which are supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> in wounds.

SARDANAPALUS

Pages 106-106

the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, whose character is one of the most infamous in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He is said to have sunk so far in depravity, that, as far as he could, he changed his very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He clothed himself as a woman, and spun amidst companies of his concubines. He painted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and behaved in a most lewd manner than the most lascivious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a>. In short, he buried himself in the most unbounded sensuality, quite regardless of sex and the dictates of nature. Having grown odious to all his subjects, a rebellion was formed against him by Arbaces the Mede and Belis the Babylonian. They were attended, however, with very bad success at first, being defeated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter in three pitched battles. With great difficulty Belis prevailed upon his men to keep the field only five days longer; when they were joined by the Bactrians, who had come to the assistance of Sardanapalus, but had been prevailed upon to renounce their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to him. With this reinforcement they twice defeated the troops of Sardanapalus, who shut himself up in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of his empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> held out for three years; at the end of which, Sardanapalus finding himself unable to hold out any longer, and dreading to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an enraged enemy, retired into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of which he caused a vast pile of wood to be raised; and heaping upon it all his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> apparel, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> inclosing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> and concubines in an apartment within the pile, he set fire to it, and so destroyed himself and all together.

SARDINIA

Pages 106-107

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> slaps another without premeditated malice, within four hours after quarrelling with him, he is not liable to be hanged. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> affords no protection to the guilty. The Sardinians are not at all bigotted; and, next to the Spaniards, the English are their favourites. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was formerly subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, who enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sardinia. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAGLIARI">CAGLIARI</a>. It is now under the dominion of the French. There is in this island a pleasing variety of hills and valleys, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fruitful; but the inhabitants are a fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, and cultivate but a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> there is a fishery of anchovies and coral, of which they send <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>. This island is divided into two parts; the one, called Capo di Cagliari, lies to the south; and the other Capo di Ligure, which is leated to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Cagliari the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Oristagno, and Safarri.

SARDIS

Pages 107-107
or SARDES, now called Sardo, or Sart, is an ancient town of Natolia in Asia, about 40 miles east of Smyrna. It was much celebrated in early antiquity, was enriched by the fertility of the soil, and had been the capital of the Lydian kings. It was seated on the side of Mount Tmolus; and the citadel, placed on a lofty hill, was remarkable for its great strength. It was the seat of King Croesus, and was in his time taken by Cyrus; after which the Persian satrapas or commandant resided at Sardis as the emperor did at Sufa. The city was also taken, burnt, and then evacuated by the Milesians in the time of Darius, and the city and fortresses surrendered on the approach of Alexander after the battle of Granicus. Under the Romans Sardis was a very considerable place till the time of Tiberius Caesar, when it suffered prodigiously by an earthquake. The munificence of the emperor, however, was nobly exerted to repair the various damages it then sustained. Julian attempted to restore the heathen worship in the place. He erected temporary altars where none had been left, and repaired the temples if any vestiges remained. In the year 400 it was plundered by the Goths, and it suffered considerably in the subsequent troubles of Asia. On the incursion of the Tartars in 1324, the Turks were permitted to occupy a portion of the citadel, separated by a strong wall with a gate, and were afterwards murdered in their sleep. The site of this once noble city is now green and flowery, the whole being reduced to a poor village, containing nothing but wretched huts. There are, however, some curious remains of antiquity about it, and some ruins which display its ancient grandeur. See Chandler's Travels in Asia ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor, p. 251, &c. There is in the place a large caravansary, where travellers may commodiously lodge. The inhabitants are generally shepherds, who lead their sheep into the fine pastures of the neighbouring plain. The Turks have a mosque here, which was a Christian church, at the gate of which there are several columns of polished marble. There are a few Christians, who are employed in gardening. E. Long. 28. 5. N. Lat. 37. 51.

SARDONIUS RISUS

Pages 107-107

Sardonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUGHTER">Laughter</a>; a convulsive involuntary laughter; thus named from the herba fardonia, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ranunculus, and is said to produce such convulsive motions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> as resemble those motions which are observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> during a fit of laughter. This complaint is sometimes specifiedly fatal. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the ranunculus happens to be the cause, the cure must be attempted by means of a vomit, and frequent draughts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROMEL">hydromel</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>.

SARDONYX

Pages 107-107

a precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> consisting of a mixture of the calcined and carnelian, sometimes in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, but at other times blended together. See MINEROGY.

SARIMPATAM

Pages 107-107

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Indofan, lying at the back of the dominions of the Samorin of Malabar, and which, as far as we know, was never subdued by any foreign power. Mr Grofe relates, that "it has been constantly a maxim with the inhabitants of this country never to make any but a defensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and even then, not to kill any of their adversaries in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, but to cut off their noses. To this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> were peculiarly trained up, and the dread of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> proved sufficiently strong to keep their neighbours, not much more martial than themselves, from effectually attacking them." SARMENTOSÆ (from sarmentum, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> shoot like that of a vine); the name of the 11th clas in Linnaeus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Method, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which have climbing stems and branches, that, like the vine, attach themselves to the bodies in their neighbourhood for the purpose of support. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>.

SAROCOLLIA

Pages 105-105

a concrete juice brought from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, in small whitish-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> grains, with a few of a reddish and sometimes of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> mixed with them; the whitest tears are preferred, as being the freshest: its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is bitter, accompanied with a dull kind of sweetness. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>.

SAROS

Pages 107-107

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of 223 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word is said to be Chaldean, signifying restitution, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> return of eclipses; that is, conjunctions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the ecliptic. The Saros was a cycle like to that of Meto.

SAROTHRA

Pages 107-107

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 20th order, Rotaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SARPLAR OF WOOL

Pages 107-107

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, otherwise called a pocket, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half-sack; a sack containing 80 tod; a tod two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> 14 pounds.—In Scotland it is called sarplath, and contains 80 stone.

SARRACONIA

Pages 107-107

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Mifeellanea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SARRASIN

Pages 107-107
or SARRAZIN, in fortification, a kind of portcullis, otherwise called a herse, which is hung with ropes over the gate of a town or fortress, to be let fall in case of a surprize. SARSAPARILLA. See SMILAX, BOTANY and Materia Medica Index.

SASHES

Pages 108-108

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> dress, are badges of distinction worn by the officers of most nations, either round their waists <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> over their shoulders. Those for the British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were made of crimson <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; for the Imperial army crimson and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; for the Prussian army <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> silk and silver; the Hanoverian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> silk; the Portuguese crimson silk with blue tassels.

SASINE

Pages 108-108
or SEISIN. See LAW, No. clxv. i5, &c. SASSA. See MYRRH, OPICALPASUM, MATERIA MEDICA Index, and BRUCE'S TRAVELS, vol. v. p. 27, &c.

SATAN

Pages 108-108

a name very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Scripture, means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the fallen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. See DEVIL.

SATELLITE

Pages 108-108

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>, the same with a secondary planet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. SATIRE. See SATYR.

SATRAPA

Pages 108-108
or SATRAPE, in Persian antiquity, denotes an admiral; but more commonly the governor of a province.

SATTIN

Pages 108-108

a glossy kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> fluff, the warp of which is very fine, and stands so as to cover the coarser woof.

SATTINET

Pages 108-108

a slight thin kind of sattin, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> striped, and is employed for different purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> dress.

SATURATION

Pages 108-108

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a>, is the impregnating an acid with an alkali, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vice versa, till either receive no more, and the mixture then become neutral.

SATURDAY

Pages 108-108

the seventh and last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, so called from the idol Seater, worshipped on this day by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxons, and thought to be the same as the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> of the Latins.

SATUREIA

Pages 108-108

SAVORY, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didyma class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, VERTICILLACE. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SATURN

Pages 108-109

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the Pagan deities, was the son of Caelus and Terra, and the father of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He deposed and castrated his father; and obliged his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Titan to resign his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to him, on condition of his bringing up none of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue, that the succession might at length devolve on him. For this purpose he devoured all the sons he had by his wife Rhea <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cybele: but she bringing forth at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Jupiter and Juno, she presented the latter to her husband, and sent the boy to be nursed on Mount Ida; when Saturn being informed of her having a son, demanded the child; but in his stead his wife gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> swaddled up like an infant, which he instantly swallowed. Titan finding that Saturn had violated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> he had made with him, put himself at the head of his children, and made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on his brother, and having made him and Cybele prisoners, confined them in Tartarus: but Jupiter being in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time grown up, raised an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, went to his father's assistance, defeated Titan, and restored Saturn to the throne. Some time after, Saturn being told that Jupiter intended to dethrone him, endeavoured to prevent it; but the latter being informed of his intention, deposed his father, and threw him into Tartarus. But Saturn escaping from thence fled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he was kindly received by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, who afflicated him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: whence Italy obtained the name of Saturnia Tellus; as also that of Latium, from latro, "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> hid." There Saturn, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and mildness of his government, is said to have produced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Saturn is represented as an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with four wings, armed with a lyre; sometimes he is delineated under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> with its tail in its mouth. This is emblematic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, which roll perpetually in the same circle. Sometimes also Saturn is painted with a wand-glas in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The Greeks say, that the story of his mutilating his father and destroying his children is an allegory, which signifies, that Time devours the past and present, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> also devour the future. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him, built a temple, and celebrated a festival which they called Saturnalia. During this festival no business or profession was allowed to be carried on except cookery; all distinctions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> ceased; slaves could say what they pleased to their masters with impunity; they could even rally them with their faults before their faces.

SATURNALIA

Pages 109-109

in Roman antiquity, a festival observed about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the god <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, whom Lucan introduces giving an account of the ceremonies observed on this occasion, thus, "During my whole reign, which lasts but for one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, no public business is done; there is nothing but drinking, singing, playing, creating imaginary kings, placing servants with their masters at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, &c. There shall be no disputes, reproaches, &c. but the rich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, masters and slaves, shall be equal," &c. On this festival the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sacrificed bare-headed, contrary to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> at other sacrifices.

SATURNINE

Pages 109-109

an appellation given to persons of a melancholy disposition, as being supposed under the influence of the planet <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>.

SATYAVRATA

Pages 109-109
or MENU, in Indian mythology, is believed by the Hindoos to have reigned over the whole world in the earliest age of their chronology, and to have resided in the country of Dravira on the coast of the eastern Indian peninsula. His patronymic name was Vivasvata, or child of the sun. In the Bha-gavat we are informed, that the Lord of the universe, intending to preserve him from the sea of destruction, caused by the depravity of the age, thus told him how he was to act. "In seven days from the present time, O thou tamer of enemies, the three worlds will be plunged in an ocean of death; but, in the midst of the destroying waves, a large vessel, sent by me for thy use, shall stand before thee. Then shalt thou take all medicinal herbs, all the variety of seeds; and, accompanied by seven saints, encircled by pairs of all brute animals, thou shalt enter the spacious ark and continue in it, secure from the flood on one immense ocean without light, except the radiance of thy holy companions. When the ship shall be agitated by an impetuous wind, thou shalt fasten it with a large sea-serpent on my horn; for I will be near thee: drawing the vessel, with thee and thy attendants, I will remain on the ocean, O chief of men, until a night of Brahma shall be completely ended. Thou shalt then know my true greatness, rightly named the supreme Godhead; by my favour, all thy questions shall be answered, and thy mind abundantly instructed." All this is said to have been accomplished; and the story is evidently that of Noah disguised by Asiatic fiction and allegory. It proves, as Sir William Jones has rightly observed, an ancient Indian tradition of the universal deluge described by Moses; and enables us to trace the connexion between the eastern and western traditions relating to that event. The same learned author has shown it to be in the highest degree probable, that the Satyavrata of India is the Cronus of Greece and the Saturn of Italy. See SATURN; and Asiatic Researches, vol. i. p. 230, &c.

SATYR

Pages 109-109
or SATIRE, in matters of literature, a discourse or poem, exposing the vices and follies of mankind. See POETRY, Part II. sect. x. The chief satirists among the ancients are, Horace, Juvenal, and Persius: those among the moderns are, Regnier and Boileau, in French; Butler, Dryden, Rochester, Buckingham, Swift, Pope, Young, &c. among the English; and Cervantes among the Spaniards. SATYRIASIS. See MEDICINE Index.

SATYRIUM

Pages 109-109

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order ranking under the 4th order, Verticillate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SATYRS

Pages 109-109

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of demi-gods who dwelt in the woods. They are represented as monsters, half-men, and half-goats; having horns on their heads, a hairy body, with the feet and tail of a goat. They are generally in the train that follows <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. As the poets supposed that they were remarkable for piercing eyes and keen raillery, they have placed them in the same pictures with the Graces, Loves, and even with Venus herself.

SAUCISSE

Pages 118-118
or Saucisson, in mining, is a long pipe or bag, made of cloth well pitched, or sometimes of leather, of about an inch and a half diameter, filled with powder, going from the chamber of the mine to the entrance of the gallery. It is generally placed in a wooden pipe called an auger, to prevent its growing damp. It serves to give fire to mines, caissons, bomb-chests, &c.

SAUCISSON

Pages 118-118

is likewise a kind of fascine, longer than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ones; they serve to raise batteries and to repair breaches. They are also used in making emplacements, in stopping <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, and in making traverses over a wet ditch, &c.

SAUMUR

Pages 120-120

a considerable town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Saumurais, with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle. The town is small, but pleasantly situated on the Loire, across which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> through a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Saumur was anciently a most important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over the river, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was frequently and fiercely disputed by either party, during the civil wars of France in the sixteenth century. The fortifications are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength, and Henry IV. on the reconciliation which took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between him and Henry III. near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, in 1589, demanded that Saumur should be delivered to him, as one of the cities of safety. The castle overlooks the town and river. It is built on a lofty eminence, and has a venerable and magnificent appearance, and was lately used as a prison of state, where persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> were frequently confined. The kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and dukes of Anjou of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Valois, who descended from John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, often resided in the castle of Saumur, as it constituted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their Angevin dominions. E. Long. o. 2. N. Lat. 47. 15.

SAUNDERS

Pages 120-120

a kind of wood brought from the East Indies, of which there are three kinds; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. See Pterocarpus and Santalum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAUNDERSON

Pages 120-122

Dr Robert, an eminent casuist, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROTHERHAM">Rotherham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> on the 19th September 1687, and was descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. He attended the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school at Rotherham, where he made such wonderful proficiency in the languages, that at 13 it was judged proper to send him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1688 he was appointed logic reader in the same college. He took orders in 1691, and was promoted successively to several benefices. Archbishop Laud recommended him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. as a profound casuist; and that monarch, who seems to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> admirer of casuistical learning, appointed him one of his chaplains in 1631. Charles proposed several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to him, and received so great satisfaction from his answers, that at the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>'s attendance he told him, that he would wait with impatience during the intervening 11 months, as he was resolved to be more intimately acquainted with him, when it would again be his turn to officiate. The king regularly attended his sermons, and was wont to say, that "he carried his ears to hear other preachers, but his conscience to hear Mr Saunderson." In 1642 Charles created him regius professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Oxford, with the canonry of Christ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> annexed: but the civil wars prevented him till 1646 from entering on the office; and in 1648 he was ejected by the visitors which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> had commissioned. He must have stood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; for in the same year in which he was appointed professor of divinity, both houses of parliament recommended him to the king as one of their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> for settling the affairs of the church. The king, too, repose great confidence in his judgement, and frequently consulted him about the state of his affairs. When the parliament proposed the abolition of the episcopal form of church-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> as incompatible with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, Charles desired him to take the subject under his consideration, and deliver his opinion. He accordingly wrote a treatise entitled, Episcopacy as established by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in England not prejudicial to regal power. At taking leave, the king advised him to publish Cases of Conscience: he replied, that "he was now grown old and unfit to write cases of conscience." The king said, "it was the simplest thing he ever had heard from him; for no young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was fit to be a judge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> write cases of conscience." Walton, who wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Dr Saunderson, informs us, that in one of these conferences the king told him (Dr Saunderson), or one of the rest who was then in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, that "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of two errors did much affect him; which were his affections to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Strafford's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and the abolishing of episcopacy in Scotland; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> God ever restored him to the peaceable possession of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, he would prove his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> by a public confession and a voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, by walking barefoot from the Tower of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, or Whitehall, to St Paul's church, and would desire the people to intercede with God for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>." Dr Saunderson was taken prisoner by the parliament's troops and conveyed to Lincoln, in order to procure in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> a Puritan divine named Clark, whom the king's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> had taken. The exchange was agreed to, on condition that Dr Saunderson's living should be restored, and his person and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> remain unmolested. The first of these demands was readily complied with: and a stipulation was made, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> should be observed; but it was impossible to restrain the licentiousness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. They entered his church in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, interrupted him when <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> prayers, and even had the audacity to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> book from him, and to tear it to pieces. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Boyle, having read a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Dr Saunderson's entitled De juramentis obligatione, was so much pleased, that he inquired at Bishop Barlow, whether he thought it was possible to prevail on the author to write Cases of Conscience, if an honorary pension was assigned him to enable him to purchase books, and pay an amanuensis. Saunderson told Barlow, "that if any future tract of his could be of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to mankind, he would cheerfully set about it without a pension." Boyle, however, sent him a present of £50, sensible no doubt, that, like the other royalists, his finances could not be great. Upon this Saunderson published his book De Conscientia. When Charles II. was reinstated in the throne, he recovered his professorship and canonry, and soon after was promoted to the bishopric of Lincoln. During the Saunderson, the two years and a half in which he possessed this new office, he spent a considerable sum in augmenting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> vicarages, in repairing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Bugden, &c. He died <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 29, 1662-3, in his 76th year. He was a man of great acuteness and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgement. "That staid and well-weighted man Dr Saunderson (says Dr Hammond) conceives all things deliberately, dwelleth upon them discreetly, discerns things that differ exactly, puffeth his judgement rationally, and expresses it aptly, clearly, and honestly." Being asked, what books he had read most? he replied, that "he did not read many books, but those which he did read were well chosen and frequently perused." These, he said, were chiefly three, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, Aquinas's Summa Secunda, and Tully's Works; especially his Offices, which he had not read over less than 20 times, and could even, in his old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, recite without book." He added, that "the learned civilian Dr Zouch had written Elementa juris prudentiae, which he thought he could also say without book, and that no wise man could read it too often." He was not only conversant with the fathers and schoolmen, with casuistical and controversial divinity; but he was well acquainted with all the histories of the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, was a great antiquary, had searched minutely into records, and was well skilled in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a> and genealogy. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> now be proper to give a short account of his works. 1. In 1615 he published Logicae Artis Compendium, which was the system of lectures he had delivered in the University when he was logic-reader. 2. Sermons, amounting in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to 36, printed in 1681, folio, with the author's life by Walton. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> Cases of Conscience resolved; first collected in one volume, in 1678, 8vo. 4. De juramenti obligatione. This book was translated into English by Charles I., while a prisoner in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, and printed at London in 1665, 8vo. 5. De Obligatione conscientiae. 6. Censure of Mr Antony Ascham his book of the confusions and revolutions of government. 7. Pax Ecclesiae concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREDESTINATION">Predestination</a>, or the five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. 8. Episcopacy, as established by law in England, not prejudicial to the regal power, in 1661. Besides these, he wrote two Discourses in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s writings. Saunderson, Dr Nicholas, was born at Thrufstone in Yorkshire in 1682, and may be considered as a prodigy for his application and success in mathematical literature in circumstances apparently the most unfavourable. He lost his sight by the smallpox before he was a year old. But this disaster did not prevent him from searching after that knowledge for which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had given him an ardent desire. He was initiated into the Greek and Roman authors at a free-school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENRITH">Penrith</a>. After spending some years in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the languages, his father (who had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>) began to teach him the common rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. He soon surpassed his father; and could make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and difficult calculations, without having any sensible marks to assist his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. At 18 he was taught the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> by Richard West of Underbank, Esq., who, though a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of fortune, yet, being strongly attached to mathematical learning, readily undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of so uncommon a genius. Saunderson was also assisted in his mathematical studies by Dr Nettleton. These two gentlemen read books to him and explained them. He was next sent to a private academy at Attercliffe near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, where Saunderson, logic and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a> were chiefly taught. But these sciences not fitting his turn of mind, he soon left the academy. He lived for some time in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> without any instructor; but such was the vigour of his own mind, that few instructions were necessary: he only required books and a reader. His father, besides the place he had in the excise, possessed also a small estate; but having a numerous family to support, he was unable to give him a liberal education at one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. Some of his friends, who had remarked his perspicuous and interesting manner of communicating his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, proposed that he should attend the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> as a teacher of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. This proposal was immediately put into execution; and he was accordingly conducted to Cambridge in his 25th year by Mr Joshua Dunn, a fellow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Christ's college. Though he was not received as a member of the college, he was treated with great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and respect. He was allowed a chamber, and had free access to the library. Mr Whiston was at that time professor of mathematics; and as he read lectures in the way that Saunderson intended, it was naturally to be supposed he would view his project as an invasion of his office. But, instead of meditating any opposition, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was no sooner mentioned to him than he gave his consent. Saunderson's reputation was soon spread through the university. When his lectures were announced, a general curiosity was excited to hear such intricate mathematical subjects explained by a man who had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> from his infancy. The subject of his lectures was the Principia Mathematica, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, and Arithmetica Universalis of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton. He was accordingly attended by a very numerous audience. It will appear at first incredible to many that a blind man should be capable of explaining optics, which requires an accurate knowledge of the nature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and colours; but we must recollect, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of vision is taught entirely by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and is subject to the rules of geometry. While thus employed in explaining the principles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he became known to its illustrious author. He was also intimately acquainted with Halley, Cotes, De Moivre, and other eminent mathematicians. When Whiston was removed from his professorship, Saunderson was universally allowed to be the man best qualified for the succession. But to enjoy this office, it was necessary, as the statutes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, that he should be promoted to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. To obtain this privilege the heads of the university applied to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset, who procured the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> mandate to confer upon him the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. He was then elected Lucasian professor of mathematics in November 1711. His inauguration speech was composed in classical Latin, and in the style of Cicero, with whose works he had been much conversant. He now devoted his whole time to his lectures, and the instruction of his pupils. When George II., in 1728, visited the university of Cambridge, he expressed a desire to see Professor Saunderson. In compliance with this desire, he waited upon his majesty in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and was there, by the king's command, created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws. He was admitted a member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in 1736. Saunderson was naturally of a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; but having confined himself to a sedentary life, he at length became scrofulous.
