For several years he felt a numbness in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1739, brought on a mortification in his foot; and, unfortunately, his blood was so vitiated by the scurvy, that assistance from medicine was not to be expected. When he was informed that his death was near, he remained for a little space calm and silent; but he soon recovered his former vivacity, and conversed with his usual ease. He died on the 19th of April 1739, in the 57th year of his age, and was buried at his own request in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> at Boxworth. He married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the reverend Mr Dickens, rector of Boxworth, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, and by her had a son and daughter. Dr Saunderson was rather to be admired as a man of wonderful genius and affability, than to be loved for amiable qualities. He spoke his sentiments freely of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and praised or condemned his friends as well as his enemies without reserve. This has been ascribed by some to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of defamation; but perhaps with more propriety it has been attributed by others to an inflexible love of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, which urged him upon all occasions to speak the sentiments of his mind without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, and without considering whether this conduct would please or give offence. His sentiments were supposed unfavourable to revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. It is said, that he alleged he could not know God, because he was blind, and could not see his works; and that, upon this, Dr Holmes replied, "Lay your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> upon yourself, and the organization which you will feel in your own body will dissipate so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>." On the other hand, we are informed, that he had desired the sacrament to be given him on the evening before his death. He was, however, seized with a delirium, which rendered this impossible. He wrote a system of algebra, which was published, in two volumes 4to, at London, after his death, in the year 1740, at the expense of the university of Cambridge. Dr Saunderson invented for his own use a Palpable Arithmetic; that is, a method of performing operations in arithmetic solely by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of touch. It consisted of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> raised upon a small frame, so that he could apply his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with equal ease above and below. On this table were drawn a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> lines which were crossed by others at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; the edges of the table were divided by notches half an inch distant from one another, and between each notch there were five parallels; so that every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inch was divided into a hundred little squares. At each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the squares where the parallels intersected one another, a hole was made quite through the table. In each hole he placed two pins, a big and a small one. It was by the various arrangements of the pins that Saunderson performed his operations. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this method of making calculations by his table is given under the article Blind, No. 38, though it is there by mistake said that it was not of his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. His sense of touch was so perfect, that he could discover with the greatest exactness the slightest inequality of surface, and could distinguish in the most finished works the smallest oversight in the polish. In the cabinet of medals at Cambridge he could single out the Roman medals with the utmost correctness; he could also perceive the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, while some gentlemen were making observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, he took notice of every little cloud that passed over the sun which could interrupt their labours. When any object passed before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, even though at some distance, he discovered it, and could guess its size with considerable accuracy. When he walked, he knew when he passed by a tree, a wall, or a house. He made these distinctions from the different ways his face was affected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. His musical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> was remarkably acute; he could distinguish accurately to the fifth of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. In his youth he had been a performer on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>; and he had made such proficiency, that if he had cultivated his talents in this way, he would probably have been as eminent in music as he was in mathematics. He recognized not only his friends, but even those with whom he was slightly acquainted, by the tone of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>; and he could judge with wonderful exactness of the size of any apartment into which he was conducted.

SAURIN

Pages 124-126

James, a celebrated preacher, was born at Nîmes in 1677, and was the son of a protestant lawyer of considerable eminence. He applied to his studies with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success; but at length being captivated with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he relinquished them for the profession of arms. In 1694 he made a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADET">cadet</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and soon afterwards obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of colours in the regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Renault which served in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy having made peace with France, he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and resumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> under Turretin and other professors. In 1700 he visited <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, then came to England, where he remained for several years, and married. In 1703 he returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, where he fixed his residence, and preached with the most unbounded applause. To an exterior appearance highly prepossessing, he added a strong harmonious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. The sublime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> which he recited before his sermon was uttered in a manner highly affecting. Nor was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> excited by the prayer dissipated by the sermon: all who heard it were charmed; and those who came with an intention to criticise, were carried along with the preacher and forgot their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. Saurin had, however, one fault fault in his delivery; he did not manage his voice with sufficient skill. He exhausted himself so much in his prayer and the beginning of his sermon, that his voice grew feeble towards the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. His sermons, especially those published during his life, are distinguished for judicious thought, force of reasoning, and an eloquent unaffected style. The first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the celebrated Abbadie heard him preach, he exclaimed, "Is it an angel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who speaks?" Saurin died on the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1732, aged 53 years. He wrote, 1. Sermons, which were published in 12 vols 8vo and 12mo; some of which display great genius and eloquence, and others are composed with negligence. One may observe in them the imprecatory and the aversion which the Calvinists of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> were wont to utter against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. Saurin was, notwithstanding, a lover of toleration; and his sentiments on this subject gave great offence to some of his fanatical brethren, who attempted to obscure his merit, and embitter his life. They found fault with him because he did not call the pope Antichrist, and the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> the whore of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. But these prophetic metaphors, however applicable they may be, were certainly not intended by the benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> to be bandied about as terms of reproach; which would teach those to rail who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them, and irritate, without convincing, those to whom they were applied. Saurin, therefore, while he perhaps interpreted these metaphors in the same way with his opposers, discovered more of the moderation of the Christian spirit. Five volumes of his sermons were published in his life, the rest have been added since his decease. 2. Discourses Historical, Critical, and Moral, on the most memorable Events of the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. This is his greatest and most valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. It was printed first in two volumes folio. As it was left unfinished, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a> and Roques undertook a continuation of it, and increased it to four volumes. It is full of learning: it is indeed a collection of the opinions of the best authors, both Christian and Heathen; of the philosophers, historians, and critics, on every subject which the author examines. 3. The State of Christianity in France, 1725, 8vo. In this book he discusses many important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of controversy, and calls in question the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the miracle said to be performed on La Folie at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. 4. An <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">Abridgment</a> of Christian Theology and Morality, in the form of a Catechism, 1722, 8vo. He afterwards published an abridgment of this work. A Dissertation which he published on the Expediency of sometimes disguising the Truth, raised a multitude of enemies against him. In this discourse his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was, to state the arguments of those who affirm that, in certain <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it is lawful to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> truth, and the answers of those who maintain the contrary. He does not determine the question, but seems, however, to incline to the first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. He was immediately attacked by several adversaries, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> controversy ensued; but his doctrines and opinions were at length publicly approved of by the synods of Campen and of the Hague. The subject of this controversy has long been agitated, and men of equally good principles have supported opposite sides. It would certainly be a dangerous maxim that falsehood can ever be lawful. There may, indeed, be particular cases, when the motives to it are of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as to diminish its criminality in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; but to lessen its guilt is a very different thing from justifying it by the laws of morality. Saurin, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, a geometrician of the academy of Sciences at Paris, was born at Courtoison in the principality of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, in 1659. His father, who was a minister at Grenoble, was his first preceptor. He made rapid progress in his studies, and was admitted minister of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EURE">Eure</a> in Dauphiny when very young; but having made use of some violent expressions in one of his sermons, he was obliged to quit France in 1683. He retired to Geneva, and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, where he obtained a considerable living. He was scarcely settled in his new habitation, when some theologians raised a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against him. Saurin, hating controversy, and disgusted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where his talents were entirely concealed, repaired to Holland. He returned soon after to France, and surrendered himself into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Bolluet bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, who obliged him to make a recantation of his errors. This event took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1690. His enemies, however, suspected his sincerity in the abjuration which he had made. It was a general opinion, that the desire of cultivating science in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of France had a greater effect in producing this change than religion. Saurin, however, speaks of the reformers with great asperity, and condemns them for going too far. "Deceived in my opinions concerning the rigid system of Calvin, I no longer regarded that reformer in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> but as one of those extravagant geniuses who are carried beyond the bounds of truth. Such appeared to me in general the founders of the reformation; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> idea which I have now obtained of their character has enabled me to shake off a load of prejudices. I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> which have separated them from us, such as the invocation of saints, the worship of images, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of meats, &c., that they had much exaggerated the inevitable abuses of the people, and imputed these to the Romish church, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sanctioned by its doctrines. Besides, that they have misrepresented these doctrines which were not connected with any abuse. One thing which surprised me much when my eyes began to open, was the false idea, though in appearance full of respect, for the word of God, which the reformers entertained of the perfection and perspicuity of the Holy Scriptures, and the manifest misinterpretation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which they bring to support that idea (for that misinterpretation is a point which can be proved). Two or three articles still raised some objections in my mind against the Romish church; to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, Transubstantiation, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the sacrament, and the infallibility of the church. The adoration of the sacrament I considered as idolatry, and, on that account, removed from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. But soon after, the Expulsion of the bishop of Meaux, a work which can never be sufficiently admired, and his Treatise concerning changes, reversed all my opinions, and rendered me an enemy to the Reformation." It is said also, that Saurin, appeased his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> Poiret's Cogitationes rationales. This book is written with a view to vindicate the church of Rome from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of idolatry. If it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of distinction that induced Saurin to return. return to the Romish church, he was not disappointed; for he there met with protection and support. He was favourably received by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. obtained a pension from him, and was treated by the Academy of Sciences with the most flattering respect. At that time (1717), <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> formed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> occupation. He adorned the Journal des Scavans with many excellent treatises; and he added to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the Academy many interesting papers. These are the only works which he has left behind him. He died at Paris on the 29th December 1737, in his 78th year, of a fever. He married a wife of the family of Crouas in Switzerland, who bore him a son, Bernard Joseph, distinguished as a writer for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. Saurin was of a bold and impetuous spirit. He had that lofty deportment which is generally mistaken for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>. His philosophy was austere; his opinions of men were not very favourable; and he often delivered them in their presence: this created him many enemies. His <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was attacked after his decease. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was printed in the Mercure Suiffe, said to be written by Saurin from Paris, in which he acknowledges that he had committed several crimes which deserved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Some Calvinist ministers published in 1757 two or three pamphlets to prove the authenticity of that letter; but Voltaire made diligent enquiry, not only at the place where Saurin had been discharging the facerdotal office, but at the deans of the clergy of that department. They all exclaimed against an imputation so opprobrious. It must not, however, be concealed, that Voltaire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> which he has published in his general <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Saurin's conduct, leaves some unfavourable impressions upon the reader's mind. He intimates, that Saurin sacrificed his religion to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; that he played upon Boissot, who believed he had converted a clergyman, when he had only given a little fortune to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>.

SAURURUS

Pages 126-126

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hepandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> order, Piperita. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAUSSURE

Pages 126-126

Horace Benedict de, a celebrated naturalist, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and born in 1740. His father was an intelligent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, who lived at Conches, about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from Geneva, which no doubt contributed, in addition to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, to increase the physical strength of young Saussure, so requisite for a naturalist who intends to travel. He went daily to town for public instruction; and as he lived at the foot of a mountain, he frequently amused himself in ascending its steep and rugged sides. Thus environed by the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and afflicted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, it was to be expected that he would soon conceive a predilection for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> was his most early and favourite study, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which was powerfully encouraged by his local situation, and was the means of introducing him to the acquaintance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Haller, to whom he paid a visit in 1764, and was astonished at his intimate acquaintance with every branch of the natural sciences. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the study of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was also increased by his connection with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">Bonnet</a>, who had married his aunt, and who put a proper estimate on the talents of his nephew. He was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, to which Saussure was also induced to turn his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and published the result of his researches under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Saussure of Observations on the Bark of Leaves. About this time the philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> at Geneva became vacant, and was given to Saussure at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21. Rewards conferred too early have been thought to extinguish some zeal for the increase of knowledge, but this was not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with de Saussure, who taught physics and logic alternately with equal success. For physics, however, he had the greatest taste, as affording the means of perfecting the study of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, and other kindred sciences. He now began his travels through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, not for the purpose of studying, as formerly, their flowery decorations, but their constituent parts, and the disposition of their masses. During the first fifteen years of his professorship, he was alternately engaged in discharging the duties of his office, and in traversing the mountains in the vicinity of Geneva; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his talents as a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> were fully displayed. He extended his researches on one side to the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and on the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. He travelled to Auvergne to examine the extinguished volcanoes, going afterward to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, England, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. It is proper to remark that these were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> journeys, but were undertaken purely with the view of studying nature; and in all his journeys he was surrounded with such instruments as would be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to him; together with plans of his procedure previously drawn up. Readily <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> our readers believe this great philosopher when he asserts, that he found such a method extremely beneficial. The first volume of his travels through the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> was published in 1779, which contains a circumstantial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the environs of Geneva, and an excursion as far as Chamouni, a village at the foot of Mont Blanc. It contains a description of his magnetometer, with which philosophers will probably be delighted. In proportion as he examined mountains, the more was he persuaded of the importance of mineralogy; and that he might study it with advantage, he acquired a knowledge of the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. In the last volumes of his travels, the reader will see how much new mineralogical knowledge he had acquired. During the troubles which agitated Geneva in 1782, he made his beautiful and interesting experiments on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYGROMETRY">hygrometry</a>, which he published in 1783. This has been pronounced the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that ever came from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, and completely established his reputation as a philosopher. De Saussure resigned his chair to his pupil and fellow labourer, Picquet, who discharged the duties of his office with reputation, although rendered difficult to him by succeeding so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. He projected a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> in the education of Geneva, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of which was, to make young people acquainted with the natural sciences and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at an early period, and wished that their physical education should not be neglected, for which purpose he proposed gymnastic exercises. This plan found admirers in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but the poverty of its funds was an obstacle in the way of any important innovation. It was dreaded too, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> established forms were changed, they might be altered for the worse. The attention of De Saussure was not wholly confined to public education, for he superintended the education of his own two sons and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who have since

SAUVAGEISIA

Pages 126-127

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAUVEUR

Pages 127-127
JOSEPH, an eminent French mathematician, born at La Flèche in 1643. He was absolutely dumb until he was seven years of age; and even then his organs of speech were not evolved so fully as to permit him to speak without great deliberation. Mathematics were the only studies he had any relish for, and these he cultivated with extraordinary success; so that he commenced teacher at 20 years of age, and was soon in vogue, that he had Prince Eugene for his scholar. He became mathematical professor in the royal college in 1686; and ten years after was admitted a member of the Academy of Sciences. He died in 1716; and his writings, which consist rather of detached papers than of connected treatises, are all inserted in the Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences. Vol. XVIII. Part II. He was twice married; and by the last wife had a son, Sauveur who, like himself, was dumb for the first seven years of his life.

SAVAGE

Pages 109-117

RICHARD, one of the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> that is to be met with perhaps in all the records of biography, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> countess of Macclesfield by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>, according to her own confession; and was born in 1698. This confession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> was made in order to procure a separation from her husband the earl of Macclesfield: yet, having obtained this desired end, no sooner was her impious offspring brought into the world, than, without the dread of shame <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poverty to accuse her, she discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of disowning him; and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived, treated him with the most unnatural cruelty. She delivered him over to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> woman to educate as her own; prevented the earl of Rivers from leaving him a legacy of 6000l. by declaring him dead: and in effect deprived him of another legacy which his godmother Mrs Lloyd had left him, by concealing from him his birth, and thereby rendering it impossible for him to prosecute his claim. She endeavoured to send him secretly to the plantations; but this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> being either laid aside or frustrated, she placed him apprentice with a shoemaker. In this situation, however, he did not long continue: for his nurse dying, he went to take care of the effects of his supposed mother; and found in her boxes some letters which discovered to young Savage his birth, and the cause of its concealment. From the moment of this discovery it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for him to become dissatisfied with his situation as a shoemaker. He now conceived that he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to share in the affluence of his real mother; and therefore he directly, and perhaps indirectly, applied to her, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of every art to awaken her tenderness and attract her regard. But in vain did he solicit this unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>: she avoided him with the utmost precaution, and took <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to prevent his ever entering her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on any pretence whatever. Savage was at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> so touched with the discovery of his birth, that he frequently made it his practice to walk before his mother's door in hopes of seeing her by accident; and often did he warmly solicit her to admit him to see her; but all to no purpose: he could neither soften her heart nor open her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> time, while he was affiduously endeavouring to rouse the affections of a mother in whom all natural affection was extinct, he was destitute of the means of support, and reduced to the miseries of want. We are not told by what means he got rid of his obligation to the shoemaker, or whether he ever was actually bound to him; but we now find him very differently employed in order to procure a subsistence. In short, the youth had parts, and a strong inclination towards literary pursuits, especially <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. He wrote a poem; and afterwards two plays, Woman's a Riddle, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in a Veil: but the author was allowed no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the profits from the first; and from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> he received no other advantage than the acquaintance of Sir Richard Steele and Mr Wilks, by whom he was pitied, cared for, and relieved. However, the kindness of his friends not affording him a constant supply, he wrote the tragedy of Sir Thomas Overbury; which not only procured him the esteem of many persons of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, but brought him in 200l. The celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill, Esq.; was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to him in correcting and fitting this piece for the stage and the press; and extended his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> still farther. But Savage was, like many other wits, a bad manager, and was ever in distresses. As fast as his friends raised him out of one difficulty, he sunk into another; and, when he found himself greatly involved, he would ramble about like a vagabond, with scarce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> on his back. He was in one of these situations during the time that he wrote his tragedy above-mentioned; without a lodging, and often without a dinner: so that he used to scribble on scraps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> picked up by accident, or begged in the shops, which he occasionally stepped into, as thoughts occurred to him, craving the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, as it were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to take a memorandum. Mr Hill also earnestly promoted a subscription to a volume of Miscellanies, by Savage; and likewise furnished part of the poems of which the volume was composed. To this miscellany Savage wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, in which he gives an account of his mother's cruelty, in a very uncommon strain of humour. The profits of his Tragedy and his Miscellanies together, had now, for a time, somewhat raised poor Savage both in circumstances and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; so that the world just began to behold him with a more favourable eye than formerly, when both his fame and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were endangered by a most unhappy event. A drunken frolic in which he one night engaged, ended in a fray, and Savage unfortunately killed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, for which he was condemned to be hanged; his friends earnestly solicited the mercy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, while his mother as earnestly exerted herself to prevent his receiving it. The counsellors of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a> at length laid his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Caroline, and Savage obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. Savage had now lost that tenderness for his mother which the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of her cruelty had not been able wholly to repress; and considering her as an implacable enemy, whom nothing but his blood could satisfy, threatened to harass her with lampoons, and to publish a copious narrative of her conduct, unless she consented to allow him a pension. This expedient proved successful; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Tyrconnel, upon his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of laying aside his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his mother's cruelty, took him into his family, treated him as an equal, and engaged to allow him a pension of 200l. a-year. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> part of Savage's life. He was courted by all who endeavoured to be thought men of genius, and cared for by all who valued themselves upon a refined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. In this gay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his life he published the Temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a> and Mirth, on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of Lady Tyrconnel from a languishing illness; and The Wanderer, a moral poem, which he dedicated to Lord Tyrconnel, in strains of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>: but these praises he in a short time found himself inclined to retract, being discarded by the man on whom they were bestowed. Of this quarrel Lord Tyrconnel and Mr Savage assigned very different reasons. Our author's known character pleads too strongly against him; for his conduct was ever such as made all his friends, sooner or later, grow weary of him, and even forced most of them to become his enemies. Being thus once more turned adrift upon the world, Savage, whose passions were very strong, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> was very small, became extremely diligent in exposing the faults of Lord Tyrconnel. He, moreover now thought himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to take <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> upon his mother.—Accordingly he wrote The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a>, a poem, remarkable for the vivacity of its beginning (where he finely enumerates the imaginary advantages of base birth), and for the pathetic conclusion, wherein he recounts the real calamities which he suffered by the crime of his parents.—The reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be displeased with a transcript of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in the opening of the poem, as a specimen of this writer's spirit and manner of versification. Blest be the bastard's birth! thro' wondrous ways, He shines eccentric like a comet's blaze. No sickly fruit of faint compliance he; He! stamp'd in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>'s mint with ecstacy! He lives to build, not boast, a gen'rous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; No tenth transmitter of a foolish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. I'e, kindling from within, requires no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, He glories in a bastard's glowing name. —Nature's unbounded son, he stands alone, His heart unbias'd, and his mind his own. —O mother! yet no mother!—tis to you My thanks for such disingui'th'd claims are due. This poem had an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; and its appearance happening at the time when his mother was at Bath, many persons there took frequent opportunities of repeating <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> from the Bastard in their hearing. This was perhaps the first time that ever the discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of shame, and on this occasion the power of wit was very conspicuous: the wretch who had, without scruple, proclaimed herself an adulteress, and who had first endeavoured to starve her son, then to transport him Savage, him, and afterwards to hang him, was not able to bear the representation of her own conduct; but fled from reproach, though she felt no pain from guilt; and left Bath with the utmost haste, to shelter herself among the crowds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> (a). Some time after this, Savage formed the resolution of applying to the queen; who having once given him life, he hoped she might farther extend her goodness to him, by enabling him to support it.—With this view, he published a poem on her birthday, which he entitled The Volunteer-Laureate; for which she was pleased to send him £50, with an intimation that he might annually expect the same bounty. But this annual allowance was nothing to a man of his strange and singular extravagance. His usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was, as soon as he had received his pension, to disappear with it, and secrete himself from his most intimate friends, till every shilling of the £50 was spent; which done, he again appeared, penniless as before: But he would never inform any person where he had been, or in what manner his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> had been dissipated.—From the reports, however, of some, who found means to penetrate his haunts, (a) Mr Boswell, in his life of Dr Johnson, has called into question the story of Savage's birth, and grounded his suspicion on two mistakes, or, as he calls them, falsehoods, which he thinks he has discovered in his friend's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of that extraordinary man. Johnson has said, that the earl of Rivers was Savage's godfather, and gave him his own name; which, by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, was inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St Andrew's, Holborn. Part of this, it seems, is not true; for Mr Boswell carefully inspected that register, but no such entry is to be found. But does this omission amount to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, that the person who called himself Richard Savage was an impostor, and not the son of the earl of Rivers and the countess of Macclesfield? Mr Boswell thinks it does; and, in behalf of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, appeals to the maxim, *fallum in uno, fallum in omnibus*. The solidity of this maxim may be allowed by others; but it was not without surprise that, on such an occasion, we found it adopted by the biographer of Johnson. To all who have compared his view of a celebrated cause, with Stuart's letters on the same subject addressed to Lord <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>, it must be apparent, that, at one period of his life, he would not have deemed a thousand such mistakes sufficient to invalidate a narrative otherwise so well authenticated as that which relates the birth of Savage. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that the omission of the name in the register of St Andrew's may be easily accounted for, without bringing against the wretched Savage an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of imposture, which neither his mother nor her friends dared to urge when provoked to it by every possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> that can influence <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> conduct. The earl of Rivers would undoubtedly give the direction about registering the child's name to the same person whom he entrusted with the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; but that person, it is well known, was the countess of Macclesfield, who, as she had resolved from his birth to disown her son, would take care that the direction should not be obeyed. That which, in Johnson's life of Savage, Mr Boswell calls a second falsehood, seems not to amount even to a mistake. It is there stated, that "Lady Macclesfield having lived for some time upon very uneasy terms with her husband, thought a public confession of adultery the most obvious and expeditious method of obtaining her liberty." This Mr Boswell thinks cannot be true; because, having perused the journals of both houses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> at the period of her divorce, he there found it authentically ascertained, that so far from voluntarily submitting to the ignominious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of adultery, she made a strenuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> by her counsel. But what is this to the purpose? Johnson has nowhere said, that she confessed her adultery at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of either house of parliament, but only that her confession was public; and as he has taught us in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, that whatever is notorious or generally known is public; public, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, that confession certainly was, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> made to different individuals, in such a manner as showed that she was not anxious to conceal it from her husband, or to prevent its notoriety. She might, however, have very cogent reasons for denying her guilt before parliament, and for making a strenuous defence by her counsel; as indeed, had she acted otherwise, it is very little probable that her great fortune would have been restored to her, or that she could have obtained a second husband. But Mr Boswell is of opinion, that the person who assumed the name of Richard Savage was the son of the shoemaker under whose care Lady Macclesfield's child was placed; because "his not being able to obtain payment of Mrs Lloyd's legacy must be imputed to his consciousness that he was not the real person to whom that legacy was left." He must have a willing mind who can admit this argument as a proof of imposture. Mrs Lloyd died when Savage was in his tenth year, when he certainly did not know or suspect that he was the person for whom the legacy was intended, when he had none to prosecute his claim, to shelter him from oppression, or to call in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the assistance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. In such circumstances he could not have obtained payment of the money, unless the executors of the will had been inspired from heaven with the knowledge of the person to whom it was due. To these and a thousand such idle cavils it is a sufficient answer, that Savage was acknowledged and patronized as Lady Macclesfield's son by Lord Tyrconnel, who was that lady's nephew; by Sir Richard Steele, the intimate friend of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Brett, who was that lady's second husband; by the queen, who, upon the authority of that lady and her creatures, once thought Savage capable of entering her mother's house in the night with an intent to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> her; and in effect by the lady herself, who at one time was prevailed upon to give him £50, and who fled before the satire of the Bajard, without offering, either by herself or her friends, to deny that the author of that poem was the person whom he called himself, or to infirmate so much as that he might possibly be the son of a shoemaker. To Mr Boswell all this seems strange; to others, who look not with so keen an eye for spurious births, we think it must appear convincing. Vol. XVIII. Part II. it would seem that he expended both his time and his cath in the most fordid and despicable feniality; parti- cularly in eating and drinking, in which he would in- dulge in the most unloose manner, fitting whole days and nights by himself, in obscure houses of entertain- ment, over his bottle and trencher, immersed in filth and filth, with scarce decent apparel; generally wrapped up in a horseman's coat; and, on the whole, with his very homely countenance, altogether, exhibiting an ob- ject the most disgusting to the sight, if not to some other of the fenses. His wit and parts, however, still raised him new friends as fast as his behaviour lost him his old ones. Yet such was his conduct, that occasional reliefe only fur- nished the means of occasional excesses; and he defeated all attempts made by his friends to fix him in a decent way. He was even reduced so low as to be destitute of a lodging; infomuch that he often passed his nights in those mean houses that are set open for casual wander- ers; sometimes in cellars amidst the riot and filth of the most profligate of the rabble; and not seldom would he walk the streets till he was weary, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> on a bulk, or in winter with his associates among the attics of a glas-house. Yet, amidst all his penury and wretchedness, had this man so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an opinion of his own merit, that he ever kept up his spirits, and was always ready to repulse, with scorn and contempt, the least ap- pearance of any slight or indignity towards himself, in the behaviour of his acquaintance; among whom he looked upon none as his superior. He would be treat- ed as an equal, even by persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. We have an instance of this profligacy and insensible pride, in his refusing to wait upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who was desirous of relieving him when at the lowest ebb of distress, only because the message signified the gen- tleman's desire to see him at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning. Sa- vage could not bear that any one should presume to prescribe the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his attendance, and therefore he absolutely rejected the proffered kindness. This life, unhappy as it may be already imagined, was yet ren- dered more unhappy, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the queen, in 1738; which stroke deprived him of all hopes from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His pension was discontinued, and the in- sensitive manner in which he demanded of Sir Robert Walpole to have it restored, for ever cut off this consi- derable supply; which possibly had been only delayed, and might have been recovered by proper application. His distress became now so great, and so notorious, that a scheme was at length concerted for procuring him a permanent relief. It was proposed that he should retire into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, with an allowance of 50l. per annum, on which he was to live privately in a cheap <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, for ever quitting his town-haunts, and re- signing all farther pretensions to fame. This offer he seemed gladly to accept; but his intentions were only to deceive his friends, by retiring for a while, to write another tragedy, and then to return with it to London in order to bring it upon the stage. In 1739, he set out in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> stage-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWANSEA">Swansea</a>, and was furnished with 15 guineas to bear the expense of his journey. But, on the 14th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after his departure, his friends and benefactors, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom was no other than the great Mr Pope, who expected to hear of his arrival in Wales, were surprised with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Savage, informing them that he was yet upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and could not proceed for want of money. There was no other method than a remittance; which was sent him, and by the help of which he was enabled to reach Bristol, from whence he was to pro- ceed to Swansea by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. At Bristol, however, he found an embargo laid upon the shipping; so that he could not immediately obtain a passage. Here, there- fore, being obliged to stay for some time, he, with his usual facility, to ingratiate himself with the principal inhabitants, that he was frequently invited to their hou- ses, distinguished at their public entertainments, and treated with a regard that highly flattered his vanity, and therefore easily engaged his affections. At length, with great reluctance, he proceeded to Swansea; where he lived about a year, very much dissatisfied with the diminution of his salary; for he had, in his letters, treated his contributors so insolently, that most of them withdrew their subscriptions. Here he finished his tra- gedy, and resolved to return with it to London; which was strenuously opposed by his great and constant friend Mr Pope; who proposed that Savage should put this play into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Mr Thomson and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, in order that they might fit it for the stage, that his friends should receive the profits it might bring in, and that the author should receive the produce by way of annuity. This kind and prudent scheme was rejected by Savage with the utmost contempt.—He declared he would not submit his works to any one's correction; and that he should no longer be kept in leading strings. Accordingly he soon returned to Bri- stol in his way to London; but at Bristol, meeting with a repetition of the same kind treatment he had before found there, he was tempted to make a second stay in that opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> for some time. Here he was again not only cared for and treated, but the sum of 30l. was raised for him, with which it had been happy if he had immediately departed for London: But he never considered that a frequent repetition of such kindness was not to be expected, and that it was possible to tire out the generosity of his Bristol friends, as he had be- fore tired his friends everywhere else. In short, he remained here till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was no longer welcome. His visits in every family were too often repeated; his wit had lost its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> behaviour grew troublesome. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a> came upon him before he was aware; his money was spent, his clothes were worn out, his appearance was shabby; and his presence was disgusting at every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. He now began to find every man from home at whose house he called; and he found it difficult to obtain a dinner. Thus reduced, it would have been prudent in him to have withdrawn from the place; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and Savage were never acquainted. He stood, in the midst of poverty, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, and contempt, till the mistress of a coffee-house, to whom he owed about eight pounds, arrested him for the debt. He remained for some time, at a great ex- pense, in the house of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s officer, in hopes of procuring bail; which expense he was enabled to defray, by a present of five guineas from Mr Nash at Bath. No bail, however, was to be found; so that poor Savage was at last lodged in Newgate, a prison so named in Bristol. But it was the fortune of this extraordinary mortal always to find more friends than he deserved. The keeper of the prison took compassion on him, and greatly softened the rigours of his confinement by every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>; he supported him at his own table, gave him a commodious room to himself, allowed him to stand at the door of the gaol, and even frequently took him into the fields for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>: so that, in reality, Savage endured fewer hardships in this place than he had usually suffered during the greatest part of his life. While he remained in this not intolerable prison, his ingratitude again broke out, in a bitter satire on the city of Bristol; to which he certainly owed great obligations, notwithstanding the circumstances of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>; which was but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of an individual, and that attended with no circumstances of injustice or cruelty. This satire he entitled London and Bristol delineated; and in it he abused the inhabitants of the latter, with such a spirit of resentment, that the reader would imagine he had never received any other than the most injurious treatment in that city. When Savage had remained about six months in this hospitable prison, he received a letter from Mr Pope, (who still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to allow him 20l. a-year) containing a charge of very atrocious ingratitude. What were the particulars of this charge we are not informed; but, from the notorious character of the man, there is reason to fear that Savage was but too justly accused. He, however, solemnly protested his innocence; but he was very uneasily affected on this occasion. In a few days after, he was seized with a disorder, which at first was not suspected to be dangerous; but growing daily more languid and dejected, at last a fever seized him; and he expired on the 1st of August 1743, in the 46th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Thus lived, and thus died, Richard Savage, Esq., leaving behind him a character strangely chequered with vices and good qualities. Of the former we have seen a variety of instances in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of his life; of the latter, his peculiar situation in the world gave him but few opportunities of making any considerable display. He was, however, undoubtedly a man of excellent parts; and had he received the full benefits of a liberal education, and had his natural talents been cultivated to the best advantage, he might have made a respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in life. He was happy in a quick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, a retentive <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and a lively flow of wit, which made his company much coveted; nor was his judgment both of writings and of men inferior to his wit: but he was too much a slave to his passions, and his passions were too easily excited. He was warm in his friendships, but implacable in his enmity; and his greatest fault, which is indeed the greatest of all faults, was ingratitude. He seemed to think every thing due to his merit, and that he was little obliged to any one for those favours which he thought it their duty to confer on him: it is therefore the less to be wondered at, that he never rightly estimated the kindness of his many friends and benefactors, or preserved a grateful and due sense of their generosity towards him. The works of this original writer, after having long lain dispersed in magazines and fugitive publications, have been lately collected and published in an elegant edition, in 2 vols 8vo; to which are prefixed, the admirable Memoirs of Savage, written by Dr Samuel Savage Johnson. Savage is a word so well understood as scarcely to require explanation. When applied to inferior animals, it denotes that they are wild, untamed, and cruel; when applied to man, it is of much the same import with barbarian, and means a person who is untaught and uncivilized, or who is in the rude state of uncultivated nature. That such men exist at present, and have existed in most ages of the world, is undeniable; but a question naturally occurs respecting the origin of this savage state, the determination of which is of considerable importance in developing the nature of man, and ascertaining the qualities and powers of the human mind. Upon this subject, as upon most others, opinions are very various, and the systems built upon them are consequently very contradictory. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers maintained that man sprung at first from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> like his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> vegetables; that he was without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and without speech; and that many ages elapsed before the race acquired the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, or attained to greater knowledge than the beasts of the forest. Other sects again, with the vulgar, and almost all the poets, maintained that the first mortals were wiser and happier, and more powerful, than any of their offspring; that mankind, instead of being originally savages, and rising to the state of civilization by their own gradual and progressive exertions, were created in a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection; that, however, they degenerated from that state, and that all nature degenerated with them. Hence the various ages of the world have almost everywhere been compared to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, the golden having been always supposed to be the first age. Since the revival of letters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and especially during the present century, the same question has been much agitated both in France and England, and by far the greater part of the most fashionable names in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> science have declared for the original savagery of men. Such of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> as held that opinion were countenanced by the atheistic cosmogony of the Phoenicians, and by the early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of their own nations; the moderns build their system upon what they suppose to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the human mind, and upon the late improvements in arts and sciences. As the question must finally be decided by historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, before we make our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to facts, we shall consider the force of the modern reasonings from the supposed innate powers of the human mind; for that reasoning is totally different from the other, and to blend them together would only prevent the reader from having an adequate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of either. Upon the supposition that all mankind were originally savages, destitute of the use of speech, and, in the strictest sense of the words, mutium et turpe pecus, the great difficulty is to conceive how they could emerge from that state, and become at last enlightened and civilized. The modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for the universality of the savage state remove this difficulty by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of instincts or internal senses, with which they suppose the human mind endowed, and by which the savage is, without reflection, not only enabled to distinguish between right and wrong, and prompted to do everything necessary to the preservation of his existence, and the continuance of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but also led to the discovery Savage of what will contribute, in the first instance, to the ease and accommodations of life. These instincts, they think, brought mankind together, when the reasoning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, which had hitherto been dormant, being now raised by the collisions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, made its observations upon the consequences of their different actions, taught them to avoid such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> showed to be pernicious, and to improve upon those which they found beneficial; and thus was the progress of civilization begun. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> is opposed by objections which we know not how to obviate. The bundle of instincts with which modern idleness, under the denomination of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, has so amply furnished the human mind is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> chimera. (See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">Instinct</a>.) But granting its reality, it is by no means sufficient to produce the consequences which are derived from it. That it is not the parent of language, we have shown at large in another place (see Language, No. 1—7); and we have the confession of some of the ablest advocates for the original savagism of man, that large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> must have been formed before language could have been invented. How societies, at least large societies, could be formed and kept together without language, we have not indeed been told; but we are assured by every historian and every traveller of credit, that in such societies only have mankind been found civilized. Among known savages the social force is very much confined; and therefore, had it been in the first race of men of an enlarged nature, and as safe a guide, as the instinctive philosophers contend that it was, it is plain that those men could not have been savages. Such an appetite for society, and such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of conduct, instead of enabling mankind to have emerged from savagism, would have effectually prevented them from ever becoming savage; it would have knit them together from the very first, and furnished opportunities for the progenitors of the human race to have begun the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of civilization from the moment that they dropt from the hands of their Creator. Indeed, were the modern theories of internal senses and social affections well founded, and were these senses and affections sufficient to have impelled the first men into society, it is not easy to be conceived how there could be at this day a savage tribe on the face of the earth. Natural causes, operating in the same direction and with the same force, must in every age produce the same effects; and if the social affections of the first mortals impelled them to society, and their reasoning faculties immediately commenced the process of civilization, surely the same affections and the same faculties would in a greater or less degree have had the same effect in every age and on every tribe of their numerous offspring; and we should everywhere observe mankind advancing in civilization, instead of standing still as they often do, and sometimes retreating by a retrograde <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. This, however, is far from being the case. Hordes of savages exist in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe; and the Chinese, who have undoubtedly been in a state of civilization for at least 2000 years, have during the whole of that long period been absolutely <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, if they have not lost some of their ancient arts. (See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>.) The origin of civilization, therefore, is not to be looked for in human instincts or human propensities, carrying men forward by a natural progress; for the supposition of such propensities is contrary to fact; and by fact and historical evidence, in conjunction with what we know of the nature of man, must this great question be at last decided. In the article <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, No. 7, it has been shewn that the first men, if left to themselves without any instruction, instead of living the life of savages, and in process of time advancing towards civilization, must have perished before they acquired even the use of fome of their senses. In the same article it has been shewn (No. 14—17), that Moses, as he is undoubtedly the oldest historian extant, wrote likewise by immediate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; and that therefore, as he represents our first parents and their immediate descendants as in a state far removed from that of savages, it is vain to attempt to deduce the originality of such a state from hypothetical theories of human nature. We have, indeed, heard it observed by some of the advocates for the antiquity and universality of the savage state, that to the appeal to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> they have no objection, provided we take the Mosaic account as it stands, and draw not from it conclusions which it will not support. They contend, at the same time, that there is no argument fairly deducible from the book of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> which militates against their position. Now we beg leave to remark, that besides the reasoning which we have already used in the article just referred to, we have as much positive evidence against their position as the nature of the Mosaic history could be supposed to afford. We are there told that God created man after his own image; that he gave him dominion over every thing in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in the air, and over all the earth; that he appointed for his food various kinds of vegetables; that he ordained the Sabbath to be observed by him, in commemoration of the works of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; that he prepared for him a garden to till and to dress; and that, as a test of his religion and submission to his Creator, he forbade him, under severe penalties, to eat of a certain tree in that garden. We are then told that God brought to him every animal which had been created; and we find that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> was so well acquainted with their several natures as to give them names. When, too, an helpmate was provided for him, he immediately acknowledged her as bone of his bone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of his flesh, and called her woman, because she was taken out of man. How these facts can be reconciled to a state of ignorant savagism is to us absolutely inconceivable; and it is indeed strange, that men who profess Christianity should appeal to reason, and stick by its decision on a question which revelation has thus plainly decided against them. But it is agreeable to their theory to believe that man rose by slow steps to the full use of his reasoning powers. To us, on the other hand, it appears equally plausible to suppose that our first parents were created, not in full maturity, but mere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, and that they went through the tedious process of childhood and youth, &c., as to suppose that their minds were created weak, uninformed, and uncivilized, as are those of savages. But if it be granted that Adam had a tolerable share of knowledge, and some civilization, nothing can be more natural than to suppose that he would teach his descendants what he knew himself; and if the Scriptures are to be believed, we are certain that some of them possessed more than savage knowledge, and better Savage than savage manners. But instead of going on to further perfection, as the theory of modern philosophers would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to suppose, we find that mankind degenerated in a most astonishing degree; the causes of which we have already in part developed in the article Polytheism, No. 4, &c. This early degeneracy of the human race, or their sudden progress towards <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and savagery, appears to lead to an important <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. If men so very soon after their creation, possessing, as we have seen they did, a considerable share of knowledge and of civilization, instead of improving in either, degenerated in both respects, it would not appear that human nature has that strong propensity to refinement which many philosophers imagine; or that had all men been originally savage, they would have civilized themselves by their own exertions. Of the ages before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> we have no certain account anywhere but in Scripture; where, though we find mankind represented as very wicked, we have no reason to suppose them to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> savages. On the contrary, we have much reason, from the short account of Moses, to conclude that they were far advanced in the arts of civil life. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>, we are told, built a city; and two of his early descendants invented the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> and organ, and were artificers in brass and iron. Cities are not built, nor musical instruments invented, by savages, but by men highly cultivated; and surely we have no reason to suppose that the righteous posterity of Seth were behind the apostate descendants of Cain in any branch of knowledge that was really useful. That <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> and his family were far removed from savagery, no one will controvert who believes that with them was made a new covenant of religion; and it was unquestionably their duty, as it must otherwise have been their wish, to communicate what knowledge they possessed to their posterity. Thus far then every confident Christian, we think, must determine against original and universal savagery. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> discourse to Sketches of the History of Man, Lord Kames would infer, from some facts which he states, that many pairs of the human race were at first created, of very different forms and natures, but all depending entirely on their own natural talents. But to this statement he rightly observes, that the Mosaic account of the Creation opposes insuperable objections. "Whence then (says his Lordship) the degeneracy of all men into the savage state? To account for that dismal catastrophe, mankind must have suffered some dreadful convulsion." Now, if we mistake not, this is taking for granted the very thing to be proved. We deny that at any period since the creation of the world, all men were sunk into the state of savages; and that they were, no proof has yet been brought, nor do we know of any that can be brought, unless our fashionable philosophers choose to prop their theories by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTRESS">buttress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANCHONIATHO">Sanchoniatho</a>'s Phenician cosmogony. (See Sanchoniatho.) His Lordship, however, goes on to say, or rather to suppose, that the confusion at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>, &c., was this dreadful convulsion: For, says he, "by confounding the language of men, and scattering them abroad upon the face of all the earth, they were rendered savages." Here again we have a positive assertion, without the least shadow of proof; for it does not at all appear that the confusion of language, and the scattering abroad of the people, was savage—a circumstance such as could induce universal savagery. There is no reason to think that all the men then alive were engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the tower of Babel; nor does it appear from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> original that the language of those who were engaged in it was so much changed as the reader is apt to infer from our English version. (See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILOLOGY">Philology</a>, No. 8—16.) That the builders were scattered, is indeed certain; and if any of them were driven, in very small tribes, to a great distance from their brethren, they would in process of time inevitably become savages. (See Polytheism, No. 4—6, and Language, No. 7;) but it is evident, from the Scripture account of the peopling of the earth, that the descendants of Shem and Japheth were not scattered over the face of all the earth, and that therefore they could not be rendered savage by the catastrophe at Babel. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> which relates that wonderful event, the generations of Shem are given in order down to Abram; but there is no indication that they had suffered with the builders of the tower, or that any of them had degenerated into the state of savages.
