The saw, instead of fig. 4, &c., being allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in a vertical groove as it cuts the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, is attached to a lever or beam FG, sufficiently strong; this lever has several holes pierced through it, and so has the vertical piece ED, which is likewise moveable towards either side of the frame in grooves in the top and bottom pieces AI, DM. Thus, the length KG of the radius can be varied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the curvature of NO; and as the saw is moved to and fro by proper machinery, in the direction CB, BC, it works lower and lower into the block, while, being confined by the beam FG, it cuts the cylindrical portion from the block P, as required. When a completely cylindrical pillar is to be cut out of one block of stone, the first thing will be to ascertain in the block the position of the axis of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>: then lay the block so that such axis shall be parallel to the horizon, and let a cylindrical hole of from one to two inches diameter be bored entirely through it. Let an iron bar, whose diameter is rather less than that of this tube, be put through it, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> room to slide freely to and fro as occasion may require. Each end of this bar should terminate in a screw, on which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> and frame may be fastened: the nut frame should carry three flat pieces of wood or iron, each having a slit running along its middle nearly from one end to the other, and a screw and handle must be adapted to each slit: by these means the framework at each end of the bar may readily be so adjusted as to form equal isosceles or equilateral triangles; the iron bar will connect two corresponding responding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of these triangles, the saw to be used two other corresponding angles, and another bar of iron or wood the two remaining angles, to give sufficient strength to the whole frame. This construction, it is obvious, will enable the workmen to place the saw at any proposed distance from the hole drilled through the middle of the block; and then, by giving the alternating motion to the saw frame, the cylinder may at length be cut from the block, as required. If it were proposed to saw a conic frustum from such a block, then let two frames of wood or iron be fixed to those parallel ends of the block which are intended to coincide with the bases of the frustum, circular grooves being previously cut in these frames to correspond with the circumferences of the two ends of the proposed frustum; the saw being worked in these grooves will manifestly cut the conic surface from the block. This, we believe, is the contrivance of Sir George Wright. The best method of drilling the hole through the middle of the proposed cylinder seems to be this: on a carriage running upon four low wheels let two vertical pieces (each having a hole just large enough to admit the borer to play freely) be fixed two or three feet apart, and so contrived that the pieces and holes to receive the borer may, by screws, &c., be raised or lowered at pleasure, while the borer is prevented from sliding to and fro by shoulders upon its bar, which are larger than the holes in the vertical pieces, and which, as the borer revolves, press against those pieces: let a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORING">boring</a> bar between the two vertical pieces be square, and a grooved wheel with a square hole of a suitable size be placed upon this part of the bar; then the rotatory motion may be given to the bar by an endless band which shall pass over this grooved wheel and a wheel of a much larger diameter in the same plane, the latter wheel being turned by a winch handle in the usual way. See boring of ordnance. Circular saws, acting by a rotatory motion, have been long known in Holland, where they are used for cutting wood used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENEERING">veneering</a>. They were introduced into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, we believe, by General Bentham, and are now used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>-yard at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, and in a few other places: but they are not, as yet, so generally adopted as might be wished, considering how well they are calculated to abridge labour, and to accomplish with expedition and accuracy what is very tedious and irksome to perform in the usual way. Circular saws may be made to turn either in horizontal, vertical, or inclined planes; and the timber to be cut may be laid upon a plane inclined in any direction; so that it may be sawn by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> making any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> whatever, or at any proposed distance from each other. When the saw is fixed at a certain angle, and at a certain distance from the edge of the frame, all the pieces will be cut of the same size, without marking upon them by a chalked line, merely by causing them to be moved along and keeping one side in contact with the side of the frame; for then, as they are brought one by one to touch the saw revolving on its axle, and are pressed upon it, they are soon cut through. Mr Smart, of Ordnance wharf, Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, has several circular saws, all worked by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> in a moderate sized walk; one of these, intended for cutting and boring tenons used in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, is represented in fig. 6. NOPQR is a hollow frame, under which is part of the wheel-work of the horse-mill. —A, B, D, C, E, F, are pulleys, over which pass straps or endless bands, the parts of which out of sight run upon the rim of a large vertical wheel: by means of this simple apparatus, the saws S, S', are made to revolve upon their axles with an equal velocity, the same band passing round the pulleys D, C, upon those axles; and the rotatory motion is given to the borer G by the band passing over the pulley A. The board I is inclined to the horizon in an angle of about 30 degrees; the plane of the saw S' is parallel to that of the board I, and about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch distant from it, while the plane of the saw S is vertical, and its lowest point at the same distance from the board I. Each piece of wood K out of which the tenon is to be cut is four inches long, an inch and a quarter broad, and five-eighths of an inch thick. One end of such piece is laid so as to slide along the ledge at the lower part of the board I; and as it is pushed on, by means of the handle H, it is first cut by the saw S', and immediately after by the saw S: after this the other end is put lowest, and the piece is again cut by both saws: then the tenon is applied to the borer G, and as soon as a hole is pierced through it, it is dropped into the box beneath. By this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, at least 30 tenons may be completed in a minute, with greater accuracy than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> could make one in a quarter of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, with a common hand-saw and gimlet. The like kind of contrivance may, by slight alterations, be fitted for many other purposes, particularly all such as may require the speedy sawing of a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pieces into exactly the same size and shape. Gregory's Mechanics, II. Saxe, Maurice <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of, was born the 13th October 1666. He was the natural son of Frederic Augustus II, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and of the countess of Konigsmarck, a Swedish lady, celebrated both for her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. He was educated along with Frederic Augustus the electoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, afterwards king of Poland. His infancy announced the future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>. Nothing could prevail on him to apply to his studies but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of being allowed, after he had finished his talk, to mount on horseback, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> himself with arms. He served his first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> commanded by Prince Eugene and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, when only twelve years old. He signalized himself at the sieges of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAY">Tournay</a> and Mons, and particularly at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALPLAQUET">Malplaquet</a>. In the evening of that memorable day, he was heard to say, "I'm content with my day's work." During the campaign of 1710, Prince Eugene and the duke of Marlborough made many public encomiums on his merit. Next year the young count accompanied the king of Poland to the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRALSUND">Stralsund</a>, the strongest place in Pomerania, and displayed the greatest intrepidity. He swam across the river in flight of the enemy, with a pistol in his hand. His valour shone no less conspicuously on the bloody day of Gaedeluck, where he commanded a regiment of cavalry. He had a horse killed under him, after he had three times rallied his regiment, and led them on to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. Soon after that campaign, his mother prevailed on him to marry the countess of Lubin, a lady both rich and beautiful. This union lasted but a short time. In 1721, the count procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; a step of which he afterwards repented. The countess left him with regret; but this did not prevent her from marrying soon after. The count of Saxe was too fond of pleasure and variety to submit to the duties which marriage imposes. In the midst, however, of the pleasures in which he sometimes indulged, he never lost sight of his profession. He carried along with him wherever he went a library of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> books; and even when he seemed most taken up with his pleasures, he never failed to spend an hour or two in private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. In 1717 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> had an army of 15,000 men under the command of Prince Eugene. Young Count Saxe was present at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>, and at a battle which the prince gained over the Turks. On his return to Poland in 1718, he was made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> eagle. The wars in Europe being concluded by the treaties of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> and Passarowitz, Count Saxe went to France. He had always professed a partiality for that country. French, indeed, was the only foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which during his infancy he was willing to learn. He spent his whole time during the peace in studying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, fortification, and mechanics, sciences which exactly suited his genius. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of exercising troops had struck his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> when very young. At 16 he invented a new exercise, which was taught in Saxony with the greatest success. Having obtained a regiment in France in 1722, he formed it himself according to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. From that moment the Chevalier Folard, an excellent judge of military talents, predicted that he would be a great man. In 1726 the states of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a> chose him for their sovereign. But both Poland and Russia rose in arms to oppose him. The Czarina wished to bestow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> on Menzikoff, a happy adventurer, who from a pastry-cook's boy became a general and a prince. Menzikoff sent 800 Russian troops to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, where they besieged the new-chosen duke in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Count Saxe, who had only 60 men, defended himself with astonishing intrepidity. The siege was raised, and the Russians obliged to retreat. Soon after he retired to Ulmiz, and prepared to defend his people against the two hostile nations. Here he remained with only 300 men, till the Russian general approached at the head of 4000 to force his retreat. That general invited the count to a conference, during which he intended to surprise him, and take him prisoner. The count, informed of the plot, reproached him for his baseness, and broke up the conference. About this time he wrote to France for men and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Mademoiselle le Couvreur, a famous actress, pawned her jewels and plate, and sent him the sum of 40,000 livres. This actress had formed his mind for the fine arts. She had made him read the greater part of the French poets, and given him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which he retained even in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The count, unable to defend himself against Russia and Poland, was obliged in the year 1729 to leave his new dominions, and retire into France. It is said that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Ivanowa, duchess dowager of Courland, and second <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the tsar Ivan Alexievitch, had given him hopes of marriage, and abandoned him at that time because she despaired of fixing his wavering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>.—This infatuation lost him not only Courland, but the throne of Russia itself, which that princess afterwards filled. Count Saxe, thus stript of his territories, devoted himself for some time to the study of mathematics. He composed also, in 13 nights, and during the intervals of anague, his Reveries, which he corrected afterwards. This book is written in an incorrect but forcible style; it is full of remarks both new and profound, and is equally useful to the soldier and the general. The death of the king of Poland his father, in 1733, kindled a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Europe. His brother, the elector of Saxony, offered him the command of all his forces, but he preferred the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and repaired to the marshal of Berwick's army, which was encamped on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. "Count," said that general, who was preparing to attack the enemy's entrenchments at Ettingen, "I was going to send for 3000 men, but your arrival is of more value than theirs." When the attack began, the count, at the head of a regiment of grenadiers, forced the enemy's lines, and by his bravery decided the victory. He behaved at the siege of Philipburgh with no less intrepidity. For these services he was, in 1734, rewarded with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general. Peace was concluded in 1736; but the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI, emperor of Germany kindled a new war almost immediately. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> was besieged by the count of Saxe in 1742, near the end of November, and taken the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> by assault. The conquest of Egra followed that of Prague. It was taken a few days after the trenches were opened. This success gave so much joy to the emperor Charles VII, that he wrote a congratulatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the conqueror with his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. In 1744 he was made marshal of France, and commanded a part of the French army in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. During that campaign he displayed the greatest military conduct. Though the enemy was superior in number, he observed their motions so skilfully that they could do nothing. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1745, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> was concluded at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a> between the queen of Hungary, the king of England, and the States of Holland. The ambassador of the States General, meeting Marshal Saxe one day at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, asked his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>. "I think (says he), that if the king my master would give me an unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, I would read the original at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> before the end of the year." This answer was not a bravado; the marshal was capable of performing it. He went soon after, though exceedingly ill, to take the command of the French army in the Low Countries. A gentleman seeing the feeble condition in which he left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, asked him how he could in that situation undertake so great an enterprise. "The question (replied he) is not about living, but setting out."—Soon after the opening of the campaign, the battle of Fontenoy was fought. Marshal Saxe was at the point of death, yet he caused himself to be put into a litter, and carried round all the posts. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he mounted on horseback, though he was so very weak that his attendants dreaded every moment to see him expire. The victory of Fontenoy, owing entirely to his vigilance and capacity, was followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Tournay, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, Ghent, Oudenaarde, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and... SAX and Brufels: This last city was taken on the 28th February 1746; and very soon after the king sent to the marechal a letter of naturalization conceived in the most flattering terms. The succeeding campaigns gained him additional honours. After the victory of Raucoix, which he gained on the 11th October 1746, the king of France made him a present of six pieces of cannon. He was, on the 12th of January of the following year, created marechal of all the French armies, and, in 1748, commander-general of all those parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> which were lately conquered. Holland now began to tremble for her safety. Maastricht and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom had already fallen, and nothing but misfortunes seemed to attend the further prosecution of the war. The States General, therefore, offered terms of peace, which were accepted, and a treaty concluded on the 18th October 1748. Marechal Saxe retired to Chambord, a country seat which the king of France had given him. Some time after he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, where the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> received him as Alexander would have received Caesar.—On his return to France, he spent his time among men of learning, artists, and philosophers. He died of a fever, on the 30th November 1750, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 54. Some days before his death, talking to M. Senac his physician about his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, "It has been (says he) an excellent dream." He was remarkably careful of the lives of his men. One day a general officer was pointing out to him a poll which would have been of great use. "It will only cost you (says he) a dozen grenadiers. That would do very well," replied the marechal, "were it only a dozen lieutenant-generals." It was impossible for Marechal Saxe, the natural brother of the king of Poland, elected sovereign of Courland, and possessed of a vigorous and restless imagination, to be destitute of ambition. He constantly entertained the notion that he would be a king. After losing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Russia by his inconstancy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, he formed, it is said, the project of assembling the Jews, and of being the sovereign of a nation which for 1700 years had neither possessed chief nor country. When this chimerical idea could not be realized, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his eyes upon the kingdom of Corsica. After failing in this project also, he was busily employed in planning a settlement in some part of America, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, when death surprized him. He had been educated and died in the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. "It is a pity (said the queen of France, when she heard of his death) that we cannot say a single De profundis (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> for the dead) for a man who has made us sing so many Te Deums." All France lamented his death. By his will, which is dated at Paris, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1. 1748, he directed that his body should be buried in quicklime: "that nothing (says he) may remain of me in this world but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of me among my friends." These orders, however, were not complied with; for his body was embalmed, put into a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, which was inclosed in another of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and this covered with one of wood, bound about with iron. His heart was put into a silver gilt box, and his entrails into another coffin. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. was at the charge of his funeral. By his order his corpse was interred with great pomp and splendor in the Lutheran church of St Thomas, at Straiburg, on the 8th February 1751. The marechal was a man of ordinary stature, of a robust <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and extraordinary strength. To an aspect, noble, warlike, and mild, he joined the excellent qualities of the heart. Affable in his manners, and disposed to sympathize with the unfortunate, his generosity sometimes carried him beyond the limits of his fortune. On his death-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> he reviewed the errors of his life with remorse, and expressed much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a>. The best edition of his Reveries was printed at Paris 1757, in two vols. It was compared with the greatest attention with the original manuscript in the king's library. It is accompanied with many designs exactly engraved, and a Life of the Author. The Life of Marechal Saxe was written by M. d'Epagnac, two vols. 12mo. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is written in the panegyrical style. The author is, however, impartial enough to remark, that in the three battles upon which the reputation of Marechal Saxe is founded, he engaged in the most favourable circumstances. "Never did a general (says he) stand in a more advantageous situation. Honoured with the confidence of the king, he was not restrained in any of his projects. He always commanded a numerous army: his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were steady, and his officers confessed great merit."

SAXIFRAGA

Pages 134-134

SAXIFRAGE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulente. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAXO-GRAMMATICUS

Pages 134-135

descended from an illustrious family, was born about the middle of the 12th century. Stephens, in his edition of Saxo-Grammaticus, printed at Soroe, indubitably proves, that he must have been alive in 1156, but cannot ascertain the exact <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his birth. See Stephens's Prolegomena to the Notes on Saxo-Grammaticus, p. 8, to 24; also Holberg; vol. i. p. 269; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Antiqu. vol. i. p. 4. On account of his uncommon learning, Saxo was distinguished by the name of Grammaticus. He was provost of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Roskilde, and warmly patronized by the learned and warlike Abaloni, the celebrated archbishop of Lunden, at whose instigation he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. His epitaph, a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> in bad Latin verses, gives no account of the era of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened, according to Stephens, in 1204. His history, consisting of 16 books, begins from the earliest account of the Danish annals, and concludes with the year 1186. According to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of an accurate writer, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, which relates to the origin of the Danes, and the reigns of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings, is full of fables; but the eight last books, and particularly those which regard the events of his own times, deserve the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. He wrote in Latin; (A) Some authors have erroneously conjectured, from his name Saxo, that he was born in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; but Saxo was no uncommon appellation among the ancient Danes. See Olaus Wormius Monumenta Danica, p. 186, and Stephens's Prolegomena, p. 10. La'in; the style, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider the barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he flourished, is in general extremely elegant, but rather too poetical for history. Mallet, in his Histoire de Dänemark, vol. i. p. 182, says, "that Sperling, a writer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> erudition, has proved, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the assertions of Stephens and others, that Saxo Grammaticus was secretary to Abfalon; and that the Saxo provost of Roskild was another person, and lived earlier."

SAXONY

Pages 135-137

the name of two circles of the German empire, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same. The lower circle is bounded to the south by the circle of Upper Saxony, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of that of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the duchy of Sleswick, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and the Baltic; to the west, by the circle of Westphalia and the North <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and to the east by the circle of Upper Saxony. The states belonging to it are the dukes and princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> and Bremen, Zell, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRUBENHAGEN">Grubenhagen</a>, Calenburg, Wolfenbuttle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALBERSTADT">Halberstadt</a>, Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Güstrow, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>-Glückstadt, Holstein-Gottorf, Hildesheim, Saxe-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUENBURG">Lauenburg</a>; the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>; the principalities of Schwerin, Ratzeburg, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANKENBURG">Blankenburg</a>, Ranzau; the imperial cities of Lubeck, Gotzlar, Mühlhausen, Nordhausen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, and Bremen. The dukes of Bremen and Magdeburg are alternately directors and summoning princes; but, ever since the year 1682, the diets which used generally to be held at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a> have been discontinued. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the empire, which, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the empire in 1681, was settled at 40,000 men, this circle was to furnish 1322 horsemen and 2707 foot; and of the 300,000 florins granted to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> in 1707, its quota was 31,271 florins; both which affections are the same with those of Upper Saxony, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, Swabia, and Westphalia. This circle at present nominates only two electors in the chamber-judicatory of the empire, of one of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Brunswick-Lunenburg has the nomination, who must be a Lutheran, and is the ninth in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The inhabitants of this circle are almost all Lutherans. The circle of Upper Saxony is bounded by that of Franconia, the Upper Rhine, and Lower Saxony; and also by the Baltic sea, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and contains the following states; viz., the electors of Saxony and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, Saxe-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, Saxe-Eisenach, Saxe-Cobourg, Saxe-Gotha, Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Querfurt, the Higher and Farther Pomerania, Camin, Anhalt, Quiltenburg, Gernrode, Walkenried, Schwarzburg, Sonderhausen, Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, Mansfeld, Stolberg, Barby, the counts of Reußen, and the counts of Schönberg. No diets have been held in this circle since the year 1683. The elector of Saxony has always been the sole summoning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of it. Most of the inhabitants profess the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. When the whole empire furnishes 40,000 men, the quota of this circle is 1322 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 2707 foot. Of the 300,000 florins granted by the empire in 1707, it contributed only 31,271 florins, 28 krutiziers, being rated no higher than those of Westphalia, Lower Saxony, Swabia, and Burgundy, though it is much larger. Agreeable to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and regulation in 1654, this circle nominates now only two electors of the chamber-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The electorate consists of the duchy of Saxony, the greatest part of the margravate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, a part of Saxony, the Vogtland, and the northern half of the landgraviate of Thuringia. The Lusatias also, and a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Henneberg, belong to it, but are not part of this circle. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the electoral dominions lying in this circle is in general exceeding rich and fruitful, yielding corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> in abundance, together with hops, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, aniseed, wild saffron, wood; and in some places woad, wine, coals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> clay, terra sigillata, fullers-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, fine fliver, various sorts of beautiful marble, serpentine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and almost all the different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Sulphur also, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and free-stone, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, turf, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, arsenic, cobalt, and other minerals, are found it. This country, besides the above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, contains likewise valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and abounds in many places with horned cattle, sheep, horses, and venison. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> by which it is watered are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, the Schwarze-Elster, the Mulde, the Saale, the Unstrut, the Weiße-Elster, and the Pleisse. These rivers, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and rivulets, abound in fish; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-Elster are found beautiful pearls. This electorate is extremely well cultivated and inhabited, and is said to include about 250 great and small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, upwards of 3000 villages, 106 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> manors, and near as many royal castles, besides private estates, and commanderies. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> diets here consist of three classes. The first is composed of the prelates, the counts, and lords, and the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Leipzig and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a>. To the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> belong the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> in general, immediate or mediate, that is, such as stand immediately under the fief-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> or the aulic judicatories, and such as are immediately under the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMAN">amman</a>. The third class is formed of the towns in general. The general provincial diets are ordinarily held every five years; but there are others, called Selektion diets, which are convened <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> every two years. We would here observe, that not only these diets, but those in most of the other states of Germany, are at present extremely insignificant and unimportant, retaining little more than the shadow of their former power and privileges; for even the petty princes, though they depend upon their more potent neighbours, are almost as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> in their respective territories as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seignior himself. As to religion, it was in this country that the reformation took its rise in the 16th century, to which it hath ever since adhered, according to the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>. The two late electors, when they embraced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> in order to qualify themselves to be elected kings of Poland, gave the most solemn assurances to their people, that they would inviolably maintain the established religion and its professors in the full and free enjoyment of all their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, privileges, and prerogatives whatsoever, in regard to churches, worship, ceremonies, usages, universities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, benefices, incomes, profits, jurisdictions, and immunities. The electoral families still continue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, though they have lost the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Poland, for which they at first embraced Popery. With respect to ecclesiastical matters, the country is divided into parishes, and these again into spiritual inspections and consistories, all subordinate to the ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and upper consistory of Dresden, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and Leipzig the Calvinists and Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> Catholics enjoy the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religion. Learning flourishes in this electorate; in which, besides the free-schools and gymnasia in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns, are the two celebrated universities of Wittenberg and Leipzig, in the last of which are also <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> for the liberal arts and the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with bookellers and printers of the greatest eminence. A great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are also carried on in this country. The principal are those of fine and coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, thread, fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, fine glazes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>; porcelain, equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; iron, bras, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares; manufactures of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; gloves, caps, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>; in which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions mentioned above, together with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, an important foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is carried on. A great addition has been made since the year 1718 to the electoral territories, by the extinction of the collateral branches of Zeitz, Merleburg, and Weissenfels, whose dominions devolved to the elder electoral branch, descended from the margraves of Meissen. The first of these, who was elector of Saxony, was Frederick the Warlike, about the beginning of the 15th century. This elector styles himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony, Juliers, Cleve, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>, as also of Engern and Westphalia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-marshals and elector of the Holy Roman empire, landgrave in Thuringia, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of Meissen, and of Upper and Lower Lusatia, burgrave of Magdeburg, princely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Henneberg, count of La Mark, Ravenberg, Barby, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANAU">Hanau</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Ravenstein. Among the electors he is reckoned the fifth, as great-marshal of the empire, of which he is also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, during an interregnum, in all places not subject to the vicariate of the count palatine of the Rhine. He is moreover sole director of the circle; and in the vacancy of the see of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> claims the directorium at the diet of the empire. His matricular affluence, on account of the electorate, is 1984 florins, besides what he pays for other districts and territories. To the chamber-courts he contributes, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, the sum of 1545 rix-dollars, together with 83 rix-dollars and 62 kruitzers on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mansfeld. In this electorate, subordinate to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, are various colleges for the departments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, foreign affairs, the finances, fees, mines, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, and ecclesiastical affairs, together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tribunals and courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, to which appeals <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> from the inferior. The revenues of this electorate are as considerable as those of any prince in the empire, if we except those of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. They arise from the ordinary and extraordinary subsidies of the states; his own demesnes, consisting of 72 bailiwicks; the impost on beer, and the fine porcelain of the country; tenths of corn, fruit, wine, &c.; his own silver mines, and the tenths of those that belong to particulars; all which, added together, bring in a yearly revenue of between 700,000l. and 800,000l. yet the electorate is at present deeply in debt. The regular troops commonly amount to 20,000 men, exclusive of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> of the ban, the arriere-ban, and the body of miners and hunters, who are obliged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war to bear arms. The whole electorate is divided into circles. The electoral circle, or the duchy of Saxony, is bounded by the circles of Meissen, Leipzig, and Thuringia, the principality of Anhalt, the marche of Brandenburg, and Lusatia. The principality of Anhalt lies across it, and divides it into two parts. Its greatest length and breadth is computed at about 40 miles; but though it is watered by the Elbe, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Elster, and the Mulde, it is not very fruitful, the soil for the most part consisting of sand. It contains 24 towns, three boroughs, between 400 and 500 villages, 164 noblemen's estates, 11 superintendencies, three inspections under one consistory, and 11 prefectures or districts. The present duchy of Saxony is not to be confounded with the old; for the latter was of a much greater extent, and contained in it those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tracts anciently called Eastphalia, Engern, and Westphalia, of which the electoral circle was no part, but was taken by Albert the Bear, margrave of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALZWEDEL">Salzwedel</a>, from the Veneti. His son Bernard obtaining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of duke of Saxony from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic I. the name of duchy was given to this country; and the electoral dignity having been afterwards annexed to the duchy, it acquired thereby also the name of the electoral circle. The country of Saxony is remarkable for being the mother of the present English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but concerning the Saxons themselves, previous to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, we have very few particulars. The Saxons (says Mr Whitaker) have been derived by our historians from very different parts of the globe; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the north of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the forests of Germany. And their appellation has been equally referred to very different causes; the name of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> progenitor, the plundering disposition of their Asiatic fathers, and the short hooked weapons of their warriors. But the real origin of the Saxons, and the genuine derivation of their name, seem clearly to be these. In the earlier period of the Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the Celtæ of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> crossed the Rhine in considerable numbers, and planted various colonies in the regions beyond it. Thus the Voconii Teutofages settled on one side of the Hercynian forest and about the banks of the Neckar, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELVETII">Helvetii</a> upon another and about the Rhine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, the Boii beyond both, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENONES">Senones</a> in the heart of Germany. Thus also we see the Treviri, the Nervii, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEVI">Suevi</a>, and the Marcomanni, the Chatti, the Venedi, and others, in that country; all plainly betrayed to be Gallic nations by the Gallic appellations which they bear, and all together possesting the greatest part of it. And, even as late as the conclusion of the first century, we find one nation on the eastern side of this great continent actually speaking the language of Gaul, and another upon the northern using a dialect nearly related to the British. But as all the various tribes of the Germans are considered by Strabo to be γενος Ραλαδιου, or genuine Gauls in their origin; so those particularly that lived immediately beyond the Rhine, and are asserted by Tacitus to be indubitably native Germans, are expressly denominated Ραλαδιου, or Gauls, by Diodorus, and as expressly declared by Dio to have been distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> appellation of Celtæ from the earliest period. And the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> line of nations, which extended along the ocean, and reached to the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, was all known to the learned in the days of Diodorus, by the same significant appellation of Ραλαδιου, or Gauls. Of these, the most noted were the Si-Cambri and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>; the former being seated near the channel of the Rhine, and the latter inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>. And the denominations of both declare their original; original; and show them to have been derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock of the Celtæ, and to be of the same Celtic kindred with the Cimbri of our own <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and the Cymbri or Cambrians of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The Cimbri are accordingly denominated Celtæ by Strabo and Appian. And they are equally asserted to be Gauls by Diodorus; to be the descendants of that nation which sacked the city of Rome, plundered the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, and subdued a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and some of Asia. Immediately to the south of these were the Saxons, extending from the isthmus of the Cherlonebus to the current of the Elbe. And they were equally Celtic in their origin as their neighbours. They were denominated Ambrones as well as Saxons; and, as such, are included by Tacitus under the general appellation of Cimbri, comprehended in Plutarch under the equal one of Celtio-Scythæ. And the name of Ambrones appears particularly to have been Gallic; being common to the Saxons beyond the Elbe, and the Ligurians in Cisalpine Gaul; as both found to their surprise, on the irruption of the former into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with the Cimbri. And, what is equally surprising, and has been equally unnoticed by the critics, the Welsh distinguish England by the name of Loegr or Liguria, even to the present moment. In that irruption these Saxons, Ambros, or Ligurians, composed a body of more than 30,000 men, and were principally concerned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> to pieces the large armies of Manlius and Capito. Nor is the appellation of Saxons less Celtic than the other. It was originally the same with the Belgic Sueftones of Gaul; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that tribe being now intitled Sufiones by the French, and the name of the Saxons pronounced Saifon by the Welsh, Sufon by the Scotch, and Sufenach or Saxenach by the Irish. And the Sueftones or Saxones of Gaul derived their own appellation from the position of their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> on a river, the stream at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a> being now denominated the Aisne, and formerly the Axon; Ueffon or Axon importing only waters or a river, and S-ueffon or S-ax-on on the waters or the river. The Sueftones, therefore, are actually denominated the Uffiones by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; and the Saxones are actually intitled the Axones by Lucan. These, with their brethren and allies the Cimbri, having been more formidable enemies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by land, than the Samnites, Carthaginians, Spaniards, Gauls, or Parthians, in the second century applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and became nearly as terrible by sea. They soon made themselves known to the inhabitants of the British isles by their piracies in the northern channels, and were denominated by them Lochlyn or Lochlynnach; luced-lyn signifying the people of the wave, and the d being quiescent in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>. They took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORKNEY_ISLANDS">Orkney <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, which were then merely large shoals of sand, uncovered with wood, and overgrown with rushes; and they landed in the north of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and ravaged the country. Before the middle of the third century they made a second <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the latter, disembarked a considerable body of men, and designed the absolute subjection of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Before the conclusion of it, they carried their naval operations to the south, infested the British channel with their little vessels, and made frequent descents upon the coasts. And in the fourth and fifth centuries, acting in conjunction with the Picts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a> and the Scots of Ire- land, they ravaged all the eastern and south-eastern shores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, began the formal conquest of the country, and finally settled their victorious soldiery in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>.

SCABIOSA

Pages 137-137

SCABIOUS; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, Aggregata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCABRITA

Pages 137-137

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clasps. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SCÆVOLA, C. MUCIUS, a young Roman of illustrious birth, is particularly celebrated in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for a brave but unsuccessful attempt upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Porfena <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Hettruria, about the year before Christ 504. See the article Rome, No. 71. SCÆVOLA, a genus of plants belonging to the pentandra clasps. See BOTANY Index.

SCAFFOLD

Pages 137-137

also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised in the manner of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, for the more commodious viewing any show <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>: it is also used for a stage raised in some public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the execution of criminals.

SCALA-NOVA

Pages 137-137

anciently Neapolis, called by the Turks Koubadafes, is situated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, on the slope of a hill, the houses rising one above another, intermixed with minarets and tall slender cyprresses. "A street, through which we rode (says Dr Chandler), was hung with goat-skins exposed to dry, dyed of a most lively <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. At one of the fountains is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> used as a cistern. The port was filled with small craft. Before it is an old fortress on a rock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cliff frequented by gulls and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-mews. By the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-side is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and good khan, at which we passed a night on our return. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> belonged once to the Ephesians, who exchanged it with the Samians for a town in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>."

SCALADO

Pages 137-137
or SCALLADE, in the art of war, a furious assault made on the wall or rampart of a city, or other fortified place, by means of ladders, without carrying on works in form, to secure the men.

SCALD-CREAM

Pages 137-138

sometimes also called Clouted cream; a curious method of preparing cream for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, almost peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Dr Hales, in Philosophical Transactions volume xlix. p. 342, 1755, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. gives some account of the method of preparing this delicate and luxurious article; other writers also speak of it. With an elucidation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two, we shall nearly quote Mr Feltham's account from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, volume lxii. Part II. It is there observed, that the purpose of making scald-cream is far superior butter than can be procured from the usual raw cream, being preferable for flavour and keeping; to which those accustomed are so partial, as seldom to eat any other. As leaden cisterns would not answer for scalding cream, the dairies mostly adopt <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> pans, which hold from three to five gallons for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and that which is put into those pans one morning, stands till the next, when, without disturbing it, it is set over (on a trivet) a steady brick wood fire, devoid of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, where it is to remain from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to fifteen minutes, according to the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in it: the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of removing it from the fire must be particularly attended to, and is, when the surface begins to wrinkle or to gather in a little, showing signs of being near the agitation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, which it must by no means do; it is then instantly to be taken off, and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a> until the next morning, when the fine cream is thrown up, and may be taken for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or for butter, into which it is now soon converted by stirring it with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Some know when to remove it from the fire by touching the pan with the finger, it being then less formidable; but this can only be acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Dr Hales observes, that this method of preparing milk takes off the ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which it sometimes acquires from the cows feeding on turnips, cabbage, &c.

SCALDS

Pages 138-138

in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of literature, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants of the northern countries to their poets; in whose writings their history is recorded.

SCALE

Pages 138-138

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a line divided into equal parts, placed at the bottom of a map <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> draught, to serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to all the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, or all the distances and places of the map.

SCALENE

Pages 138-138
or SCALENOUS TRIANGLE, Scalenum, in Geometry, a triangle whose sides and angles are unequal. See GEOMETRY.

SCALIGER

Pages 138-139

Julius Caesar, a learned critic, poet, physician, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at the castle of Ripa, in the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, in 1484; and is said to have been descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> princes of Verona, though this is not mentioned in the letters of naturalization he obtained in France in 1528. He learned the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin tongue in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and in his 12th year was presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, who made him one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. He served that emperor 17 years, and gave Scaliger signal proofs of his valour and conduct in several expeditions. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> in April 1512, in which he had the misfortune to lose his father Benedict Scaliger, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Titus; on which his mother died with grief: when being reduced to necessitous circumstances, he entered into the order of the Franciscans, and applied himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; but soon after changing his mind with respect to his becoming a monk, he took arms again, and served in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a physician persuaded him to study physic, which he did at his leisure hours, and also learned Greek; and at last the gout determined him, at 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to abandon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He soon after settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a>, where he married, and began to apply himself seriously to his studies. He learned first the French tongue, which he spoke perfectly in three months; and then made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the Gallic, Italian, Spanish, German, Hungarian, and Slavonian; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of his studies was polite literature. Meanwhile, he supported his family by the practice of physic. He did not publish any of his works till he was 47 years of age; when he soon gained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> name in the republic of letters. He had a graceful person, and so strong a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, even in his old age, that he dictated to his son 200 verses which he had composed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> before, and retained without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. He was so charitable, that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was as it were an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and sick; and he had such an aversion to lying, that he would have no correspondence with those who were given to that vice; but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he had much vanity, and a satirical spirit, which created him many enemies. He died of a retention of urine in 1558. He wrote in Latin, 1. A Treatise on the Art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. 2. Exercitations against Cardan; which works are much esteemed. 3. Commentaries on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Animals, and on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. 4. Some Treatises on Physic. 5. Letters, Orations, Poems, and other works, in Latin. Scaliger, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Justus, one of the most learned critics and writers of his time. He was the son of the former, and was born at Agen in France in 1540. He studied in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Bordeaux; after which his father took him under his own care, and employed him in transcribing his poems; by which means he obtained such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for poetry, that before he was 17 years old he wrote a tragedy upon the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a>, in which he introduced all the poetical ornaments of style and sentiment. His father dying in 1558, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the year following, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to apply himself to the Greek tongue. For this purpose he for two months attended the lectures of Turnebus; but finding that in the usual course he should be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time in gaining his point, he shut himself up in his closet, and by constant application for two years gained a perfect knowledge of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. After which he applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, which he learned by himself with great facility. He made no less progress in the sciences; and his writings procured him the reputation of one of the greatest men of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other age. He embraced the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at 22 years of age. In 1563, he attached himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Caffeignier de la Roch Pozay, whom he attended in several journeys; and in 1593, was invited to accept of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of honorary professor. professor of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, which he complied with. He died of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1629. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>; was never married; and was so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> a student, that he often spent whole days in his study without eating; and though his circumstances were always very narrow, he constantly refused the presents that were offered him. He published many works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Notes on Seneca's Tragedies, on Varro, Aulonius, Pompeius Festus, &c. 2. His Latin Poems. 3. A Treatise de Emendatione Temporum. 4. Eusebius's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, with Notes. 5. Canones Iofogici; and many other works. The collections entitled Scaligeriana, were collected from his conversations by one of his friends; and being ranged into alphabetical order, were published by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius. SCALLOP. See Ostrea, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In the Highlands of Scotland, the great scallop shell is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for skimming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. In old times, it had a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> place; being admitted into the halls of heroes, and was the cup of their festivity when the tribe assembled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of their chieftain.

SCALPEL

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> used in anatomical dissections and operations in surgery.

SCALPER

Pages 139-139
or Scalping-Iron, a surgeon's instrument used for scraping foul carious bones.

SCALPING

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, in practice among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> warriors, of taking off the tops of the heads of the enemies' skulls with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on. They preserve them as trophies of their victories, and are rewarded by their chiefs according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of heads they bring in.

SCALPRA DENTALIA

Pages 139-139

instruments used by surgeons to take off those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, livid, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> crusts which adhere to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and not only loosen and destroy them, but taint the breath.

SCAMMONY

Pages 139-139

a concreted vegetable juice of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of convolvulus, partly of the resin, and partly of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> kind. See Convolvulus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCANDALUM MAGNATUM

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a defamatory speech <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the injury of a person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; for which a writ that bears the same name is granted for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of damages.

SCANDERBEG

Pages 139-139

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of George Castriot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, dependent on the Ottoman empire. He was delivered up with his three elder brothers as hostages, by their father, to Amurath II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the Turks, who poisoned his brothers, but spared him on account of his youth, being likewise pleased with his juvenile <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and amiable person. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he became one of the most renowned generals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and revolting from Amurath, he joined Humiade Corvin, a most formidable enemy to the Ottoman power. He defeated the sultan's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, took Amurath's secretary prisoner, obliged him to sign and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> an order to the governor of Croia, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Albania, to deliver up the citadel and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> to the bearer of that order, in the name of the sultan. With this forged order he repaired to Croia; and thus recovered the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and maintained the independency of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the numerous armies of Amurath and his successor Mahomed II. who was obliged to make peace with this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in 1461. He then went to the assistance of Ferdinand of Arragon, at the request of Pope Pius II., and by his assistance Ferdinand gained a complete victory over his enemy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Anjou. Scanderbeg died in 1467. SCANDEROON. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRETTA">Alexandretta</a>.

SCANDINAVIA

Pages 139-140

a general name for the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, anciently under the dominion of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The inhabitants of these countries, in former times, were excessively addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. From their earliest years they applied themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, and accustomed themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, fatigue, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. Even the very sports of youth and childhood were dangerous. They consisted in taking frightful leaps, climbing up the steepest rocks, fighting naked with offensive weapons, wrestling with the utmost fury; so that it was usual to see them grown up to be robust men, and terrible in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 15. At this early age the young men became their own masters; which they did by receiving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, a buckler, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed at some public meeting. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> named the youth in public; after which he was obliged to provide for his own subsistence, and was either now to live by hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by joining in some incursion against the enemy. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> care was taken to prevent the young men from too early connections with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and indeed they could have no hope to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the affection of the fair, but in proportion to the courage and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> they had shown in their military exercises. Accordingly, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> song, we find Bartholin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Norway, extremely surprised that his ministers should prove unkind, as he could perform eight different exercises. The children were generally born in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>; and being inured from their infancy to behold nothing but arms, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood, and slaughter, they imbibed the cruel disposition of their fathers, and when they bore forth upon other nations, behaved rather like furies than like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> creatures. The laws of this people, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, resembled those of the ancient Lacedemonians. They knew no virtue but bravery, and no vice but cowardice. The greatest penalties were inflicted on such as fled from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The laws of the ancient Danes declared such persons infamous, and excluded them from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Among the Germans, cowards were sometimes suffocated in mud; after which they were covered over with hurdles, to show, says Tacitus, that though the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of crimes should be public, there are certain degrees of cowardice and infamy which ought to be buried in oblivion.
