Kenneth II. upon his conquest of the Piets in the ninth century, having made Scone his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence, delivered his laws, called the Macalpine laws, from a tumulus, named the Mote Hill of Scone. The old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was begun by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Gowrie; but was completed by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Murray of Gopshie, the favourite of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James VI. to whom that monarch had granted it; and the new pellier in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to his benefactor put up the king's arms in several parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It was built around two courts. The dining room was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome; and had an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and magnificent chimney-piece, and the king's arms, with this motto: Nobis hæc invicta miserunt centum fæs proavi. Beneath were the Murray arms. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> room was some good old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, with an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. In a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber was a medley scripture-piece in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with a border of animals, said to be the work of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> during her confinement in Loch Leven castle. The gallery was about 155 feet long; the top arched, divided into compartments filled with paintings in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours. The pieces represented were various kinds of huntings; that of Nimrod, and King James and his train, appear in every piece. But the whole of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> we believe has been demolished, and a most magnificent pile erected in its place by the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>, who is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> keeper. Till the destruction of the abbey, the kings of Scotland were crowned here, sitting in the famous wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> which Edward I. transported to Westminster abbey, to the great mortification of the Scots, who looked upon it as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, was crowned in the chapel at Scone. The old pretender resided for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Scone in 1715; and his son paid it a visit in 1745.

SCONES

Pages 198-198

small forts, built for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of some pals, river, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Some scones are made regular, of four, five, or six bastions; others are of smaller dimensions, fit for passes or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; and others for the field.

SCOPARIA

Pages 198-198

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 40th order, Perforatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SCOPE <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> SCUPPER HOLES, in a ship, are holes made through the sides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the deck, to carry off the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> that comes from the pumps.

SCOPOLIA

Pages 198-198

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th clas, Sarmentaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCORIA

Pages 198-198
or Dross, among metallurgists, is the recrement of metals in fusion; or, more determinately speaking, is that mass which is produced by melting metals and ores; when cold, it is brittle, and not dissoluble in water, being properly a kind of glass.

SCORIFICATION

Pages 198-198

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, is the art of reducing a body, either entirely <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, into scoria. SCORPÆNA, a genus of fishes belonging to the order thoracici. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCORPIO

Pages 198-198

a genus of insects belonging to the order of aptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Scorpion, Scorpion, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the eighth sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a> denoted by the character η. See Astronomy. SCORPION Fly. See Panorpa, Entomology Index.

SCORPIURUS

Pages 198-198

Caterpillars, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCORZONERA

Pages 198-199

SCORZONERA, VIPPER-GRASS, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCOT

Pages 199-199

a customary contribution laid upon all subjects, according to their abilities. Whoever were afflicted in any sum, though not in equal proportions, were said to pay scot and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Scot, Michael, of Balwirie, a learned Scottish author of the 13th century. This singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> made the tour of France and Germany; and was received with some distinction at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic II. Having travelled enough to gratify his curiosity <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his vanity, he returned to Scotland, and gave himself up to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. He was skilled in languages; and, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proficient in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and medicine. He translated into Latin, from the Arabic, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of animals by the celebrated physician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>. He published the whole works of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, with notes, and affected much to reason on the principles of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He wrote a book concerning The Secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, in which he treats of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, physiognomy, and the signs by which we judge of the temperaments of men and women. We have also a tract of his On the Nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>. He there speaks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> operation, as it is termed by alchemists, and is exceedingly solicitous about the projected powder, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE">philosopher's <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. He likewise published what he calls Mensa Philosophica, a treatise replete with astrology and chiromancy. He was much admired in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and was even suspected of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>; and had Roger <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> and Cornelius Agrippa for his panegyrists. Scot, Reginald, a judicious writer in the 16th century, was the younger son of Sir John Scot of Scot's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, near Smeethe in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-hall in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; after which he retired to Smeethe, where he lived a studious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and died in 1599. He published, The perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">Platform</a> of a Hop-Garden; and a book intitled, The Discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">Witchcraft</a>; in which he showed that all the relations concerning magicians and witches are chimerical. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was not only censured by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. in his Daemonology, but by several eminent divines; and all the copies of it that could be found were burnt.

SCOTAL

Pages 199-199
or SCOTALE, is where any officer of a forest keeps an ale-house within the forest, by colour of his office, making people come to his house, and there spend their money for fear of his displeasure. We find it mentioned in the charter of the forest, cap. 8. "Nulus forestariss faciat Scotallas, vel garbas colligat, vel aliquam collectam faciat," &c. Manwood, 216.—The word is compounded of feet and ale, and by transposition of the words is otherwise called alefoot.

SCOTALES

Pages 199-199

were meetings formerly held in England for the purpose of drinking ale, of which the expense was paid by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> contribution. Thus the tenants of South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALLING">Malling</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, which belonged to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, were, at the keeping of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to entertain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> with a drinking, or an ale; and the stated quotas towards the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> were, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should pay threepence halfpenny for himself and his wife, and a widow and cottager a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> halfpenny. In the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Feering, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and under the same jurisdiction, it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the tenants named to make a feotale of fifteenpence halfpenny, and to allow out of each sixpence a penny halfpenny for the bailiff. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> feotales in taverns, at which the clergy were not to be present, are noticed in several <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> canons. They were not to be published in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> by the clergy or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>; and a meeting of more than ten persons of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> or vicinage was a feotale that was generally prohibited. There were also common drinkings, which were denominated feet-ale, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>-ale, clerk-ale, church-ale. To a feet-ale probably all the residents in a manorial district were contributors; and the expense of a bride-ale was defrayed by the relations and friends of a happy <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, who were not in circumstances to bear the charges of a wedding dinner. This custom prevails occasionally in some districts of Scotland even at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, under the denomination of a penny bride-ale, and was very common about half a century ago. The clerk's-ale was in the Easter holidays, and was the method taken to enable clerks of parishes to collect their dues more readily. Mr Warton, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, has inserted the following extract from an old indenture, which clearly shows the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of a church-ale. "The parishioners of Elveton and Okebrook, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, agree jointly to brew four ales, and every ale of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of malt, betwixt this and the feast of St John the Baptist next coming; and that every inhabitant of the said town of Okebrook shall be at the several ales. Every husband and his wife shall pay twopence, every cottager one penny; and all the inhabitants of Elveton shall have and receive all the profits and advantages coming of the said ales, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and behoof of the said church of Elveton." The give-ales were the legacies of individuals, and from that circumstance entirely gratuitous. They seem to have been very numerous, and were generally left to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; though, from the largeness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ale enjoined to be brewed, it must have been sometimes intended that others were to partake of them. These bequests were likewise made to the altar of a saint, with directions for ringing masses at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBIT">obit</a>, or anniversary of the testator. The give-ales were sometimes dispensed in the church, and frequently in the church-yard, by which means Godde's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was made a tavern of glutons. Such certainly would be Chalk-church, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in it was kept the give-ale of William May of that parish; for he ordered his wife "to make in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> six bushels of wheat, and in drink ten bushels of malt, and in cheese 20d. to give to poor people, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>;" and he ordered that, after the decease of his wife, his executors and feoffees, should continue the custom for evermore." SCOTER. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAS">ANAS</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCOTO

Pages 398-398

Irish, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an epithet applied, by some writers on Scottish antiquities, to the colony of Irish, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Dalriads <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dalriadians, who, in the beginning of the fifth century, established themselves in the district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>; and formed a distinct tribe, till, under the reign of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> Kenneth II., they united with the Picts, whom they had nearly subdued. See Chalmers's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>, vol. i. and SCOTLAND, from n° 31. to n° 85. SCOTO-Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is by Mr Chalmers applied to that period of Scottish history which elapsed from the accession of Edgar, the son of Malcolm Canmore, to the throne of Scotland in the year 1097, to the reign of Robert Bruce in 1306. See SCOTLAND from n° 86. to n° 164.

SCOTOMIA

Pages 398-398

in Medicine, a vertigo, accompanied with dimness of sight, frequently the forerunner of an apoplexy.

SCOTT

Pages 398-398

JOHN, an eminent English divine, was born in 1638, and became minister of St Thomas's in Southwark. In 1684 he was collated to a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of St Paul's. Dr Hickes tells us, that, after the revolution, "he first refused the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, because he would not take the oath of homage; and afterwards another bishopric, the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, and a prebend of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, because they were all places of deprived men." He published several excellent works, particularly The Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, &c. and died in 1695. He was eminent for his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, affability, sincerity, and readiness to do good; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for preaching was extraordinary.

SCOUGAL

Pages 398-399

HENRY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Patrick Scougal, bishop of Aberdeen, was born <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1650, at Salton in East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>, where his father, the immediate predecessor of Bishop Burnet, was rector. His father, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> him for the sacred ministry, watched over his infant mind with peculiar care; nor was his care belied in vain. He had soon the satisfaction of perceiving the most amiable dispositions unfold themselves, and his understanding rise at once into the vigour of manhood. Relinquishing the amusements of youth, young Scougal applied to his studies with ardour; and, agreeable to his father's wish, at an early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he directed his thoughts to sacred literature. He perused the historical parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> with peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and then began to examine its contents with the eye of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He was struck with the peculiarities of the Jewish dispensation, and felt an anxiety to understand the reason why its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and ceremonies were abolished. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and evidences of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> also occupied his mind. He perused sermons with pleasure, committing to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which most affected him, and could comprehend and remember their whole scope. Nor was he inattentive to polite literature. He read the Roman classics, and made considerable proficiency in the Greek, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and other oriental languages. He was also well versed in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. His diversions were of a manly kind. After becoming acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman history</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with some of his companions he formed a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> where orations of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> were delivered. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fifteen he entered the university, where he behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, sobriety, and diligence. He disliked the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> then taught, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy; that philosophy which has now happily got such footing in the world, and tends to enlarge the faculties. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, we may here observe, that when he was yet about eighteen years of age, he wrote the reflections and short essays since published; which, though written in his youth, and some of them left unfinished, breathe forth so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, and such an exalted <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, as must convince us his conversation was in heaven. In all the public meetings of the students he was unanimously chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and had a singular deference paid to his judgement. No sooner had he finished his courses, than he was promoted to a professorship in the university of Aberdeen, where he conscientiously performed his duty in training up the youth under his care in such principles of learning and virtue as might render them ornaments to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state. When any divisions and animosities happened in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, he was very instrumental in reconciling and bringing them to a good understanding. He maintained his authority among the students in such a way as to keep them in awe, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and esteem. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> evenings were spent with his scholars in discouraging against vice and impiety of all kinds, and encouraging religion in principle and practice. He allotted a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his yearly income for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; and many indigent families, of different persuasions, were relieved in their straits by his bounty; though so secretly that they knew not whence their supply came. Having been a professor of philosophy for four years, he was at the age of twenty-three ordained a minister, and settled at Auchterlees, a small village about twenty miles from Aberdeen. Here his zeal and ability for his great great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> were eminently displayed. He catechised with great plainsness and affection, and used the most endearing methods to recommend religion to his hearers. He endeavoured to bring them to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> attendance to public worship, and joined with them himself at the beginning of it. He revived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of lectures, looking on it as very edifying to comment upon and expound <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portions of Scripture. And though he endured several outward inconveniences, yet he bore them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and meekness. But as God had designed him for an eminent station, where he could be of more universal use in his church, he was removed from his private <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to that of training up youth for the holy ministry and the care of souls. In the twenty-fifth year of his age he was admitted professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, Aberdeen; and though he was unanimously chosen, yet he declined a station of such importance, from a modest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his unfitness for it: And as he had been an ornament to his other stations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, so in a particular manner he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of this office. After he had guarded his students against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> artifices of the Romish missionaries in making proselytes, he proposed two subjects for public exercises; the one, of the pastoral care; the other, of casuistical divinity: but there were no debates he was more cautious to meddle with than the decrees of God; sensible that secret things belong to God, and to us things revealed. The inward dispositions of this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> are best seen in his writings; and the whole of his outward behaviour and conversation was the constant practice of what he preached; as we are assured by the concurring testimony of several respectable persons who knew him. How unsuitable then would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> be, where the subject was full of humility? and therefore let it suffice to say, that after he began to appear publicly, you see him as a professor, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> at once to improve his scholars in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> and sacred learning; as a pastor, he ceased not to preach the word, to exhaust, to reprove, and to rebuke with all authority: and as a professor of divinity, he bestowed the utmost pains to convince the candidates for the ministry, of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and importance of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> office; that it was not to be followed for lucre, but purely to promote the worship of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of men. Again, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider his private life, how meek, how charitable, and how self-denied! how disinterested in all things, how resigned to the divine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>! and above all, how refined his sentiments with regard to the love of God! How amiable must he then appear! How worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, and of the universal regret at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>! In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> we see clearly that the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> is blessed. At length his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> began to be impaired by incessant study, and about the twenty-seventh year of his age he fell into a consumption, which waited him by slow degrees. But during the whole time of his sickness he behaved with the utmost resignation, nor did he ever show the least impatience. When his friends came to visit him, he would say, "he had reason to blest God it was no worse with him than it was. And (says he) when you have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to remember me in your prayers, do not think me a better man than I am; but look on me, as indeed I am, a miserable sinner." Upon the twentieth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of June 1678 he died, in the greatest calmness, in the twenty-eighth year of his age, and was buried in the King's College church in Old Aberdeen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Scougal is a small treatise intitled, The Life of God in the Soul of Man. This book is not only valuable for the sublime spirit of piety which it breathes, but for the purity and elegance of its style; qualities for which few English writers were distinguished before the revolution.

SCOUTS

Pages 399-399

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are generally horsemen sent out before, and on the wings of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two, to discover the enemy, and give the general an account of what they see.

SCRATCH PANS

Pages 399-399

in the English <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works, a name given to certain leaden pans, which are usually made about a foot and an half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and three inches deep, with a bow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circular handle of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, by which they may be drawn out with a hook when the liquor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to receive a scalding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, known by the name of soft scratch, which falls during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the salt-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. See the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Salt.

SCREED

Pages 399-399

with platterers, is the floated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> behind a cornice, and is only necessary when a cornice is to be executed without bracketing.

SCREW

Pages 399-399

one of the six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL_POWERS"><a class="xref" h</a>ref="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> powers, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> cut into several concave surfaces, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather a channel or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> made in a cylinder, by carrying on two spiral planes the whole length of the screw, in such a manner that they may be always equally inclined to the axis of the cylinder in their whole progress, and also inclined to the base of it in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, p. 66, No. 131. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>'s Screw. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a>, No. 328. Endless or Perpetual Screw, one so fitted in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> machine as to turn a dented wheel; so called, because it may be turned for ever without coming to an end. See Mechanics, p. 67, No. 135.

SCRIBE

Pages 399-400

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> סופר, is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in scripture, and has several significations. It signifies, 1. A clerk, writer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> secretary. This was a very considerable employment in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the kings of Judah, in which the scripture often mentions the secretaries as the first officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Seraiah was scribe or secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> (2 Sam. viii. 17). Shevah and Shemaiah exercised the same office under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> (2 Sam. xx. 25.). In <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> we find Elihoephe and Ahia secretaries to that prince (1 Kings iv. 4); Shebna under Hezekiah (2 Kings xix. 2); and Shaphan under Josiah (2 Kings xxii. 8.). As there were but few in those times that could write well, the employment of a scribe or writer was very considerable. 2. A scribe is put for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> or muster-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, who makes the review of the troops, keeps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> or roll, and calls them over. Under the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UZZIAH">Uzziah</a> king of Judah, there is found Jei the scribe who had under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the king's armies (2 Chr. xxvi. 11.). And at the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, it is said the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, among other considerable persons, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> scribe of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a>, or secretary at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which muttered the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> (2 Kings xxv. 19.). 3. Scribe is put for an able and skilful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a man of learning that understands affairs. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>, David's uncle by the father's side, was a counsellor. counsellor, a wife man, and a scribe (1 Chr. xxvii. 32.). Baruch, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and secretary to Jeremiah, is called a scribe (Jer. xxxvi. 26.). And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> is celebrated as a skilful scribe in the law of his God (Ezra vii. 6.). The scribes of the people, who are frequently mentioned in the Gospel, were public writers and professed doctors of the law, which they read and explained to the people. Some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the original of scribes under Moses; but their name does not appear till under the judges. It is said, that in the wars of Barak against Sihera, “out of Machir came <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> governors, and out of Zebulun they that handle the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of the writer.” (Judges v. 14.) Others think that David first instituted them, when he established the several classes of the priests and Levites. The scribes were of the tribe of Levi; and at the time that David is said to have made the regulations in that tribe, we read that 6000 men of them were constituted officers and judges (1 Chr. xxiii. 4); among whom it is reasonable to think the scribes were included. For in 2 Chr. xxiv. 6, we read of Shemaiah the scribe, one of the Levites; and in 2 Chr. xxxiv. 13, we find it written, “Of the Levites that were scribes and officers.” The scribes and doctors of the law, in the scripture phrase, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the same thing; and he that in Mat. xxiii. 35, is called a doctor of the law, or a lawyer, in Mark xii. 28, is named a scribe, or one of the scribes. And as the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Jews at that time chiefly consisted in pharisaical traditions, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> that was made of them to explain the scripture; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the doctors of the law, or of the scribes, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; and we almost always find them joined together in scripture. Each of them valued themselves upon their knowledge of the law, upon their studying and teaching it (Mat. xxii. 52): they had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of knowledge, and sat in Moses’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> (Mat. xxiii. 2). Epiphanius, and the author of the Recognitions imputed to St Clement, reckon the scribes among the sects of the Jews; but it is certain they made no feet by themselves; they were only distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the law.

SCRIBONIUS

Pages 400-405

LARGUS, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physician in the reign of Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tiberius, was the author of several works; the best edition of which is that of John Rhodius. SCRIMZEOR or SCRIMGEOUR, Henry, an eminent reformer of learning, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a> in the year 1506. He traced his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the ancient family of the Scrimzeours of Didepe or Duthope, who obtained the office of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> standard-bearers to the kings of Scotland in 1557. At the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school of Dundee our author acquired the Greek and Latin languages to an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, and that in a shorter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than many scholars before him. At the university of St Andrew’s his successful application to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> gained him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his studies was the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and their more particular object the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Two of the most famous civilians of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Eguinard Baron and Francis Duaren (A), were then giving their lectures to crowded circles at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>. The fame of these professors occasioned his removal from Paris; and for a considerable time he prosecuted his studies under their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. At Bourges he had an opportunity of becoming acquainted with the celebrated James Amiet, Greek professor in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, well known in the learned world by his translation of Plutarch’s Lives, and distinguished afterwards by his advancement to great honours in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and finally to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. Through the recommendation of this eminent person, Mr Scrimzeor engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of two young gentlemen of the name of Buchereil, whom he instructed in the belles lettres, and other branches of literature, calculated to accomplish them for their station in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. This connection introduced him to Bernard Bonnetel bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RENNES">Rennes</a>, a person famed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> world for having served the state in many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> embassies. Accepting an invitation from this prelate to accompany him to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Mr Scrimzeor greatly enlarged the sphere of his literary acquaintance, by his conversation and connection with most of the distinguished scholars of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Francis Spira (B) happened during his visit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; and as the character and conduct of this remarkable person at that time engaged (A) “Francis Duaren was the first of the French civilians who purged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the civil law <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> from the barbarisms of the Glossaries, in order to introduce the pure sources of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>. As he did not desire to share that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with any one, he looked with an envious eye on the reputation of his colleague Eguinard Baron, who also mixed good literature with the knowledge of the law. This jealousy put him upon composing a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, wherein he endeavoured to lessen the esteem that people had for his colleague. The maxim, ‘Pacituri in vivis livor; poëta fata quiete,’ was verified remarkably in him; for after the death of Baron, he showed himself most zealous to eternize his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and was at the expense of a monument to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the deceased.” From the Translation of Bayle’s Dict. of 1710, p. 1143-4. (B) Francis Spira was a lawyer of great reputation at Cittadella in the Venetian state, at the beginning of the 16th century. He had imbibed the principles of the Reformation, and was accused before John de la Cata, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, the pope’s nuncio at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. He made some concessions, and asked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of the papal minister for his errors. But the nuncio insisted on a public recantation. Spira was exceedingly averse to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>; but at the pressing instances of his wife and friends, who represented to him that he must lose his practice and ruin his affairs by persisting against it, he at last complied. Shortly after he fell into a deep melancholy, lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and was removed to Padua for the advice of physicians and divines; but his disorders augmented. The recantation, which he said he had made from cowardice and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, filled his mind with continual horror and remorse; inasmuch that he sometimes imagined that he felt the torments of the damned. No means being found to restore either his health or his peace of mind, in 1548 he fell a victim to his miserable situation. See Collyer’s Dict.—Spira. engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the world, Mr. Scrimzeor is said to have collected <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of him in a publication entitled, "The Life of Francis Spira, by Henry of Scotland." This performance, however, does not appear in the catalogue of his works. After he had stored his mind with the literature of foreign countries, and satisfied his curiosity as a traveller, it was his intention to have revisited Scotland. He might without vanity have entertained hopes, that the various knowledge which he had treasured up would have won him a partial reception among his countrymen. An ambition of being usefully distinguished among them as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters is justly supposed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of his desire to return; but the most languid projects of life are often strangely diverted by accident, or rather perhaps are invisibly guided by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, from their purposed course. Mr. Scrimzeor, on his journey homewards, was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. His fame had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> forerun his footsteps. The syndics and other magistrates, on his arrival, requested him to set up the profession of philosophy in that city; promising a compensation suitable to the exertion of his talents. He accepted the proposal, and established the philosophical chair. After he had taught for some time at Geneva, a fire broke out in his neighbourhood, by which his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was consumed, and himself reduced to great distress. His late pupils, the Bucherels, had not forgotten their obligations to him, and sent a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to his relief. At this time flourished at Augsburg that famous mercantile family (c), the Fuggers. Ulric Fugger was then its representative; a man possessed of prodigious wealth, passionately fond of literature, a great collector of books and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and a munificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learned men. Being informed, by means of his literary correspondence, of the misfortune which had befallen Mr. Scrimzeor in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of his house, he immediately sent him a pressing invitation to accept an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> beneath his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> till his affairs could be re-established. Mr. Scrimzeor, gladly availing himself of such a hospitable kindness, lost no time in going to Germany. Whilst residing at Augsburg with Mr. Fugger, he was much employed in augmenting his patron's library by vast collections, purchased from every corner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Manuscripts of the Greek and Latin authors were then of inestimable value, and seem to have been more particularly the object of Mr. Scrimzeor's researches. He did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a life of yawning indolence amidst these treasures, and, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> unfeeling collector, leave them unenjoyed. As librarian, he was not contented to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eunuch to his literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>. He seems to have forgotten that he was not its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>, and accordingly ranged at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> among surrounding beauties. He composed many works of great learning and ingenuity, whilst he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a situation so peculiarly agreeable to the views and habits of a scholar. When his manuscripts were ready for the press, he was desirous of returning to Geneva to print them. His patron, Fugger, recommended him for this purpose to the very learned Henry Stephens, one of his pensioners, and at that time one of the most celebrated printers in Europe. Immediately on his arrival at Geneva, 1563, he was earnestly solicited by the magistrates to resume the chair of philosophy. Notwithstanding his compliance, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of it the dedication of much of his time to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physics, he, two years afterwards, instituted a course of lectures in the civil law, and had the honour of being its first founder and professor at Geneva. As soon as he was settled again in this city, he hoped, amidst his other occupations, to prosecute the great object of his literary fame, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of his various works. But a suspicion which Henry Stephens entertained, that it was his intention to set up a rival press at Geneva, occasioned great differences between them. The result of the quarrel was, that the republic of letters, during Mr. Scrimzeor's life, was deprived of his valuable productions. They fell most of them at his death into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Calaubon, who has been accused of publishing considerable portions of them as his own. Some account of Mr. Scrimzeor's several performances will give an idea of his extensive erudition. He wrote critical and explanatory notes upon Athenaeus's (d) Deipnosophists, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> conversations of Philosophers and Learned Men of Antiquity; having first collated several manuscripts of his author. This work Calaubon published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1600; but without distinguishing his own notes from those of Scrimzeor. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> and Emendations of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> of Strabo were among our author's literary remains. These were published in Calaubon's Parisian edition of Strabo, 1620. Henry Stephens, from an idea of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> due to Scrimzeor's literary fame, notwithstanding the violent animosity which had subsisted betwixt them, reproaches Calaubon for adopting our Scottish critic's lucubrations on Strabo without acknowledgment—Dempster affirms us, that Scrimzeor, in his manuscript letters, mentions his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of publishing this performance; whence, it is probable, that his work appeared to himself of considerable consequence, and had taken up much of his attention. Although Calaubon, in his ampli notes exhibited at the foot of Strabo's text, makes no confession of having derived any thing from Scrimzeor, it must not be concealed, that in an epistle to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Young, our critic's nephew, through whom the Commentary and Emendations of Strabo came into his hands, Calaubon acknowledges how very useful to him they might be made; for speaking there of his intended (c) They were ennobled by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> in 1519, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Barons of Kirkberg and Weissenborn. (d) Athenaeus was a grammarian of Naucrates in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century. His Deipnosophists is a very curious and learned work, in 15 books. It is full of interesting anecdotes and descriptions of ancient manners, and has preserved many relics of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> not to be found elsewhere. tended edition of Strabo, he says, "It cannot be expressed how much assistance I may obtain from your notes of Scrimzeor." Edward Herriton, a Scottish author, in his Commentary on Plutarch's Book concerning the Inconsistencies of the Stoics, informs us, that Scrimzeor collated different manuscripts of all the works of Plutarch. This undertaking appears sufficient to have occupied half the life of an ordinary critic. Every one knows how voluminous an author was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the historian, and orator of Chaeronea. Whether our learned critic had meant to publish an edition of Plutarch's works is not known; but such an intention seems highly probable from this laborious enterprise of collating them. The 10 books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius on the Lives, Opinions, and Apophthegms of the Philosophers, were collated from various manuscripts by Scrimzeor. His corrected text of this author, with notes full of erudition, came also into Cæsabon's possession, and is supposed to have contributed much to the value of his edition of the Grecian Biographer, printed at Paris in 1593. The works of Phormatus and Palaeaphatus were also among the collations of Mr Scrimzeor. To the latter of these authors he made such considerable additions, that the work became partly his own. These were two ancient authors who explain the fables of the heathen deities. The former wrote De Naturâ Deorum, seu de Fabulârum Poeticarum Allegoris Speculatio, "On the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> of the Gods, or the Allegorical Fictions of the Poets." The latter entitled his book Amiri, Sive de falsis Narrationibus, "Things incredible, or concerning false Relations." These works were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, 1570; whether in Greek or Latin is uncertain. They have been published since in both languages. The manuscripts of them were for some time preserved in the library of Sir Peter Young, after that of his uncle Scrimzeor, which was brought into Scotland in 1573, had been added to it. What became of this valuable bequest at the death of the former, is uncertain. Our learned philologer also left behind him in manuscript the orations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, Aeschines, and Cicero, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Eusebius, all carefully collated. Among his literary remains was a collection of his Latin epistles. The men of letters in the 15th and 16th centuries seem to have kept their republic, as it is called, more united and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> than it is at present, by an epistolary intercourse in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, then the universal medium of literature and science. This general spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> could not but contribute greatly to the advancement of learning, as well as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and, we may add, to the importance, of those who were engaged in its pursuit. The intercourse and union of enlightened men, able and disposed to promote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of their fellow-creatures, cannot be too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. From such intellectual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> alone it is, that uniformity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, moral, and political principles, to its greatest attainable degree, can ever be expected; or, in other words, the greatest possible benefit derived from the cultivation of letters. Of the many performances which had exercised his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, it does not appear that any were immediately published by himself but his Translation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOVELS">Novels</a> into Greek. This was printed at Paris in 1558, and again with Holonder's Latin version at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1575. This work has been highly extolled, both for the purity of its language and the accuracy of its execution, and is likely, according to some respectable opinions, to hold its estimation as long as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> or memory of the civil law shall exist. A Latin translation of the Basilica, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASILICS">Basilics</a>, as they are called by our civilians, is the last we have to mention of this author's performances. This is a collection of Roman Laws, which the eastern emperors Basil and Leo, who reigned in the fifth century, commanded to be translated into Greek, and which preserved their authority till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the eastern empire. The Basilics comprehend the institutes, digests, code, and novels, and some of the edicts of Justinian and other emperors. Of 60 original books, 41 only remain. Mr Scrimzeor collated them with various manuscripts, probably before he commenced his translation. From the foregoing recital of the learned labours of this profound scholar and critic, it will be concluded, that almost the whole of his life, although long, was spent in his library, and that the biographer, having now terminated the catalogue of his writings, is probably not distant from the conclusion of his life. Different years have been assigned for the time of his death; but it appears most likely, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the different accounts of this event, that it happened very near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of 1571, or at the beginning of the succeeding year, about the 66th year of his age. He died in the city of Geneva. The characteristic features of Scrimzeor are few, but they are prominent and striking, and remote posterity may regard him with no inferior degree of respect. His industry and perseverance in the pursuit of knowledge and erudition were equalled only by the exquisite judgment which he displayed in his critical annotations and commentaries on the errors and obscurities of ancient books and manuscripts. His acquisitions in the Greek, Latin, and oriental languages, were reckoned much beyond those of most of the professed linguists of his time. The great Cujacius used to say, "That he never quitted Mr Scrimzeor's conversation without having learned something new." But that which gave peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> to such superiority, was the amiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> which on all occasions was observed to accompany it. From the commendation given him by the illustrious civilian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, it will be concluded, that he did not brood, with a jealous reserve, over unopened treasures of erudition; but that, conscious of possessing stores too ample to be soon exhausted, at the same time that he avoided an ostentatious profusion of them, he obliged and delighted his friends by a liberal communication. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> at which he lived, considered with the nature and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his studies, and his abilities in prosecuting them, he may be deservedly ranked among those eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> who have most successfully contributed their exertions to the revival of letters in Europe. SCRIPTURE is a word derived from the Latin Scriptures scriptura, and in its original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is of the same import of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, signifying "any thing written." It is, however, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used to denote the writings of the Old and New Testaments; which are sometimes called the Scripture, the Scriptures, sometimes the sacred or holy Scriptures, and sometimes canonical Scripture. These books are called the Scriptures by way of eminence, as they are the most important of all writings; they are said to be holy or sacred on account of the sacred doctrines which they teach; and they are termed canonical, because when their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and authenticity were ascertained, their names were inserted in ecclesiastical canons, to distinguish them from other books; which, being of no authority, were kept as it were out of sight, and therefore styled apocryphal (A). The authenticity of the Old Testament may be proved from the character of the Jews, from internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, and from testimony. 1. The character of the Jews affords a strong presumptive evidence that they have not forged or corrupted the Old Testament. Were a person brought before a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice on suspicion of forgery, and yet no presumptive or positive evidence of his guilt could be produced, it would be allowed by all that he ought to be acquitted. But farther, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the forgery alleged were inconsistent with the character of the accused; if it tended to expose to disgrace and reproach his general principles and conduct; or if we were assured that he considered forgery as an impious and abominable crime—it would require very strong testimony to establish his guilt. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> now mentioned corresponds exactly with the character and situation of the Jews. If a Jew had forged any book of the Old Testament, he must have been impelled to do bold and dangerous an enterprise by some very powerful motive. It could not be national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, for there is scarcely one of those books which does not severely censure the national manners. It could not be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of fame; for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> would have taught him to flatter and extol the national character; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, if detected, would have been infamy and death. The love of wealth could not produce such a forgery; for no wealth was to be gained. The Jews were selected from among the other nations of the world, and preserved a distinct people from the time of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> from Egypt to the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, a period of 892 years. The principal purposes for which they were selected was to preserve in a world running headlong into idolatry the knowledge and worship of the one true God, and to be the guardians of those sacred books that contained the prophecies which were to prove to future ages the divine mission of the Redeemer of mankind. To fit them for these important truths, the spirit of their laws and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> had the strongest tendency. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a> were openly performed, to convince them that the God of Israel was the God of all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and that he alone was to be worshipped. Public calamities always befell them when they became apostates to their God; yet they continued violently attached to idolatry till their captivity in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> made them forever renounce it. The Jews then had two opposite characters at different periods of their history: At first they were addicted to idolatry; afterwards they acquired a strong antipathy against it. Had any books of the Old Testament been forged before the Babylonish captivity, when the Jews were devoted to idolatry, is it to be conceived that the impostor would have inveighed so strongly against this vice, and so often imputed to it the calamities of the state; since by such conduct he knew that he would render himself obnoxious to the people and to those idolatrous monarchs who persecuted the prophets? But it may next be supposed, that "the sacred books were forged after the Babylonish captivity, when the principles of the Jews would lead them to inveigh against the worship of idols." But these principles would surely never lead them to expose the character of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and to detail their follies and their crimes. Never had any people more national pride, or a higher veneration for their ancestors, than the Jews. Miracles and prophecies ceased soon after their return to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; and from that period their respect for the sacred books approached to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. They preserved them with pious care, they read them often in their synagogues, and they considered every attempt to alter the text as an act of sacrilege. Is it possible that such men could be guilty of forgery, or could false writings be easily imposed on them? 2. There is an internal evidence in the books of the Old Testament that proves them to have been written by different persons, and at distant periods; and enables us with precision to ascertain a time at or before which they must have been composed. It is an undeniable fact that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> ceased to be the living language of the Jews during the Babylonish captivity, and that the Jewish productions after that period were in general written either in Chaldee or in Greek. The Jews of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, some ages before the coming of our Saviour, were unable, without the assistance of a Chaldee <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a>, to understand the Hebrew original. It necessarily follows, therefore, that every book which is written in pure Hebrew was composed either before or about the time of the Babylonish captivity. This being admitted, we may advance a step farther, and contend that the period which elapsed between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the most ancient and the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> book of the Old Testament was very considerable; or, in other words, that the most ancient books of the Old Testament were written many ages before the Babylonish captivity. No language continues <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>; and the Hebrew, like other tongues, passed through the several stages of infancy, youth, manhood, and old age. If therefore, on comparison, the several parts of the Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> are found to differ not only in regard to style, but also in regard to character and cultivation, we have strong internal marks that they were composed at different and distant periods. No classical scholar would believe, independent of the Grecian history, that the poems ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> were written in the age of Demosthenes, the Orations of Demosthenes in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, or the Commentaries of Origen in the time of Lactantius and Chrysoloras. For the very same reason, it is certain that the five books which are ascribed to Moses were not written in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, the Psalms. (A) From ἀποκρύψις, to put out of sight, or conceal. Scripture. Psalms of David in the age of Isaiah, nor the prophecies of Isaiah in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>; and since the Hebrew became a dead language about the time of the Babylonish captivity, the book of Malachi could not have been written much later. Before that period therefore were written the prophecies of Isaiah, still earlier the Psalms of David, and much earlier than these the books which are ascribed to Moses. 3. Let us now consider the evidence of testimony for the authenticity of the Old Testament. As the Jews were a more ancient people than the Greeks or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and for many ages totally unconnected with them, it is not to be expected that we should derive much evidence from the historians of those nations: it is to the Jews alone we must look for information. But it has unfortunately happened that few of their works except the Scriptures themselves have been preserved to posterity. Josephus is the most ancient of the Jewish historians to whom we can <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>. He informs us, that the Old Testament was divided into three parts, the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa or poetical books. No man, says he, hath ever dared to add or take away from them. He tells us also, that other books were written after the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a>; but as they were not composed by prophets, they were not reckoned worthy of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. Since the promulgation of the Christian religion, it is impossible that any material alterations or corruptions could have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the books of the Old Testament; for they have been in the hands both of Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> from that period. Had the Jews attempted to make any alterations, the Christians would have detected and exposed them; nor would the Jews have been less severe against the Christians if they had corrupted the sacred text. But the copies in the hands of Jews and Christians agree; and therefore we justly conclude, that the Old Testament is still pure and uncorrupted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> mentioned by our Saviour into the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, corresponds with that of Josephus. We have therefore sufficient evidence, it is hoped, to convince even a deaf, that the Old Testament existed at that time. And if the deaf will only allow, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was a personage of a virtuous and irreproachable character, he will acknowledge that we draw a fair conclusion when we assert that the Scriptures were not corrupted in his time; for when he accused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a> of making the law of no effect by their traditions, and when he enjoined his hearers to search the Scriptures, he could not have failed to mention the corruptions or forgeries of Scripture, if any in that age had existed. But we are assured, by very respectable authority, that the canon of the Old Testament was fixed some centuries before the birth of Jesus Christ. Jesus the son of Sirach, the author of Ecclesiasticus, makes evident references to the prophecies of Isaiah *, Jeremiah †, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> ‡, and mentions these prophets by name. He speaks also of the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> prophets §. It appears also from the prologue, that the law and the prophets, and other ancient books, existed at the same period. The book of Ecclesiasticus, according to the calculations of the best chronologers, was written in Syriac about A.M. 3772, that is, 232 years before the Christian era, and was translated into Greek in the next century by the grandson of the author. The prologue was added by the translator; but this circumstance does not diminish the evidence for the antiquity of Scripture; for he informs us, that the law and the prophets, and the other books of their fathers, were studied by his grandfather: a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that they existed in his time. As no authentic books of a more ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, except the sacred writings themselves, have reached our time, we can ascend no higher in search of testimony. There is, however, one remarkable historical fact, which proves the existence of the law of Moses at the dissolution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Israel, when the ten tribes were carried captive to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a> by Shalmanezer, and dispersed among the provinces of that extensive empire; that is, about 741 years before Christ. It was about that time the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a> were transported from Assyria to repeople the country, which the ten captive tribes of Israel had formerly inhabited. The posterity of the Samaritans still inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of their fathers, and have preserved copies of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, two or three of which were brought to this country in the seventeenth century. The Samaritan Pentateuch is written in old Hebrew characters (see <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILOLOGY">Philology</a>, No. 28), and therefore must have existed before the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>. But so violent were the animosities which subsisted between the Jews and Samaritans, that in no period of their history would the one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> have received any books from the other. They must therefore have received them at their first settlement in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a> from the captive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> whom the Assyrian monarch sent to teach them how they should fear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> (2 Kings xvii.). The canon of the Old Testament, as both Jewish and Christian writers agree, was completed by Ezra and some of his immediate successors (see Bible). In our text, copies of the sacred books are divided into 39. The Jews reckoned only 22, corresponding to the number of letters in the Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. They united the books of Judges and Ruth; they joined the two books of Samuel; the books of Kings and Chronicles were reckoned one; Ezra and Nehemiah one; the Prophecies and Lamentations of Jeremiah were taken under the same head; and the 12 minor prophets were considered as one book—so that the whole number of books in the Jewish canon amounted to 22. The Pentateuch consists of the five books, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUTERONOMY">Deuteronomy</a>. Several observations have been already made respecting the authenticity of these under the article Pentateuch; but several additional remarks have occurred, which may not improperly be given in this place. For many of these we acknowledge ourselves indebted to a sermon published by the reverend Mr Marti, whose research, learning, and critical accuracy, will be acknowledged by every reader of discernment. One of the strongest arguments that have occurred to us in support of the authenticity of the Pentateuch, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of the writer, has already been given under the article Religion, No. 14, &c., which see: But we shall in this place present two arguments of a different kind, which would be sufficient to prove at least the former of these conclusions. We argue from the language and contents of the Mosaic writings, and from the testimony of the other books of Scripture. From the contents and language of the Pentateuch there arises a very strong presumption that Moses was its author. The very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in the four last books discovers an author <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the events which he relates; every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, both religious and political, is a proof that the writer was present at each respective scene; and the legislative and historical parts are so interwoven with each other, that neither of them could have been written by a man who lived in a later age. The account which is given in the book of Exodus of the conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> towards the children of Israel, is such as might have been expected from a writer who was not only acquainted with the country at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but had frequent access to the court of its sovereign: and the minute geographical description of the passage through <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> is such, as could have been given only by a man like Moses, who had spent 40 years in the land of Midian.
